name: Gürcan Keman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68446/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 13 November 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr S. Özay, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 26 April 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The General Directorate appealed the decision dated 14 January 1992. The Ankara Administrative Court awarded the applicant a certain amount of compensation for pecuniary damage. The court further decided that legal costs should be shared by the parties, given that it partially acceded to the applicant's claims for compensation. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the request for rectification of the decision on 30 May 2002. The General Directorate argued that the applicant had not suffered any damage and that therefore the legal costs for him should be borne by him. The appeal was dismissed on 31 October 2001. The applicant brought a new action against the General Directorate on an unspecified date.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Manisa, Turkey. In 1991 the applicant sat a competition for admission to the civil service. Following his success in the competition, the General Directorate of Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution conducted a pre-employment background investigation. It found that the applicant had not mentioned his criminal record in his application form. In 1980 the applicant was convicted of issuing threats against one of his teachers and had been sentenced to four months and twenty days' imprisonment, which had then been converted into a fine. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant was awarded compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The General Directorate appealed the decision, arguing that the applicant had not suffered any damage and that therefore the legal costs should be borne by him. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the Ankara Administrative Court's ruling was in conformity with law and procedure. The court further decided that legal costsShould be shared by the parties, given that it partially acceded to the applicant's claims for compensation. The decision was made in accordance with Law no. 657. The application was rejected on the grounds that it did not meet the requirements of the vacant post.

name: Sofiika Vasileva
train_texts: The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 9.30 p.m. on 11 August 1995. The applicant invokes Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. By a decision of 30 April 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Danish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Hans Klingenberg of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The charge with the offence of refusing to reveal her identity was not followed up by an indictment. The applicant collapsed and was hospitalised for three days diagnosed with high blood pressure. The outcome of the applicant's dispute with the bus company is unknown. The claim for compensation made by the applicant as regards the detention has not yet been decided. The decision can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice. The application is still pending in the Supreme Court of Norway. The case was brought by a Norwegian woman and has been heard by the Court of Appeal of the High Court of Justice in Oslo. The trial began on 12 August 1995 and was adjourned until 12 September 1995. The judge ruled on the case on 18 July 1996. The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision, but on 31 July 1996 she complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg. The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. She brought her claim for compensation before the City Court of Århus. Four police officers were heard as witnesses on 17 September 1998. The two police officers who made the arrest explained inter alia that the applicant twice had refused to give her name and address on their request, once after they had warned her that she would be arrested. It had been difficult to get in touch with the applicant, who screamed and appeared hysterical. A woman was arrested in 1996 after refusing to reveal her name to police. She was held in a detention cell for many hours before being released. The City Court ruled that she should be compensated in the amount of DKK 2,200. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice. The decision was handed down on 25 September 1998, and the case is still pending. It is currently being heard at the Court of Appeal in Copenhagen, Denmark, and is expected to be heard later this month. The case is being heard by the District Court for the City of Copenhagen, which is based on a decision made by the City Court in 1996. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. The applicant's appeal was rejected in February 1999. On 11 February 1999 the High Court gave judgment against the applicant stating as follows: “Having breached section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act [the applicant] could be arrested pursuant to section 755, subsections 1 and 2 of the Justice Act.” The applicant was released as soon as she revealed her name and address. Under these circumstances, there is no basis for granting [ the applicant] compensation pursuant tosection 1018 a, subsection 1 of the justice act.

The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 9.30 p.m. on 11 August until 11 a.m on 12 August 1995. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. By a decision of 30 April 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal, the highest court in Denmark. The charge with the offence of refusing to reveal her identity was not followed up by an indictment. The applicant complained about the detention to the Chief Constable of Århus. The outcome of the applicant's dispute with the bus company is unknown. The claim for compensation for having been detained by the police has not yet been decided on by the Ministry of Justice. On 14 June 1996 the applicant claimed compensation. The Chief Constable decided on the matter on 18 July 1996, and in so far as relevant his letter of the same day to the applicant reads as follows: “In connection with your previous complaint ... you received a ... letter of 14 September 1995 from Chief Superintendent HJH. [My] reply to your complaint... will not differ essentially from the content of [that letter] The applicant's behaviour necessitated the arrest and the length of the detention. The two police officers who made the arrest explained inter alia that the applicant twice had refused to give her name and address on their request. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station. She had handed over various belongings among those, she believed, various letters from public authorities bearing her name. A court session was held on 26 June 1998. Four police officers were heard as witnesses on 17 September 1998. The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. The applicant was arrested for breaching the Administration of Justice Act. She refused to reveal her name and address and was detained for hours. The City Court ruled that she was entitled to compensation. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice. The High Court ruled in favor of the applicant and the fine was reduced from DKK 2,200 to DKK 1,000. The case is still pending at the Supreme Court of Denmark. The application has been adjourned until the end of the month until a decision can be made on whether or not to order the fine to be reduced to the amount of DKK 500. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. The applicant amended slightly her statement given before the City Court in that she admitted that the police had asked her before and after the arrest to provide them with her personal data, but that she had refused because she had been angry. On 11 February 1999 the High Court gave judgment against the applicant stating as follows: “Having breached section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act [the applicant] could be arrested pursuant to section 755, subsections 1 and 2”

However, in view of your relatively advanced age I find reason to regret that you were not, as promised, attended to by a doctor in connection. with your stay in the detention cell. This decision can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice... The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station. The applicant was detained for breaching section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act. She was denied medical treatment during her time in a detention cell. The City Court ruled she was entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice in Copenhagen. The High Court ruled in favour of the applicant and ordered the prosecution to pay back the money. The appeal was dismissed on appeal on September 4, 1998. The application was brought by a woman in her seventies, who was detained at the Århus Police Station in Denmark on July 9, 1996. She refused to reveal her name and address to two police officers. The officers were unable to establish her identity until 10.45 a.m. the next day. The High Court of Western Denmark gave judgment against the applicant in February 1999. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. Under these circumstances, there is no basis for granting [the applicant] compensation pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of the administration of Justice Act. Also, as no circumstances has been established, [the court finds for the prosecution.]’ The High Court ruled that the applicant could be arrested pursuant tosection 755, subsections 1 and 2 of the Administration of Justice Act.

Under these circumstances, there is no basis for granting [ the applicant] compensation pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of the administration of Justice Act. name: Karlheinz Schmidt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 13580/88) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mr Karlheinz Schmidt, on 11 August 1987. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court gave the lawyer in question leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig, Mr Vögtle, Mr Weitzel and Mr Olbrich. On 30 April 1982 the relevant municipal authorities required Mr Schmidt to pay a fire service levy (Feuerwehrabgabe) of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978. The Commission produced various documents as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The Sigmaringen Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgericht) dismissed his appeal on 18 August 1983. The Administrative Appeals Court stated that it endorsed the opinion expressed in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 5 July 1983. In its view, the case raised no issue of principle (grundlegende Bedeutung) On the question whether the imposition of a fire service levy was in breach of the Constitution, it concluded that it was not, in conformity with a judgment of 17 October 1961. It would only be possible to refer the issue back to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsbergericht) in 1986. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the appeal for adjudication, on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. It noted, inter alia: “... The Federal Constitutional court has already held, in its judgment of 17 October 1961 ..., concerning the provision which corresponds to the present section 43 para. 2, first sentence, of the Baden-Württemberg Fire Brigades Act, that there had been no violation of the principle of equal treatment.’ The court said there had still been no general change in legal opinion; the fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be justified on account of the risks.

name: Şemsettin Gümüşten
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 10 February 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation. The Diyarbakır Assize Court acquired jurisdiction over the applicant's case after the promulgation of Law no. 3953 on 27 December 1993. It held that the offence fell within the scope of Article 168 § 2 and that the statutory time limit under Articles 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code had expired. It accordingly ordered that the criminal proceedings against the applicant be terminated. On 10 September 1998 the judgment became final in respect of the applicant. The applicant was released from detention on 29 July 1990. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation, which quashed the judgment on the ground that the Martial Law Court had misinterpreted the domestic law.

name: Krzysztof Nurzyński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46859/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to respect for his family life had been infringed. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was heard by the Court on 11 December 2008. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3 of the convention, now Article 29§ 1) The applicant and his wife were granted a divorce on 27 June 2007. The applicant's pre-trial detention was lifted on 8 October 2008. After that date he was visited by his mother on 11 occasions. On 29 July 2008 the Łódź District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment. applicant's mother was granted permission to visit the applicant in prison. He was released on 2 July 2009 after serving half his sentence. He now lives in a suburb of Warsaw with his wife and two children. He has been married to his wife for seven years and has a son and daughter.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47114/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Sean Marc Taylor-Sabori, was granted legal aid, but never actually claimed it. Using a ‘clone’ of the applicant’s pager, the police were able to intercept messages sent to him. The pager system used by the applicant and intercepted by the police operated as follows. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The applicant was arrested and charged with conspiracy to supply a controlled drug. He was convicted and sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against conviction and sentence. One of the grounds was the admission in evidence of the pager messages. The Court of Appeal, dismissing the appeal on 13 September 1998, upheld the trial judge’s ruling that the messages had been intercepted at the point of transmission on the private radio system, so that the 1985 Act did not apply. The messages were admissible despite having been intercepted without a warrant. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the 1984 Act had not been applied in this case.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7070/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been subjected to ill-treatment in a gendarmerie station and that the criminal proceedings subsequently brought against her had not been fair. On 29 November 2007 the President of the Court's Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) In two statements made during meetings with the prosecutor and the judge the applicant admitted to being a member of the PKK. Edirne Magistrates' Court, which ordered her pre-trial detention in prison. The applicant rejected the allegations against her and alleged that, before she was brought before the prosecutor, she had been beaten up by gendarme officers and threatened with rape. She also alleged that she had was stripped naked by the gendarmes during her detention. In the letter she alleged, in particular, that while she was being detained in the gendarmerie station she was insulted, beaten up and drenched with water. During the proceedings the applicant was represented by a lawyer. On 9 October 2001 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. Threats of rape and death, directed at her and her mother, had also been made. Other than the statements taken from his client by the gendarmerie and then by the prosecutor and the judge on 9 March 2000, there was no evidence against her. The Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's conviction on 8 July 2002. The applicant appealed against her conviction and argued, in particular, that the decision of the trial court had not been adequately reasoned. The Government were requested to submit to the Court a copy of the “cassette of questioning” referred to above (see paragraph 16 above)  domestic judicial authorities to produce the cassette, stated in their letter of 21 May 2008 that they had “no records of the cassette being handed over to the Edirne prosecutor’s office”. In the letter, they said they had no record of the tape being handed to the prosecutor, and that they did not know of any plans to present it to the court. The cassette was never presented to the prosecution, and was returned to the family of the victim, who died in May 2009, in an undisclosed location in France. The prosecutor alleged that the applicant had left Turkey in 1996 and had been taken to the PKK's training camp in Lavrion, Greece, where she had received training. Following her training she had obtained a false German passport in order to enter the Netherlands. The applicant's lawyer told the trial court that his client's questioning had been in breach of the applicable procedure and legislation. On 9 October 2001 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. On 8 July 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's conviction. The jury was not allowed to consider the case until April 19, 2013, when it was acquitted of all charges and the case was dismissed. name: Alois Unterpertinger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against the Republic of Austria, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980 by an Austrian citizen, Mr. Alois Unterpertinger. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30) The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) The President of the Chamber, Mr. Wiarda, had ascertained, through the Deputy Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and Mr. Unterpertinger’s representative on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). On 24 April, he directed that the applicant’’ representative should have until 6 June 1985 to submit a memorial. On 3 February 1986, the Commission supplied to the Registrar certain documents which he had requested. The hearings were held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Government and the applicant produced documents at the hearings. The applicant was charged with causing actual bodily harm to his step-daughter on 14 August 1979 and to his wife on the following 9 September. He claimed that his wife had inflicted several head wounds with a paper-knife and gashed his forehead close to his eyebrow. Miss Tappeiner admitted having called her step-father a ‘convict’ that morning, and said that he had responded by slapping her in the face, but without injuring her. She added that a doctor she had consulted had issued a certificate in respect of her own injury. The applicant's wife said that she had been slapped in the. face and beaten by her husband, who had grabbed her daughter by the hair to. stop her running away. Wörgl police sent the Kufstein District Court a report (Strafanzeige) “concerning Alois Unterpertinger and Rosi Unter pertinger, suspected of causing actual bodily harm (Körperverletzung)“ The report indicated that the applicant’s injuries had been described as “slight“ by the doctor. The police went on to say that they had already had to intervene in several quarrels in the household. They added that the three protagonists had given conflicting accounts of the incident on 14 August. Miss Tappeiner, who had been questioned as an informant (Auskunftsperson), had clearly taken her mother's side. An X-ray at the hospital next day had shown that her right thumb was swollen. Alois Unterpertinger accused of injuring his wife with a broken thumb. He claimed she had tried to hit him with a hairbrush, but had hit the stair-rail instead. The couple had had a quarrel on 9 September, during which he had kicked his wife’s right arm. Mrs. Unter PERtinger was acquitted of causing actual bodily harm contrary to Article 152(1)(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. She was allowed to refuse to give evidence because she was the wife of the accused (Beschuldigter) The case was heard by the Kufstein District Court on 9 November 1979. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. The applicant pleaded not guilty. He admitted that he had hit his step-daughter on the head, but not that he. had injured her. He said he had not seen his wife come into contact with the stair-rail and added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. The Regional Court then called Mrs. Unterpertinger and Miss Tappeiner. On being told by the court of their right to refuse to give evidence (see paragraph 16 above), they replied that they wished to avail themselves of that right. Mr. Unterpertinger was convicted of causing actual bodily harm and causing grievous bodily harm to his wife and step-daughter. He was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. He appealed on 9 April 1980. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. The appeal proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal in Dusseldorf. The verdict was returned on 14 November 1980. Mr Unter PERtinger has since remarried and moved to a new town. He has a son and a daughter from a previous marriage. He is now the father of a young girl. Mr. Unterpertinger asked the Innsbruck Court of Appeal to quash the conviction of 10 March and acquit him. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of the applicant’s brother. She was unable to say whether the applicant's former wife had had a bandage on her. The applicant requested that evidence should be taken from a number of people and an expert opinion (Sachbefund) obtained. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. The court refused to admit the remaining evidence proffered, as to part, on the ground that the circumstances to which it related were of no importance. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. Except for his sister-in-law, it was unnecessary to hear the witnesses the applicant had sought to have called, since he had referred to them in connection with matters that were either ofno importance or else extremely vague. Consequently, Mr. Unterpertinger's conviction on the two counts against him was justified; he had not been acting in self-defence. The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The Commission declared the application admissible on 8 July 1983. In its report of 11 October 1984 the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Court was requested by the Government, “to find that the Republic of Austria violated several provisions of the Convention in these criminal proceedings“ and to require the Republic to pay appropriate compensation“.

The Public Prosecutor’s Department asked the Regional Court to read out the various statements made to the police, including the police reports, the accused's criminal record and two files relating to previous convictions of his. Mr. Unterpertinger was found guilty of causing actual bodily harm and causing grievous bodily harm to his wife and step-daughter. He was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. The appeal proceedings began on 9 April 1980 and ended on 9 October 1980. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Germany, which ruled in favour of Mr. Untterperninger. The ruling was the first of its kind to be made by the Court of Appeal of Germany. The sentence was quashed on appeal. The Court of Appeal sat on 4 June 1980. Counsel for the applicant submitted the grounds of appeal and requested, inter alia, that additional witnesses be called by the court. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of Mr. Unterpertinger’s brother. The prosecution sought to have the appeal dismissed. Failing this, he asked it to review his sentence in the light of the degree of his guilt. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. Except for his sister-in-law, it was unnecessary to hear the witnesses the applicant had sought to have called, since he had referred to them in connection with matters that were either of no importance or else extremely vague. Consequently, Mr. Unterpertinger's conviction on the two counts against him was justified; he had not been acting in self-defence. The sentence imposed was consistent with the degree of his guilt (schuld) The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The Commission declared the application admissible on 8 July 1983. In its report of 11 October 1984, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. At the hearing on 17 February 1986, the Court was requested by the Government, “to find that the Republic of Austria violated several provisions of the Convention in these criminal proceedings“

name: Helmut Malek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 60553/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) An Austrian national, Mr Helmut Malek (“the applicant”), filed the application on 30 June 2000. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case continues. In August 1995, after the case had been taken over by another Investigating Commissioner, the latter agreed with the Vienna Federal Police Directorate (Bundespolizeidirektion) to question the police officers involved in the traffic control at issue. On 3 November 1995 he filed letters rogatory with the Donaustadt District Court (Bezirksgericht) which were subsequently transferred to the Josefstadt District Court. On 8 February 1996 the Investigating commissioner submitted his report to the Disciplinary Council. On 24 February 1997 the Constitutional Court, in proceedings unrelated to the present one’s, issued a decision concerning the composition of the Dis disciplinary Council. The Disciplinary Council ordered him to pay an additional fine of ATS 10,000 as he had already been ordered to pay ATS 25,000 in four other sets of disciplinary proceedings. It found that he had misbehaved towards intervening police officers during a traffic control by threatening them with job-related troubles in case they charged him with traffic offences. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) about the length of the proceedings and claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length into account as a mitigating circumstance. This decision was served on the applicant on 6 April 2000.

The applicant's spouse and the two police officers submitted that they could not appear at that date and the hearing was cancelled. The case was adjourned and the case was re-opened on 9 February 1998. The file at issue had meanwhile been transmitted to an other administrative authority, and the Disciplinary council filed a appeal against the decision. The applicant challenged two members of the Disciplinary Council for bias. He was convicted under section 10 § 2 of the Lawyers Act. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) He claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length of the proceedings into account as a mitigating circumstance. This decision was served on the applicant on 6 April 2000. The application was dismissed on 14 June 1999. The Bar Chamber’s Prosecutor submitted his observations in reply on 11 January 1999. On 15 December 1998 the applicant filed an appeal against this decision. On 29 February 2000 the constitutional court dismissed the applicant's complaint.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 70213/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Four Polish nationals, Mr Maciej Zys-Kowalski, Mrs Danuta Kowalska, Mr Krzysztof Kowaltski and Ms Marta KowALSka (‘the applicants’) were represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki and, subsequently, by Ms S. Jaczewska and Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard at the Łódź Court of Appeal on 19 May 2000. On 30 June 2000 the applicants lodged a cassation appeal. On 11 January 2002 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) refused to deal with the appeal. The decision was upheld on 14 December 2001 by the court of cassation.

This expert must possess special professional qualifications and have a special authorisation from the Federal Ministry of Health (sections 47 and 50) The 1975 Act involves a derogation from the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure in so far as expert evidence is concerned. train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 5 February 2003. The applicant alleged that his conviction and fine for failing to reply to questions about specific offences violated Article 6. The parties did not file observations on the merits. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required. The case was heard by the Court's Fourth Section (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) on 23 November 2004 and declared admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27. 1 of the conventions) was constituted as provided in Rule 26. 1. The applicant was required to attend at Woodbourne Police Station on 26 June 1998. The investigation. was into whether any person had benefited from theft or false accounting, contributing to the resources of a proscribed organisation or from contraventions of betting regulations. The Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation. On 25 February 1999, the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of GBP 200. The applicant refused to answer questions at an interview. The judge took the view that once he had been questioned by the police and charged, the applicant had a right to not answer questions that would have tended to incriminate him. Lord Justice Carswell, giving judgment, considered, in the light of R. v. Hertfordshire County Council, ex parte Green Environmental Industries Ltd ([2000] AC 326), that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention is directed towards the fairness of the trial itself. The appeal was upheld, and the applicant's conviction confirmed. The criminal proceedings for false accounting and conspiracy to defraud were struck out on grounds of delay by the Belfast Magistrates' Court. DPP asked him to state a case for the Court of Appeal. name: Marlène Kress
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39594/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained of the excessive length of administrative proceedings she had brought against Strasbourg Hospital. She also complained under Article 6 of the Convention that she had not had a fair trial. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In a decision of 2 February 1999 the Third Section decided to communicate the application to the Government for written observations. The Third Section confirmed its decision to relinquish jurisdiction in accordance with Rule 72 of the Rules of Court. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 11 October 2000 (Rule 59 § 2) It involved a woman who was left 90% disabled after a gynaecological operation under general anaesthetic at Strasbourg Hospital in 1986. She is now hemiplegic, has difficulty coordinating her upper limbs, can speak only with difficulty and suffers from double vision. The case was settled out of court in 1990 but the case was adjourned until the following year. The hearing was eventually listed for 19 April 1990. The Bar applied for leave to intervene under Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61. The President of the Court gave leave and the Bar produced a memorial in July 2000. The case was brought against Strasbourg Hospital in 1990. The court found that the hospital was not liable for the damage caused to the applicant's shoulder. The Strasbourg Administrative Court assessed the amount of damage sustained by the applicant as a result of her scalded shoulder at 5,000 French francs. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the circumstances of the hospitalisation had not disclosed any failure to provide information about the nature of the operation and its foreseeable consequences. The applicant, represented by a member of the Court of Cassation and Conseil d’Etat Bar, appealed on points of law against that judgment and filed full pleadings on 11 October 1993. Strasbourg Hospital filed a defence on 12 September 1994 and the applicant replied on 16 January 1995. The case was heard in public on 18 June 1997 by the 5th and 3rd sections sitting together. The Conseil d’Etat dismissed the applicant’s appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the evidence submitted to the courts below that Mrs Kress underwent a hysterectomy on 8 April 1986 at the Strasbourg Regional Hospital Centre. Following that operation, which took place normally, post-operative complications, which supervened twice, caused serious, disabling after-effects and damage.”

The applicant, then 44, underwent a gynaecological operation under general anaesthetic at Strasbourg Hospital in April 1986. name: Samuel Betteridge
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1497/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below) The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings against the Parole board, the delay in fixing a hearing. The panel was not satisfied that sufficient evidence exists that your risk of sexual and/or violent offending has yet reduced to a level such that that risk can be safely managed out of closed conditions. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk ... and an insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments.’ The panel made no recommendation to the Secretary of State. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” The judge considered that it followed ‘inevitably’ from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. He added: ‘It is common ground that Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires there to be a speedy hearing an independent judicial body’ Article 5(4) requires a speedy hearing to determine the lawfulness of the detention. The lack of man power in the Parole Board has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel. ‘Speedy’ does not indicate a particular period, and I accept entirely that it is fact sensitive, but, one has to see in an individual case what has been the cause of the delay. The judge concluded that the September 2008 advisory opinion in the applicant’s case could not address the question whether the post-tariff detention was lawful. However, it did mean that any breach would not require payment of damages, because it was plain that in any case the Par parole board would not have ordered the applicant's release. The applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September, but that remedy was no longer pursued. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order, observing that it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to “jump the queue” at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. “I am satisfied, as I have said, that the Parole Board was correct to accept that there is here, a breach of Article 5(4), because, and only because, in the circumstances of this case the reason why it was not heard at an earlier date was because of the lack of necessary manpower,” he said. Judge says measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. He warns it is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) The court cannot do the impossible, he adds, and we cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others. A more flexible approach by the Board to consideration of cases which do need priority should be taken into account, he says. The sooner a prisoner has a hearing the better, the judge adds. The parole board will now be required to get on top of this problem and to ensure that the hearings that are required are provided, and that the requirements of Article 1 of the Constitution are met. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions. The Secretary of State accepted the recommendation. The applicant was released in September 2009. A ParoleBoard review subsequently took place on 13 January 2010. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to ensure that that situation does not continue. In. special circumstances, claims of this nature should now be discouraged. But, this has at least brought home to the court, and enabled the court to make the point, that the situation that existed was unsatisfactory, potentially contrary to law.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the period of his detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section on 1 November 2004. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was brought before the Istanbul State Security Court in 1994. The applicant was convicted of being a member of an illegal organisation and committing the offence of armed robbery. He was sentenced to thirty-two years and six months’ imprisonment. On 28 December 2001 the applicant was released from detention on remand. In 2004 the case was transferred to the Istanbul 11th Assize court. The case is still pending.

name: Arthur Hutchinson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 57592/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In October 1983, the applicant broke into a family home, stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son and repeatedly raped their 18 year‑old daughter. On 14 September 1984, at Sheffield Crown Court, he was convicted of aggravated burglary, rape and three counts of murder. The trial judge sentenced the applicant to a term of life imprisonment and recommended a minimum tariff of 18 years to the Secretary of State for the Home Office. On 10 July 2013 the complaint under Article 3 was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 6 October 2008. On 16 May 2008, Tugendhat J handed down judgment in the applicant's case ([2008] EWHC 860 (QB), finding that there was no reason for deviating from the Secretary of State's decision. The seriousness of the offences alone was such that the starting point was a whole life order. In addition, there were a number of very serious aggravating factors. There were no mitigating factors. The surviving victim described “sadistic as well as sexual conduct’. The appeal was dismissed on 7 October 2008, with the appeal judge saying that there were 'no mitigating factors'

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2369/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was given priority, in accordance with Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The court relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence with which he was charged and the need to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings. train_texts: The Adolf case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Republic of Austria. The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Commission on 7 June 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by an Austrian citizen, Mr. Gustav Adolf. The request refers to Articles 44 and 48. The Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court. The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 November 1981. The applicant, an Austrian citizen born in 1918, lives in Innsbruck where he practises. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Herndl, Mr. Linke and Mr. Okresek for the Government and by. Melchior and Hoffmann for the Commission, as well as. their replies to questions put by the Court. Those appearing before the Court filed several documents during the hearings. The application was denied on grounds of the right to a jury trial. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. An 85-year-old woman, Irmgard Proxauf, reported to the Innsbruck public prosecutor's office that three days earlier during a quarrel Mr. Adolf had thrown at another person, Mrs. Anneliese Schuh, a bunch of keys which had then struck her. In her letter headed “request to inquire into a set of facts“, she called on the prosecutor'sOffice to take criminal proceedings against the applicant. The applicant denied the facts alleged against him and denounced the complaint as being knowingly false. He said that the object alleged to have caused the injury was, in fact, an envelope containing a single key, and that he had not thrown it. Dr. Gustav Adolf was charged with inflicting bodily harm. He denied that he had injured Mrs. Proxauf, whether by throwing a bunch of keys or otherwise. He called on the District Court either to acquit him after trial or to terminate the proceedings pursuant to section 90 par. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 21 below). He requested that fresh medical evidence be taken forthwith. The District Court terminated the proceedings - on an unspecified date - in pursuance of section 451 par. 2 of the Criminal Procedure. Mr. Adolf filed an application for appeal on 4 January 1978, and was served with a decision on 10 January 1978. Irma Proxauf alleged that the accused had caused her an injury, namely a bruise on her left arm and another below her left breast, with a bunch of keys. The key first struck the back of the right hand, causing a superficial abrasion, and then bounced against the left side of the above-named person's chest. No injury could be established on the chest. The injury found (festgestellte) is insignificant as it does not exceed the three-day limit. The fault (Verschulden) of the accused may be described as insignificant (geringfügig), and his character gives cause to expect that he will conduct himself properly in future. In both cases, the decisions would be taken without the formal hearing of evidence (Beweisverfahren), something which should in principle precede any finding of guilt (Schulderkenntnis) In the submission of the Generalprokurator, section 42 of the Penal Code was not appropriate where, on the basis of the complaint or the preliminary enquiries, no offence could be established on the facts or existed in law. A court decision terminating proceedings in accordance with section 42 could therefore only be grounded on a “suspected state of affairs’ (Verdachtslage) as disclosed by the case-file. Mr. Adolf appealed to the Supreme Court to annul the decision of the Innsbruck District Court. He claimed that the decision in issue was not capable of causing Mr. Adolf any direct prejudice. He relied on section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which places the judge under a duty to satisfy himself, before bringing the proceedings to a close, that the conditions stipulated under section 42 of the Penal Code are met. He alleged a breach of Article 6 par. 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art.6-3-d) of the Convention. In particular, he disputed the interpretation given by the Generalprokurator to section 42, which required the court to make a positive finding of an act. The Supreme Court rejected the application for annulment on 28 February 1980. In the opinion of the Supreme Court, the application of section 42 par. 1 of the Penal Code did not place the suspect in a worse position than where the case is closed for some other reason. Section 42 is not at all meant to be used to terminate proceedings when it is certain that an offence cannot be proved on the facts or does not exist in law. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified. The decision contains a negative ruling on the merits of the case and does not amount to a declaration, equivalent to a finding of guilt, that the suspect has committed a punishable act. The judgment of the Supreme Court was reproduced in an Austrian legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. The professional association to which Mr. Adolf belongs has not instituted any disciplinary proceedings against him in respect of the facts underlying Mrs. Proxauf's complaint. According to Mr Adolf, the file on his case, including the Innsbruck District Court's decision dated 10 January 1978, has been produced in evidence in a civil action. The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor may have preliminary enquiries (Vorerhebungen) carried out by the investigating judge, the district courts and the police authorities. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty on the person concerned. The decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides: “If the court is satisfied that the conditions laid down in section 42 are met, it shall terminate the proceedings by a decision.’” In cases before a district court, the decision whether or not the conditions of paragraph (1) hereof are met shall be taken by the court. The public prosecutor may lodge an appeal against any such decision. Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on 1 January 1975. It is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. As a result of the present case, two circulars were issued on 15 January 1979 and 24 March 1980 by the relevant Austrian authorities drawing the attention of the courts to the problems raised. The Commission accepted the application on 6 July 1979. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been breach of paragraph 2 of Article 6 (art. 6-2) (nine votes to six, with one abstention) The report contains three dissenting opinions. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The applicant applied for a State pension from the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Adjudication Officer issued on 31 October 1997. He stated that she had applied ‘too early’, and was only entitled to a pension from 65. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Birmingham Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 12 March 1998. name: Gisela Kirsten
train_texts: The case was brought by a woman who had worked as a dancer in the German Democratic Republic. The case was decided by the Court of Justice of Germany on 2 May 2005. The Government of Germany was represented by the Minister of Justice. The judge ruled in favor of the woman and the case was dismissed. The decision was made on the basis that the former dancer had received an old-age allowance. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the dancer and the application was thrown out. The matter was returned to the Minister of Justice for reconsideration. The court of appeal decided that the case should be dismissed on the grounds that the woman had not been paid for her work as a ballet dancer. The allowance was granted on 1 January 1991. The court ruled that the allowance was no longer valid. The Court of Appeal then ruled that there was no reason to continue paying the allowance. The decision was reversed on 28 May 1998. The bill for the allowance has now been paid for 12 years in a row. The case was decided by the court of appeals. The cost of the allowance is now estimated to be around £100,000. It has been paid out in full for the past 12 years. The allowance will be paid out of the proceeds of the sale of the German War Museum to a fund set up by the German government to help the unemployed. The ballet dancers' allowance was not to be transferred into the united German legal system. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint of approximately fifty pages with the Federal Constitutional Court. She complained that the length of the proceedings - which were still pending before the Federal Labour Court - violated Article 6 of the Convention. The decision was served on the applicant's lawyer on 3 August 2002. It referred to its leading judgment of 28 April 1999, pursuant to which the pension rights acquired in the GDR fell within the scope of Article 14 of the German Basic Law protecting the right to property provided that the German Unification Treaty recognised them as legal claims.

The case was brought by a woman who had worked as a dancer in the German Democratic Republic (GDR) for many years. The court decided to rule on the merits of the case. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favour of the former dancer. The judge ruled in favor of the woman's claim of a right to a pension. She had been paid an allowance by the GDR since leaving the stage in 1979. The Court of Appeal ruled that the allowance was illegal. The decision was appealed, but the case was not overturned because the judge did not agree with the original decision. The Supreme Court of Germany agreed with the decision. The allowance was due to be paid from 1 January 1992. The court ruled that the date could not be set as it was in breach of the German Unification Treaty. The final payment was made on 31 January 1998. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Germany. The case was appealed to the High Court of Justice, who ruled in favour of the end of the allowance. The ruling was upheld on the grounds that the payment was not required to be made after December 31, 1991. The cost of paying the allowance was reduced from £3,000 to £1,000. The amount of the annual allowance was then reduced to £2,000 per year. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint of approximately fifty pages with the Federal Constitutional Court. She inter alia complained that the length of the proceedings - which were still pending before the Federal Labour Court - violated Article 6 of the Convention. It referred to its leading judgment of 28 April 1999, pursuant to which the pension rights acquired in the GDR fell within the scope of Article 14 of the German Basic Law protecting the right to property. The allowance did accordingly not fall within thescope of Article14. explicitly that the allowance was to be transferred into the united German legal system.

The case was decided by the Supreme Court of Germany on May 21, 2006. The decision was made on the basis that the former dancer had made a good use of the allowance. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the dancer, and the case was dismissed. The original complaint was filed on May 1, 2006, by a man who had worked in the East German Democratic Republic (GDR) for more than 20 years. The allowance was set to end on 31 December 1991. The court ruled that the allowance was not required to end after that date. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice in July 1998. The allowance has been paid since the end of the first half of the 1990s. The final payment of the allowance will be made on December 31, 1998. It will be paid out of a fund set up by the German Ministry of the Interior. The fund will be known as the German National Pension Fund (GNP) The fund was set up to pay the German national pension fund. It was created to pay for the cost of the National Pension System (NPP) The ballet dancers' allowance was not to be transferred into the united German legal system. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint of approximately fifty pages with the Federal Constitutional Court. She complained that the length of the proceedings - which were still pending before the Federal Labour Court - violated Article 6 of the Convention. On 2 July 2002 the Federal constitutional court delivered a leading decision on the allowance. The decision was served on the applicant's lawyer on 3 August 2002. It referred to its leading judgment of 28 April 1999, pursuant to which the pension rights acquired in the GDR fell within the scope of Article 14 of the German Basic Law protecting the right to property. eval_texts: The case was lodged with the Court of Appeal on 1 May 2002. The case was brought by a former dancer who was paid an allowance for her time on the stage. The Court ruled that the payment was legal. The decision was made on the basis of Article 29 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) The case will be heard again on 2 May 2013, when the judge will rule on the merits of the case. The judge will then make a decision on whether or not to issue a new ruling. The court of appeal has until the end of this year to make a final decision on the case, which could be appealed or not. The allowance was to be paid out of the German government's budget until 31 December 1998. The German government claimed the allowance was valid until the end of 1998. But the court ruled that the allowance should not have been paid at all until then. The court also ruled that it was illegal for the government to use the allowance for personal expenses. The decision was later overturned on appeal by the Supreme Court of Germany. The ruling means that the taxpayer will not be compensated for the cost of the allowance. The cost of paying the allowance will now be determined by a formula that will be decided by the court. It is not known whether or not the cost will be less than the amount of money spent on the allowance per year. The ballet dancers' allowance was granted by the Federal Labour Court in 1998. She complained that the length of the proceedings violated Article 6 of the Convention. In July 2002 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint with reference to its leading decision of 2 July 2002. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 3 August 2002. It was decided that the pension rights acquired in the GDR fell within the scope of Article 14 of the German Basic Law protecting the right to property provided that the German Unification Treaty recognised them as legal claims within the united German legal system.

name: Hugh Jordan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24746/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer and that there had been no effective investigation into, or redress for, his death. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 ° 1. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy. By a decision of 4 April 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Jordan. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when PearseJordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The post mortem report found that he had been struck by three bullets which had come from behind and to the left. The four witnesses gave the following account of the shooting, which is not accepted by the Government. Four civilians heard a crash behind them and turned to see on the opposite side of the road the red police car pulling alongside a car (Pearse Jordan’s) and ramming it up onto the footpath. Pearse Jordan emerged from the immobilised car, and appeared shaken. He staggered across the road towards the four men followed by four police officers. An officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. Sergeant A was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. He had been at a briefing at 11 a.m. the day before concerning reports of a planned distribution of kit and munitions, including weapons, explosives and mortars, by the Provisional IRA. A surveillance operation was to be mounted and he was in charge of the teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. He and his teams left Woodbourne police station to wait at Andersontown police station. They heard reports there of a build up of activity at the back of two houses in Arizona street, which were under surveillance. The red car from the leisure centre arrived in Arizona Street. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment taking place. Sergeant A said that he called out ‘Police. Halt’ or ‘Halt. Police’ The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. He arrived back at the station at about 5.30 to 6.00 p.m. Sergeant A had clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon.Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. The RUC concluded its inquiry into the shooting in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions. The DPP issued a direction of ‘no prosecution’ on 16 November 1993. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995. Pearse Jordan’s family were not provided with any indication as to the nature of the RUC's findings. The Coroner ruled that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the preferment of disciplinary charges against the police officers concerned. A number of civilians made statements to the police and gave evidence at the inquest. The Coroner decided to protect certain categories of information from disclosure on the grounds of national security. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995, at the request of Pearse Jordan’s family, to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence from the taxi driver, to reconsider the decision whether or not to bring a prosecution. The applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. Legal aid was granted to the applicant for this purpose. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia (a) the. refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses before. they gave evidence at the inquest and (b) the decision of the. coroner to grant anonymity to RUC witnesses. Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 4 October 1996. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses who were to appear at the inquest and copies of any statements which the Coroner proposed to read out. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The applicant stated that the case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. The application was dismissed on 2 October 2000. The inquest into the death of Pearse Jordan was opened and adjourned on 4 April 2001. The Coroner has decided to hold an inquest into his death.

When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Inspector M gave an interview in which he explained why he had considered that his life was in danger, given that he could not confirm that the dead man was armed. The RUC concluded its inquiry into Pearse Jordan's death in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) The DPP’s department issued a direction of “no prosecution” in respect of the fatal shooting. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995 and ended on 4 February 1994. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal, sitting at the High Court in London. The jury was returned a verdict of unlawful killing. The sentence was commuted to a life sentence with a minimum term of 14 years. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. On 4 January 1995, the Coroner’s inquest commenced. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The DPP decided that the evidence remained insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person. On 10 March 1995, the applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia (a) the. refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses before they gave evidence at the inquest and (b) the decision of the Cor. to grant anonymity to RUC witnesses. The Coroner adjourned the inquest pending these proceedings. Leave was granted to bring judicial review proceedings against the coroner on 2 June 1995. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. Inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. However, it was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. The applicant stated that the case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On 7 December 1992, the applicant instituted civil proceedings, alleging death by wrongful act. On 24 October 1995 the Ministry of Defence served their defence, together with a request for further and better particulars of the statement of claim. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. On 2 October 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995.
