eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer. He invoked Articles 2, 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The President decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of McKerr v. the United Kingdom, no. 28883/95, Kelly and Others v the United UK,No. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the U.K. no. 37715/97. The applicant's son, Pearse Jordan, 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. A. Treacy. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy and declared the application admissible on 4 April 2000. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when Pearse. Jordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The hearing was held at the Royal Courts of Justice in Belfast. Four civilians stopped in the road after hearing a crash and seeing a police car ramming a car. Pearse Jordan emerged from the immobilised car, and appeared shaken. He staggered across the road towards the four men followed by four police officers. As he reached the white line in the centre of the road, an officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. The Independent Commission for Police Complaints will supervise the RUC investigation. Sergeant A thought that this was possibly the re-supply of terrorist equipment taking place. He was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. The car possibly reached the speed of 60, maybe 70 miles per hour at the fastest. The Orion slowed falling behind and then shot past on the passenger side, accelerating down the Falls Road in the direction of the city. Sergeant A told his driver to pursue him and force him off the road. He split his crews in two, his own team (call signs 8 and 12) to approach from the city side and the crews with call signs 3 and 9 to approachfrom the country side. Sergeant A said that he called out ‘Police. Halt.’ or ‘Halt. Police’ The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. The military took over the first aid. Sergeant A said that he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved in the incident. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. In his statement of 6 December 1992, Sergeant H, from the car call sign 11, stated that on arrival at the scene he had instructed car 12 to be moved to facilitate the movement of a bus which had stopped very close to the injured man. RUC report on investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) on 25 May 1993. On 16 November 1993, the DPP’s department issued to the Chief Constable of the RUC a direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting of Pearse Jordan. It had been concluded that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The Coroner wrote to interested parties informing them that the inquest would begin on 4 January 1995. The inquest was held at Westminster Coroner's Court. The verdict of unlawful killing was returned by the Court of Appeal. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The proceedings were adjourned on 16 January 1995, at the request of Pearse Jordan’s family, to enable the DPP, in the light of new evidence from the taxi driver, to reconsider the decision whether or not to bring a prosecution. In March 2000, the applicant was granted leave to bring judicial review proceedings against the Chief Constable, challenging his decision not to provide further documents to the applicant. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 7 December 1992, the applicant instituted civil proceedings, alleging death by wrongful act. The applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings on 5 October 1995. On 24 October 1995 the Ministry of Defence served their defence. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On a date unspecified between 4 April and 2 October 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995.

It was the first case to be settled by a court in Germany since the fall of communism in Germany in 1970. name: Mohammad Kuranbay Babajanov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49867/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 17 October 2008. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. Yılmaz, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 7 April 2015 the Chamber decided to invite the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. On 16 July 2015 the Government replied to the submissions of the applicant. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Turkey. He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan because of pressure from the police. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he decided to flee from Iran following deportation threats. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. On 18 November 2007 the applicant entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. Following a preliminary interview, the applicant was referred to the UNHCR office in Van. The Van office issued him with an asylum seeker certificate. He was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008. The applicant and Iran were forcibly deported to Iran on 12 September 2008. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. The Uzbek asylum seekers, including the applicant, were captured and held hostage by people smugglers, who demanded 5,000 United States dollars to spare their lives. The asylum seekers contacted some other Uzbeks who had managed to escape deportation from Turkey and obtained the ransom fee. The smugglers made them walk for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. The applicant arrived in Turkey in 2007 from Uzbekistan. On 12 September 2008 he was deported to Iran along with other Uzbek nationals. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. He is living in hiding and his application for refugee status under the mandate of the UNHCR is still under consideration. He was interviewed by officers from the UNHCR’s Ankara office on 4 December 2013 and 28 March 2014. The application to be granted refugee status has not yet been approved by the UNHCR. The applicant's application for asylum in Turkey has been rejected by the Turkish government on the basis that it is not in line with Turkish law. The Turkish government has the right to deport the applicant if it so chooses. The applicant cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities. He does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. According to a document signed by two police officers and one military officer, submitted by the Government, twenty-nine Uzbek and Afghan nationals, including the applicant, were deported on 12 September 2008. The Government, the applicant was not deprived of his liberty. Moreover, his identity documents were not confiscated.

The case originated in an application (no. 49867/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Uzbek national, Mr Mohammad Kuranbay Babajanov. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. Yılmaz, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The Court asked the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Government replied to the submissions of the applicant. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Turkey. He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan in 1999 because of pressure from the police, who suspected him of anti-constitutional activities. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he decided to flee from Iran following deportation threats. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. On 18 November 2007 the applicant entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. The Van office issued him with an asylum seeker certificate. He was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008 and was ordered to report to the police three times a week for signature. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The asylum seekers contacted some other Uzbeks who had managed to escape deportation from Turkey and obtained the ransom fee. The smugglers made them walk for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. They requested legal advice from the Van Bar Association, which, along with two Turkish non-governmental organisations, published a report on 28 September 2008 regarding the Uzbek asylum seekers’ collective expulsion. It was argued in the report, inter alia, that the expulsion of the Uzbek by the Turkish State authorities had had no legal basis. The applicant and other Uzbek nationals were deported to Iran in 2008. He has been in hiding in Turkey since then. His application for refugee status is still under consideration by the UNHCR. The applicant has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. He is seeking a temporary residence permit to stay in Turkey until his case is heard in court. He also wants to be allowed to return to Uzbekistan where he had lived for a year before being sent to Iran. He wants to apply for a permanent residency permit to live in Turkey. He would then be able to work in Turkey for as long as he was allowed to work. The applicant cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. According to a document signed by two police officers and one military officer, submitted by the Government, twenty-nine Uzbek and Afghan nationals, including the applicant, were deported on 12 September 2008. The applicant does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public. He does not have a legal residence permit for fear of being deported again to Iran like the other Uzbek asylum seekers who were deported in October 2008.

The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. It is alleged that the expulsion had been motivated by political considerations to improve relations with Uzbekistan, which had been strained following the acceptance by Turkey of members of Uzbek opposition groups as asylum seekers. The applicant has been living in Turkey in hiding since 2007. His application for refugee status under the mandate of the UNHCR is still under consideration. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. The applicant is still waiting to hear if he will be allowed to stay in Turkey after his application for asylum is rejected by the UNHCR. He is also waiting to find out if he is allowed to return to his native Uzbekistan before the end of this year. The application was denied on the basis that the applicant was not a resident of the country and was therefore not eligible to apply for asylum in Turkey. He was also denied the right to stay on in Turkey under the terms of his asylum application. The applicant applied for asylum in Turkey in December 2007. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. He cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities. He does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public. The Government says the applicant was not deprived of his liberty. According to a document signed by two police officers and one military officer, submitted by the Government, twenty-nine Uzbek and Afghan nationals, including the applicant, were deported on 12 September 2008.

name: Ronald Easterbrook
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48015/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his tariff as a discretionary life prisoner had not been set at trial by a judge but had been fixed by the Secretary of State after a long delay and without an oral hearing. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible in a decision of 26 September 2002. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant fired six shots, wounding one police officer in the leg. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. In sentencing him, the judge made reference to his long, violent criminal record and the dangerous nature of his character. The Court of Appeal refused the applicant’s renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction, leave having already been refused by a single judge. The Home Secretary agreed to certify that the applicant should be subject to the arrangements for the release of discretionary life prisoners, despite having previously qualified the applicant as someone serving a mandatory life sentence. The decision of 5 February 1998 also set the tariff of the applicant's sentence at 16 years, exp exp. The applicant’s solicitors made written submissions as to the appropriate length of the tariff and submitted that the applicant should be entitled to an oral hearing before the Lord Chief Justice. On 27 November 1998, the Prison Service informed the applicant”s solicitor that the Home Secretary had decided on a tariff of 12.5 years, to expire in May 2000. On 8 January 1999, the applicant made an application for judicial review. The application was dismissed on 11 February 1999. The applicant became eligible for Parole Board review procedures. He has stated however that he has decided not to participate in the procedures due to his continuing belief that the Government have breached his human rights and still refuses to acknowledge those breaches.

name: John Hirst
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40787/98) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that there had been undue delay between the reviews by the Parole Board of his continued detention as a prisoner serving a sentence of discretionary life imprisonment. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 March 2000, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant was sentenced to 15 years in prison in 1989. He was transferred to a Category B prison in 1993. His tariff period expired on 25 June 1994. The Parole Board agreed to the transfer of the applicant to Category C prison. A psychiatric report issued about the same time stated that the applicant’s personality, described as psychopathic, had shown some capacity for change. The applicant agreed to follow and successfully completed in July 1996 a drugs awareness course. Reports noted that he had made considerable progress over the preceding six years but would need phased re-introduction into society. In April 1996, the Court of Appeal refused leave to apply for judicial review. The DLP did not recommend release but transfer to a Category D prison. following a long period of institutionalisation and a lack of family support. The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of both decisions, alleging inter alia that the DLP had wrongly applied an ‘exceptional circumstances’ test. Mr Justice Potts refused leave against DLP’s recommendation but granted leave to appeal against Secretary of State's decision. The application was refused on 11 April 1997. On 21 October 1997, the applicant re-applied for leave for. judicial review. He was granted leave in respect of the decision of the Secretary of. State. The DLP again considered the applicant’s case on 15 July 1998, the DLP declined to recommend release but did recommend transfer to a Category D (open) prison. The panel took into account the nature of the index offence, your violent disruptive early prison career, the fact that you are still seen as having a psychopathic personality, and the remaining areas of concern identified by [Mrs B, a higher psychologist] The panel also considered that the sexual ambivalence referred to by [Dr G] merited further investigation. In all these circumstances, the panel considered that you still presented too great a risk to the public to justify your release. The panel did recommend that you be transferred to open conditions. In coming to this conclusion, the panel took into account the length of time you have spent in custody. The panel considered that you would be unable to cope in the community, were you to be released directly or via a pre-release employment scheme. The Secretary of State did not agree that these matters could be safely addressed in open prison conditions. He noted that the applicant had failed to attend further courses in anger management, social skills and communications. He also had regard to an intervening incident which had occurred on 31 July 1998 when the applicant was being escorted to court by a female officer. The applicant was found guilty under the Prison Rules of assault and using threatening, abusive or insulting words. The applicant's application for leave to judicially review the DLP’s decision of October 1996, which had been dormant since 21 October 1997, was listed for hearing before the Court of Appeal. His request to amend his grounds of application to add complaints about a lack of independence was refused. The Court of appeal rejected his application for left to apply for judicial review. It was however agreed that his next review should take place in July 2000. The Secretary of State saw no justification in allowing him to progress further towards release. He was sentenced to five years in prison, suspended for a year, and fined £100,000. The sentence was suspended for five years, and the fine was reduced to £150,000, but the sentence was not suspended.

name: Aziz Binbir
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29913/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the case a success. The case was joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95,. 26699/96, 26700/96,. 29701/96 and 29702/96). The applicant was represented by Mrs Semra Dural Esim, a lawyer practising in Muğla (Turkey). The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The applicant was convicted of involvement in the THKP/C and in some of the alleged crimes. However, the court did not indicate the applicant’s sentence in its judgment. The application was found admissible on the grounds that the applicant had not been convicted of any crime. The judge also ruled that the application was not a breach of the Turkish Constitution. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the first instance court had failed to establish the applicant's involvement in certain crimes. The Appeal Court upheld the conviction of the applicant. The applicant was convicted under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to seven years and six months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision of the latter court, and decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The case was settled in a settlement between the applicant and the Turkish government. The applicant was never sentenced to prison and the case was dismissed. The application was dismissed by the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice. The judge said that the application was based on a false premise that the applicant was guilty of a criminal offence. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the prosecution had been unsuccessful.

The case originated in an application (no. 29913/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the case to be settled. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52§ 1) The applicant appealed against his conviction in 1984 but the appeal was quashed on the grounds that the first instance court failed to establish certain of the alleged crimes. The applicant was convicted in 1984, but the court did not indicate the applicant's sentence in its judgment. The applicant was convicted under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to seven years and six months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision of the latter court, and decided that the criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The case was closed on 18 April 1995. The applicant was later acquitted of all charges against him by the Turkish court of appeals. The decision was made by the High Court of Justice on 6 June 1997. The conviction was quashed on 6 April 1998 and the case was settled on 4 January 1998. The application was dismissed by the Court of Appeals on 1 January 2000.

The Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, acquired jurisdiction over the case and the case was transferred to it. name: Necmettin Alkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right of access to court had been breached by the domestic court’s refusal to grant him legal aid. The application was made on 11 April 2007. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant requested a total of 200,000 Turkish liras (TRY) (approximately 100,000 euros (EUR) at the time) in respect of both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s legal aid request, stating that pursuant to the Code of Civil Procedure, the case is well-founded and that the plaintiff does not have the means to pay the required court fees. Court informed the applicant that he was to pay a total of TRY 2,719 (approximately EUR 1,400 at the time) in court fees within thirty days for the proceedings to be continued. Court decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings on 10 January 2007 because the applicant had not paid the necessary court fees for the case to continue. The applicant received a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtar) attesting to his father's poverty. The certificate stated that neither the applicant nor anyone else from his household was employed.

He lodged an appeal with the Court of Cassation but it was not heard until September 1997.

name: Detlef Bayer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8453/04) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr D. Herrmann, a lawyer practising in Karlsruhe. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applications for admissibility and merits of the application were heard at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was accused of having hindered the audit of his professional conduct on three occasions and of falsifying and then charged for disbursements and fees without any legal basis on 541 occasions. He was acquitted of the criminal charges on 12 December 1991 and the criminal proceedings were thus terminated. The formal disciplinary investigations were closed and a first formal report was drawn up on 20 October 1995. The charges were received by the Disciplinary Chamber of the Frankfurt Administrative Court on 12 January 2000. On 21 March 2001 the applicant was scheduled to be heard but failed to attend. On 1 June 2001 the revised charges of 11 May 2001 were submitted. On 6 July and 23 November 2000 oral hearings were held. The applicant had been found responsible for 519 misdemeanours between 27 November 1987 and 3 November 1990. The applicant appealed to the Kassel Administrative Court of Appeal. The court dismissed the applicant's appeal on 1 July 2003. On 7 August 2003 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court regarding the length of the proceedings and the interpretation and application of procedural rules and substantial provisions of disciplinary law. The Federal Constitutional court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons on 10 September 2003. The application was dismissed on 5 July 2001 and the applicant was removed from office on 1 October 2001. The case was heard at the Frankfurt Administrative Court, which found that Article 6 of the Convention was not applicable to disciplinary proceedings.

name: Shayan Baram Saadi
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13229/03) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been detained in breach of Article 5. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52: 1 of the Rules of Court) On 27 September 2005 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section. On 11 July 2006 a Chamber composed of the same judges delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 1. The Chamber further held, unanimously, that it was not necessary to consider Article 14 separately. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 16 May 2007. The applicant, an Iraqi Kurd, was born in 1976 and now lives and works as a doctor in London. He fled the Kurdish Autonomous Region of Iraq when, in the course of his duties as a hospital doctor, he treated and facilitated the escape of three fellow members of the Iraqi Workers’ Communist Party who had been injured in an attack. He arrived at Heathrow Airport on 30 December 2000 and immediately claimed asylum. The immigration officer contacted the Oakington Reception Centre but there was no immediate room there, so the applicant was granted “temporary admission” to stay at a hotel of his choice and return to the airport the following morning. The applicant met at Oakington with a lawyer from the Refugee Legal Centre. The lawyer then wrote to the Home Office requesting the applicant’s release on the grounds that it was unlawful. When refused, the applicant applied for judicial review of the decision to detain him. Collins J on 7 September 2001 (R. (on the application of Saadi and others) v. Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 670) found that the Secretary of state had such a power to detain under the Immigration Act 1971. The following day he was released and again granted temporary admission pending the determination of his appeal. The appeal was allowed and he was granted asylum. Appeal court ruled in favour of detention of an asylum-seeker. The decision was overturned on appeal by the Court of Appeal in 2001. Lord Phillips of Worth Matravers, Master of the Rolls, gave the lead judgment. He said it was in the interests of all asylum-seekers to have their status determined as quickly as possible. The average monthly number of applications from July to September 1999 was nearly 7,000: 60% higher than the previous year. The Home Office minister said ‘no responsible government can simply shrug their shoulders and do nothing’ ... A short period of detention designed to ensure that the regime operates without dislocation cannot be ignored. House of Lords unanimously dismissed the applicant’s appeal. Court of Appeal next considered whether the detention fell within the first limb of Article 5 § 1 (f) ‘It is clear that detention to achieve a quick process of decision-making for asylum-seekers is not of itself necessarily and in all cases unlawful’ ‘There must be some other factor which justifies the exercise of the power to detain such as the likelihood of the applicant absconding, committing a crime or acting in ways not conducive to the public good. ...’. ‘In the circumstances such detention can properly be described as a measure of last resort.’ It is regrettable that anyone should be deprived of his liberty other than pursuant to the order of a court but there are situations where such a course is justified. Far from being arbitrary, it seems to me that the Secretary of State has done all that he could be expected to do to palliate the deprivation of liberty of the many applicants for asylum here. Getting a speedy decision is in the interests not only of the applicants but of those increasingly in the queue. Accepting as I do that the arrangements made at Oakington provide reasonable conditions, both for individuals and families and that the period taken is not in any sense excessive, I consider that the balance is in favour of recognising that detention is proportionate and reasonable.

An Iraqi national, Mr Shayan Baram Saadi (“the applicant”), on 18 April 2003. The applicant alleged that he had been detained in breach of Article 5 and Article 14 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. On 27 September 2005 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section. On 11 July 2006 a Chamber composed of the same judges delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Articles 5 and 14. The Grand Chamber decided to refer the case to the Court in accordance with Article 43 of the convention. The applicant, an Iraqi Kurd, was born in 1976 and now lives and works as a doctor in London. The applicant met at Oakington with a lawyer from the Refugee Legal Centre, who contacted the Home Office to enquire why the applicant was being detained and to request his release. When refused, the applicant applied for judicial review of the decision to detain him, claiming it was contrary to domestic law and Article 5 of the Convention. Collins J on 7 September 2001 (R. (on the application of Saadi and others) v. Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 670) found that the Secretary of state had such a power to detain under the Immigration Act 1971. On 14 January 2003 his appeal was allowed and he was granted asylum. Appeal court said that detention of asylum-seekers was unlawful under domestic law. Court of Appeal unanimously overturned this judgment on 19 October 2001. Lord Phillips of Worth Matravers, Master of the Rolls, gave the lead judgment. He observed that over recent years applications for asylum to the United Kingdom and other countries had been escalating. In the UK the average monthly number of applications from July to September 1999 was nearly 7,000: 60% higher than the previous year. He continued: “We share the doubts expressed by Collins J as to whether detention is really necessary to ensure effective and speedy processing of asylum applications.” House of Lords unanimously dismissed the applicant’s appeal ([2002] UKHL 41) Court of Appeal next considered whether the detention fell within the first limb of Article 5 § 1 (f) It found that the right to liberty in Article 5 was intended to preserve the sovereign power of member States to decide whether to allow aliens to enter their territories on any terms whatsoever. It ruled that detention of an alien would be covered by the sub-paragraph unless and until entry was authorised, subject to the proviso, derived from Chahal v. the United Kingdom (15 November 1996, Reports 1996-V), that the asylum or deportation procedure should not be prolonged unreasonably. ‘The State has power to detain without violating Article 5 until the application has been considered and the entry ‘authorised’ ... There remains the issue whether, even if detention does fall within Article 5 (1) (f), ‘detention was unlawful on grounds of being a disproportionate response to the reasonable requirements of immigration control’’ ‘The need for highly structured and tightly managed arrangements, which would be disrupted by late[ness] or non-attendance of the applicant for interview, is apparent. ... name: Loukas Nicola
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18404/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 26 January 2008. The decision was published in full by the European Court of Human rights on 11 January 2008, and is available on the Commission's website here. Since 1974 the applicant had been unable to return to his home and property in the northern part of Cyprus. On 9 December 1990 he took part in a car convoy organised by persons from three villages in Kyrenia and from Trypimeni. The participants in the convoy had informed the commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intention to return home. They drove to the ‘buffer zone’ checkpoint on the main road linking Nicosia and Famagusta. There they stopped and asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return. They requested him to transmit their demand to the Turkish military authorities.

name: Wiktor Kucharczyk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3464/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The application was made by a Polish national, Mr Wiktor Kucharczyk (“the applicant”), in 2005. The Kielce Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on 6 July 2005. On the same day, the applicant requested the court to allow him a legal-aid lawyer to lodge a cassation appeal on his behalf. He based his request on his difficult financial situation and his lack of legal knowledge. The applicant revoked the power of attorney of his lawyer, G.P., on 12 July 2005 and voluntarily relinquished free legal aid. The appeal was dismissed on 25 July 2005, relying on the fact that since 1991 the applicant had been represented before the courts by a legal adviser and that he had terminated the latter's power of Attorney. The applicant lodged a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Kielce Regional Court found that there had been a period of inactivity on the part of the Kielcé District Court between 23 December 2003 and 18 October 2004. The court found that in the remaining periods the proceedings had been conducted without undue delays. The appeal was rejected as inadmissible in law. The applicant was awarded 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) in just satisfaction. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of Poland, where the judge ruled in favor of the applicant and awarded him PLN 2,000.

train_texts: The Schmidt and Dahlström case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Commission’). The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects on 9 June 1972. On 15 October 1974, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges required to sit as members of the Chamber. The five judges so selected were Mr H. Mosler, Mr E. Rodenbourg, Mr. A. Favre, Mr G. Wiarda and Mr P. O’Donoghue. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on 25 September 1975. There appeared before the Court: Mr. H. Danelius, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr. B. HÅRDEFELT, Chief Legal Adviser at the Finance, Mr. G. NORMARK and Mr. O. BERGQVIST, Advisers. At the hearing the Commission produced the document recently called for by the Court. The Court heard the addresses of Mr. Fawcett and. Mr. Schmidt for the Commission and for the Government, as well as their replies to questions. The applicants are members of trade unions affiliated to two of the main federations representing Swedish State employees. In 1971, after expiry of one collective agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement, the applicants’ unions called selective strikes not affecting the sectors in which they worked. The applicants complain that on conclusion of the new agreement they were denied certain retroactive benefits paid to members of other trade unions and to non-union employees who had not participated in the strikes. The case was heard by the Labour Court, which had jurisdiction in disputes relating to the interpretation or application of collective agreements, but proceedings could be adjourned until a later date. The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. It is also the right to negotiate regarding conditions of employment. The 1965 State Officials Act (statstjänstemannalag) has virtually assimilated State employees to employees in the private sector. It imposes on the other party an obligation to enter into negotiations, to attend meetings for negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. The Act made the 1928 Collective Agreement Act, the 1928 Labour Court Act and the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate applicable in the public sector. The Act provided for collective agreements to be concluded, subject to certain exceptions, between the National Collective Bargaining Office (Statens Avtalsverk) and the organisations of State employees. According to the information at the disposal of the Court, these federations represent the large majority of Swedish State employees: more than 450,000 out of the 500,000 whose terms of employment are negotiated by the Office. About forty trade unions are affiliated to these organisations. The few independent trade unions represent only about 2,000 State employees in all. The Royal Order of 30 June 1965 relating to Certain Public Collective Agreements includes the following provisions: “Collective agreements as to such conditions of employment or service as are determined by the King-in-Council or by Parliament.“ Collective agreements in Sweden are normally concluded for a period of two or three years. For various reasons, however, the new collective agreement is often concluded some time after the previous agreement has expired. In such cases the new agreement has often specifically provided that its terms shall apply retroactively as from the date of expiry of previous agreement. In the case of a strike during the bargaining period, on the other hand, employers - both in the public and private sector - have customarily refused to grant retroactive benefits. The law described above at paragraphs 10 to 17 has in recent years undergone various changes which, being subsequent to the facts at issue, are not relevant for the present case. The question whether an individual employee has any means of challenging his union’s decision to go on strike is a matter exclusively governed by the internal rules of the union concerned. The Office retaliated and, on 19 February 1971, about 30,000 members of SACO and SR were locked out. This affected all university teachers belonging to SACo, including Mr. Schmidt, and some officers belonging to SR, but not Mr. Dahlström. New strikes and lock-outs were proclaimed, but did not become effective. The previous collective agreement was reinstated on 13 March 1971 for a period of six weeks and all strikes and lock-outs terminated forthwith. negotiations before the Commission of Conciliation resulted in June 1971 in a new global agreement for the years 1971 to 1973. According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits applicable under the agreement, unless the Collective Bargaining Office decides otherwise” This declaration also concerns other officials if they took part in any such industrial action. Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. Mr. Schmidt, following the conclusion of the collective agreement, gave notice to the Office that, through his special treatment in regard to wages, his right to organise had been violated. The Labour Court unanimously rejected the claim of the applicants’ unions. The Court found that no such purpose on the part of the State could be established. The adoption of such a position, and its enforcement after a conflict, were not to be regarded in themselves as an attack on the right to organise. The employer’s duty to respect this right did not include any obligation in principle to pay equal wages to union and non-union employees or to members of different organisations. No support had appeared for the idea that the State intended to induce members of SACO and SR to switch over to TCO-S and SF. In the case before it, the Court did not consider the granting of retroactive benefits to non- union employees who had not organised industrial action. In the Court’s opinion, the parties had not been able to present anything more than quite uncertain information on the total number of non-union officials or on their field of employment. The uncertainty in regard to these circumstances argued in favour of the States declaration that its purpose did not extend beyond upholding the principle that a strike destroys retroactivity. The Commission confirmed its opinion, previously expressed in the report in the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union case, that Article 11 para. 1 (art. 11-1) may legitimately extend to cover State responsibility in the field of labour-management relations and thus to provide some protection for unions against interference by employers. The report contains a separate concurring opinion. The opinion says the differential treatment complained of was in the circumstances justified as an industrial relations policy. There had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report also says there was no violation of Article 14-1 (Art. 14-2) and Article 11-1-1. The report concludes that there had been no violation of any of these articles or of any other articles or provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) or of the Convention on Economic and Social Rights.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. He was charged under Articles 168 (2), 497 (2) and 522, 55 (3), 33 and 40 of the former Criminal Code. On 29 April 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Istanbul State Security Court, finding that the classification of the applicant's offence had been erroneous. On 5 February 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was sentenced to 16 years and eight months' imprisonment in January 2003 for attempting to undermine the constitutional order. He appealed against this judgment arguing, inter alia, that his acquired rights had not been protected. On 2 December 2003 the Court of Cassation upheld the reasoning in the judgment of the Istanbul State Security Court, and dismissed the appeal. In the meantime, following his release, the applicant fled to Switzerland, where he currently resides. Following the entry into force of the new Criminal Code on 1 June 2005, the Istanbul Assize Court reopened the proceedings against the applicant in order to review his sentence. As an interim measure, on 11 October 2005 the applicant was conditionally released pending the outcome of the proceedings. On 13 November 2007 the applicant's appeal was rejected.

name: Wanda Lidia Gordon-Krajcer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5943/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made by a Polish national, Ms Wanda Lidia Gordon-Krajcer (“the applicant”), on 3 January 2007. Between 9 June 1993 and 21 February 2003, the District Court scheduled 28 hearings, 6 of which were adjourned due to the failure of the applicant’s husband to appear. She sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Warszawa District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 2,500 euros (EUR) The court held that the 2004 Act did not have retroactive effect and examined the applicant’s claim only in respect of the period between the entry into force of the2004 Act on 17 September 2004 and the date on which the complaint had been lodged. The court awarded the applicant PLN 2,000 (apprehended EUR 526 euros) in just satisfaction.

The left side of the letter has been cut open and then resealed with sellotape.

name: Darren Omoregie
train_texts: The case originated in an applications (nos. 265/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the decision to expel the first applicant to Nigeria with a prohibition of re-entry into Norway for a period of five years constituted a violation of Article 8. The Court declared the application admissible on 22 November 2007. The application was brought by Mr Louis Osaze Darren Omoregie, a Nigerian national; Mrs Elisabeth Skundberg Darren, a Norwegian national; and their daughter Selma, a Norway national. The first applicant was ordered to leave Norway by 30 September 2002. He appealed the decision but the Immigration Appeals Board refused to stay his expulsion. On 14 February 2003 the first applicant applied for a work permit on the ground of family reunification. The Directorate of Immigration rejected the application on 26 April 2003. The first applicant again appealed and requested stay of execution. On 19 October 2003 local police notified him of the decision and ordered him to leave the country by 30 October 2003. No judicial appeal was lodged against the above decisions, which became final on 2 February 2003. For confidential support call the Samaritans on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org for details. The Directorate of Immigration on 4 July 2003 warned him that it was contemplating to expel him pursuant to section 29(1)(a) of the Immigration Act. The Directorate considered that he had seriously contravened the provisions of the Act and had evaded implementation of the order to leave the country. The Immigration Appeals Board upheld the Directorate's rejection of his request for family reunification and its decision that the basic conditions for expelling the first applicant were fulfilled. The Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals board's decision of 21 July 2004 as being invalid. It found that the applicant's alleged ignorance of the unlawfulness of his gainful occupation was no excuse. The High Court found it established that the applicant had stayed lawfully in Norway from 25 August 2001 to 30 September 2002. He had worked unlawfully for nine months and had resided unlawfully for four and a half months. This was, relatively speaking, not a very serious offence, which fact counterbalanced his relatively weak links to Norway. To impose a prohibition on re-entry for five years would constitute a disproportionate measure towards the applicant and his family in the sense of section 29 of the Immigration Act. It could easily lead to the dissolution of the family. Even if the first applicant could apply for re- entry after two years, he would most probably only be granted permission to come for shorter visits. The High Court observed that the central issue was the one of proportionality. He had arrived in Norway aged 22 years, without any links to the country. At the time of the impugned decision he had lived there for less than three years. Already after less than two years he had been warned of expulsion. His stay in Norway had been very short and could not have given him any legitimate expectation of being able to live there. This was not significantly altered by his marriage to the second applicant, which had been entered into shortly before the disputed decision. It was not uncommon for a person whose expulsion had been decided to marry a Norwegian citizen and use this as an argument to have the expulsion order invalidated. The High Court, taking into account the Strasbourg Court's case law, did not find that the disputed decision would be incompatible with Article 8 of the Convention. The High Court considered that the balance of interest was not in his favour. The only countervailing consideration was his marriage to the second applicant. However, this could not be decisive; otherwise it would leave open a practice which would completely undermine the authorities' implementation of the Immigration Act. The applicants filed an application under the Convention, which was received at the Registry on 3 January 2007. They complained that the first applicant's expulsion would entail a splitting of the family in breach of Article 8. The first applicant's lawyer told the Court that they wished to maintain their application notwithstanding the refusal to apply Rule 39. They submitted that, having regard to the minor character of his breaches of the Immigration Act, the enforcement of the expulsion order would constitute a disproportionate interference with the applicant's family life. The Immigration Appeals Board dismissed an appeal by the first applicant against a rejection by the Directorate of Immigration of 30 October 2006. The request had been made on the basis of a provision in the Immigration Regulation which was applicable to cases of unmarried parents and therefore did not cover the applicants' case. Nor did the Board see any other reason for altering its earlier decision in the case. On 7 March 2007 the Implementation Group of the Oslo Police District expelled the first applicants back to Nigeria.

name: William Condron
train_texts: An Irish citizen, Mr William Condron, and a British citizen, Mrs Karen Condron (“the applicants”), on 13 November 1996. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing on account of the fact that the trial judge left the jury with the option of drawing an adverse inference from their silence during police interview. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 7 September 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 2000. The applicants were arrested at 12.45 p.m. on 28 April 1995. In the flat were found sixteen wraps of heroin weighing between 0.07 and 0.09 g and a further quantity of heroin weighed 1.19 g. The applicants' solicitor, Mr Delbourgo, noted that the first applicant, who seemed to be in the early stages of withdrawal, was unfit to be interviewed. However, after a 10- to 15-minute examination, the Force Medical Examiner, Dr Youlten, stated that the applicant was fit for interview. The applicant was an opiates addict with symptoms and signs of withdrawal but that he was thinking clearly and able to answer questions. Both applicants were legally aided and represented by counsel. were interviewed separately in the presence of their solicitor. The applicants were asked to explain their actions in apparently passing to, and being passed items from, flat 50. Both simply responded to these questions with the words ‘no comment’ The defence case for the applicants was that the heroin found in the flat had been for their own personal use and had been purchased in bulk by the first applicant the evening before their arrest. The judge accepted that the interviews had been short and were not conducted in an oppressive manner. He also considered that Mr Delbourgo had been wrong in his analysis that the applicants had been unfit to be questioned. The applicants' co-accused, Mr Curtis, testified at the trial that the applicants had never given him heroin. He confirmed the applicants' account of their friendship with him and his frequent borrowing. When he was arrested he was told that he would not get bail which made him angry and ‘bloody-minded’ so he decided not to help the police by answering their questions. The trial judge's direction to the jury was: “I turn to a new topic in our law ... It is the law that these defendants did not mention certain facts when questioned about them in interview by the police. In the past that would not have been evidence that could in any way be held against them but now it is for you to judge whether in fact you do hold it against them” The applicants were each convicted by a majority of nine to one of being concerned in supplying heroin and possessing heroin with intent to supply. The first applicant was sentenced to a total of four years. Failure to mention the points in interview cannot on its own prove guilt but depending on the circumstances you may hold it against him or her when deciding whether he or she is guilty. You should decide whether in the circumstances which existed at the time of the interview the matters were ones which the defendant concerned could reasonably be expected then to mention. It is for you to decide whether it is proper to do so.” The applicants' conviction and appeal were successful. The applicants' counsel contended that the trial judge should have excluded the “no comment” interviews as they were a direct result of following their solicitor's honest advice. The Court of Appeal pointed to problems with that argument in situations where solicitors advised their clients tactically or dishonestly to refuse to answer questions. The judge, as the fact-finding tribunal in the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury), had been correct in his decision to include the notes of interviews in evidence. The second applicant was sentenced to a total of three years' imprisonment. James Curtis, the co-accused, was acquitted on both charges. The Court of Appeal did not find that this lacuna in the summing-up meant that the convictions were unsafe, having regard to the weight of the other evidence. Lord Justice Stuart-Smith explained in this connection: “We have already referred to the substantial, almost overwhelming evidence of drug supply from what was found in the [applicants'] house.” The acquittal of Curtis shows that the jury regarded the evidence of the interviews as insignificant. Curtis also failed to answer questions in interview. The applicants' appeal in its judgment delivered on 17 October 1996 was dismissed by the court of appeal. The appeal was dismissed in October 1996.

The case originated in an application (no. 35718/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing on account of the fact that the trial judge left the jury with the option of drawing an adverse inference from their silence during police interview. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 7 September 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Counsel. The applicants and Mr Curtis were observed from 24 to 28 April 1995 by police and recorded on video from 25 April 1995 onwards. The applicants were seen to pass various items to Mr Curtis including a plastic bottle for smoking crack cocaine and silver foil for smoking heroin. Mr Curtis was also charged with the same offences as the applicants, namely being concerned with the supply of heroin and possession of heroin with intent to supply, but was acquitted. The prosecution also alleged that a polythene sheet in the flat had been used to make heroin wraps. The first applicant was an opiates addict with symptoms and signs of withdrawal but that he was thinking clearly and able to answer questions. The second applicant was also seen to have withdrawal symptoms but again was stated by the Force Medical Examiner to be thinking clearly. Both applicants were legally aided and represented by counsel. were interviewed separately in the presence of their solicitor. In a pre-trial hearing counsel for the applicants argued that the interviews should not be put before the jury as they had been carried out whilst the applicants were suffering from drug withdrawal symptoms. Their solicitor, Mr Delbourgo, testified that he had been of the firm view that neither should embark upon what might prove to be a very lengthy interview given their condition. The judge noted that the doctor had considered them fit to be interviewed, that they were thinking clearly and able to answer questions, and that both applicants had stated in response to direct questions that they understood the charges against them. The applicants' co-accused, Mr Curtis, testified at the trial that the applicants had never given him heroin. They stated that the polythene sheet had been planted there by the police after they had been brought to the police station. When asked about the incident recorded on 26 April 1995 in which the second applicant was seen receiving and then returning a packet to the occupant of flat 50, the applicants gave explanations which they had not mentioned to police in their interviews. The first applicant stated no drugs had ever passed between the flats and that the packet contained either cigarettes or money. The second applicant stated that it was simply an exchange of a packet of cigarettes. The applicants were each convicted by a majority of nine to one of being concerned in supplying heroin and possessing heroin with intent to supply. The first applicant was sentenced to a total of four years. Failure to mention the points in interview cannot on its own prove guilt but depending on the circumstances you may hold it against him or her when deciding whether he or she is guilty. You should decide whether in the circumstances which existed at the time of the interview the matters were ones which the defendant concerned could reasonably be expected then to mention. It is for you to decide whether it is proper to do so. Members of the jury that is all I have to say at this stage about the law. The applicants' counsel contended that the trial judge should have excluded the “no comment” interviews as they were a direct result of following their solicitor's honest advice. The Court of Appeal pointed to problems with that argument in situations where solicitors advised their clients tactically or dishonestly to refuse to answer questions. The key question was the subjective reason why the applicants had not answered the questions. Both were clearly advised by their solicitor that if they failed to mention material facts at the proposed interview, they could be criticised if the matter came to trial. At the beginning of the interview both were given the caution in its current form. Both indicated that they understood that caution. The Court of Appeal did not find that this lacuna in the summing-up meant that the convictions were unsafe, having regard to the weight of the other evidence. All but one of the jury must have rejected the [applicants'] explanation of the police observations, much of which was recorded on video, the presence of the matching wraps in Curtis' flat and the elaborate security arrangements at the applicants' own flat. The acquittal of Curtis shows that the jury regarded the evidence of the interviews as insignificant. Curtis also failed to answer questions in interview.” The Court of appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal in its judgment delivered on 17 October 1996.

Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Counsel, Ms S. Chakrabati, Counsel. The applicants were arrested at 12.45 p.m. on 28 April 1995. In the flat were found sixteen wraps of heroin weighing between 0.07 and 0.09 g and a further quantity of heroin weighed 1.19 g. The applicants' solicitor, Mr Delbourgo, noted that the first applicant, who seemed to be in the early stages of withdrawal, was unfit to be interviewed. However, after a 10- to 15-minute examination, the Force Medical Examiner, Dr Youlten, stated that the applicant was fit for interview. The second applicant was also seen to have withdrawal symptoms but again was stated by the Force medical Examiner to be thinking clearly and able to answer questions. The applicants were interviewed separately in the presence of their solicitor. At one point the first applicant's solicitor specifically suggested that this might happen. The applicants were asked to explain their actions in apparently passing to, and being passed items from, flat 50. Both simply responded to these questions with the words ‘no comment’ The defence case for the applicants was that the heroin found in the flat had been for their own personal use and had been purchased in bulk by the first. applicant the evening before their arrest. The judge considered that Mr Delbourgo had been wrong in his analysis that the applicants had been unfit to be questioned and allowed their interviews to stand as evidence. The applicants' co-accused, Mr Curtis, testified at the trial that the applicants had never given him heroin. He confirmed the applicants' account of their friendship with him and his frequent borrowing. When he was arrested he was told that he would not get bail which made him angry and “bloody-minded” so he decided not to help the police by answering their questions. Both applicants stated that their solicitor's advice that they were not in a condition to do so, given their withdrawal from heroin, had been conclusive. They stated that the polythene sheet had been planted there by the police after they had been brought to the police station. The applicants were each convicted by a majority of nine to one of being concerned in supplying heroin and possessing heroin with intent to supply. The first applicant was sentenced to a total of four years in prison. The applicants' conviction and appeal were upheld by the Court of Appeal. The defendants explained that their 'no comment' answers, speaking generally because of course they put it in more detail, the [applicants] said they were suffering from withdrawal symptoms and relied on Mr Delbourgo, their solicitor's advice. The law is ... that you may draw such inferences as appear proper from a defendant's failure to mention the points I have referred to in their respective interviews. It is for you to decide whether it is proper to do so. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal on two primary grounds: the inclusion of the police interviews and the contents of the judge's direction. James Curtis, the co-accused, was acquitted on both charges. The second applicant was sentenced to a total of three years' imprisonment. The judge, as the fact-finding tribunal in the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury), had been correct in his decision to include the notes of interviews in evidence. The applicants' counsel contended that the trial judge should have excluded the “no comment” interviews as they were a direct result of following their solicitor's honest advice. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants' appeal in its judgment delivered on 17 October 1996. The acquittal of Curtis shows that the jury regarded the evidence of the interviews as insignificant. Curtis also failed to answer questions in interview. All but one of the jury must have rejected the [applicants'] explanation of the police observations, much of which was recorded on video, the presence of the matching wraps in Curtis' flat and the elaborate security arrangements at the applicants’ own flat.” The Court of appeal did not find that this lacuna in the summing-up meant that the convictions were unsafe, having regard to the weight of the other evidence.

Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors led to their father’s death. The application was declared partly inadmissible on 18 December 2012 as being manifestly ill-founded. The Government of the United Kingdom, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36, did not make use of this right. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. German doctor U. was recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U. had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. He had applied to be admitted to one of the Medical Performers Lists maintained by each of the local PCTs. Once a GP is admitted to a PCT’s Performers List he may work in the area of any other PCT in England. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany where he arrived the following day. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. He explained that when treating the deceased he had committed a grave mistake with fatal outcome that had resulted from the confusion between the drugs pethidine and diamorphine. On the day of the incident he had further been overtired following his journey from Germany to the United Kingdom and had found himself in a tremendous stress situation. U. apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment and again explained that he had confused the opiates and referred to the stress situation he was subject to. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United. Kingdom established as the cause of Mr Gray’S death diamorphin poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication and hypertensive heart disease. Cambridgeshire Constabulary made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) on 5 March 2008. The request was forwarded to the competent Bochum police department which provided the police with the requested information and documentation by mid-March 2008. In June 2008 the BoChum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray. In Article 152 § 2 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure in conjunction with Articles 222 and 7 § 2 no. 1 of theGerman Criminal Code (see Relevant domestic and international law and practice below) In July 2008 German and British police officers visited U. at his surgery in Witten, Germany, and informed him that criminal investigations were pending against him in Germany and the United Kingdom. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. The originals of the protocols of the witness hearings conducted as well as the material obtained in the course of the investigations were handed over to Cambridgeshire police. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U.'s treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. None of the information gathered in the course of the. investigations carried out jointly by German and British police officers on the occasion of their visits to Germany would be disclosed to U., Mr Gray. or their respective counsel. U. had notified the incident to his professional indemnity insurance company. U. was accused of causing the death of Mr Gray with an overdose of morphine. U., represented by counsel, had declared that he would accept the envisaged sentence of suspended prison sentence of 9 months as well as a payment of 5,000 euros (EUR) to the treasury. A draft of the penal order was attached to the application. U. was convicted of having caused Mr Gray’S death through negligence pursuant to Article 222 of the Criminal Code. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation on 13 March 2009. Cambridgeshire police asked the Bochum public prosecution authorities for information about the procedure to be followed by the German authorities after transmission of the EAW. The Hamm General Prosecutor (Generalstaatsanwalt) was the competent authority to deal with questions regarding U.’s extradition and pointed out that extradition might be hindered on the ground that criminal proceedings were also pending against U. in Germany. By a decision of the same day, the District Court determined that the probation period for U. was two years starting from the date the penal order became final. It is not clear on what date between 14 April and 19 May 2009 counsel actually obtained access to the file. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U.’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. U. was granted access to the files in the terminated criminal proceedings against U. in August 2009 and April 2010. A meeting between representatives of the Bochum prosecution authorities, the CPS and Cambridgeshire police took place at Eurojust in The Hague on 1 July 2009. The content of these discussions is confidential. Criminal investigations in the United Kingdom were discontinued. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. for breach of his professional duties in connection with the incidents on 16 February 2008. The proceedings regarding U.’s fitness to practice medicine before the Arnsberg District Government were discontinued at the end of 2010. There was nothing to establish that U. would commit a similar error of treatment in Germany or that he lacked the necessary qualifications for practising medicine. He was reprimanded for having disregarded the standards of the medical profession. U. committed himself to refrain from practising. medicine abroad in the future. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cam Bridgeshire PCT.
