In Article 152 § 2 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure in conjunction with Articles 222 and 7 § 2 no. 1 of theGerman Criminal Code (see Relevant domestic and international law and practice below) Cambridgeshire police officers visited Germany on several occasions in the period from July until September 2008. They were provided with assistance by the German police in their investigations against U. The investigations focussed on the authenticity of the certificates U. had submitted to the English health authorities as evidence of his medical qualifications. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U.’S treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. Cambridgeshire Constabulary requested the German public prosecution authorities to assure that no criminal proceedings would be instituted against U. in Germany prior to finalisation of the investigations in the United Kingdom. None of the information gathered in the course of the. investigations carried out jointly by German and British police officers on the occasion of their visits to. Germany would be disclosed to U., Mr Gray's relatives or their respective counsel. An arrest warrant was issued against U. on 27 February 2009 by the Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court, Cambridgeshire. On 12 March 2009 the Colchester Magistrates' Court issued a European Arrest Warrant (”EAW’) against U for allegedly having caused the death of Mr Gray with an overdose of morphine. On the same day, the Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ordered that the preliminary criminal proceedings against U be terminated and applied to the Witten District Court for a penal order (Strafbefehl) to be issued against him. U., represented by counsel, had declared that he would accept the envisaged sentence. U. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment and had thus violated basic principles of the medical profession. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued the penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U. as applied for by the prosecution authorities. By a decision of the same day, the District Court determined that the probation period for U. was two years starting from the date the Penal order became final. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. The Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U.’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. The content of these discussions is confidential. C. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. U. was reprimanded for having disregarded the standards of the medical profession on the occasions of three patient consultations on 16 February 2008 in the United Kingdom. The proceedings regarding U.’s fitness to practice medicine before the Arnsberg District Government were discontinued at the end of 2010. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. The verdict that the deceased had been unlawfully killed as a consequence of the inadequate treatment administered by U.D. pointed explicitly to the deficiencies in the recruitment, training and supervision of foreign locum doctors in the United Kingdom. U. in particular for having committed a grave error in the treatment of Mr Gray, and fined him 7,000 EUR. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cam Bridgeshire PCT. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants.

train_texts: The case originated in eight applications against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, who are of Kurdish ethnic origin, were students at various faculties attached to Istanbul University at the time of the events. In November 2001 they petitioned the University Rector’s office requesting that Kurdish language classes be introduced as an optional module. Around the same time similar petitions were submitted by students studying at various universities in Turkey.Upon receipt of these petitions a disciplinary investigation was initiated by the University. On 25 January 2011 the applications were communicated to the Government. The applicants claim that following this disciplinary sanction they were denied access to the University facilities, they were branded as terrorists by the University authorities, their names were put on notice boards and they were shunned by their friends and other students. The applicants lodged separate actions with the Istanbul Administrative Court, requesting a stay of execution of the disciplinary decisions, with a view to their subsequent annulment. In 2004 the applicants each lodged an application with the Supreme Administrative Court to have the sanctions in question annulled on the grounds that they were unlawful. In its decisions, the court noted, inter alia, that there was nothing in the content of the petitions or in the manner in which they were submitted to warrant disciplinary sanctions. Istanbul Administrative Court awarded compensation to the applicants on the grounds that they had been denied their right to sit exams. Court quashed the judgments of the first-instance court and dismissed the actions. Court held that following the stay of execution of the disciplinary sanctions the University administration had permitted the students to take repeat exams in July, compensating for the exams which they were unable to sit in the spring semester. The conditions for awarding non-pecuniary damage had not been met, the court ruled. The court ruled that the students had not graduated from the University within the minimum time allowed (4 years) The court also ruled that it was not possible to award damages for damage caused by the actions of the University. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17081/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. On 2 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was filed by four Turkish nationals and the Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) was represented by Ms Nuran Özdemir. Toğay Gültekin died at the GATA Hospital on 27 March 2004. No autopsy was performed. An investigation was carried out at the military unit where he had been doing his military service. On 28 September 2004 the applicants initiated compensation proceedings against the Ministry of Defence before the Supreme Military Administrative Court (“the Military Administrative court”) They argued, in particular, that Toğay tokin had not received prompt or adequate medical care in his regiment. A total of eleven military personnel who knew or had had dealings with toğay  were questioned by their superiors. The military officers who carried out the investigation concluded, on the basis of the statements referred to above, that the military authorities had acted in accordance with their duties. Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with his medical problems. A blood test had been conducted, but the results had not revealed any abnormalities. The following day he was put on a bus and sent to the hospital. The applicants argued that it had been these inordinate delays that had caused Toğay’s death. They pointed out that To Turkey had been under an obligation to protect his well-being and to ensure timely medical treatment for him. Toğay Gültekin started his military service on 22 August 2003. On 2 January 2004 he was treated for a retractile testicle at Çorlu Military Hospital. He was prescribed medication at the regiment’s infirmary for an upper respiratory tract infection on 5 January 2004. On 17 March 2004 the regimentalinfirmary doctor decided to refer him to an infectious diseases clinic, but that was not done. On 20 March 2004 he. was diagnosed with and treated for an infection of the upper respiratory. tract. On 22 March 2004, he was referred to the University Hospital with suspected. hepatitis and he was sent there. On 23 March 2004 his condition deteriorated and he died on 27 March 2004 as a result of fulminant hepatitis. Toğay Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses within a short period of time. His liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) The Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18) and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for ToğayGülTekin’s death. No mention was made in the complaint regarding the failure to transfer to hospital on 17 March 2004. The Military Administrative Court refused to entertain the rectification request lodged by the applicants. in failing to refer Toğay Gültekin to hospital between 17 and 23 March 2004. On 28 December 2005, the court ruled in favor of the applicants and denied the request to rectify the mistake. The decision was made on the basis of a letter written by the court to the Turkish Ministry of Health in March 2004, which said that the hospital had failed to refer Gül Tekin for treatment. The court ruled that this was not the case, and he was not sent to hospital. The case was settled out of court in December 2005.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38663/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 of the. Convention in proceedings concerning the enforcement of their claims for maintenance against. their father. On 23 October 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The applicants were represented by Mr R. Gabl, a lawyer practising in Linz. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent. The applicants did not have any funds. The debtor claimed he would risk losing his property rights over the objects seized for enforcement. The applicants were not heard in the proceedings. It held that an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court was not admissible. It ordered both kinds of enforcement to be postponed until the decision on the action under Section 35 of the Enforcement Act was rendered and re-setting the deposit at EUR 1,000. They were obliged to reimburse legal costs amounting to EUR 305.40 to the debtor. The decision was overturned on appeal by the Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) on August 2, 2006.

name: Patrick Benjamin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28212/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had not had available to them a procedure by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 October 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court in 2001. The first applicant, Mr Patrick Benjamin, was sentenced to life imprisonment for rape in 1983. Mr Hueth Wilson was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. In August 1989, he was made the subject of a transfer direction and a restriction order under, respectively, sections 47 and 49 of the Mental Health Act 1983 (the 1983 Act) and transferred to Broadmoor Special Hospital. On 9 January 2001, the MHR Tribunal recommended his discharge. Home Department refused to certify the applicants as eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. Leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions was granted on 17 May 1993. In June 1993, following consultation with the trial judge and the Lord Chief Justice, the Secretary of State decided that the second applicant should be regarded as a “technical lifer”. On appeal, on 19 July 1994, the Court of Appeal reversed the High Court's decision in part. The applicants were informed by letter of 18 May 1995 that the House of Lords had refused leave to appeal.

train_texts: The applicant was arrested on 14 May 2002 on suspicion of having intimidated witnesses. On the second day of the trial the witness who had identified the applicant did not attend and the trial had to be aborted. The applicant was subsequently charged with five counts of doing acts tending and intended to pervert the course of public justice. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 1 March 2004. On 16 February 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was duly acquitted. On his counsel's application for a defendant's costs order, the judge refused to make an order and stated: “That order will be refused. There is clear evidence on the court papers. The Crown have taken the view that they are not going to compel this witness. Verdicts must follow.” The applicant's attempted appeal was dismissed on 14 November 2003 as “to be appealable as a sentence, the order must be contingent upon conviction. As the defendant’s costs order only arises when a prosecution is unsuccessful, it cannot be a sentence and cannot be appealed at the Court of Appeal Criminal Division”.

name: Piotr Rachwalski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The application was filed under former Article 25 of the. Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants produced their identity cards and the registration card of the car, whose owner was asleep in the house. The police were not satisfied with their explanation and the dispute became more intense. In reaction to the opinions expressed about the intervention, in particular by D. S., the policemen used truncheons. The applicants were ordered to stand against a fence. They were pushed and jostled and the policemen insulted them referring to them as “scum”, “slobs” and “queers” (hołota, brudasy, pedały). It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The second applicant had objected in a pretentious tone (“pretensjonalny ton głosu”) to having been woken up and to the check on the car taking place at night. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. As he had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated, it had been decided that he should be taken to a police car. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. Nothing in the behaviour of the persons present had justified the use of force. The police had entered private property and effected a search. They had also felt threatened by the presence of other persons at the scene of the incident. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the intervention of the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault.

S. had been behaving aggressively, direct force had been used against him, including the use of truncheons and handcuffs. The appeal against the prosecutor’s decision was rejected by the court of appeal. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. name: Selim Kabasakal
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applications were allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications (Rule 42 § 1) The Court declared the applications admissible on 8 March 2005. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicants were born in 1979 and 1977 respectively and were serving their prison sentences in Ordu prison. The applicants say they were arrested for trying to join the armed forces of the TDP. Both repudiated the statements they had given to the police, claiming that they had been made under duress. The applicants also said that they were boycotting the court and were not going to give any statements. The court took some procedural decisions and heard several of the co-accused, including the second applicant who maintained that he had nothing to say. The civilian judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time in July 1999. On 5 October 1999 before the court two persons filed petitions to intervene as third-parties in the proceedings. The applicants were sentenced to twelve years and six months in prison. The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation against the judgment of the State Security Court. On an unspecified date, the applicants were released from prison. This decision was pronounced, in the absence of the applicants’ representative, on 14 June 2000. The court examined and dismissed the requests of the Applicants to be released. The application was dismissed and the appeal was dismissed on 5 June 2000, the court upheld the first‑instance court’s judgment. The appeal was rejected on 6 December 1999, and the applicants appealed again on 11 December 1999. The applications were dismissed on 9 December 1999 and 2 December 2000, respectively. The appeals were dismissed by the court on 8 November 1999 and 10 November 1999.

name: Helmut Kucera
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40072/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complains that he had not been able to attend the oral hearing on his appeal against sentence before the Vienna Court of Appeal. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 14 March 2002 the Court declared the applicant’s remaining complaint admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 25: 1). On 5 September 1993 he had raped E.P., had beaten and strangled her, had forced her to swallow drugs, had burned her skin with cigarettes and had cut her vagina with a knife. He was convicted of both offences of aggravated rape and sentenced to 14 years’ imprisonment. In assessing the penalty, the court considered as mitigating circumstances the applicant’s partial confession and that he had acted under the influence of alcohol and drugs. As aggravating circumstances, it considered the applicant's criminal record and his extreme brutality when committing the offences. In his appeal against sentence the applicant submitted that the Court of Assizes had failed to give sufficient weight to the requested witnesses from Poland. The applicant did not request to attend the hearings before the Supreme Court or the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The applicant’s partial confession was merely a contribution to the establishment of the truth (Beitrag zur Wahrheitsfindung) and did not qualify as a mitigating circumstance. A neglected education and difficult childhood could not be considered as the applicant was now an adult and it could not explain his excessive use of brutality. No weight could be given to his intoxication because he should have known about the effects of alcohol on his person, and experts had stated that it had no bearing on him committing the offences.

A neglected education and difficult childhood could not be considered as the applicant was now an adult and it could not explain his excessive use of brutality. No weight could be given to his intoxication because he should have known about the effects of alcohol on his person.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52690/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that upon his arrival in the Białystok Remand Centre, on 14 December 1989, he had been beaten and insulted by the prison guards. He claimed that in consequence of the excessive use of force against him he had sustained a spinal injury and suffered permanent disability. On 24 August 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The applicant had filed a civil action for compensation against the State Treasury- Szczecin Remand Centre. He claimed PLN 2,500 in compensation for an accident which had occurred in 1983, during his detention. The applicant was heard before the Trzcianka District Court. Between 18 September and 18 November 1997 the trial court held four hearings. The Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s allegations that the incident had caused a spinal injury and dismissed the remainder of his claims for compensation. In May 1998 the Białystok Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) held a hearing and examined the appeal lodged by the State treasury. The applicant had lodged a civil action on 28 January 1991 and despite the fact that he had not contributed to their length, the proceedings were still pending before the District Court. The applicant relied on the 2004 Act on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The court examined only the course of the proceedings after the remittal of the case by the appellate court on 13 November 2002 and found no delays on the part of the district court. As result, the court found that during this period the District court had not violated the applicant’s right to have his case heard within areasonable time. On 7 January 2005 the Szczecin Regional Court dismissed his complaint. The case. occurred before the Regional Court during the period between 24 May 1991 when the case was transferred to it and 14 May 2002 when the court gave a judgment. According to the provisions [of the 2004 Act] the. Regional Court examining the complaint lodged by [the applicant] that the proceedings in his case. before the District Court exceeded a reasonable time is not entitled to examine the course of the proceedings before the Szczecin Regional Court. The civil proceedings in this case are pending before the Szczec in District Court. It appears that the civil proceedings are pending in that court as well as the regional court.

name: Lasse Lilja
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36689/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of aggravated tax fraud and an aggravated bookkeeping offence in relation to the declaration of value-added tax and employers’ contributions for the period July 1994 – September 1996 by Latem AB, a building company wholly owned by him. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. In the absence of an appeal from the prosecutor, the latter judgment acquired legal force in March 2004. Latem AB was found liable for value-added tax and employers’ contributions. The company was ordered to pay tax surcharges amounting to 20% of the increased tax liability. Latem AB appealed to the County Administrative Court. On 2 October 2003 the Supreme Administrative Court (Regerings-rätten) refused leave to appeal. On 15 February 2002 the applicant complained to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (Justitieombudsmannen) about the preliminary investigation against him. On 12 February 2003, the appellate court held an oral hearing and, by a judgment of 10 March 2003, it upheld the Court’s judgments. The matter was referred to the Director General of the National Economic Crimes Bureau. Latem AB was declared bankrupt on the basis of unpaid taxes and surcharges totalling approximately SEK 10.7 million. The applicant further requested compensation for suffering caused by his detention in 1996. On 2 June 2004 the Chancellor of Justice awarded him SEK 35,000 for suffering and SEK 2,500 for legal costs. The Director General found that the prosecutor should have decided whether to bring an indictment at the latest during the autumn of 1999 and thus disagreed with the prosecutor’s opinion that he had to await the outcome of the tax proceedings.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of aggravated tax fraud and an aggravated bookkeeping offence in relation to the declaration of value-added tax and employers’ contributions for the period July 1994 – September 1996 by Latem AB, a building company wholly owned by him. He was detained by a decision of the District Court (tingsrätten) of Stockholm on 23 October 1996 and released from detention on 3 December 1996. The preliminary investigation, which concerned 20 companies, was concluded on 25 April 1998. The trial commenced on 2 September 2003. In the absence of an appeal from the prosecutor, the latter judgment acquired legal force on 19 March 2004. On 6 September 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible. Latem AB was ordered to pay tax surcharges amounting to 20% of its increased tax liability for value-added tax and employers’ contributions. The company appealed to the County Administrative Court. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The applicant complained to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (Justitieombudsmannen) about the preliminary investigation against him. The application was dismissed on 2 October 2003. The case was settled out of court in October 2002. Latem AB is now the subject of a criminal investigation into alleged irregularities in the company’s tax affairs. The investigation has been adjourned pending the outcome of the criminal investigation. The applicant further requested compensation for suffering caused by his detention in 1996. On 2 June 2004 the Chancellor of Justice, pursuant to the Act on Compensation for Deprivations of Liberty, awarded him SEK 35,000 for suffering and SEK 2,500 for legal costs. Latem AB was declared bankrupt on the basis of unpaid taxes and surcharges totalling approximately SEK 10.7 million in 2003. The Director General of the National Economic Crimes Bureau criticised the responsible prosecutor for the delays in the preliminary investigation. He found that the prosecutor should have decided whether to bring an indictment at the latest during the autumn of 1999 and thus disagreed with the prosecutor’s opinion that he had to await the outcome of the tax proceedings.

name: Esat Bayram
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75535/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant’s brother Halim Bayram, who was a Turkish citizen of Kurdish origin, was called up for military service in 1998. His superior was Mr Hüseyin Arabacı. At about 12.30 p.m. he was seriously wounded by one bullet and he was immediately taken to the Çanakkale Military Hospital, where he was operated upon. A few days later the applicant received a. telephone call from his brother, who stated that he was being bullied by his superior. He told the. applicant that he had been threatened with death by Hü.seyin. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. Halim Bayram allegedly told the applicant: ‘I saw Hüseyin Arabacı approaching and I remembered his death threats. I do not remember what happened but I am sure that I did not shoot myself’ The applicant’s brother told him that he wanted to be transferred to Istanbul. Witnesses to the incident gave statements to the court. The applicant was able to speak to his brother briefly at the hospital. He also spoke to Mr Kazım Ağın, who allegedly told him he had been pressurised by his superior. He told the court that he had written a letter to be sent to his parents should anything happen to him. The applicant’s brother developed disseminated intravascular coagulation and was transferred to the GATA Military Hospital in Istanbul. He died from internal bleeding in the ambulance during the transfer. The applicant wanted to transfer his brother to another hospital but the doctors refused. He stated that he doubted that his brother had shot himself and requested an autopsy. A military investigation board delivered its report and concluded that no fault could be attributed to Mr Hüseyin Arabacı or the hospital. A second autopsy was conducted on Halim's body by the Morgue Expertise on 17 September 1998. The report stated that a bullet entry hole was observed in the stitched wound in the chest area. Halim Bayram shot himself in the back in 1998. A bullet had entered his back and exited from the right below the xiphoid process. Miss Emrah Baynal gave a statement to the gendarmes. She told them she had been friends with Halim for nearly two years. She explained that they loved each other and denied that she was engaged to somebody else. The case was transferred to the Gölcük Military Prosecutor. The Prosecutor delivered a non-jurisdiction decision and transferred the file to the Çanakkale Public Prosecutor on 28 September 1998. The Forensic Medicine Institute delivered its report concerning the chemical examination of these two pieces of skin. On 21 January 2000 the Forensic Laboratory Department delivered its final report. The report concluded that although the autopsy report dated 26 February 1999 had stated that the entrance hole had been in the back, as following the chemical examination no nitrite and nitrate ions had been found on Halim Bayram’s clothes, this should indicate that the bullet must have entered from the xiphoid process. In the report, it was further stated that there was no indication to determine whether the shot had been fired from close range or point blank range. On 30 March 2000 the Military Prosecutor decided not to prosecute. The applicant appealed against that decision and the Military Court rejected the appeal. On 20 July 2001 the applicant obtained a medical report from Mr Christopher Milroy.

Thereby, she would commit regulatory offences under the Railway Construction and Operation Act and the Assembly Act. The applicant was detained in a cell in the Lüneburg Police Station from 7 p.m. onwards. The applicant’s small cell, equipped with a mattress and a chair, was lighted at least via a ventilation slot and by electric light. She went outside for a walk on the banks of the Ilmenau river with the police officers three times during that period. The applicant was detained in the Braunschweig Police Station from 8 November 2008, 2.10 a.m. until her release on 9 November 2008. name: Inga Allard
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The applicant's mother owned a number of houses on Marum 1:8. Two of the houses were used by the applicant's two sisters. A third house situated on the property was considered too small for the applicant’s needs. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) On 9 September 1987, the committee granted a permit for the building of a new house further away from the shore. The new house was built in 1988. In 1991 one of the joint owners applied for the sale of the two estates at a public auction. On 22 February 1992 the District Court decided to stay those proceedings. By a partial division on 29 June 1991, the new house is transferred to the applicant. In 1994 the District Court’s removal judgment was upheld on appeal by the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) She later requested, inter alia, that no further action be taken on the case pending the outcome of division proceedings which she had begun in October 1990. In these proceedings, the applicant claimed that the joint ownership of the two estates should be dissolved and individual plots be assigned to the family members. On 7 March 1996 the Office ordered the applicant to remove the house before 3 April 1996 or risk having it demolished by the Office at her own expense. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. However, at a session held on 3 June 1996 the Court. of Appeal had already examined the case and, by a decision. delivered the following day, refused the applicant leave to appeal against the. District Court's decision of 15 May 1996. Thus, no further stay was granted. this could preserve the house and reduce the risk of adverse consequences for the applicant. The house in issue was demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. This claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996. The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. The Real Estate Court decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. It agreed with the opinion given by the Central Office of the National Land Survey on 14 March 1996. This decision was upheld on appeal by the Court of Appeal on 2 November 1998. On 28 April 1997 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The applicant and her sister had claimed that several other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8 should remove buildings they had erected on the estates. However, the District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. Furthermore, considering that the claimants did not have a legitimate interest in having their cases heard, the court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. With effect from the date of the judgment, the legal aid previously awarded was withdrawn. The Court of Appeal upheld the legal-aid decision on 3 October 1997. On 16 January 1998 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Building Committee granted the applicant building permits for the reconstruction of the demolished house.

She later requested, inter alia, that no further action be taken on the case pending the outcome of division proceedings which she had begun in October 1990. On 7 March 1996 the applicant was ordered to remove the house before 3 April 1996 or risk having it demolished by the Office at her own expense. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. The appeal was not heard until the evening of 5 June, as she had been at the site of the house in issue. It appears from the court that the applicant was not given a ten-day respite to complete her appeal by 12 midnight on 5 June 1996. The Court of appeal refused the applicant leave to appeal against the decision of 15 May 1996. The house in issue was demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken). The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 25 June 1996 the Enforcement. Office declared that the house had been demolished and that accordingly the removal. judgment had been duly enforced. This decision was appealed against by the other joint owners on the ground that the building material had not been removed from the property. The applicant and her sister had claimed that several other joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8 should remove buildings they had erected on the estates. However, the District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. The court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The applicant's mother owned a number of houses on the land managed by the applicant’s mother – which formed part of Marum 1:8. A third house situated on the property was considered too small and it was decided to enlarge it. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) on 9 September 1987. On 21 December 1989 practically all the other joint owners of the two estates brought proceedings against the applicant in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Södra Roslag. The court stated, inter alia, that it was the applicant who owned the house and that she had built it without the necessary consent. The applicant began division proceedings in October 1990. She claimed that the joint ownership of the two estates should be dissolved and individual plots be assigned to the family members. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) and requested that no further action be taken on the case pending the outcome of division proceedings. Following several decisions taken by the Real Estate Formation Authority and the courts, the case had to be referred back by the Court of Appeal to the REFA for re-examination as the latter had made procedural errors. Subsequently, by a decision of 1 December 1995, theREFA allowed the creation of four individual plots on Marum 1:8 but rejected the applicant’s request for the. creation of an individual plot around the new house. The house was to be demolished by a construction firm on 3 June 1996. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. The Appeal Court refused the applicant leave to appeal against the District court's decision of 15 May 1996. It appears from the court that the applicant was not given a ten-day respite to complete her appeal by 12 midnight on 5 June 1996, as she had been at the site. The house in issue was therefore demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. However, this claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996. The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 22 November 1996 the Real Estate Court gave judgment in the division proceedings. It decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. In this respect, the real estate court agreed with the opinion given by the Central Office of the National Land Survey on 14 March 1996. The applicant and her sister were joint owners of Marum 1:6 and 1:8. They claimed that several other joint owners should remove buildings they had erected on the estates. The District Court rejected the claims, finding that the buildings had been erected before 1991. The court also decided that further litigation in this respect should not be paid for through public legal aid. After an appeal, the declaratory judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 26 February 1998. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force. By decisions of 4 February 1997 and 29 February 2000 the Building Committee granted the applicant building permits for the reconstruction of the demolished house and the construction of two smaller outbuildings.

name: Manuel Tejedor García
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 October 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25420/94) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Spanish national, Mr Manuel Tejedor García, on 4 August 1994. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1997. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991. The accused, Mr Manuel Tejedor García, who was born on 11 October 1948 and has no criminal record, was at the material time a police officer stationed in the Mataró (Barcelona) police station. On 21 May 1989, while off duty, he was in Gallur (Saragossa) where he joined members of his family and friends to celebrate his niece’s first communion. At about 8.30 p.m., after a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, in addition to the wine that accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of the cognac, he drank a glass of wine. Manuel Tejedor García shot into the ceiling of a café in Gallur. He then kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. These events provoked the indignation and disapproval of the people present who gathered round the police officer and his prisoners after following them from the café. The accused came out of the building in an aggressive manner on several occasions. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. The investigating judge sent the case file to the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial, competent for criminal proceedings regarding members of the security forces. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution (acusación particular) against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out and decided, in accordance with Article 789 of the CCP (see paragraph 16 below) In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside (recurso de reforma) or, in the alternative, an appeal (see paragraph 16 below), dated 13 September 1990. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected the ANPU’s observations and held that the application had been made in time. As to the merits he stated that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial. On 12 February 1991 the investigating judge made a final discontinuance order (Articles 637 no. 2 and 790 no. 6 of the CCP) in respect of the two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. On 6 November 1991 the Audiencia Provincial dismissed the preliminary objection that the public prosecutor’s application had been made out of time and found the applicant guilty of the alleged offences. It sentenced him to six months and fifteen days’ imprisonment, and a fine of 200,000 pesetas, and ordered him to pay compensation to the victims. He was also suspended from duty for six months. On 28 May 1993 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. The court ruled that the application was not in breach of the law. The court said that the interpretation of the case was consistent with the Constitution. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the case had already been decided by the trial court. The case is still pending at the Supreme Court of the Court of Appeal. The judge said that he would have to review the case again if he were to make an appeal to the High Court. The high court is yet to make a decision on whether or not to overturn the appeal. The decision is expected to be made by the end of the month. For more information on the case click here: http://www.cnn.com/2013/01/20/politics/the-trial-of-the-charter-of the-crown-and-culling-of the-law-to-prove-that-it-isn't-legal-that the appeal is illegal.

Manuel Tejedor García, who was dressed in plain clothing, did not consider the documents satisfactory and, showing his police identification, fired a shot into the ceiling of the café. He then kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them, using the psychological pressure of the gun, to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. The ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside (recurso de reforma) or, in the alternative, an appeal. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. However, no annotation appears on the file attesting service on the publicProsecutor. In an order (providencia) of 8 November 1990, the investigating judge held that the application for an order setting aside the decision that no further action be taken had been made in the correct form. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application was not a breach of the law. The court said the application did not have to be approved by the court because it was based on a broad interpretation of the constitution. The ruling was made on the basis that the interpretation was consistent with the law, not that it was a violation of the Constitution. The case was settled at the Constitutional Court of South Africa’s Supreme Court, not the Supreme Court of the Republic, which was supposed to decide whether the application should be allowed to go ahead or not. The Court of Appeal ruled the application had no grounds for appeal, and therefore the appeal was not valid.

name: Arnold Fragner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18283/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor's fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time. The Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board refused to pay the fees claimed as the applicant is not a specialist doctor but a general practitioner. On 19 June 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The case was brought before the Joint Arbitration Committee (Paritätische Schiedskommission) on 4 September 1996. Because of a tie vote, the Committee could not take a binding decision. The applicant filed an application for the transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommmission) On 11 December 1996 the Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's claim as it found that the applicant had failed to obtain the necessary visa from a chief physician. On 9 May 1997 the applicant filed a complaint with Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) and on 13 October 1999 that court quashed the Commission's decision. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the right to a fair trial and upheld the contested decision. It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their function and no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality and independence had arisen in the present case. This decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal. The verdict was handed down on 27 September 2005 and the appeal was heard on 30 November 2005, with the final decision served on 1 December 2005. It was the first time the appeal had been heard by a court of appeal. The appeal was the last to be heard before the Supreme Court of Justice.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor's fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time. He claimed payment for these treatments from the Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board. The Board refused to pay the fees claimed as the applicant is not a specialist doctor but a general practitioner. On 19 June 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The applicant filed an application for the transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommission) on 23 September 1996. The applicant's lawyer argued that the applicant was professionally competent to do the interventions at issue and that to give such treatment was his basic contractual obligation. The Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's claim on 10 December 2004. It was not persuaded that there had actually been a situation of emergency allowing the applicant not to obtain the necessary visa from a chief physician beforehand. The Constitutional Court found that the alleged unlawfulness of the restriction excluding general practitioners from administering certain types of therapy was a preliminary question which the Appeals Commission had failed to address. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging a breach of the principle of equal treatment. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the right to a fair trial and upheld the contested decision. It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their function and no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality and independence had arisen in the present case. This decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. 2005. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who was awarded the case against the Regional appeals commission. The decision was made on 27 September 2005 and the case was heard in court on 29 October 2005.

The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. State Security Courts were abolished by constitutional amendments introduced on 7 May 2004. On 31 January 2005 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in accordance with Article 146 of the Criminal Code. However, on an unknown date the Court of Cassation quashed the decision of the first-instance court once again. The applicant's case was also heard by the Istanbul State Security Court, but he was not convicted. The case has been adjourned until the end of the year, when it is expected to be re-examined by the court.

The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation. In their application lodged with the Commission on 11, the German authorities claim they have been subject to surveillance by the G 10. The G 10 authorises measures of surveillance of telephone and telegraphic communications. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used. The court may decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security and dismiss the application on that ground. In urgent cases, the decision may be taken by the public prosecutor’s department but to remain in effect it must be confirmed by a court within three days. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Articles 6, 8 and 13 (art. 6, art. 8 and art. 13) of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’;. The present case didn’t disclose any breaches of Article6 para. 5-1;. name: Gisèle Augusto
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71665/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in Vouziers. By a decision of 17 May 1996 the occupational counselling and redeployment board (“the COTOREP”) gave the applicant a 50 to 79% disability rating and issued her with a card certifying that she found it difficult to remain in a standing position. On 18 November 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal on points of law on 27 May 1998. In further pleadings her lawyer filed with the Court of Cassation on 23 October 1998, she invoked, inter alia, a violation of ‘the requirements of the rights of the defence’ and of “equality of arms in a fair trial within the meaning of Article 6” of the Convention. The accredited doctor of the national tribunal for claims relating to disability and level of insurance coverage for accidents at work observes the following: ‘On 1 June 1996 the subject was in a fit state to carry on working without seriously jeopardising her health’ In the light of the above medical opinion, the court decides to uphold the impugned decision. The Employment and Welfare Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal in the following terms. “Without laying itself open to the objection raised in the ground of appeal, the national disability tribunal, in the light of the findings of its accredited doctor and having analysed the different evidence adduced, considered, as it was within its exclusive jurisdiction to do, that Ms Augusto's disability rate was less than 50%.” “The applicant was therefore not entitled to a retirement pension on the grounds of incapacity to work,” the court added. ‘For these reasons, the appeal ... is dismissed.

Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Ms Gisèle Augusto (‘the applicant’), on 31 August 2000. The Employment and Welfare Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal in the following terms: ‘Without laying itself open to the objection raised in the ground of appeal, the national disability tribunal, in the light of the findings of its accredited doctor and having analysed the different evidence adduced, considered, as it was within its exclusive jurisdiction to do, that Ms Augusto's disability rate was less than 50%.’ For these reasons, the appeal ... is dismissed.’ The appeal was dismissed on 2 March 2000, and the case was dismissed. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled that Augusto was entitled to a pension on the grounds of incapacity.

name: Ayhan Işık
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33102/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints under Articles 6 and 13. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was arrested and taken into custody in Istanbul on suspicion of involvement in the activities of the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers' Party, an illegal organisation) The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The case was heard between 30 April 1999 and 14 May 2003. The Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The court awaited the enactment of a new provision to replace the annulled Section 1 § 4 of Law no. 4616. The applicant was released in October 2004. The new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 June 2005. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court on 9 December 2003 and the applicant was served with the committal order concerning the execution of his sentence on 28 April 2004. On 14 June 2005 the Istanbul Assize Court reviewed the applicant's conviction and reduced his sentence of imprisonment to six years and three months.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) from 25 to 27 December 2014. On an unknown date the applicant was transferred to Goleniów Prison. The applicant signed a protest letter but was only one of 140 prisoners who had signed the letter. The Szczecin Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 29 November 2011. The court held that the decision to impose the regime of 8 September 2011 had been justified. The following one taken on 6 December 2011 had not indicated any new circumstances justifying the continuing application of the regime and its reasoning had been scarce. The regime was imposed on the applicant for a total of five months and seven days. The Commission decided to lift the ‘dangerous detainee’ regime on 14 February 2012.

The applicant was wounded in the hip and his cousin in the leg during the incident as a result of ricochet bullets. On the same day, a major from the District Gendarmerie wrote to the Yüksekova Public Prosecutor and requested authorisation to search the two vehicles which had been stopped by the gendarmes. Upon receipt of authorisation, the gendarme officers searched the two lorries. They found sixty‑six barrels of smuggled fuel in the first lorry and forty-five barrels in the applicant's cousin’s lorry. No other illegal items were found in the vehicles. Gendarmes ordered the driver of the lorry to stop on suspicion of fuel smuggling. When the driver failed to obey, shouting from the window that the brakes had failed, they opened fire. The applicant was shot in the hip but was able to stop the vehicle by using the handbrake. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The court found that the applicant had benefited from the commission of the offences in the amount of GBP 2,092,569.20. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment under section 1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1906 on each of the twelve counts, to be served concurrently. On 2 September 1996, following an application on behalf of the Ministry of Defence in separate civil proceedings, the applicant was declared bankrupt. The High Court, which appointed the Receiver under section 80(2) of the 1988 Act on application by the CPS, ordered that the Receiver’s powers were not to be exercised until the interests of the restrained properties had been determined. The Order was made under section 371 of the Insolvency Act 1986 in favour of Ms S.D. in her capacity as the applicant’s Trustee in Bankruptcy. The application was based on the grounds that the Trustee was of the opinion that communications concerning remittances and useful information might be forwarded to the applicant's address. The grounds invoked were supported by an affidavit sworn on 27 September 1996, which affirmed that it was necessary for postal packets to be intercepted immediately and without notice to the apply. The applicant expressed particular concern that apparently privileged material was being intercepted. On 2 December 1996 the Receiver and Trustee replied that no mail from the Police, Legal Aid, the Legal Aid Board, the National Council for Civil Liberties or the European Commission of Human Rights was intercepted. Re-direction Order expired on 27 December 1996. Sender’s names would be stamped on envelopes. National Council for Civil Liberties and European Court of Human Rights would be opened in the future. The applicant issued a summons for a stay of the receivership proceedings pending the determination of his application to the Commission. The. applicant has not informed the Court of any subsequent developments in the. receivership. proceedings. The appeal was dismissed on 25 February 1997.

name: Ümit Onur
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Ümit Onur, is a Turkish national who was born in 1978 and now lives in Turkey. In 1989 the applicant, who was then eleven years old, arrived in the United Kingdom with his father, his brother and his four sisters to join his mother, who had arrived six weeks earlier. In 1999 the applicant and his other family members were granted Indefinite Leave to Remain. One of the applicant’s sisters left the United UK for Turkey in 1993 and the family believe she may be in Iraq. The applicant was convicted on seven occasions for a number of different offences. His relationship with his partner ended when he was imprisoned. Shortly afterwards, in 2000, his partner gave birth to a daughter. The applicant is not named as the father on the birth certificate although his mother cared for the child until she was three years old. In 2005 the applicant was found guilty of a road traffic offence and a failure to surrender to custody. He was given a sentence of twenty-eight days’ imprisonment, a fine of GBP 200 and disqualified from driving for nine months. In April 2006 the Secretary of State for the Home Office admitted that 1023 foreign national criminals, who should have been considered for deportation or removal, had completed their prison sentences. The applicant was served with an undated Notice of Decision to Make a Deportation Order on 1 October 2006. The applicant appealed to the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal (“the AIT”), relying, inter alia, on Article 8 of the Convention. The relevant paragraph of the Immigration Rules, paragraph 364, had changed on 20 July 2006. Before the AIT, the applicant argued, first, that the decision to deport him was not in accordance with the law. The post-20 July 2006 version of the rule established a presumption that the public interest required deportation. The Secretary of State would consider all relevant factors in considering whether the presumption was outweighed in a particular case, but it would be only in exceptional circumstances. The applicant argued that the decision to deport him had been taken on 6 July 2006 and thus his case should have been considered under the old version of paragraph 364. He also submitted a report prepared by a consultant clinical psychologist who diagnosed him as having mild to moderate depression, panic disorder, mild mental retardation, borderline intellectual functioning and dyslexia. The applicant’s application for statutory review was dismissed by the High Court on 16 May 2007. On 8 June 2007 the deportation order in respect of the applicant was signed and it was served on him on 27 June 2007. He was deported to Turkey on 12 July 2007. The High Court dismissed the judicial review application on 10 October 2007. Convention of the Convention was held on 17 July 2008 in New York City. The convention was the first to be held since the end of World War II in 1945. It was held under Article I, Section 8 of the Treaty of Versailles. The Convention was officially opened with a speech by U.S. President George H.W. Bush at 11:30 a.m. ET on July 17, 2008. The speech was followed by a statement by Mr. Bush on July 18, 2008, at 12:30 p.m., and a vote by the Convention at 3:30pm on July 19, 2008; the vote was then followed by an announcement by the convention at 4:45pm. The vote was approved by a majority of both houses of Congress.

The court found that the accused was aware that a human life counted for little with Schwarzenberger. The accused was so intensely involved in the planning and in the choice of a weapon that his actions did not merely constitute supportive measures, but an autonomous part of the action, the court said. The court said the accused wanted to slay his sleeping victim, thus perfidiously exploiting his unsuspecting victim’s defencelessness. These offences had been committed jointly with the applicant in order to get the loot from the murder. The jury found the accused guilty of two counts of attempted murder and one count of attempted attempted murder of the adoptive mother of the accused. The applicant was extradited to Germany on 22 April 1997. On 12 February 1999 the main hearing was opened before a chamber of the Heilbronn Regional Court. name: David Smith
train_texts: Case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained that they were denied a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The applications were introduced on 18 August and 10 December 1997 and were registered on 25 August and 19 December 1997 under file nos. 37475/97 and 39036/97, respectively. The Court heard the cases on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the applications fell to be examined by the Court. The Government responded by letter dated 20 November 1998, stating that the Government did not have any observations to make on the admissibility of the applications. The applicants’ subsequent petitions and appeals, as far as the full Courts-Martial Appeal Court, were unsuccessful. March 1999 the Chamber decided to join the cases and not to hold a hearing on the merits. The Chamber also declared the applications admissible. Mr Smith was found guilty of, inter alia, four disciplinary offences of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline contrary to section 69 of the 1955 Act. He was sentenced to be dismissed from the army, although section 69 provides for a maximum sentence of two years’ imprisonment. Mr Ford was convicted of three counts of common assault contrary to Criminal Justice Act 1988 and sentenced to six months' imprisonment.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18837/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fact that she was not allowed to attend the hearing of the prosecution's appeal against her being granted bail had breached her rights under Article 5. and Article 6. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The application was made by a British national, Ms Susan Anne Allen (“the applicant”), on 2 May 2006. She was charged with two offences of conspiracy to supply Class A drugs. Judge Globe declined the request, reasoning that the applicant could be given a full report of what had happened from her counsel. He emphasised that this was a re-hearing and rather unusual as it was the prosecution which had sought to appeal the Deputy District Judge's ruling on bail. In refusing the applicant permission to attend, Judge Globe stated: “I am not going to alter my view in relation to [the applicant] being present during the hearing. I will listen to your submissions.” He added that if there is anything during your submissions that causes me to hear evidence from her or to have to do something different to what I am doing at the moment, I will reconsider it. The applicant applied for permission to apply for judicial review of the decision not to allow her to attend the hearing on the ground that her rights under the Convention had been breached. Mr Justice Sullivan refused the application. The applicant's first application to the High Court was rejected on the grounds that she did not contend that the ultimate decision to refuse her bail was unreasonable. Her second application was refused on the basis that she was entitled to be present if, in an exceptional circumstances, she could not be seen by the judge. The application was rejected again on the reasoning that a person was only entitled to see the judge if she was present in exceptional circumstances. The applicant's grounds for applying for permission to seek judicial review did not explain why hers was an exceptional case or why the interests of justice required her attendance whilst she was legally represented. Mr Justice Sullivan took into account Judge Globe's clear indication that he would be prepared to reconsider his view and allow the applicant to be present if there was anything that would require him to hear evidence from her in person. The applicant's counsel argued that the decision to refuse her admission to the hearing of the prosecution's appeal had breached her rights under Article 5 § 3, or alternatively, Article 5 ° 4 of the Convention. It was asserted that the production of the applicant before the Deputy District Judge did not fulfil the requirements of Article 5§ 3 because the judge was not a judge authorised to exercise judicial power. Mr Justice Gibbs said Mr. was authorised to exercise judicial power as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and clearly had exercised it. The decision was subject to immediate appeal and was not put into effect pending appeal. The legal framework covering applications for bail, including appeals, did in Mr Justice Gibbs view enable her to take proceedings whereby the lawfulness of her detention could be decided speedily by a court. There was, in his judgment, nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5§ 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances. Where prosecution appeals against refusal of bail were concerned, Rule 19.17 (4) provided a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant.
