The application was examined at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29§ 3) The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by Mr D. Taylor, a lawyer practising in Liverpool. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Willmott, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. Judge Globe refused the applicant's request to attend the hearing. He said it would be unfair to treat the applicant more favourably if she was not present. The applicant's counsel argued that she was a ' respectable woman of good background and a vulnerable person' Judge Globe said that he would not change his view if he heard evidence that caused him to reconsider his previous decision to grant bail to the applicant. The application for bail had been made on the basis of ‘common humanity’ and ‘not technical’. The judge ruled that the case. was being dealt with fairly and he further clarified that the basis for his application was “ common humanity” and “ not technical”. The applicant applied for permission to apply for judicial review of the decision not to allow her to attend the hearing on the ground that her rights under the Convention had been breached. On 9 November 2005 Mr Justice Sullivan refused the application. The applicant's case was heard at the High Court in London. The hearing was held in the applicant's absence. The judge refused to grant the application to review the decision to refuse her bail. The application was dismissed on the grounds that it was not in breach of the Convention. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal and the decision was upheld by the Supreme Court. The appeal was heard by the Appeal Court and the ruling was upheld. The decision was made to deny the applicant bail. The applicant's counsel argued that the decision to refuse her admission to the hearing of the prosecution's appeal had breached her rights under Article 5 § 3. Mr Justice Sullivan took into account Judge Globe's clear indication that he would be prepared to reconsider his view and allow the applicant to be present if there was anything that would require him to hear evidence from her in person. The applicant's grounds for applying for permission to seek judicial review did not explain why hers was an exceptional case or why the interests of justice required her attendance whilst she was legally represented, Mr Justice Gibbs ruled in her favour on 7 December 2005. He found that the Deputy District Judge had not fulfilled the first exception to Rule 19.17 (4) as the applicant was not acting inperson. Mr Justice Gibbs said the judge was authorised to exercise judicial power as required by Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and clearly had exercised it. The judge's decision was subject to immediate appeal and was not put into effect pending appeal. He said the legal framework covering applications for bail, including appeals, did in Mr Justice Gibbs view enable her to take proceedings whereby the lawfulness of her detention could be decided speedily by a court. There was, in his judgment, nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5§ 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances, he said. He ruled that there was a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant in cases in which he or she was not permitted to bePresent.

Having been affiliated to this company since 1975, she claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. As an employee of the Berlin Land, she was entitled to allowances covering half of her medical expenses; the private health insurance was to cover the other half. The court found that the experts had convincingly shown that the applicant had been for at least the last three years under the constraint of living according to these tendencies and that there was a high probability that the she would not change these tendencies in the future. The psychiatrist Dr H., having examined the applicant in January 1993, delivered his opinion in February 1993. In his conclusions, he confirmed the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her transsexuality had to be regarded as a disease. Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s claims. The court considered that the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her condition had to be regarded as a disease. The expert concluded that the gender reassignment operation formed part of the curative treatment of a mental disease. the fact that transsexuals accepted themselves and their bodies contributed to their stabilisation. According to him, many transsexuals reached such stability only after an operation. In his view, this was the case for the applicant and an operation should therefore be approved. The question whether the treatment in question was recognised by medical science was irrelevant. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal. In its reasoning, the court found the applicant ought first to have had recourse to an extensive course of 50 to 100 psychotherapy sessions. According to the opinion of the expert Dr H., her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. In its view, the applicant’s “fear of bigger boys” at school was not gender-specific. Furthermore, applying to join the armed forces did not indicate female feelings. name: Juan Manuel Palomo Sánchez
train_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared admissible the applications (nos. 28955/06, 28957/06,. 28959/06 and 28964/06) lodged by Mr Juan Manuel Palomo. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010. The applicants sought to secure recognition by the employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status. They sought to be covered by the corresponding social-security regime. The Court heard addresses by them and heard evidence from the applicants' lawyers. The application was dismissed on the grounds that there had been no violation of Article 10 of the Convention. The case was brought by Mr José Antonio Aguilera Jiménez and Mr Francisco Beltrán Lafulla. The Government was represented by Mr Irurzun Montoro. The applicants informed the company P. of the setting-up of a branch of the trade union inside the company, of its composition, and of their appointment as members of the executive committee of that workplace branch. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. On 3 June 2002 the company notified the applicants of their dismissal on grounds of serious misconduct, namely for impugning the reputations of G., A. and B., under Article 54 §§ 1 and 2 (c) of the Labour Regulations. In a judgment of 8 November 2002, the applicants were dismissed. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. Employees complained about cartoons and an article published on noticeboard in their workplace. The first article contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything.” The text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which A and B. had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all. But your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. And you let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept, because when you’ve rented out your arse, you can’t shit when you please. High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain upheld the High Court’s decision. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker's obligations under the contract and his freedom of expression. For the court, the publication of the offending drawing and articles had clearly been harmful to the dignity of the persons concerned and had overstepped the limits of admissible criticism. Relying on Article 24 (right to a fair hearing) of the Spanish Constitution, the applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. dismissed their appeal on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of 31 July 1992, was not pertinent. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company because of the judicial proceedings they had brought against it"  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions. The application of that jurisprudence to the present case leads the Court to the conclusion that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. The Court concludes that they used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation. [Those cartoons] were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which they wished to complain, and were therefore gratuitous.

The applicants complained that they had been dismissed by way of reprisal for belonging to a trade union and on account of its demands. The applications relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the convention. The Court declared the applications admissible and decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time, as allowed by former Article 29 § 3 (now Article 29§ 1) and Rule 54A of the Rules of Court. The application was heard by the Court's Third Section on 17 November 2009. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber. On 8 December 2009 the Chamber delivered a judgment (Aguilera Jiménez and Others v. Spain) in which it held, by six votes to one, that there had been no violation of Article 10 of the Convention. The applicants sought to secure recognition by the employer of their special “salaried worker” status, as confirmed by judgments of 2 May and 30 December 1995 of the High Court of Justice of Catalonia, in order to be covered by the corresponding social-security regime. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. The union NAA published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. Inside the newsletter were two articles which vehemently denounced the fact that those two individuals had testified in favour of the company P. in proceedings that the applicants had brought against their employer. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which, in a judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed their claims. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’n shit when you please” read as following: ‘If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies’ In the old days, you were a rebel who criticised the system. You were caustic, dynamic, cutting, impulsive, jovial. But a couple of favours received have gradually cooled your fiery temperament, stoked your self-esteem and put the dampers on your feelings. From time to time you have a pang of nostalgia and you would like to fart, but your sphincter is sealed, because you’ve rented out your arse and can’t shit when you please. You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all ... but your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain upheld the High Court's decision. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment. It also referred to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker’s obligations under the contract and his freedom of expression. The balancing exercise had to enable it to be determined whether or not the reaction of the company that dismissed the employee was legitimate. Appellants tried to overturn dismissal on grounds of freedom of expression and association. Constitutional Court found appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. Court said there was not enough evidence to show the company’s action was intended to restrict, hamper or prevent the exercise of their right to freedom of association. The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Six Spanish nationals, Mr Juan Manuel Palomo Sánchez, Mr Francisco Antonio Fernández Olmo, Mr Agustín Alvarez Lecegui and Mr Francisco José María Blanco Balbas, lodged the applications on 13 July 2006. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status, as confirmed by judgments of the High Court of Justice of Catalonia. They were employed as delivery men by the company P., against which they brought several sets of proceedings in employment tribunals. The applicants set up the trade union Nueva Alternativa Asamblearia (NAA) to defend their interests and those of the other delivery staff who were under pressure from the company to renounce their claim to salaried status. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). The applicants informed the company P. of the setting-up of a branch of the trade union inside the company, of its composition, and of their appointment as members of the executive committee of that workplace branch. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union published a monthly newsletter. The March 2002 [sic] issue reported on the judgment of 2 April 2002 of Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, which had partly upheld the applicants’ claims. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk. Employees claim they were insulted by cartoon on noticeboard in their workplace. Cartoon showed caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. Text underneath read: ‘We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything’ The article was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which A and B. had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. You’re fed up with your work, pissed off, anxious, stressed and in despair. You can see the injustices meted out on your colleagues, the totally irrational way of dealing with their problems and the constant persecution to which they are subjected, but say nothing, for fear of drawing attention to yourself. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all ... but your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. You let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept, because when you’ve rented out your arse, you can’t shit when you please. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain upheld the High Court’s decision. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. The appeal was dismissed and the court found that the dismissal could not be declared null and void, since it was based on serious misconduct as provided for by law, and found that applicants’ fundamental rights had not been breached. The company P. had, moreover, duly shown that the application was not a measure of reprisal. Appellants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The court dismissed their appeal on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of 31 July 1992, was not pertinent. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company because of the judicial proceedings they had brought against it to assert their rights ...” In line with what this court has repeatedly said, such evidence does not consist of a mere allegation of a constitutional violation. The Court said freedom of expression does not extend to expressions that are offensive or defamatory. The court said the cartoons and comments were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which the appellants wished to complain. It said they were therefore gratuitous and not necessary to the exercise of freedom of speech in a trade-union context. The Court concluded that the appellant’s right to free speech has not been infringed, since they used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons andComments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation.

The applicants sought to secure recognition by the employer of their special “salaried worker” status, as confirmed by judgments of 2 May and 30 December 1995 of the High Court of Justice of Catalonia, in order to be covered by the corresponding social-security regime. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 26 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention and Rule 24. The Court heard addresses by them and also the memorials filed by the applicants and the Government. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. On 3 August 2001 the applicants informed the company P. of the setting-up of a branch of the trade union inside the company. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed. The union NAA published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which, in a judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed their claims. The first article, entitled “Whose witnesses? Theirs, of course’, contained caricatures of A. and B., showing them gagged by a handkerchief tied behind their heads. The text underneath read as follows: “We knew who they were and how they behaved, but we didn’t know how far they were prepared to go in order to hold onto their seats and cushy jobs without doing anything.” The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which A and B. had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. The newsletter was distributed to staff and displayed on the trade union’s noticeboard. The employment tribunal observed at the outset that the cause of the dismissal was the content of the newsletter and not the applicants’ trade-union membership. It referred in its judgment to the exercise of the right to freedom of expression in the context of labour relations and to the fact that it was not unlimited. It found that the limits to this right had to be interpreted in accordance with the principle of good faith, which in labour relations had to involve respect for the interests of the employer and the minimum requirements of coexistence. The tribunal ruled that the applicant had not breached any law. The tribunal took the view that the cartoon and speech bubbles on the cover, together with the articles inside, were offensive and exceeded the limits of freedom of expression and information. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain upheld the High Court’s decision. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment and to the necessary balance that judicial decisions had to strike between a worker's obligations under the contract and his freedom of Expression. The applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company’s ...” The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of 31 July 1992, was not pertinent. The Court held recently in judgment no. 39/2005 of 28 February that the Constitution does not prohibit the use of hurtful, embarrassing or vituperative expressions in every circumstance.  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20§ 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions. The application of that jurisprudence to the present case leads the Court to the conclusion that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation. [Those cartoons] were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which they wished to complain, and were therefore gratuitous.

name: Peter Sutter
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8209/78) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission in 1978. The request and the application sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mrs. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court. The President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mr. W. Ganshof van der Meersch, Mr. L. Liesch, Sir Vincent Evans and R. Bernhardt. The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 30 September. On 20 December 1982, the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on 21 March 1983. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Trechsel, Mr. Weitzel and Mr. Minelli for the Commission and by. Voyame and Barras for the Government, as well as their replies to its. questions and a question put by one of its members. On 15 December 1983, the Commission filed two documents which the Registrar, acting on the President's instructions, had asked it to produce. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. Peter Sutter, a Swiss national born in 1949, was a student and resident in Basel. He was subjected to five and seven days’ strict arrest for refusing to comply with Article 203 bis of the service regulations, relating to hair-cuts. A copy of the decision was sent to the applicant on 23 June 1977. On 2 July 1977, within the prescribed period of ten days from service of the judgment, the applicant filed a memorial containing a “final“ statement (section 189 para. 3 of the 1889 Act) of his grounds of appeal. He submitted that the decision appealed against had infringed his rights. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It could have done so only if the judgment had been quashed and the sole ground for the quashing had been misapplication of the law. The President requested a judge whom he had designated from amongst his colleagues to draft a report containing a reasoned proposal. This document was circulated, together with the papers in the case, amongst the other members of the Court. On 21 October 1977, the Court ofCassation deliberated on the matter in camera and dismissed the case. It thus did not rule on the merits of the case; according to the provisions then in force (section 194 of the 1889 Act), it could have do so onlyif the judgment was quashed. Military criminal procedure was governed by the 1889 Act (see paragraph 15 above) This Act drew a distinction according to the level of the court concerned. The 1889 Act was repealed by the Federal Military Criminal Procedure Act of 23 March 1979 (‘the 1979 Act’) The existing system was maintained for proceedings before the Divisional Courts, and was extended to the Courts of Appeal which were set up by the same statute. As regards the Military Court of Cassation, the 1979 Act provides that “There shall be no oral hearings“ (section 189 para. 1). The Act did, however, make two innovations: in future, the Court was to deliver judgment in open court and could in no circumstances itself rule on the merits of the case. The Sutter judgment of 21 October 1977 appeared in 1983 in volume 9 (covering the years 1973 to 1979) of the judgments of the Military Court of Cassation, under the number 136. Anyone who can establish an interest may consult or obtain a copy of the full text on application to the Chief Military Prosecutor or the military court registries. If judgments contain features that are novel or of importance for the interpretation of the law, they are subsequently published in printed form. In its report of 10 October 1981, the Commission expressed the opinion by ten votes to eight that there had been no violation of Article 6 para. 6-1. The Swiss Government invited the Court “to hold that Switzerland has not violated Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention’. The court rejected the Government’s claim that Switzerland had violated the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Swiss government appealed the decision to the European Court of Human Rights. The case was heard between February and March 1983. The judge ruled in favour of the Swiss government on July 3, 1982. The trial was adjourned until April 4, 1984. The appeal was rejected on May 3, 1984, and the case was dismissed on May 5, 1985. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Government on May 9, 1986.

The case originated in an application (no. 8209/78) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission in 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The request and the application sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Article 6 para. 1. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3) The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 30 September. On 10 November, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegates would submit their own observations at the hearings. On 20 December, he transmitted to the Registrar the applicant's claims under Article 50 (art. 50) The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 March. The Court heard addresses by Mr Trechsel, Mr. Weitzel and Mr. Minelli for the Commission and by Mr Voyame and Mr Barras for the Government, as well as their replies to its questions and a question put by one of its members. Peter Sutter was sentenced to ten days' imprisonment for two counts of insubordination and failure to observe service regulations. Sutter claimed that the decision appealed against had infringed on his right to a fair trial. The decision was made by the Divisional Court no. 5 of the Federal Army (Constitution of Courts and Criminal Procedure) Act of 28 June 1889 - “the 1889 Act’. The application was brought by Mr Sutter, a Swiss national born in 1949, who was a student and resident in Basel at the time of the events giving rise to the case. The court's decision was delivered in public on 16 May 1977, at the close of a hearing. Sutter argued that the military courts were not tribunals within the meaning of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention. He also argued that it was not consonant with Article 6 to conduct proceedings entirely in writing. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal and did not rule on the merits of the case. On 21 October 1977, the President of the Military Court of. Cassation requested a judge whom he had designated from amongst his colleagues to draft a. report containing a reasoned proposal. This document was circulated, together with the papers in the. case, amongst the other members of the Court ofCassation. The decision was returned to the Chief Military Prosecutor, who could have filed observations, but instead submitted that the appeal should be dismissed. The 1889 Act was repealed by the Federal Military Criminal Procedure Act of 23 March 1979 (“the 1979 Act’). The existing system was maintained for proceedings before the Divisional Courts, and was extended to the Courts of Appeal which were set up by the same statute. In future, the Court of Cassation was to deliver judgment in open court (sections 48 para. 3 and 194 para. 1) and could in no circumstances itself rule on the merits of the case. As regards the Military Court ofCassation, the 1979 Act provides that “There shall be no oral hearings“ (section 189 para.1). Anyone who can establish an interest may consult or obtain a copy of the full text on application to the Chief Military Prosecutor or the military court registries. If judgments contain features that are novel or of importance for the interpretation of the law, they are subsequently published in printed form. The report contains two separate opinions, one being dissenting. The Commission declared the remainder of the application admissible on 11 July 1979. The case was dismissed on the grounds that there had been no violation of Article 6 para. 6-1. The Government of Switzerland asked the Court “to hold that Switzerland has not violated Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention’. The case was heard for the first time in March 1983. The court heard the case for the second time in May 2013. The hearing was adjourned until November 2014. The last hearing was held on March 25 and 27, 2014. It was ruled in favor of Switzerland on March 28 and 29, 2014, but not on March 30 and 31, 2015, respectively. The decision was made on March 22, 2013, and it was decided on March 29, 2013.

If judgments contain features that are novel or of importance for the interpretation of the law, they are subsequently published in printed form. Mr. Sutter complained that the military courts were not independent and impartial. He also claimed that the principle of equality of arms had been infringed since he had had access neither to the report of the grand juge nor to the submissions of the Chief military Prosecutor. The Government invited the Court “to hold that Switzerland has not violated Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention’. The hearing was held on 21 March 1983. The Court ruled on the matter in January 1986. The case is still pending in the European Court of Human Rights, which will decide on the case again in April 2014. The Swiss government has said it will appeal the decision to the Supreme Court of the European Union. name: Said Mohammed Hilal
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his expulsion to Tanzania placed him at risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 8 February 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was decided in favour of the applicant by the Court in February 2000. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. In November 1994 the applicant was detained at a police station in Zanzibar. He was hung upside down with his feet tied together until he bled through the nose. In January 1995 the police came looking for him while he was out. He decided to leave his country fearing for his safety. In February 1995 he claimed asylum in the UK. He said he had been tortured for three months. The application was rejected on the grounds that it was based on a false premise. The applicant died in January 1995 in hospital after he was admitted with severe head injuries. He had been a member of the CUF since 1992. He died of a heart attack in February 1995. The applicant's appeal to a special adjudicator was dismissed on 8 November 1996. During the proceedings the applicant claimed that the Tanzanian authorities intercepted the letters he was sending home, knew that he had claimed asylum. He provided correspondence from the Royal Mail concerning his enquiries about money which had gone missing from a registered letter dated 27 November 1995 which he had sent to his parents in Tanzania. On 29 June 1995 the Secretary of State refused asylum, finding the applicant’s account implausible and noting inconsistencies in his answers. He placed considerable weight on the fact that the applicant had not mentioned his arrest and torture at his first asylum interview and did not accept the applicant's explanation that he was having difficulties with the interpreter. Leave to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal was refused on 10 January 1997. The applicant obtained a copy of his brother’s death certificate and a medical report which recorded that his brother died on 20 January 1995, after being brought to hospital from prison with a history of severe chest pain and general body weakness associated with a fever. He also obtained the summons from the Pemba police headquarters to his parents dated 25 November 1995. He made representations to the Secretary of State dated 30 January 1997, providing copies and requesting that his letter be considered as a fresh asylum application. By letter dated 5 February 1997 he decided not to refer the material in question to the special adjudicator. The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s refusal to refer the new material to the special adjudicator. He submitted an expert opinion confirming that the documents were genuine. On 1 July 1998 the application for leave was rejected by the High Court. In its judgment it noted that the hospital records showed that his brother had died of fever. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the refusal was wrong in law and ‘Wednesbury unreasonable’ The High Court ruled that the decision to refuse asylum had been ‘unreasonable’ and that the applicant could live safely on the mainland. The applicant's wife arrived in the United Kingdom and claimed asylum shortly afterwards. She had been detained for one day in April 1995 and questioned about her husband’s whereabouts. The police came to her house on 12 February 1999, wanting to know if her husband was back in Zanzibar. They were angry because he had claimed asylum and tarnished the name of the President. They threatened to arrest her instead. there was no evidence to suggest that the conclusion reached by the Secretary of State that the applicant could live without harassment on the mainland was wrong. There was a rumour that the U.K. had sent back most of the asylum-seekers from Zanzibia.

The case originated in an application (no. 45276/99) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his expulsion to Tanzania placed him at risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment and that he would not receive a fair trial if he were returned to Tanzania. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The case for asylum in the UK was brought against the ruling party, the Communist Party of Tanzania (CCM), and its members. The case was brought by a man who had been tortured for three months by the CCM. He claimed that he had been held in a cell full of water for days at a time and had been hung upside down with his feet tied together until he bled through the nose. The man claimed he was forced to leave the country because he feared for his safety. He was granted asylum and returned to the UK in March 1995. In an interview, he said he had no problem obtaining a passport as he was a member of the CUF and had contributed to them. The applicant claimed asylum in Tanzania in 1995. He said he had been arrested because he gave money to the CUF. He was hung upside down and given electric shocks before being released. The Secretary of State refused asylum, finding the applicant’s account implausible and noting inconsistencies in his answers. The applicant's appeal to a special adjudicator was dismissed on 8 November 1996. The judge noted inconsistencies between the evidence given by the applicant before him and the answers given in his asylum interviews. He placed considerable weight on the fact that the applicant had not mentioned his arrest and torture at his first asylum interview and did not accept the applicant's explanation that the interviewing officer told him it was not necessary to give details. The applicant obtained a copy of his brother’s death certificate and a medical report which recorded that his brother died on 20 January 1995, after being brought to hospital from prison with a history of severe chest pain and general body weakness associated with a fever. He also obtained the summons from the Pemba police headquarters to his parents dated 25 November 1995. He made representations to the Secretary of State dated 30 January 1997, providing copies and requesting that his letter be considered as a fresh asylum application. By letter dated 5 February 1997 he decided not to refer the material in question to the special adjudicator under section 21 of the Immigration Act 1971. name: Salih Olcar
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 76096/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant's stores and goods were burned and destroyed in the course of an armed clash between members of the State Security Forces and militants from the PKK. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Salih Olcar (“the applicant”), on 10 September 2001. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant filed an action with the Diyarbakır Administrative Court and requested compensation for the damage suffered as a result of the destruction of his stores. The Ministry of the Interior did not respond to the applicant's request for compensation within the 60-day period prescribed by Law no. 2577. The applicant appealed against this judgment as well and, according to the information in the case file, the proceedings are still pending before the Supreme Administrative Court. The court reasoned that, under Article 13 of Law. no.2577, an action of this kind could be filed only after the administrative authorities had refused the litigant's request.

name: Stanisław Goc
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48001/99) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. By a decision of 23 October 2001 the Chamber of the Fourth Section declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The District Court gave a preliminary decision (postanowienie wstępne) on 22 December 1989. It determined that the house in question consisted of two apartments, basements and an attic. On 9 July 1990, on the applicant’s appeal, the Regional Court quashed this decision. On 8 March 1991 the court decided to join his application to the merits of the proceedings concerning the division of the property. In April 1993 the parties paid an advance fee towards the costs of the inspection, as ordered by the court. On 27 April 1994 the District Court ordered that expert evidence be obtained from the Institute of Construction Technology (Instytut Techniki Budowlanej) The case was sent to the Institute of Construction Technology in order to have the report prepared within a two-month period. The court requested the Institute to expedite the preparation of the report. On 22 November 1995 the court received the expert report and served copies on the parties. On 20 March 1996 the applicant again filed with the District Court an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment. On 16 September 1999 the applicant submitted information about B.G.’s sole heir and requested that the proceedings be resumed. On 30 August 2000 the court appointed G.G., the petitioner, as guardian of the estate. The applicant died on 2 December 2000 at the age of ninety-six. The Warsaw-Praga District Court ruled that the applicant’s sons, T.G. and E.G., were the heirs to his estate. The proceedings are still stayed and, therefore, remain pending before the Warsaw- praga District court. Later, the lawyer of T. g. requested the court to resume the proceedings. On 23 October 2001 T.g.'s lawyer requested the President of the Civil Division of the District Court to expedite the proceedings, which have not yet been heard by the court. The case is still pending and is expected to continue until the end of 2011.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38629/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal in proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant asked the Office to review its decision under chapter 20, section 10 a of the 1962 Act. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. It considered that the Office’s first decision had been based on insufficient information and that it should therefore have reviewed that decision at the applicant's request. The National Social Insurance Board (Riksförsäkringsverket; hereinafter ‘the Board’) appealed against the County. Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten). The applicant made submissions in response to the Board’s appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative Court of Appeal to hold an oral hearing in the case during which the person in charge of the case at the Office should give evidence. The applicant also asked the court to obtain the opinion of a medical expert. The latter request was granted by a decision of 30 December 1992. By 3 votes to 2, it quashed the County Administrative Court's judgment and confirmed the Office's decision. The case can be determined notwithstanding a failure to submit such written observations. The Applicant is invited to state the further circumstances he wishes to invoke and submit his final written observations within two weeks after having been notified of this decision. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) of 12 July 1991. The dissenting judges considered that the applicant was entitled to the disability allowance granted to him by the County Administrative Court and that, for this reason, there were exceptional reasons to change the Office’s decision. The applicant complained about the lack of an oral hearing in the Administrative Court of Appeal. On 24 February 1997 the Supreme administrative court refused the applicant leave to appeal. On 9 October 1996 the applicant made a renewed request for a disability allowance. By a decision of 12 December 1996 the Office found that he had special needs and costs due to his handicap which made him eligible for disability benefits under the 1962 Act.

name: Paul H. Schmitz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30493/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his preventive detention of an indefinite duration violated his right to liberty. The case was adjourned until a judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above) has become final. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court) The applicant was convicted of sexual offences including attempted rape, sexual abuse of children, sexual assault, attempted sexual assault and dangerous assault. The Cologne Regional Court found the. applicant of two counts of sexual assault. It sentenced him to five years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered his. (first) preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see. paragraphs 20-21 below) The applicant served his prison sentence until 17 January 1995 and was then held in preventive detention until 29 March 1995, when the preventive detention order was suspended on probation and the applicant released. The applicant, acting with full criminal responsibility, had again attempted to sexually assault a hitchhiker. He had threatened her with a gas pistol, but she had succeeded in wresting the pistol from him and making good her escape. The applicant was in his first preventive detention as ordered in the judgment of the Cologne Regional Court of 14 February 1990 until 15 March 2010. The Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 10 September 2003. The Federal Constitutional Court, referring to its leading judgment of 5 February 2004 in the case of M. (file no. 2 BvR 2029/01; application no. 19359/04 to this Court), declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint. On 19 July 2004, 19 July 2006 and 2 July 2008 the Aachen Regional Court refused to suspend the. applicant's preventive detention on probation. It considered that it could not be expected that the applicant, who refused to make a therapy with an external psychologist offered to him, would not reoffend on release. The Court’s judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) is executed. The sentence of preventive detention by the sentencing court is in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment. The duration of preventive. detention under Article 67d of the Criminal Code, in its version in force prior to 31 January 1998, may not exceed ten years. If a person has spent ten years in preventive detention, the court shall declare the measure terminated (only if the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released) The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period. The court held that all provisions on the retrospective extension of preventive detention were incompatible with the Basic Law. It also held that the provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot) The court ordered all provisions declared incompatible to remain applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. It ordered that the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention made by this Court in its judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above).

It sentenced him to five years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered his. (first) preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 20-21 below). It found that owing to his criminal tendencies, it was very likely that the applicant would commit further serious sexual offences comparable to those he was found guilty of on release and was dangerous to the public. The applicant served his full prison sentence imposed in the judgment of 11 November 1996 until 25 May 2000. Since 26 May 2000 the applicant has been in preventive detention in Aachen Prison. The applicant’s preventive detention, ordered by the Cologne Regional Court in 1996 under Article 66 of the Criminal Code, constituted lawful detention after conviction by a competent court within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention. The decision of the Aachen Regional Court decided that his objections against the admissibility of the execution of his preventive detention were ill-founded. The Federal Constitutional Court, referring to its leading judgment of 5 February 2004 in the case of M. (file no. 2 BvR 2029/01; application no. 19359/04 to this Court), declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint. The applicant was in preventive detention from 14 February 1990 until 15 March 2010. The Court’s judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) is executed. The sentence of preventive detention by the sentencing court for an intentional offence is added to a prison sentence if the offender has been shown to be dangerous to the public (Article 66 of the Criminal Code). The perpetrator must have been sentenced twice already, to at least one year's imprisonment in each case, for intentional offences committed prior to the new offence. The duration of preventive. detention may not exceed ten years. If a person has spent ten years in preventive detention, the court shall declare the measure terminated (only if it has expired) The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period. The court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of theriminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned, owing to specific circumstances relating to their person or their conduct, were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention made by this Court in its judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above). In its judgment, the Court stressed that the fact that the Constitution stood above the Convention was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue.

The applicant argued that preventive detention violated Article 5 of the Convention. The Cologne Court of Appeal, endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant's appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court, referring to its leading judgment of 5 February 2004 in the case of M. (file no. 2 BvR 2029/01; application no. 19359/04 to this Court), declined to consider the applicant‘s constitutional complaint. On 19 July 2004, 19 July 2006 and 2 July 2008 the Aachen Regional Court refused to suspend the applicant. It considered that it could not be expected that the applicant would not reoffend on release. The Court’s judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) provides a summary of the provisions of the Criminal Code and of the Code of Criminal Procedure governing the distinction between penalties and measures of correction and prevention. The provisions referred to in the present case provide as follows: The order of preventive detention by the sentencing court can be in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. If a person has spent ten years in preventive detention, the court shall declare the measure terminated (only if the maximum duration has expired) The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period. The court ruled that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences and if, additionally, if they had been ordered retrospectively. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention made by this Court in its judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (cited above). It stressed that the fact that the Constitution stood above the Convention was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue between the courts.

name: Gülizar Pembe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Four Turkish nationals, Ms Gülizar Pembe, Mr Mıstık Ateş, Mr İsmail Karapınar and Ms Yüksel Bozkaya (‘the applicants’), filed separate actions for compensation with the İskenderun Civil Court of First Instance. On 27 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable. On 7 October 1997 the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay İsmail Karapınar TRL 13,075,000,000 plus interest at the statutory rate. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996, when Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000 was paid.

The case originated in an application (no. 49398/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' plots of land in İskenderun were expropriated by the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways in 1993. A committee of experts assessed the value of these lands and the determined amounts were paid to them when the expropriation took place. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings to the Government. The ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board on 23 October 1996. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the İskenderun First Instance Court on 11 May, 20 May and 25 May 1998 respectively. On 8 April, 13 April, 12 May and 4 June 1999 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest. In October 1997, the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay İsmail Karapınar TRL 13,075,000,000 plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 11 September 1996, the date on which the ownership was transferred. The court also ordered Yüksel Bozkaya TRL 80,274,368,000.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 31047/04 and 43386/08) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the execution of his preventive detention violated his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, and by their permanent Deputy Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the applications at issue be resumed and granted priority to the applications. In December 1996 the applicant was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of drug trafficking. He has remained in prison since then. In a judgment dated 9 February 1998 the Aachen Regional Court convicted the applicant of unauthorised importing of drugs. The applicant claimed that he had struck a deal with the Regional Court on the latter’s proposal that the court would impose a sentence of less than ten years. The Government submitted that there was no indication in the case-file that such an agreement had been made. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed as ill-founded an appeal by the applicant on points of law. The applicant, without being represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the two judgments of the Regional Court and the judgment and the decision of the Federal Court of Justice. He complained, in particular, that preventive detention was incompatible with his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, which did not cover such a preventive measure. The applicant’s complaint was inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, the court found. The court found that the applicant had failed to submit his statement of the grounds of his appeal on points of law nor had he claimed before it that he had complained about the unconstitutionality of the amended provisions on preventive detention. The court fully agreed with the findings of a psychiatric and psychotherapeutic expert it had consulted on the applicant’s dangerousness. He was still dangerous to the public as he had to date failed to reflect sufficiently on his numerous offences. Even assuming that the security measures taken against him by the prison authorities had not been justified, this did not alter the fact that there hadn’t been a consistent treatment limiting the risk that he would reoffend after his release. The Federal Constitutional Court found, in particular, that the decisions of the courts dealing with the execution of sentences to order the applicant's placement in preventive detention had not violated his right to liberty. The Aachen Regional Court refused to suspend the execution of the preventive detention order against the applicant on probation. That decision was confirmed on appeal. In view of the courts’ assessment that the applicant was likely to commit further serious offences if released, their finding that the interest in public safety prevailed over the applicant’s right to liberty had been proportionate. The order of preventive detention by the sentencing court is a penalty in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. The provisions referred to in the present case provide as follows:. The offender has been shown to be dangerous to the public (Article 66 of the Criminal Code). Under Article 67d of the Criminal Code, in its version in force prior to 31 January 1998, the first placement in preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The court responsible for the execution of sentences (that is, a special Chamber of the Regional Court composed of three professional judges) must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person’s preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the Execution of the preventive detention order. The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period on 4 May 2011. The court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. The provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot) The court said that Article 66 of the criminal code in its version in force since 27 December 2003 was not compatible with the constitutional protection of legitimate expectations. All provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention in its judgment in the case of M. v. Germany.

Even assuming that the security measures taken against him by the prison authorities had not been justified, this did not alter the fact that there hadn’t been a consistent treatment limiting the risk that he would reoffend. The applicant had been sentenced to one term of eight years’ imprisonment and another of 8 years and six months. The Constitutional Court noted that the courts dealing with the execution of sentences had not based their decision to order preventive detention globally on the fact that the applicant had failed to prove that he was no longer dangerous in the course of such relaxations. In view of the courts’ assessment that the. applicant was likely to commit further serious offences if released, their finding that the interest in public safety prevailed over the applicant’s. right to liberty had been proportionate. The court ruled that the Aachen Regional Court, acting as the court dealing. with the Execution of sentences, had refused to suspend the execution. of the preventive detention order against the applicant on probation. Under Article 67d of the Criminal Code, in its version in force prior to 31 January 1998, the first placement in preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The court responsible for the execution of sentences must review, before completion of the prison term, whether the person’s preventive detention is still necessary in view of its objective. Termination shall automatically entail supervision of the conduct of the offender. If that is not the case, it suspends on probation the Execution of the preventive detention order. The Federal Constitutional Court delivered a leading judgment concerning the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period. The court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. The provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot), the court said. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) on 4 May 2011. The ECHR ruled that Article 66 did not comply with the constitutional protection of legitimate expectations guaranteed by the Basic Law. Constitutional Court ordered that all provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences and if, additionally, they suffered from a mental disorder. Kopp (“the applicant”) on 20 January 1997, by the European Commission of Human Rights on 22 January 1997 and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation on 27 February 1997. Marxer, Delegate, for the applicant Mr T. Poledna, of the Zürich Bar, Counsel. In 1988 Mr Kopp and his wife were accused of leaking confidential information to a newspaper. He was replaced by his wife, Mrs Kopp, who was accused of lying to the press about the source of the confidential information. The paper was later found to be a front-page story in the Swiss press. The story of the leak was made public in 1989 and led to a parliamentary inquiry into the case. The investigation found that the leak had been made by a member of staff of the Federal Office of Police. The monitoring began on 21 November 1989 and ended on 11 December 1989. applicant was monitored as a “third party’, not as a suspect. In February 1990 the Federal Court acquitted Mrs Kopp of disclosing official secrets. The investigation was closed on 6 March 1990 on the ground that there was no evidence to corroborate the suspicions that the applicant’s wife or a member of the Federal Department of Justice and Police had disclosed official secrets, namely certain passages of the letter of request which had been classified as confidential. The report concluded that the rumours to the effect that she had allowed external influences to affect the way she performed her duties were unfounded. The American citizen’s Swiss representatives had tried to obtain the confidential document in the file by applying to [the applicant]. They were hoping for privileged access to the Federal Department of Justice and Police. The suspicion that there had been a disclosure of official secrets thus proved to be unfounded. The police investigation did, however, reveal how the rumour that led to the information and the suspicion arose. The American letter of request was in the end disclosed, but only after the confidential passages had been blotted out. On the basis of these findings, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office discontinued the investigation. As he was not a civil servant, he could not have been guilty of the offence concerned. name: Gertraud Mitzinger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29762/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that she had suffered discrimination on the grounds of her birth by the application of the relevant provisions of domestic inheritance law by the national courts. On 26 May 2015 the complaint concerning alleged discrimination was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was brought by a German national, Ms Gertraud Mitzinger (“the applicant”), on 20 May 2010. The German Government were represented by one of their Agents, Ms K. Behr. The case was brought by the daughter of a man who had died. She argued that she had no right to be given copies of his estate. The court agreed with her and dismissed the case. The case was heard again in May 2013, and the case was returned to the Court of Appeal. The judge upheld the decision to not give the mother a copy of the estate, saying it was not in conformity with the Basic Law. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the father had died before the mother had been born. The father's widow was allowed to keep the copy of her father's estate, however, because she had not been born at the time of his death. The first sentence of section 12(10)(2) of the Children Born outside Marriage (Legal Status) Act had been found to be in conformity with the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the complaint, which it considered inadmissible for lack of sufficient substantiation (no. 1 BvR 2021/09). It observed, in particular, that the applicant had failed sufficiently to address the arguments of the Munich Court of Appeal’s decision. It observed that she had been obliged to give further reasons, which she had failed to do. That provision prohibited a generalised application of the first sentence.

train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicants were born in 1973, 1975, and 1980 respectively. They were detained in Elazığ Prison in Turkey. On 14 March 1999 the police raided a flat which was used as a cell by Hezbollah in Mardin. On 11 June 1999 the applicants gave statements to the police where they accepted the charges against them. The applicants denied the content of their police statements alleging that they were taken under duress. They were convicted of the offence as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. They appealed. The Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation in his written submissions recommended that the court uphold the decision.

name: Andreas Ioannou
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18364/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 28 March 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. In addition, the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene, also filed observations on the merits. The Court ruled that the application was admissible and that it had been granted legal aid. The applicant alleged that the house described under paragraph 9 (j) above had been his permanent residence. He lived there with his wife Sophia Andreou Ioannou (the applicant in application no. 18360/91), his son Michael Michael and his daughter Christina Michael. Following the 1974 intervention and the ensuing Turkish military occupation, the applicant was deprived of access to and the use of his property. He participated in various peaceful demonstrations and marches towards his village. On all occasions he was prevented from walking home by the Turkish troops. On 9 December 1990 the applicant complained that he had been prevented from leaving the house by Turkish troops and had been denied access to his house. The applicant and his fellow refugees had informed the Commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intentions. They arrived at the check point in the “buffer zone’, on the main road which links Nicosia with Ayios Amvrosios and Kyrenia. There, they asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return to their homes, property and villages. They requested the same officer to forward their demand to the Turkish military authorities. The officer replied that the latter had refused their request. The applicant was granted a stay of deportation until the case can be heard by the European Court of Human Rights.
