name: John Harding Price
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 43185/98 and 43186/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the proceedings in which they were sued in respect of property in Florida were not dealt with within a reasonable time. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 3 September 2002 the Court declared the applications partly admissible, having in the meantime joined them on 28 November 2000. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was heard in the High Court in August 1994 but was not heard until 1 November 2001. Trial of Dr Price and K began in September 1994 but was postponed until the end of September 1994 because the judge was not available for the length of time needed for the hearing. On the fourth day of trial, while K was being cross-examined, an adjournment was granted because K claimed to feel unwell. It emerged that no medical justification could be given for his continued non-attendance, but nonetheless he remained absent for the rest of the trial. Judgment was given on 27 April 1995. The applicants and Mrs Price applied to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal on 1 November 1995. On 15 January 1997 the appeal was listed for hearing, and it was heard on 16 and 17 April 1997. On 30 March 1997 the last date the court of Appeal gave judgment dismissing the appeal. The applicants and Mrs Price were refused leave to appeal by the House of Lords in 1998. The application was dismissed by Mr Price's solicitors and Mr Price was not allowed to appeal against the decision. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, in 2000. It was ruled in favour of the applicants and they were allowed to remain in the UK. The appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court of Europe in 2001. The High Court of Justice ruled in 2007 that the case should be thrown out of court. The Supreme Court ordered the appeal be allowed to be heard by the Court of Appeal. The decision was upheld on appeal.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 25 May 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12914/87) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a French national, Mr Pierre-André Melin, on 21 November 1986. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under paragraph 1 of Article 6. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President of the Court granted this request on 22 June 1992. Mr Ryssdal assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) The applicant lodged his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Gain for the Government, by Mr Soyer for the Commission and by the applicant. The applicant was Pierre-André Melin, a French national who lives off private money. The Government was represented by Mr P. Titiun, a magistrat, and Mr D. Caron, a legal officer at the Court of Cassation, Counsel. On 6 May 1985 the Nanterre Criminal Court convicted him of fraud and sentenced him to a suspended term of sixteen months’ imprisonment, combined with an order (mise à l’épreuve) requiring him, inter alia, to compensate the victim for the damage he had sustained. The applicant appealed immediately to the Versailles Court of Appeal, which, giving judgment on 15 January 1986 in Mr Melin’s presence, upheld the lower court's guilty verdict. On 14 February 1986 the appeal file reached the registry of the Court of Cassation. Three and a half months later, on 27 May, the Criminal Division dismissed the appeal because no grounds had been put forward and because the contested judgment did not disclose any procedural defect. Mr Melin asked the Chief Registrar. for the submission of a memorial. The Chief Registrar replied that as the judgment of the Court of Cassation was final, he could not appeal against it. Mr Melin had conducted his own defence, though he had been assisted by a lawyer at first instance. He was sentenced to two years in prison and one year of community service. The President of the Court granted this request on 22 June 1992. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal. Mr Ryssdal assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the French Government (‘the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant on the organisation of the proceedings. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Gain for the Government, by Mr Soyer for the Commission, and by the applicant. The applicant lodged his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The Commission produced the file on proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The applicant appealed immediately to the Versailles Court of Appeal, which, giving judgment on 15 January 1986, upheld the lower court’s guilty verdict. The typed text of the judgment was filed with the registry on the same day as its delivery. On 14 February 1986 the appeal file reached the registry of the Court of Cassation. Three and a half months later, on 27 May, the Criminal Division dismissed the appeal because no grounds had been put forward and because the contested judgment did not disclose any procedural defect. The Government maintain that there were two possibilities: either the applicant had not requested a copy and could not therefore be surprised at not receiving one; or he had in fact asked for one. Mr Melin asked the Chief Registrar for a memorial. He was told that the judgment of the Court of Cassation was final and he could not appeal against it. Mr Melin had conducted his own defence, though he had been assisted by a lawyer at first instance. The Chief Registrar replied to him that, as the judgment was final, he couldn't appeal. train_texts: Case originated from a complaint lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a Pakistani national, Ms Farida Kathoon Khan. The applicant alleged that her envisaged expulsion to Pakistan would breach Articles 8 and 6 of the convention. The case was heard by the Fifth Section of the Court on 25 November 2013. The application was given notice of the application to the Government. The Court decided to give notice to the German Government on 22 November 2013 and the case was adjourned until after the end of the third week of January 2014. The applicant had been in a state of acute psychosis. She did not acknowledge her own psychological condition. She was neither economically integrated nor sufficiently able to communicate in German, which was an obstacle to her therapy. Adequate medical care was available in Pakistan and the applicant’s family there could assist her. Article 8 of the Convention was not applicable as the applicant had no significant family relationships. The domestic court concluded that she remained a danger for the general public and a continuous stay in a psychiatric hospital had to be ordered. On 1 March 2011 the Kassel Administrative Court refused the applicant's action against the expulsion order. It upheld the decision that the applicant could be deported, on the grounds of the serious offence committed by her, lack of awareness of her own condition and high probability of reoffending. She was allowed to leave hospital and continue her treatment in Germany. The case was adjourned until May 2012 when it will be heard again. The applicant could afford treatment as she would be receiving a small pension in the amount of around 250. The woman was allowed to stay with her family. She had to continue to take her medication. name: Józef Polejowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38399/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided on the basis of the merits and the admissiblity of the case as a whole. The court held that the applicant had other additional resources and he can afford to pay the court fees in question. The court repeated the reasons given by the Regional Court. The applicant was ordered to pay PLN 11,305.5 [approx. EUR 2,826] for lodging his statement of claim on pain of having it returned. As the applicant failed to do so, his statements of claim was returned to him on 3 February 2003. The judge ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 2,000 [EUR 1,500] to the court for the cost of the appeal. The case was heard at the Polish Court of Appeal in Gdańsk.

name: Fatma Çamdereli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28433/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mrs N. Bener, a lawyer practising in Bursa. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 11 June 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of. the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was arrested on 24 April 1999 and transferred to the Forensic Medical Institute for a medical examination. The doctor noted that she had ecchymoses of 20x10 cm on her left shoulder and arm, an 8x5 cm Ecchymosis on her right shoulder and 4x5cm on her thigh. He considered that the injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for ten days. The Bursa Criminal Court of First Instance decided, in accordance with the relevant provisions of Law no. 4616, that the proceedings against the accused should be suspended and discontinued if no offence of the same or a more serious kind was committed by the offenders within a five-year period. The applicant bought an action in tort against Mr T.Ü. and Mr M.A.G. before the Bursa Civil Court of First Instance. She sought compensation in the amount of 1,500,000,000 Turkish liras (approximately 2,700 euros [EUR] at that time) for non-pecuniary damage for the treatment she had received. The applicant’s lawyer informed the court that she had been paid the amount awarded in full. The compensation proceedings were dropped after the statutory time-limit for the offence had expired, noting that the criminal proceedings against the accused had expired.

The case originated in an application (no. 28433/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, a housewife, was born in 1953 and lives in Bursa. The alleged ill-treatment of Mrs Fatma Çamdereli occurred in February 1999. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The applicant filed an official complaint about the above events and requested the prosecution of those responsible. The applicant was charged with ill-treatment and defamation in 1999. The Bursa Criminal Court of First Instance suspended the proceedings against the accused if no offence of the same or a more serious kind was committed by the offenders within a five-year period. The applicant’s objection against this decision, notably regarding the application of Law no. 4616, was dismissed on 9 January 2002. name: Dursun Sayğı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37715/11) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the national authorities had failed to carry out an effective investigation into the disappearance of her husband. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 October 2012. The case was settled in favour of the applicant on 16 March 2013. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The outcome of the case will be announced at a later date and may be appealed to the European Court of Human rights and Human Rights. The family of Mustafa Sayğı were told that he had been detained by the military. A detailed investigation was carried out by the Suruç prosecutor into the allegations. Both the police and the military authorities denied that they had detained the applicant’s husband. The prosecutor also questioned the soldiers who had been based at the temporary military station at the time of the incident. The soldiers denied, however, that they were responsible for the detention of the applicant's husband. They said they had no information to suggest that the applicant had any links with the PKK. The investigation into the disappearance of the applicants’ husband has now been reopened by the prosecutor. Mustafa Sayğı was unlawfully detained by the military in the temporary military base near Yoğurtçu village. The prosecutor did not attach any weight to the denials of the military personnel who had been on duty at the time of his detention. The applicant lodged an objection against the prosecutor’s decision with the Siverek Assize Court and submitted that nothing had been heard from her husband after his unlawful detention. She argued that similar unlawful detentions had peaked in that area in 1994 and that the relatives of those who had disappeared had been too frightened to complain to the authorities. The objection lodged by the applicant was rejected. Mustafa Sayğı disappeared while travelling on his red motorbike. 30 bones, fabrics, a small axe and the remains of a motorbike were found. The bones and the motorbike parts, together with soil samples, were taken away by gendarme soldiers for forensic examinations. Mustafa’s brother told prosecutor M.A. that he had no doubts whatsoever that the items discovered during the excavation belonged to his brother. The soil on the bones did not match the soil samples taken from the place. According to a report drawn up on 1 February 2010 by the forensic laboratory of the police. The chassis numbers and letters of theMotorbike – in Russian – are reproduced in the report of the experts. Prosecutor M.A. decided to close his investigation on the basis that the bones were not human bones. The applicant lodged an objection with the Siverek Assize Court against the prosecutor’s decision. No mention was made in the decision about the points raised by the applicant in her objection. She argued that carrying out an effective investigation was necessary in order to avoid “the State being put on trial before the European Court of Human Rights for its failure to protect the right to life of her husband” The objection was rejected by the Sivesize Assize court on 7 June 2010. No one had made any enquiries about any disappearance of a person with the name of Mustafa Sayğı.

name: Abdurrahman Dilipak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29680/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in Istanbul. He is a professional writer and journalist, and states that he is a human rights activist. He published an article on the front page of issue 84 of the weekly magazine Türkiye’de Cuma (“Friday in Turkey”), which came out on 29 August 2003. He suggested that the high-ranking officers in question should set up a political party on retirement and present their political projects to the people. The applicant tried to have the case thrown out on the grounds of his civilian status and his right to freedom of expression. The Military Court declined jurisdiction in favour of the Bakırköy Assize Court. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged an appeal on points of law against the decision to decline jurisdiction. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision declining jurisdiction and referred the case back to the Military Court. In its reasoning, the Court mentioned the need to reclassify the facts and to assess them under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code. The applicant was not apprised of the appeals onpoints of law lodged by the commanding officer and the Military Prosecutor, both of which were added to the case file. Military Court of Cassation held that even though the applicant’s article had comprised elements of both the aforementioned criminal offences, the general tenor of the impugned article had apparently concentrated on the behaviour of two specific Generals rather than the overall armed forces. Law No. 5530 of 29 June 2006 made a series of amendments to the Military Criminal Code, inter alia abolishing military court jurisdiction for trying civilians for offences such as those with which the applicant was charged. By a judgment of 14 November 2006 the military court once again decline jurisdiction and referred the case to the Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court. Bakırköy 2nd Criminal Court referred the case to the BakırKöy 16th Criminal Court on the grounds that that court was the former Bağcılar 2rd Criminal Court. The case was referred back to the Assize Court in the case of the jurisdictional dispute. By a judgment of 9 June 2010, the BakTurkish 2nd criminal court declared the proceedings statute-barred under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code. The decision was made by the Supreme Court of Turkey in April 2013. The court's decision was the first time the case had been heard by a High Court of Justice.

The applicant was accused of denigration of the State armed forces, which offence was punishable under Article 159 of the former Criminal Code. The Military Court noted that by claiming that the armed forces were led by commanding officers who appeared to have links with certain business circles and even the Mafia, the applicant had tarnished the image of the whole armed forces. The applicant was not apprised of the appeals on points. of law lodged by the commanding officer and the Military Prosecutor. The case was referred to the Bakırköy 24th Criminal Court. By a judgment of 11 March 2008, the latter court declined jurisdiction and referred the case to the Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court, which held jurisdiction for offences committed via the press. The case was dismissed by the Military Court of Cassation in May 2005. Law No. 5530 of 29 June 2006 made a series of amendments to the Military Criminal Code, abolishing military court jurisdiction for trying civilians for offences such as those with which the applicant was charged. The prosecutor referred the applicant’s file to the Medical Court of First Instance, accompanied by an opinion that the military courts had no jurisdiction in such matters. The case was referred to the Bakırköy 16th Criminal Court on the grounds that that court was the former Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court. By a judgment of 12 March 2009 the Bak Turkish Assize Court referred a jurisdictional dispute to that court. The Bak Turkish 2nd criminal court declared the proceedings statute-barred under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code on 9 June 2010. The case was finally decided in favour of the Bak Turkish 2nd Criminal Court in February 2013. The trial is expected to last for about a month and a half. The verdicts are expected to be announced on Monday.

Case originated in an application (no. 29680/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) Mr Abdurrahman Dilipak (“the applicant”) wrote an article entitled “If the pashas [the generals] refuse to obey” in the magazine Türkiye’de Cuma in August 2003. He suggested that the high-ranking officers in question should set up a political party on retirement and present their political projects to the people, instead of “deciding on the future of the nation on their own”. Military Court declined jurisdiction in favour of the Bakırköy Assize Court on the grounds that the offence at issue was not military in nature. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged an appeal on points of law against the decision to decline jurisdiction. He argued that the military criminal provision in question constituted a lex specialis vis-à-vis Article 159 of the Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision declining jurisdiction and referred the case back to the Military Court. In its reasoning, the Court mentioned the need to reclassify the facts and to assess them under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal code. The case was referred to the Bakırköy 24th Criminal Court. The court declined jurisdiction and referred the case to the Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court, which held jurisdiction for offences committed via the press. By a judgment of 14 November 2006 the military court once again decline jurisdiction. The case was heard by the Military Court of Cassation on 24 March 2006. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged a fresh appeal on points of law against the Court’s decision declining jurisdiction in 2006. He pointed out that the 3 May 2005 judgment had been delivered after the amendment to the legislation in question and that the provisions of the Military Criminal Code enabling civilians to be tried by military courts had not been amended. The case was referred to the Bakırköy 16th Criminal Court. That court was the former Bağcılar 2nd Criminal Court, which was dissolved in 2007. The case was also referred to a higher court by a jurisdictional dispute. In June 2010, the court declared the proceedings statute-barred under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code. It is not known if the case will be heard at the Supreme Court of Justice or the Court of Appeal. The appeal is expected to be heard later this year or early next year. The decision is likely to be made in favour of the Appeals Court.

name: Michael P. Hapeshis
train_texts: The case was brought by two Cypriot nationals against the Republic of Turkey under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived them of their home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 8 February 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. The first applicant lives in London, while the second applicant resides in Larnaca. The applicant alleged that until August 1974 they were living in a house owned by their father in Ayios Amvrosios. The applicants left their house on 13 August 1974, as the Turkish troops were advancing. On 17 August 1974 their father tried to visit his property but was arrested by Turkish soldiers. He was released on the same day, since he was a British citizen. On 19 May 1991 the applicants' father died. According to his will, dated 18 May 1988, the house and land in question was to be equally shared by the two applicants. On 10 July 1995 the applicants registered, in equal shares, their titles with the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Cyprus. The first applicant got the west residence, while the second applicantgot the east one.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29699/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95 and 26700/96). The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). The applicant was detained on remand and tried in the İstanbul Martial Law Court. He was convicted in 1984 and sentenced to lifetime imprisonment. The Court declared the application admissible. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The applicant appealed. the decision was upheld on 25 April 1995. The case was dismissed on 2 November 1996. The application was dismissed and the applicant was acquitted on 2 February 1997. The appeal was dismissed again on 5 February 1998. The court was adjourned until 9 March 1998, when it was upheld. The judge was convicted and sentenced to three years in prison. The conviction was quashed on 6 March 1998 and he was sentenced to two years in jail.

name: Wojciech Depa
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Kraków, Poland. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made on 26 May 1999. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The decision was taken at a public hearing at which the applicant and his lawyers were present. The case was decided to be heard by the Court of Appeal on 6 November 2011. On 13 July 1998, the applicant was indicted before the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). At a hearing held on 16 February 1999, the court prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court relied on the strong probability that the applicant had committed the offences and the advanced stage of the trial. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment in 2000. On 13 April 2000, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. On 24 August 2000 the K.K.R. gave a judgment, allowing the applicant to be released on bail. The applicant’s numerous requests for release were to no avail. His applications and appeals against the decisions to prolong his detention were dismissed at court sessions. The decisions were upheld on appeal by the Kraków Court of Appeal. The applicant was acquitted of the charge of attempted murder and his sentence was reduced to five years’ imprisonment. He then lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court of Poland (S.R.C.P.S). The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that his presence was neither obligatory nor necessary. He was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment in 2002 but this was later reduced to 5 years. On 3 June 2003 the Supreme Court partly allowed the cassation appeal, quashed the appeal court’s judgment and remitted the case. On 24 June 2004 the Krakow Court of Appeal gave a judgment. The court amended its judgment of 19 September 2002 but it upheld the applicant's sentence. The judgment became final. The applicant was sentenced to 20 years in prison. His sentence was suspended for 10 years and 10 months respectively. He was also sentenced to three years and three months in jail. The sentence was commuted to three and a half years. The case was dropped in 2005. The appeal was settled in 2007.

The case originated in an application (no. 62324/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Wojciech Depa (‘the applicant’), was born in 1975 and lives in Kraków, Poland. On 14 January 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 16 January 1998 a court decided to detain the applicant on remand. The applicant was indicted before the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on 13 July 1998. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21868/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application concerns the wounding of the first applicant, who was eleven years old at the time, and the death of the second and third applicants' sons, who were fourteen and 13 years old respectively. The applicants were represented by Mr F. Gümüş, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent) was represented by their Agent. On 10 September 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. As a result of the explosion, the first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other. The criminal investigation into the incident began on 23 April 1994. On 6 May 1997 the military prosecutor gave a decision that there was no need to initiate criminal proceedings on the ground that there had been no fault or negligence attributable to anyone except the children. The court ruled that the Ministry of the Interior had responsibility for compensation for the deaths of the three boys. The Ministry appealed. The Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity had responsibility. The court was bound by the amount requested by the applicant for pecuniary damage, but the amount determined by experts was significantly higher. The case was settled at the High Court of Justice of Turkey, which took up the case in September 2001. It was decided that the Court of Appeal was not competent to decide the issue. The appeal was settled in October 2001. The decision was made to award the applicant's claim in full. Explosion occurred in an area where rockets are launched. The origin of the grenade which caused the explosion is unknown. The rocket launcher in question is frequently used by members of the PKK terrorist organisation. The grenade might have been left by terrorists who attacked the barracks. The plaintiff should therefore be paid his claim in full, TRL 1,000,000,.0000 for pecuniary damage... although according to the expert reports, pecUniary damage in the present case could amount to TRL 19,237,229,0000. ... As regards non-pecuniary. damage, the plaintiff should be awarded TRL 100,000.000. On 19 March 1998 the Van Administrative Court awarded the applicant a certain amount of compensation. On 22 December 1998 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to determine which administrative entity, that is the Ministry of the Interior or Ministry of Defence, had responsibility for compensating the applicant. The Ministry appealed. 23 May 2002 the Supreme administrative court upheld the judgment. In respect of Ramazan Alican the court awarded the second applicant TRL 366,954,3670 in respect of pecuniary damage together with legal interest running from the date of the incident, 23 April 1994.

name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. The Court decided to give notice of the application on 16 October 2006 and examined the merits of it at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by a French national, Mr Jean-Claude Gacon (“the applicant’s” case). The case involved problems resulting from the delay in reimbursement of health care under the third-party payment system. Under this system, in order to be fully reimbursed by the social security scheme for the health care provided, Clinique du Parc had to wait for the invoice from the prosthesis supplier, which meant a delay of several days, if not weeks. The applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court, being charged in particular with having deceived thesocial security scheme and the relevant health insurance offices through fraudulent practices. In a judgment of 30 March 2001 the Lyons criminal Court held that the prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty. The applicant was sentenced to a suspended term of two years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay a fine of 120,000 euros (EUR) and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. He was also ordered, jointly and severally with his brother, to pay the sum of EUR 442,573.13 in compensation for all the damage found to have been sustained by the civil parties. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing in particular that the time available to the Principal Public Prosecutor for lodging an appeal under Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was incompatible with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

name: Kurt Nielsen
train_texts: The case originated in an application against Denmark lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 23 September 1996. The applicant complained that, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention, civil proceedings instituted by him had not been heard within a reasonable time. The Court declared the application admissible on 22 June 1999, and the case was dismissed. The case was decided by the Second Section of the Commission, which included ex officio Mr P. Lorenzen, the judge elected in respect of Denmark, and Mrs M. Tsatsa‑Nikolovska, the substitute for Mrs V. Stráznická who was unable to participate in the examination. The applicant claimed that the defendant companies should be held liable to pay, jointly and severally, a specified amount in compensation for permanent disablement and loss of working capacity. On 11 May 1988 the case was adjourned pending the outcome of the applicant’s request to the National Board of Industrial Injuries (Arbejdsskadestyrelsen, hereinafter called the NBI) The applicant was hereafter examined by two medical experts at the request of the N BI which also, on 2 February 1989, requested the Municipality of Skanderborg to provide certain information. The applicant appealed against the decision to adjourn the case to the High Court of Western Denmark which, however, upheld the decision on 1 October 1992. The case was heard by the City Court on 25 January 1995. The defendants appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Western Denmark. The High Court upheld the judgment and the judgment has become final. The applicant was accordingly examined again by medical experts following which the NBI submitted its opinion as to the applicant’s degree of disablement and working capacity on 30 June 1994. By judgment of 15 February 1995 the defendant companies were held liable to pay 950,803.60 DKK plus interest. The trial was later rescheduled to commence on 5 September 1996. It was a successful case and the applicant received a settlement of more than 1.2 million DKK.

name: Dariusz Kwiatek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20204/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. The applicant was charged with two burglaries committed as a recidivist offender and thus he was liable to a statutory maximum sentence of at least 8 years’ imprisonment. The Polish Government represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The investigation was terminated on 14 September 2000. On 15 September 2000 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court. The case file comprised at that time some 32 volumes. The prosecution had obtained voluminous evidence, including various expert reports. The first hearing was listed for 22 March 2001 but it was cancelled. On 14 May 2001 the applicant was ordered to be held in custody until 15 October 2001. On 13 November 2000 the Regional Court ordered that the case be joined to that of a certain M.K. The applicant was charged with 2 burglaries and was remanded in custody. In addition the trial court had not commenced an examination of the merits due to reasons that were beyond the court’s control. The applicant and some of his co-defendants were held in custody until 17 January 2002. The Regional Court noted that the continued detention of the applicant was necessary in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings in the case. That decision was upheld on appeal on 13 June 2001. On 30 October 2001 the Court of Appeal upheld the decision. On 22 November 2001 the trial began. However, the Regional Court was only able to hear two defendants. Two subsequent hearings had to be cancelled due to the absence of one of the defence counsel. The applicant and two other co-Defendants appealed against that decision. The case was heard at the Katowice Court of Criminal Procedure on 28 December 2001. The applicant was detained pending trial since 8 October 2001. He was charged with armed robbery, a serious offence for the commission of which an offender was liable to a minimum sentence of 3 years’ imprisonment. However, in reality the charges of armed robbery were brought against other defendants and the applicant had been, and still was, charged with 2 burglaries. The applicant appealed against that decision, but to no avail. On 20 May 2002 the Regional Court made another application to the Katowice Court of Appeal, requesting an extension of the applicant’s detention until 1 October 2002. It was granted on 29 May 2002. On 16 September 2002 the trial court made yet another application. Appeal for prolongation of applicant's detention until 15 June 2002. The trial court held hearings on the following dates: 31 January, 15 and 21 March, 11 and 25 April, 16 May 2002, 3 and 27 June, 31 July, 29 August and 12 September 2002. Four hearings were cancelled for the following reasons: the absence of some of the co-defendants and defence counsel. The applicant was convicted of one burglary and sentenced to 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment, which was nearly (less 12 days) the period he had spent in detention on remand. In sentencing the applicant the trial court took into account his two earlier convictions for similar offences. On 23 October 2003 the Katowice Court of Appeal upheld the Regional Court’s judgment in respect of the applicant.

The applicant appealed against that decision, but to no avail. The trial court made yet another application to the Court of. Appeal for an extension of the applicant’s detention until 1 October 2002. It held that the applicant was charged with armed robbery, a serious offence for the commission of which an offender was liable to a minimum sentence of 3 years’ imprisonment. In reality the charges of armed robbery were brought against other defendants and the applicant had been, and still was, charged with 2 burglaries. The trial court held hearings on the following dates: 31 January, 15 and 21 March, 11 and 25 April, 16 May 2002, 3 and 27 June, 31 July, 29 August and 12 September 2002. Four hearings were cancelled for the following reasons: the absence of some of the co-defendants and defence counsel. The applicant was convicted of one burglary and sentenced to 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment, which was nearly (less 12 days) the period he had spent in detention on remand. On 23 October 2003 the Katowice Court of Appeal upheld the Regional Court’s judgment in respect of the applicant.

name: Raja Arlewin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22302/10) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of effective access to court and that the State had failed to provide him with sufficient protection against allegations that violated his right to privacy. In the show, the applicant, who was unknown to the broader public, appeared in pictures and was mentioned by name. He was singled out as the central figure of organised crime within media and advertising and as being guilty of several counts of fraud and other economic offences. The applicant brought a private prosecution against X for gross defamation, claiming damages in the amount of 250,000 Swedish kronor (SEK; approximately 27,000 euros) X disputed the claim on the grounds, inter alia, that he was not the responsible editor of the show and that he enjoyed the freedom to communicate information. The Stockholm District Court dismissed the claim in so far as it was based on the Constitutional Law. It referred to the Supreme Court judgment in an almost identical case, NJA 2002 p. 314 (see paragraphs 28-31 below), and held that Chapters 1-9 of the Constitutional law were not relevant to the case. The Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) upheld the District Court’s decision. It held that the issue for it to determine was whether the general provisions in the Constitutional Law were applicable to the programme in question, that is, whether or not the broadcasting of the programme could be considered to have originated from Sweden. The court further held that it was possible for the applicant to bring claims before a British court. The applicant appealed, repeating what he had stated in his earlier submissions. He also submitted that Swedish courts were competent to examine the case under the Brussels I Regulation (see further paragraph 35 below) X contested the arguments and submitted that the company Viasat Broadcasting UK Ltd, whose seat was in the United Kingdom, was responsible for the programme service. The applicant asked that a question concerning the interpretation of the Brussels I Regulation be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union (ECJ) for a preliminary ruling. According to the applicant, the regulation entitled a person claiming non-contractual damages to bring actions where the harmful event occurred. The position hitherto taken by the Swedish courts ran contrary to Community law. On 21 September 2009 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s referral request and refused leave to appeal in the case. The applicant subsequently withdrew his remaining claims before the District Court since there was no practical prospect of success in a continued procedure. He was convicted of aggravated fraud and tax and bookkeeping offences and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

name: Mahfuz Türkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33086/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody and that there were no effective remedies in domestic law in respect of his grievances. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by Mr Mahfuz Türkan (“the applicant”), a Turkish national, on 9 July 2004. The applicant complained about the ill-treatment he had suffered at the hands of the police officers at the terminal building. The police officers denied the allegations made by the applicant and claimed that the bruising found on his body could have been caused by other persons with whom he had fought. The applicant filed a petition with the Eyüp Criminal Court seeking leave to become a third-party intervener in the criminal proceedings against the officers who had ill-treated him. The court then sent the applicant for a medical examination at the Eyufp Forensic Medicine Institute. On 7 August 1999 the Istanbul Criminal Court pressed charges against the three police officers for inflicting ill- treatment. The applicant was found unfit for work for five days in November 2000. A police discipline board decided not to impose any punishment on the three police officers. The applicant challenged the decision before the Eyüp Assize Court, arguing that the accused police officers’ acts should be characterised as torture within the meaning of Article 243 of the Criminal Code. The appeal was dismissed on 19 January 2004 and the judge upheld the decision of the criminal court. The case was heard at the High Court of Justice in Istanbul, where the judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal on the basis that the applicant had not been mistreated by the officers.

The case originated in an application (no. 20482/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court. The court found that the applicant described many of the paintings, and ordered an expert opinion on their origin and value. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 10 October 2007. The application was heard by the President of the Fourth Section. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The court considered that since the applicant had initiated the proceedings he should bear the costs of the opinion. The court calculated that by putting aside between ten and twenty percent of his income the applicant could have saved up PLN 5,000 since 1997. Some of the paintings had been in the possession of the other party and whose existence and ownership had been contested, as belonging to his parents. It had thus been impossible to assess those issues without the assistance of an expert. The judge ordered him to pay PLN5,000 (approximately 1,200 euros (EUR) The court found that the estate in question consisted only of a wardrobe and a grandfather clock. The applicant was awarded the latter and ordered to pay the other party PLN 2,225 and to reimburse them PLN 14,400 for the costs of the proceedings. The court found the applicant’s financial standing had not changed since 2004 when his application for exemption from the court fees for the expert opinion had been dismissed. The assessment of other evidence collected in the case leads to unequivocal conclusion that the marital property in question did not include any of the known and existing paintings of the disputed collection. It found that a total refusal to exempt the applicant from court fees would deprive him of the possibility to pursue his claim before the second-instance court. The applicant failed to pay the court fees for proceeding with his appeal. On 19 September 2005 the Wrocław District Court rejected the appeal. name: Jutta Huber
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 12794/87) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mrs Jutta Huber, a Swiss national, on 27 February 1987. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 5-3. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent her (Rule 30). The Government submitted its memorial to the Court on 31 October 1989. The applicant, for her part, decided not to submit a memorial but, on 13 February 1990, lodged her claims for just satisfaction. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Jacot-Guillarmod and Mr Levi for the Government, by Mr Schermers for the Commission and by Mr Schönenberger and Mr Mäder for the applicant. Following the hearing and at the Court’s request, the Delegate produced the copy of a document. The Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. Jutta Huber was questioned as a witness in connection with a criminal investigation concerning two persons. She admitted making a living from prostitution, but maintained that she knew Mr K. and Mr B. only by name and that she did not pass on to them any of her earnings. The District Attorney signed a detention order (Verhaftsverfügung) remanding the applicant in custody on grave suspicion of having given false evidence. She was released on 19 August 1983 and the criminal proceedings against her were closed on 12 October 1983. Mrs Huber claimed that she had no contact with the “Hell’s Angels’, which appeared unlikely to be true. The order referred to the danger of collusion and the possibility that evidence might be tampered with. District Attorney J. instituted proceedings before the Judge in Criminal Cases (Einzelrichter in Strafsachen) at the Zürich District Court (Bezirksgericht) The trial took place on 10 January 1985, after the indictment had been accepted. Mrs Huber was acquitted on the ground that she had never been validly summoned to appear as a witness (vorgeladen zur Zeugeneinvernahme), which made her testimony unlawful and inadmissible. On appeal, the Court of Appeal (Obergericht) of the Canton of Züich fined the applicant 4,000 Swiss francs for attempting to give false evidence. The court inferred from this evidence that the applicant in fact knew Mr K. and Mr B. in accordance with the system of mutual assistance in criminal matters. On the question of the issue raised under Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the Convention, the appeal court said (translation): “Finally, ... the appellant’s lawyer's objection that, on her arrest, the accused was not brought before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power is unfounded’” The Federal Court dismissed the appeal by a judgment of 24 November 1986, which was served on 18 December. The Zürich District Attorney is an ‘officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’ within the meaning of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the Convention. The status and powers of District Attorneys were laid down in the Courts Act of 13 June 1976 (Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz, “GVG”) Both Ordinary and Special District Att attorneys are subordinate to the Principal Public Prosecutor who in turn comes under the authority of the Department of Justice and the Government (Regierungsrat) of Canton of Züich. The functions of District Attorney carry out three different functions. The District Attorney is the prosecuting authority before the “Judge in Criminal Cases’ and before the District Courts in cases concerning petty offences and misdemeanours. For the higher cantonal courts (the Court of Appeal and the Assize Court - section 72 GVG), this function is performed by the Principal Public Prosecutor. The combination of the functions of investigation and prosecution has given rise to case-law - at cantonal and federal level - which has recently been confirmed. The Zürich case- law was confirmed in a judgment of 13 June 1988 (Ante Djukic geg geg) and can be found at: http://www.zurich.org/case-law. The decision to arrest was taken by an official who satisfied the requirements of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The officer who ordered the arrest is the same as the officer who drew up the indictment. The status of this officer at the time of and in relation to the decision to arrested remains the same, and the arrest, initially regarded as being lawful, cannot subsequently become unlawful on this sole ground. It is only natural that the District Attorney, as the investigating authority, should draw up an indictment after the investigation has been completed if he considers that he possesses sufficient evidence of the accused’s guilt. The possibility in question was held not to be decisive by the European Court in its judgment in the Schiesser case. The mere fact that this possibility exists is not, however, decisive in this respect. In 1989, 108 District Attorneys in the Canton of Zürich dealt with 17,647 investigations, of which 20.3% resulted in an indictment, 33.8% in the case being discontinued and 42.2% in a punishment order. The number of cases in which the District Attorney personally conducted the prosecution in court does not appear in the statistics, but according to the Government it is very low. The Government confirmed the submissions put forward in their memorial. In that document they had asked the Court to hold “that Switzerland [had] not violated the ... Convention ... on account of the circumstances which gave rise to Mrs Jutta Huber’s application’. The Government has confirmed that the submissions made in the memorial were correct. The text of the Commission's opinion and of the three separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The report is available on the Government's website at: http://www.switzerland.org.uk/government/government-commission-memorandum.html.

In the arrest and seizure report it was also noted that the applicant had false identity papers and, inter alia, a Kalashnikov rifle, bullets, night-vision binoculars and a walkie-talkie in his bag. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 April 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was charged under the former Criminal Code with membership of an illegal organisation and attempting to undermine the constitutional order. He claimed to have been beaten, given electric shocks, hung by his arms, hosed with cold water, had his genitals and fingers squeezed, been made to lie on an icy surface and been raped by one police officer with a hose. The applicant was remanded in custody and his lawyers lodged an official complaint with the Turkish authorities. He was sentenced to three years in prison in 1999 after being released on bail and sentenced to two years' probation in 2000. He is still serving his sentence and his trial is expected to last until the end of the year. The applicant filed a. complaint with the Samsun public prosecutor’s office, claiming that the applicant had been subjected to various forms of ill-treatment while being held at Samsun police. headquarters between 5 and 6 October 1999. In 2001 he began to suffer from a mental disorder. According to a report dated 19 April 2002 issued by the Medical Board of the Ankara Numune Hospital, the applicant presented psychotic symptoms. The experts could not determine whether these symptoms were due to the hunger strike (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) or to schizophrenia. The medical expert concluded that it was not possible to determine the exact cause of the injuries noted in the medical reports. The applicant was brought before the Ankara Criminal Court in order to give evidence, acting on letters rogatory. He was not able to make any statement, as he appeared to be suffering from a mental disorder. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 16 April 2003, holding that the police officer should have been charged with torture under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The Samsun Criminal Court declined jurisdiction and transferred the case to the Samsun Assize Court. In its decision the court held that while the forensic medical reports established that the applicant had been ill‑treated between 5 and 6 October 1999, the applicant could not formally identify the accused as responsible. The applicant’s lawyer applied to the Samsun Assize Court on 11 January 2010 to annul its previous decision (eski hale getirme) to serve its judgment on the applicant. In her application, the applicant's lawyer also maintained that since the applicant suffered from Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, the rogatory court should have assigned him a lawyer. According to information obtained by the Registry from the website of the Court of Cassation, on 4 May 2012 the higher court dismissed the applicant”s appeal. On 19 January 2010 the Sam Sunn Assize court held that the applicant could not lodge an appeal against the judgment of 26 September 2007 as he had not joined the proceedings as a civil party.

name: Mehmet Gürova
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 22088/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation in May 2000. He retracted his police statement but did not mention any allegations of ill-treatment or duress. On 16 February 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant declared that he had been subjected to ‘psychological torture’ in police custody. Ankara State Security Court convicted the applicant of being a member of an illegal organisation. The Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's conviction on 12 November 2002. The applicant was released from prison on 10 June 2006. He was convicted of the assassination of a number of prominent journalists and academics in Turkey. According to the prosecutor, the organisation's aim was to establish a religious regime in Turkey similar to that in Iran. The court concluded that the applicant had retracted his police custody statement in order to avoid conviction. It sentenced him to twelve years and six months' imprisonment under Article 168 of the Criminal Code. The trial court also examined the applicant’s allegation of psychological pressure in police custody. It concluded that there were no marks of injury on his body.

name: Yüksel İğdeli
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his detention in police custody lasted seven days without being brought before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. He also complained that Turkish Law does not afford any effective remedy by which the lawfulness of his detention could be decided speedily. The judge elected in respect of Turkey withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) The Government appointed Mr F. Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge (Rule 29) On 30 May 2000 the Chamber retained the applicant's complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25): this case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the PKK. He was detained in police custody until 12 June 1995. On the same day, the applicant was brought before the İstanbul State Security Court which ordered his detention on remand. The charges were brought under Article 168 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713. The applicant was sentenced to three years' imprisonment in accordance with Article 168 §§ 2 and 2918 of the Traffic Act in 1998. He has since been released pending trial. However, he has been released from prison pending trial again on 9 August 1996.

In 1992 and 1993 the prosecutor conducted an investigation in connection with the applicants’ allegedly illegal business activities. In July 1994 the applicants were indicted before the Katowice Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki). The applicants were sentenced to suspended prison terms. The applicants appealed. They relied on the 2004 Act on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 14 December 2004 the Katowice Court of Appeal dismissed the complaints. The court examined the course of the impugned proceedings only as regards the period between 2002 and 2004 when the case had been pending before the District Court. It established that the proceedings had been conducted diligently. It further held that the trial courts could not be held responsible for delays caused by the absence of witnesses or illness of the parties.

name: Romuald Kozłowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46601/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant was a retired police officer who had formerly been employed in the Civil Militia (Milicja Obywatelska) In 1974 the applicant had been dismissed from service for a disciplinary offence. He was rehired by the Police in 1991 and retired in 1994. The applicant sought compensation, which comprised damages for lost earnings from 1974 to 1990, for lost Earnings and benefits from 1990 to 1991, and for alleged moral suffering due to the loss of employment. The case was heard at the Poznań Regional Court. The applicant made a complaint about the unreasonable length of proceedings for compensation for lost earnings and benefits from 1990 to 1991 under the Act of 17 June 2004. The Supreme Court discontinued the proceedings under the 2004 Act on the ground that the civil proceedings which were the subject of the complaint had meanwhile terminated. A cassation appeal in the case was inadmissible in law. The court observed that the main purpose of the complaints was to highlight the length of the proceedings. The hearing was held on 11 May 2006 and the respondent was ordered to pay the applicant a certain amount of compensation. The Supreme Court noted that the applicant had admittedly lodged his complaint under the 2004 Act while the civil proceedings in question were still pending. In circumstances where the proceedings which were the subject of the complaint had already terminated it was no longer necessary for the court to examine the complaint. proceedings was to accelerate the proceedings before a trial court. The appellate hearing, which turned out to be final, had been scheduled prior to the applicant's complaint. The Court found that the Labour Court had not taken into account any time that could have been used for rest periods. It also stated that the overtime calculation should be based on weekly working hours rather than the monthly working time used in the expert report. On 11 September 2007 the expert revised the findings as ordered and concluded that the applicants were likely to have had a minimum of three hours for rest during a twenty-four-hour shift. The expert therefore recalculated their entitlement to overtime on the basis of twenty-one hours of actual work and compared it with the legal working week of forty‑five hours. On 26 May 2008 the İzmir Labour Court awarded the applicants compensation. The applicants' daily working time was calculated as fourteen hours. The Court of Cassation’s Civil Division said that a person can only work for 14 hours a day. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. On 18 March 2010 the Court ofCassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court's decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. As a result of that interpretation, some of the applicants' claims were dismissed entirely, while the others were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 54640/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant had requested recognition of a foreign divorce decree. The Federal Ministry of Justice refused to grant this request. The applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. The case was referred to the Constitutional Court for review. The Constitutional Court ruled that the decree was in conformity with the constitution. The judge said that the application was in breach of Article 6 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was dismissed on appeal and the case was settled on a writ of rights for the applicant’s wife and her children. The proceedings in these cases were joined to proceedings in the applicant's case. The recognition of foreign divorce decrees was closely linked to the question whether they could be enforced in Austria. proceedings at issue were concerned with the questions whether recognition was compatible with Austrian ordre public. Even assuming that Article 6 applied, the Constitutional Court held that the Administrative Court’s scope of review was sufficient, since proceedings concerning the recognition ofForeign Divorce decrees involved mainly questions of law. The decision was served on the applicant on 29 October 2001. On 5 October 2001 having resumed its proceedings, the Administrative court dismissed the applicant's complaint. The application was dismissed on 20 October 2001, and the case dismissed on 28 October 2001 after the applicant had been served with the decision.

name: Havva Kaba
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1236/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Three Turkish nationals, Ms Havva Kaba, Miss Edanur Kaba and Miss Elif Kaba (‘the applicants’), were represented by Mr A. Tizik, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent’) was represented by their Agent. On 15 September 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the Application at the same time. In January 2004 the applicants again requested legal aid to pay the court fees. The Military Supreme Administrative Court refused to grant the applicants legal aid, once again without giving reasons. The court also decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicants had not paid the necessary court fees in 2004. This decision was served on the applicants on 4 June 2004. The application was dismissed after the court ruled that as the decision dated 21 January 2004 was not a final decision on the merits of the case, a rectification or a clarification request was not possible under domestic law. The case was settled out of court in May 2004, and the case was dismissed as a result of the court's decision on 12 May 2004.

On 12 May 2004 the court examined both requests and decided that, as the decision was not a final decision on the merits of the case, it was not possible under domestic law to rectify or clarify the decision.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50424/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 11 June 2002 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The applicants are a married couple. The first applicant was born in 1945 and the second in 1940. They both live in Ożarów, Poland. The application was filed by Mrs Maria Kusiak and Mr Marian Kusiak. The Polish Government was represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki and Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. The applicants requested that the proceedings be resumed. On 5 January 1996 the court refused to resume the proceedings. On 18 June 1996, on the applicants' appeal, the Warsaw Regional Court amended the decision. On 7 February 2000 the court held a further hearing. The applicants appealed on 8 June 2001. On 11 December 2001 the court dismissed their appeal. The case is still stayed and, therefore, pending. The Minister of Justice admitted that there was a certain delay in the proceedings, and that two courts had supervised the conduct of the proceedings and had made reports on their progress. The court gave a decision and ordered a certain M.G. to join the proceedings on 19 November 1999.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24254/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant's appeal against the detention order, his subsequent appeals against decisions prolonging his detention and all his numerous applications for release were all unsuccessful. The Lublin Regional Prosecutor decided to amend the charges against the applicant on 13 November 2001. He was suspected of several counts of extortion committed while acting in an organised criminal gang. The court relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. The applicant was charged with crimes for which he was liable to a sentence of imprisonment exceeding eight years, and that the circumstances of the case indicated that there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proceedings. The Lublin Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 11 May 2004. It observed that the fact that the trial had not been terminated could not be attributed to the authorities, given the volume of evidence. The applicant was released from detention under police supervision on 30 April 2004. The court relied on the fact that almost all witnesses had been heard and thus the applicant ceased to pose a threat to the proper conduct of the proceedings. The applicant appealed on 20 January 2006. According to the applicant the appellate court remitted the case for re-examination. However, he did not submit the date or the copy of the relevant judgment. It appears that the judgment has become final and the applicant is presently serving a prison sentence imposed by the judgment of the Płońsk District Court of 3 September 2004 (case file no. II K 282/03).
