train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In a decision of 24 October 2000 the Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1). The Court ruled in favour of the applicants in December 2001. The court ruled that the first applicant's wife had wrongfully removed the child within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The court dismissed the mother's claim that the child's return would entail a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. It considered that the second applicant's return could not be hindered by the fact that the mother was her main person of reference and that returning could cause a massive trauma affecting her development. Otherwise, mothers of small. children could easily circumvent the aim of the 1980 Hague. Convention. 26 September 2002 the Court declared the applications admissible. The case was decided by the Graz District Civil Court (Bezirksgericht für Zivilrechtssachen) The court ruled that the mother of the second applicant could be expected to return to the United States. The first applicant had started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan) by a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. The Graz District Civil Court ordered the enforcement of the return order under section 19 (1) of the Non-Contentious Proceedings Act (Ausserstreitgesetz) The mother had given an interview to a local newspaper according to which she frequently changed her whereabouts and was determined not to let the child be taken away from her. The judge ruled that it was necessary to order coercive measures as there were indications that she was obstructing the child's return. The case began in December 1995 when the mother of the second applicant applied for sole custody of her daughter. The mother appealed against the decision of 27 February 1996 and the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. On 29 May 1996 the United States District Court, Eastern District of Michigan, issued an arrest warrant against the mother on suspicion of international parental kidnapping. On 18 June 1996 the first applicant made a further application for enforcement of the return order. The Graz District Civil Court transferred jurisdiction to the Leibnitz District Court in the judicial district of which the applicant had purportedly established her residence. The case was referred back to the Graz Regional Civil Court on 29 August 1996. Austrian Supreme Court dismissed an appeal by the first applicant and set aside the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention made clear that the child's well-being took priority over the Convention's general aim of preventing child abduction. Reasons of general deterrence or, in other words, the aim of showing that child abduction was not worthwhile could not justify exposing a child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. The court had to take the interests of the child’sWell-being into account, despite the fact that the return order was final, if the relevant situation had changed in the meantime. The case was referred back to the Graz District Civil Court. The Supreme Court emphasised that the particularity of the case lay in the fact that, in the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm. The child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. The question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The second applicant's mother was awarded sole custody of the second applicant by the Graz District Civil Court. Article 16 of the Hague Convention prohibited the State to which the child has been abducted from taking a decision on custody while proceedings for the child's return were pending. The decision not to enforce the return order had become final. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998. The case was settled at the Supreme Court of Austria in 1997. The second applicant was awarded full custody of her mother on 29 December 1997 and the case was dismissed. The appeal was dismissed on 9 September 1997 on the ground that it did not raise any important legal issues.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. The Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. The first applicant and the second applicant were born in 1953 and 1994 respectively. Under the law of the State of Michigan the parents had joint custody of their daughter. The first applicant's wife, without obtaining his consent, left the United States with their second applicant and took her to Austria. The court found that the first applicant had wrongfully removed the child within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The mother's claim that the child's return would entail a grave risk of physical or psychological harm was dismissed by the court. The Court declared the applications admissible on 26 September 2002 and ordered the child to be returned to her parents. The second applicant's mother was ordered to return to the U.S. in December 1995. On 19 January 1996 the Graz Regional Civil Court dismissed an appeal by the mother. On 27 February 1996 the Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal. In May 1996 the first applicant filed an application for enforcement of the return order. The first applicant had started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan). By a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Further, it awarded the first. applicant sole custody of the second applicant and ordered that the second. applicant should reside with the first Applicant in the event of her. return. The second applicant's mother appealed against. the order of 8 May. 1996. A search carried out in the house, necessitating the use of force against the second applicant.'s mother and the forceful opening of several doors, remained unsuccessful. On 29 August 1996 the Graz Regional Civil Court granted an appeal by the first applicant against the transfer of jurisdiction. The court found that, in the enforcement proceedings, the child's well-being had to be taken into account in so far as a change in the situation had occurred since the issue of the return order and the taking of coercive measures. Under Article 13 of the Hague Convention, this question was not to be examined by the court of its own motion. The United States Department of State and the Austrian Ministry of Justice acting as their respective States' Central Authorities under the Hague Convention exchanged numerous letters between May and December 1996. U.S. repeatedly requested information as to which steps had been taken to locate the second applicant and to enforce the return order of 20 December 1995. The Supreme Court dismissed an appeal by the first applicant and set aside the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. It noted in particular that the notion of the child's well-being was central to the entire proceedings. The court acknowledged that particularly difficult problems arose in cases in which the abductor had created the situation. The child had been living solely with her mother for more than a year. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. The Supreme Court emphasised that the particularity of the case lay in the fact that, in the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm (as a result of the alleged sexual behaviour of the first applicant) The case was referred back to the Graz District Civil Court. The question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The court found that there had been a change in the relevant circumstances, in that the second applicant had lost all contact with the first applicant while her ties with her mother and her maternal grandparents had become ever closer. As this relationship was indispensable for her well-being, the application for enforcement of the return order had to be dismissed. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998. The second applicant's mother was awarded sole custody of theSecond applicant by the Graz District Civil Court on 29 December 1997. It noted that Article 16 of the Hague Convention, which prohibited the State to which the child has been abducted from taking a decision on custody while proceedings for the child's return were pending, no longer applied.

The case originated in two applications (nos. 36812/97 and 40104/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In a decision of 24 October 2000 the Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. The first applicant married an Austrian citizen in April 1994. The marriage was concluded in the United States of America. On 11 September 1994 their daughter, the second applicant, was born. Under the law of the State of Michigan the parents had joint custody. On 30 October 1995 the first applicant's wife, without obtaining his consent, left the U.S. and took her to Austria. The first applicant, relying on the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (“the Hague Convention’), requested the Austrian courts to order the second Applicant's return. On 20 December 1995 the Graz District Civil Court, after having heard evidence from the first. applicant and his wife and the oral statement of an expert in child psychology, Dr. K., ordered that the second. applicant be returned. Graz Regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für Zivilrechtssachen) dismissed an appeal by the second applicant's mother. The first applicant had started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan) by a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Graz District Civil Court ordered the enforcement of the return order under section 19 (1) of the Non-Contentious Proceedings Act (Ausserstreitgesetz) on 8 May 1996. In the early hours of 10 May 1996, an attempt to enforce the return Order was made in accordance with the terms set out in Article 13 (b) of The Hague Convention. The second applicant's mother applied for sole custody of her daughter in 1996. A search was carried out in the house, necessitating the use of force against the mother. The Graz District Civil Court transferred jurisdiction to the Leibnitz District Court, in the judicial district of which the second applicant had purportedly established her residence. On the mother's appeal, the Graz Regional Civil Court granted an appeal by the first applicant against the transfer of jurisdiction and quashed the order of 8 May 1996 and referred the case back to it. The first applicant made a further application for enforcement of the return order on 18 June 1996. The court ordered the District Court to examine whether the situation had changed since the return Order of 20 December 1995. The United States Department of State repeatedly requested information as to which steps had been taken to locate the second applicant and to enforce the return order of 20 December 1995. The Austrian Ministry of Justice replied that the first applicant was represented by counsel in the Austrian proceedings and that it was up to him to take all necessary steps to obtain the enforcement of the return orders. It also pointed out that there were only rather limited possibilities to locate a child who had disappeared after a return order had been made. On 15 October 1996 the Supreme Court dismissed an appeal by the first. applicant and set aside the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. It noted in particular that the notion of the child's well-being was central to the entire proceedings. The case was referred back to the Graz District Civil Court. The first applicant had had regular contact with her until 30 October 1995, the date of her abduction. Thereafter they had had no contact at all. Since the return order had been made, a year and four months had elapsed and the first applicant was a complete stranger to the second applicant. Given that a young child needed a stable relationship with the main person of reference at least until the age of six, her removal would expose her to serious psychological harm. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The second applicant's return to the United States would cause her irreparable harm. The second applicant's mother was awarded sole custody of the second applicant by the Graz District Civil Court on 29 December 1997. Article 16 of the Hague Convention, which prohibited the State to which the child has been abducted from taking a decision on custody while proceedings for the child's return were pending, no longer applied, as the decision not to enforce the return order had become final. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998. The court noted the first applicant's statement of 28 April 1997 and his offer within the meaning of the “safe harbour” case-law but considered that this offer did not guarantee that theSecond applicant's relationship with her main person of reference would be preserved in the long run.

name: Jakub Paluch
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of Article 3 on account of the imposition on him of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime. He also complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the conventions that the proceedings before the penitentiary commission had been unfair and that no effective remedy was available against its decisions. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Ms J. Chrzanowska of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 July 2014. The applicant's cell was constantly monitored via closed-circuit television. The applicant was subjected to a body search every time he left and entered the cell. He had to strip naked in front of prison officers and was required to bend over to allow his anus to be examined. Whenever he was outside his cell, including at court hearings, the applicant had to wear joined shackles (kajdanki zespolone) on his hands and feet. The shackles consisted of handcuffs and fetters joined together with chains. On 14 July 2012 the Lublin Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission lifted the dangerous detainee regime in respect of the applicant.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland in 1997. The applicant alleged he had not been arrested on a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence and that he did not have an enforceable right to compensation in respect of these matters. German citizen Kurt Konig was murdered on 21 November 1985. The Provisional IRA claimed responsibility for his death. The Government submitted that Special Branch received intelligence that the applicant and three other persons were involved in the murder. The intelligence derived from four informants who had proved reliable in the past and had provided information leading to seizures of explosives or firearms and to prosecutions. The information given by these four informants was consistent, in that all gave the same names as being involved. None of the informants had a criminal record. The applicant was taken to Castlereagh and arrested. He was awarded damages of 2,500 pounds sterling (GBP) for an incident in Guildhall Square on 16 March 1993. The applicant was arrested on 28 December 1985 and spent six days and 13 hours in custody. He was interviewed on thirty-four occasions. The applicant was released without charge on 3 January 1986 at 9 p.m., after six days. He instituted a civil action for damages before the High Court in Northern Ireland in respect of, inter alia, assault, seizure of documents, false imprisonment and unlawful arrest. The trial judge found that the applicant’s counsel concentrated on the issues of assault and confiscation of documents. He did however raise the argument, in the context of the lawfulness of the arrest, that Detective Constable S. did not have sufficient grounds for suspicion to justify the arrest. 1990 Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. He accepted that both Mr Justice Carswell and the Lord Chief Justice had previously rejected the same submission in similar cases. The judge said that the detective constable had a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in the murder of Kurt Konig and that this suspicion was reasonably based on information given to him by a superior officers. The applicant gave notice of appeal to the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland concerning the claim of unlawful arrest and false imprisonment. On 6 May 1994 the appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer. “Notwithstanding his concern that more detail of the briefing had not been given, the learned trial judge was able to conclude: ‘(1) that the arresting officer ... did have a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in a terrorist murder and it was implicit that that suspicion was genuinely held by him.’ These were factual findings and clearly contained in our view all the essential proofs that the respondent was required to adduce to constitute lawful arrest under section 12(1)(b) of the Act.” An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, with which the other judges agreed, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. He said the arresting officer must have equipped himself with sufficient information so that he had reasonable cause to suspect before exercising the power of arrest. The information need not be based on his own observations, as he is entitled to form a suspicion based on what he has been told. His reasonable suspicion may bebased on information which has been given to him anonymously, or it may be based upon information which turns out later to be wrong. “A mere request to arrest without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion” “How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a request to arrested someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s report,” the court said. “This is not always the case, and it is accepted, and rightly accepted, that a. mere request is not enough.”

(1) In order to have a reasonable suspicion the constable need not have evidence amounting to a prima facie case. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrested. Such information may come from other officers ... train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that wording employed by a number of domestic courts had breached his right to the presumption of innocence. The case originated in an application (no. 50172/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged on 7 December 2006. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was heard by the President of the Second Section on 27 May 2009. The decision was returned to the Court on 2 June 2009. The applicant's contract of employment was terminated by the bank on 24 August 1998. The applicant appealed against the Assize Court decision, arguing that if the proceedings had not been suspended his innocence would have been proved. On 8 June 2006 the Court of Cassation decided that the decision was not appealable, because it was not a decision containing a definitive conclusion. The applicant and his two colleagues brought a case against the bank before the Trabzon Labour Court, claiming compensation for their dismissal. The applicant appealed against the decision, submitting that the criminal proceedings against him had been suspended by the Istanbul Assize Court. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision in so far as it concerned the applicable rate of interest. The bank then brought proceedings to enforce the decision with a view to recovering the money. On 19 July 2005, the Labour Court decided, in line with the court's decision, that a lower rate ofInterest should apply. An appeal lodged against this decision by the applicant was rejected by the Court ofCassation on 26 September 2005. On 26 May 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the Labour Court decision of 21 September 2004. It held that the Istanbul Assize Court decision had suspended the proceedings and not convicted the applicant. The Labour Court had erred in rejecting the applicant's claim without hearing any of the witnesses proposed by him or obtaining expert reports. The Trabzon Labour Court repeated its decision on 13 October 2005. On 24 May 2006 an appeal lodged by the applicant against the Labour court decision was rejected. This decision was communicated to the applicant on 1 August 2006. The applicant appealed against the decision of 26 May 2003. The appeal was rejected on 24 May 2005.

name: Aziz Aydın Arslan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28353/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 19 March 2007. The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Istanbul. In 1988 the applicant was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank. In 1991 he was appointed to the post of deputy director in charge of credit cards. Criminal proceedings were brought against the director of the Topkapı branch of the Bank and three other persons for having committed a fraud. The applicant and the Bank intervened in these proceedings as a third party. On 9 July 1999 the Bakırköy Assize Court in Istanbul convicted the director and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment for having abused his duty. On 29 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the above judgment. On 31 December 2004 the BakTurkish Assize court terminated the criminal proceedings against thedirector since they were time-barred. The director was sentenced to a year in prison but the other accused were acquitted.

name: Edward Szuluk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36936/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life. On 7 February 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theapplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention). The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Government, with the decision to be appealed to the European Court of Justice. The applicant was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded by the prison medical officer as criticism and that this might inhibit his relationship with his external medical specialist. He applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. On 18 September 2002 the governor of the prison in which the applicant was being detained agreed to the applicant’s request. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings leading to his conviction he had not been afforded a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal as required by Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 July 2013. The High Court gave a judgment of 5 in favour of the applicant. The Norwegian Government was represented by Mr M. Emberland of the Attorney General’s Office (Civil Matters) as their agent, assisted by Mr H. Kolderup, Attorney. The City Court did not find credible the applicant's explanation that he and Ms A had kissed and to a little extent touched one another voluntarily. In February 2009, the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), hearing the applicant’s appeal with a jury, convicted him on the attempted rape charge and sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. It ordered him to pay 60,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK) (approximately 7,500 euros at that time) in compensation to Ms A for non-pecuniary damage. The High Court described in detail how the applicant, after he had called Mr B (who could not come straight away), had attempted to obtain sexual contact with Ms A by force. After a while the situation involved into a fight between them, in which she had been physically inferior and had to come to terms with the situation. Counsel for the defence requested that J be disqualified from taking part in the further proceedings on grounds of lack of impartiality. The High Court observed that “the jury member had formed a picture [bilde] of the victim from many years ago where she at the time had experienced her as a quiet and calm person”. It pointed out that a member might be disqualified if the person in question had particular reasons for identifying himself or herself with the victim or if there were any other circumstances to the effect that he or she had a prejudging attitude because of prior knowledge. However, that was not the situation in the present case. Juror J took part in the entire trial before the High Court, including the jury’s deliberations and vote on the charge of attempted rape. The High Court did not find that such a contact was capable of influencing, in one way or another, the assessment in the criminal case. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett) arguing that her participation had been incompatible with section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act and Article 6 of the Convention. By a judgment of 26 June 2009 the Supreme court, by three votes to two, rejected the applicant’‘s appeal.’ The majority did not consider that the juror in question had formed a picture of the victim. J’s information about Ms A had emerged after she had given evidence to the High Court for one hour. At that point, the jury, including J, had a good opportunity to form an independent and updated picture of the victim as a person. That defence counsel and the assistant advocate had requested that J withdraw could not be decisive. The minority considered that the case concerned a serious and stigmatising accusation against the defendant. There was a lot at stake for the victim, as she could easily perceive a verdict acquitting the defendant to mean that the jury believed that she had made an unfounded and serious accusation. The majority shared the majority’S view that previous contacts between the victim and J could not, of their own, disqualify the latter. J said she had experienced the victim as a ‘quiet and calm person’ The timing of J’s affirmation could easily have given the impression that J expressed a positive assessment of the victim. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, “the standpoint of the accused [was] important but not decisive’ Under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act, both counsel for the defence and the assistant advocate had demanded that J recuse herself. In this case the “fear” of lack of impartiality by the applicant had been ‘objectively justified’ (see Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy, 7 August 1996, § 58, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑III).

name: Erwin Baischer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32381/96) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him relating to an administrative offence no oral hearing has been held. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 16 January 2001 the Court declared the application admissible and the application reallocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The applicant did not request a hearing, nor did he expressly waive this right. He complained that the District Administrative Authority had incorrectly applied the law and failed to sufficiently assess the evidence before it. An oral hearing would have been necessary because his appeal was not limited to points of law. In such a hearing the Independent Administrative Panel could have properly assessed this evidence, which had already been obtained at first instance, as well as fresh evidence. No oral hearing was held. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The case was then transferred to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof)

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29840/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Arzu Becerik, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The application was filed by Mr Hasan Erkan, a Turkish national, on 15 August 2003. He worked as a teacher and retired on 3 September 1973. The applicant filed an action before the Ankara Administrative Court and asked for the days he worked in 1992 to be taken into account when calculating the total period of his service. The applicant appealed on 5 May 1995 but did not pay the necessary appeal fees until 3 August 1995. In the opinion of the Council of State, the applicant should have been considered as a civil servant on the day of the appointment and not on theDay of his actually taking up his duties. The court ruled that the applicant did not have the right to advance to a higher grade. This decision was served on the applicant on 17 February 2003. The application was dismissed and the applicant was ordered to pay the court fees.

name: Artur Warsiński
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Artur Warsiński, is a Polish national who was born in 1976 and lives in Bytów. He was charged with drug trafficking and detained on remand from 6 April 2002 to 21 May 2004. On 28 May 2003 the Słupsk Regional Court found the applicant guilty of drug trafficking. On 30 December 2003 the Gdańsk Court of Appeal amended the judgment and sentenced the applicant to two years and four months' imprisonment. On 29 November 2006 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate to the Government the complaint. The applicant submitted a photocopy of an envelope sent to him on 24 October 2002 by the Court. It bears a stamp “censored on”, a handwritten date “31 October 2002’ and an illegible signature. The applicant also produced a photocopic of an enveloped sent by Amnesty International on 22 November 2002. It also appears that both envelopes had been cut open and resealed with adhesive tape. On 12 June 2003 the applicant sent a letter to the Słupsk Regional Court in which he complained about censorship of his correspondence. On 30 June 2003 he received a letter from the President of the S Polish Regional Court informing him that according to the information obtained from the Criminal Department, his correspondence had not been censored.

name: Hildegard Klaas
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the German Government (‘the Government’) on 10 August 1992 and by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15473/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 11 July 1989 by two German citizens. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) and Mr Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 March 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig for the Government, by Mr Frowein for the Commission and by Mr Stüben for the applicants, as well as replies to its questions and by two of its members individually. The Registrar consulted the applicants’ lawyer, the Agent of the Government and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). The Registrar received, on 7 December 1992, the Government’s memorial and, on 19 January 1993, the applicants' observations. The first applicant underwent two medical examinations. She was charged with obstructing a public officer in the execution of his duties contrary to Article 113 of the German Criminal Code (Strafgesetzbuch) and of driving. The blood test showed the level of alcohol in her blood to be 0.82 per ml (milligrammes per millilitre). She was subsequently released. The precise course of the events is disputed by the applicants (see paragraph 7 below) and the police officers (see paragraphs 9 and 10 below) The application was dismissed and the case against the applicant was dismissed. The appeal was rejected and the appeal was denied. Police Constable Bolte stated in his report that after Mrs Klaas had been informed that she had to undergo a blood test, she had attempted to escape into the darkness of the back-yard. Police Constable Wildschut took her left arm and twisted it behind her back. With great difficulty the officers managed to control the applicant, who was putting up a fight. They handcuffed her in order to avoid further criminal offences being committed, in particular injury to the person. On 22 April 1986 the criminal proceedings against the first applicant were discontinued by the public prosecutor’s office (Staatsanwaltschaft) at the Detmold Regional Court. First applicant laid an information against the police officers concerned. She alleged that they had assaulted her contrary to Articles 223 and 230 of the Criminal Code. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and to the Federal Constitutional Court were dismissed. On 18 September 1986, the Head of the Detmold District Administration, acting as the Police Department authority (Kreispolizeibehörde), dismissed her complaint. In the decision, it was stated in particular that after she had been informed that she would have to give a blood sample, the mildest means of achieving the objective should have been employed. The first applicant instituted civil proceedings in April 1987 against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia and the police officers concerned. She claimed compensation for the injuries sustained on 28 January 1986. On 10 July 1987 the Detmold Regional Court, in a partial judgment, dismissed her complaint against the police officer on the ground that an official acting in the exercise of his duties does not incur personal liability. The judge ruled that the use of force had been justified and was not disproportionate to the aim pursued, namely the taking of a blood test. The first applicant was awarded £2,500 for her injuries and £1,800 for her legal fees. Police Constable Wildschut confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte. He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. She had resisted arrest and had been lashing out when he had twisted her arm behind her back, but he assumed she had not intended to assault either him or his colleague. Monika was arrested with her mother and the police officers in their back-yard. She said she had managed to see through the plain glass door panel that one of the police officer had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. The Chamber is admittedly convinced that the plaintiff incurred the injuries complained of when she was arrested by the two police officers. It does not follow, however, that the defendant Land is liable in damages. The plaintiff was under suspicion of driving under the influence of alcohol in road traffic. Police officers found that the plaintiff’s breath smelt of alcohol. The arrest does not appear to be disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring that the further investigations could be carried out. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff's daughter, conflicts. Witness Klaas claims to have seen one of the police officers repeatedly knocking the plaintiff’s head against the wall by the door, the two police officers deny this. None of these three witnesses can be regarded as not having an interest in these proceedings. The two officers could certainly expect disciplinary proceedings and a resumption of the criminal investigation if these proved to be the facts. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the walls; the shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled. The Commission declared the applicants’ complaints admissible. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the various separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government in their memorial of 12 November 1992 invited the Court to find “that the applicants did not suffer violations of their rights under Article 3 or Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention’”. The Court ruled in favour of the first applicant by a majority of 14 votes to one. The second applicant, Monika Klaas, was found to have suffered no violation of her right to respect for her private life.

He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. The second applicant, Monika, gave evidence. She stated that she remembered the incident and did not have a head injury. Monika was arrested with her mother and two police officers in their back-yard. She was not aware that one of the police officers had forcibly kept the door open. Her mother and the police officer had been close to the door, approximately one metre away from it. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. The Detmold Regional Court dismissed the first applicant’s compensation claims against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia. It held as follows: “The plaintiff has no claim under Articles 839 and 847 of the Civil Code’. The plaintiff was under suspicion of having committed a criminal offence. arrest itself was not unlawful. Even if the plaintiff had no intention whatsoever to abscond, the situation nevertheless appeared otherwise to the police officers. The arrest does not appear to be disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring that the further investigations could be carried out. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police Officers went further than was necessary, by handling the plaintiff too roughly and in so doing injuring her or even by deliberately inflicting the injuries on her. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof. With respect to the origin of the graze, the evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff’s daughter, conflicts. Witness Klaas claims to have seen one of the police officers repeatedly knocking the plaintiff’s head against the wall by the door, the two police officers deny this. None of these three witnesses can be regarded as not having an interest in these proceedings. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the walls. The shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled while being restrained by the police and when the handcuffs were being put on her. For these reasons the claim must be dismissed. The arrest does not appear to be disproportionate either, but a perfectly reasonable means of ensuring that the further investigations could be carried out. Witness Klaas claims to have seen one of the police officers repeatedly knocking the plaintiff’s head against the wall by the door, the two police officers deny this. None of these three witnesses can be regarded as not having an interest in these proceedings. Two police officers could certainly expect disciplinary proceedings and a resumption of the criminal investigation if these proved to be the facts. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. Neither the balance of probability nor general experience militate in favour of accepting the plaintiff's version of events. The claim must be dismissed. The Commission declared the applicants’ complaints admissible. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the various separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government in their memorial of 12 November 1992 invited the Court to find “that the applicants did not suffer violations of their rights under Article 3 (art. 3) or Article 8 (art.-8) of the Convention’”. The Court concluded that there was no violation of the rights of the applicants and that they were entitled to a fair trial. The applicants were allowed to appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.

name: Ayten Ünal Tekeli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29865/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the refusal by the domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to protection of her private life. In that connection she relied on Article 8 of the Convention, read alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 1 July 2003 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 13 January 2004. Ayten Ünal Tekeli is a Turkish national, born in 1965 and living in İzmir. She took her husband’s name pursuant to Article 153 of the Turkish Civil Code. As she was known by her maiden name in her professional life, she continued putting it in front of her legal surname. However, she could not use both names together on official documents. On 22 November 2001 the new Civil Code was enacted. Article 187 was worded identically to the former Article 153. The decision was served on the applicant on 23 June 1995. The applicant preferred not to make use of that possibility because, in her view, the amendment in question did not satisfy her demand.

The court held that the 2004 Act did not have retroactive effect and, consequently it examined the applicant’s claim only in respect of the period between the entry into force of the2004 Act on 17 September 2004 and the date on which the complaint had been lodged.

name: Edward Wynne
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67385/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not been afforded a proper review of the lawfulness of his continued detention as a mandatory life prisoner. By a decision of 22 May 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled in the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland on 23 November 2004. The applicant learned that his ‘tariff’ period fixed by the trial judge on the manslaughter offence expired in June 1991. He was informed by a Home Office Memorandum of 5 June 1992 that his continued detention was based on the risk he represented. According to the Government's submissions, the Parole Board considered the applicant's case in September 1994 and January 1997. In 1994, it concluded that his behaviour was aggressive and intimidatory and that he represented a high risk to the public. On 10 January 1997, it conclude that he remained far too great a risk to warrant transfer to open conditions. In 1999, without holding an oral hearing, the Board declined to recommend release.

name: Stephen Andrew Benham
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 23 January 1995 by the European Commission of Human Rights. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government”) applied to have the case heard within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 5 and 6. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 November 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Emmerson and Mr Pannick. The Grand Chamber decided on 26 January 1996 that it was not necessary to hold a further hearing following the relinquishment of jurisdiction by the Chamber. Mr Benham became liable to pay a community charge of £325 on 1 April 1990. Since then he has been subject to the community charge. The case was heard by the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The Government's memorial was received on 27 July 1995 and the applicant's memorial on 7 August 1995. Poole Magistrates' Court ordered the issue of a liability order, entitling Poole Borough Council to commence enforcement proceedings against him. Mr Benham did not pay the amount owed, and bailiffs visited his parents' house but were told that he had no goods of any value there or elsewhere which could be seized by them and sold in order to pay the debt. He was not assisted or represented by a lawyer, although he was eligible for “Green Form“ legal advice and assistance before the hearing. He had started a Government Employment Training Scheme in September 1989, but had left it in March 1990 and had not worked since. His application for income support was turned down because it is not payable to those who are voluntarily unemployed. Mr Benham was released from prison after serving 11 days for failing to pay the community charge. He was represented and legally aided by his solicitor, who lodged a notice of appeal by way of case stated and an application for bail pending appeal. Legal aid was obtained for the appeal, but not for the bail application, because it is not available for such proceedings. Mr Justice Potts in the Divisional Court held that the magistrates had been mistaken in concluding that Mr Benham's failure to pay had been due to culpable neglect. He found that the decision to commit MrBenham to prison would have been wrong even if there had been evidence of culpability neglect, because he did not have the means to pay. Mr Benham was not able to apply for compensation in respect of the time he spent in prison. He was unable to show bad faith on the part of the magistrates, as was required by section 108 of the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990. The local authority could have renewed their application at a later date if Mr Benham's circumstances had changed (see paragraph 19 below). The magistrates could have suspended the term of imprisonment subject to such conditions as they thought fit, or refused to issue a warrant. They could have continued to hold him in prison until he paid the debtor in question. In the circumstances it was incumbent upon them to consider the alternatives to immediate detention.

He was taken to Dorchester prison on the same day. Mr Benham was released from prison on 5 April 1991. Mr Justice Potts in the Divisional Court held that the magistrates had been mistaken in concluding that Mr Benham's failure to pay the community charge had been due to culpable neglect. He found that the decision to commit MrBenham to prison would have been wrong even if there had been evidence of culpable. neglect, because he did not have any means with which to pay. the debt at the time of the debt. train_texts: An Iraqi national, Mr Shayan Baram Saadi, applied for asylum in the UK in 2003. He claimed his detention at Oakington Reception Centre was not compatible with Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 27 September 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The parties did not submit observations on the merit of the applicant's case. The case was heard in the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The applicant was represented by Messrs Wilson and Co., a firm of lawyers. The applicant was detained at Oakington on 5 January 2001. He was formally refused leave to enter the UK on 8 January. The applicant submitted an appeal against the asylum refusal and was released on 9 January. On 14 January 2003 the adjudicator found that the applicant was a refugee within the meaning of the 1951 Refugee Convention, and also that there was a real risk that his return to Iraq would expose him to treatment contrary to Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. The. applicant was subsequently granted asylum by the Home Office. The case was remitted to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal and the appeal was allowed. The appeal was later dismissed. The form of words was not available at the time the applicant was detained, and Collins J. regarded it as a “disgrace” that the form lagged behind the policy. Both the Court of Appeal and the House of Lords held that the detention was lawful under domestic law. The detention was therefore “to prevent ... unauthorised entry”, and in addition was not disproportionate, Lord Slynn holding: “The need for highly structured and tightly managed arrangements, which would be disrupted by late or non-attendance of the applicant for interview, is apparent”. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 31 October 2002. Oakington residents will be able to apply to live in the city if they choose to. The application process will take place over the course of several weeks. The process will then be heard by a panel of five judges, which will make a decision in July. The panel will then make a final decision on the application on whether the application can go ahead. The judge will then decide on whether or not to grant the application to move to the Oakedton area.

He was permitted to attend, without an escort, a college to follow an educational course two days a week and also a centre where he was doing community work. He had previously been granted a home visit in August 1980 and prior to the commencement of the Training for Freedom programme he spent five days on home leave in September 1981. He is expected to transfer to the formal Training for freedom (TFF) in September. Prior to that he will have a five-day home leave and while on TFF he will has weekends which he may spend at home. In particular, it was pointed out that all his mail had been posted. The reply of 2 September 1981 rejected all the various complaints raised.

name: Johannes Werner
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 October 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria on 25 November 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21835/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Johannes Werner, on 16 March 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31 of Rules of Court B). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language. The hearing in this case and in the Szücs case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weitzel, Mr Bürstmayr, Mr Schreiner, Mr Cede and Mrs Gartner. Commission had produced various documents relating to the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. A. The applicant was suspected of having aided and abetted Mr and Mrs Hauser by forging the signature on the credit card. On 1 July 1991 the police also arrested the applicant, who was detained pending trial. The claim for compensation for detention was made in 1992. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The Vienna Regional Court refused their compensation claims on the ground that, contrary to the requirements of section 2 (1) (b) of the 1969 Act, the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. They appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The appeal was dismissed on 29 October 1992, and the case was dismissed by the Vienna court of appeal in 1994. The case was decided by the court in favour of the applicant. The tribunal heard that the prosecution was abandoned because witnesses’ memories had begun to falter. No representative of the principal public prosecutor’s office attended the deliberations. The conditions which must be met under section 2 (1) (b) of the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act in order to be able to claim compensation have accordingly not been satisfied and the appellants’ claims must therefore fail, the tribunal was told. The appellants did not dispute that the police inquiries had given rise to real suspicion concerning them. That suspicion was not subsequently dispelled, but on account of some remaining doubt was simply not sufficient to support a finding of guilt.

name: Bogusław Kijowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33829/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons. The Government submitted that the child's psychological problems had been caused by the trauma of being kidnapped by the applicant. The President of the Fourth Section decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) and gave priority to the application pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with A; the applicant denied this. In May 2004 the parties and A were examined by experts from the RODK (Regional Family Consultation Centre) Their opinion was that A should live with his mother, although the applicant should enjoy extensive contact rights. The applicant continued to live with A, who changed schools; they apparently moved house more than once. In December 2004 the applicant attempted to visit B; however, his wife apparently hindered his contact with his younger son. In June 2006 the Kraków Regional Court granted the applicant his petition for divorce. On 8 March 2007 the applicant was arrested. The child ran away from his mother's house in March 2008 and went to his father's house, located 100 kilometres away. The applicant took him to the police station and A was returned to his mother. On 1 April 2008 A ran away again and joined his father in Kraków. They have been living together since then. The child stated that he preferred to live with his father and that his mother had been threatening him and had forbidden him to call his father. On 4 December 2009 the Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment. It appears that the proceedings are pending before the trial court. The judge made an interim order suspending contact between the applicant and B, which had been ordered in the divorce judgment of 30 June 2006. The child felt that he had been treated differently from his brother B. The court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother. The opinion was finally submitted to the court on 16 December 2009. According to the experts the best interests of A required that the residence order be changed to allow A to live with the applicant. The court found that the applicant had never wanted his second child, contested his paternity of him and had seen B only twice: once after B's birth in 2003 and once in connection with the preparation of a psychological opinion. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. The applicant appealed against this decision, but on 11 June 2010 the Dabrowa Tarnowska District Court rejected the appeal for failure to lodge it in accordance with formal requirements, namely by lodging it out of time. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court.

name: Osman Özçelik
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56497/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Osman Özçelik (‘the applicant’), was taken into custody by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Ankara Security Directorate. The applicant was represented by Mr M.N. Özmen, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court on 27 July 1999. He was charged with aiding and abetting members of the PKK on account of his statements made during the television programmes shown on pro-Kurdish channel MED-TV. The court held that criminal proceedings against him would be suspended and a final sentence would be imposed if he was convicted of a similar offence within five years of this decision. On 21 December 2000 new legislation (Law no. 4616) on the suspension of proceedings and the execution of sentences regarding offences committed before 23 April 1999 came into force. The judge ordered the applicant’s release from detention, having regard to the nature of the alleged offence.

name: Osman Erden
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1520/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a primary school teacher in Kahramanmaraş at the material time, was discharged from his duties and on 10 March 1989 he was reinstated. He subsequently requested the Ministry of Education to reimburse him for the salaries and other financial rights he had been unfairly deprived of during the period of inactivity. The Ministry rejected this request. He lodged an action before the Ankara Administrative Court, requesting this court to quash the Ministry's decision and to order the payment of his entitlements. The applicant was. paid 4.35 Turkish liras (TRY0)0, which corresponded to the salaries and other financial benefits. he would have received during the specified period of his discharge. The applicant was not paid any default interest on this amount to compensate the effects of inflation, pursuant to the instructions of the Ministry of Finance dated 24 May 2005 and the judgment of the Ankara Administrative Court dated 6 November 1991. He was ordered to pay back the amount he was paid by the Turkish government in accordance with the terms of his employment contract, but he has not been paid the sum as he did not pay any interest on the original sum.

He considered himself bound by the decision of the House of Lords in Kay and Price (see paragraph 42 below) Judge says he is not satisfied that Maria Buckland has herself been guilty of any offensive behaviour on site. He is satisfied that her son, who resided part of the time with her, had been involved in an incident on site in which he threatened someone with a gun. He made an order for possession against the applicant against the site manager's family on 28 July 2006. The applicant has indicated in a recent statement that she intends to move from the site when [her parents] leave, that is on or before 4pm on 24th November. I do consider it appropriate to suspend enforcement of the possession order against her until the same time and date. Lord Justice Dyson noted the impact of the amendment to the 1968 Act to allow suspension of a possession order on whether the applicant could succeed in a conventional public law challenge. The real difference between the present case and Connors is not that the appellant had been in occupation for a shorter period than was the family in Connors ... On any view, the site was her home and had been for a substantial period of time. In Connors, once the licence had been terminated, the authority was entitled to evict the occupier. Dyson LJ concluded that since the amendment to the 1968 Act, it was difficult to conceive of a case in which a public law defence would succeed. However, the parties agreed that it was not necessary to decide whether the present case could be distinguished from Connors as the distinction was only relevant for any appeal before the House of Lords. He accepted that the vulnerable position of gypsies as a minority meant that ‘some special consideration should be given to their needs and different lifestyle’ (citing Connors, § 83). He found that the main reason for the narrowing of the margin of appreciation in Connors itself was that the complete absence of any procedural safeguards was a serious interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights. The court was bound not merely to make an order for possession, but to order the eviction of an occupant such as the appellant provided that the 4 weeks’ notice was given. name: Herwig C. Emmer-Reissig
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11032/04) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Administrative Court failed to hold an oral hearing, which was in breach of Article 6. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was brought by an Austrian national, Mr Herwig C. Emmer-Reissig (“the applicant”), on 11 March 2004. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Mr F. Trauttmannsdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Lower Austria Regional Government quashed the municipality's decision on 10 January 2001 and referred the case back to the municipal council. The applicant lodged further grounds in support of his appeal on 19 March, 4 and 24 April 2001. He also submitted a statement by the Tulln Administrative District Authority and a document he referred to as a business plan. The Königstetten Municipality requested the applicant to comment on an expert opinion it had obtained from the Planning Office on 31 October 2001. It stated that by far the largest part of the land was covered by forest, which would impede serious agricultural activities. The municipal council also rejected the applicant's appeal on 29 January 2002. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and requested an oral hearing. The Administrative Court rejected the complaint as inadmissible for non-exhaustion of administrative remedies. It found that, despite its request for a detailed business plan, the applicant had failed to provide one. Accordingly, the alleged need for a shed for the so-called agricultural enterprise had not been made out. The applicant's objection of 12 March 2002 was dismissed by the Lower Austria Regional Government on 22 July 2002. On 16 September 2003, the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's complaint and rejected his request for an oral hearing. The Appeal was dismissed on 17 December 2003.

Mégevand, a lawyer practising in Geneva. The Swiss Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr P. Boillat, former Deputy Director of the Federal Office of Justice in charge of the human rights and Council of Europe Section. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. In 1976, shortly after his death, a blood-type analysis did not rule out his being the latter’s father. In 1997 the applicant contacted the Geneva University Institute of Forensic Medicine to have a private paternity test carried out, but his request was refused. In 1999 the applicant applied to the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance for revision of the judgment of 30 January 1948. In the course of the proceedings he also requested a DNA test on the mortal remains of A.H. The Court of Justice argued that the applicant was not entitled to such an amendment of the register as a result of the 1976 revise of the Civil Code abolishing the exceptio plurium constupratorum. The right to know one’s parentage cannot be absolute in scope but must be weighed against the interests relating to protection of the personal freedom of others. The applicant, who is 60 years old, has been able to develop his personality and pursue a large portion of his existence without suffering any medically attested damage to his physical or mental health. The Federal Court observed that there were no consequences of a civil-law nature that could justify implementing the measure sought. The Court of Justice was entitled to restrict the applicant's personal freedom by taking into consideration that of the respondents, in view of the lack of public interest in having this parental tie established and the disproportionate nature of the steps required to establish it.

name: Sven Olof Göthlin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, about the proportionality of the detention order under Article 5 § 1 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 September 2012. The writ of execution was lifted on 1 February 2012 after the application was sent to the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The judge will hear the case at a hearing at the Supreme Court on 14 October 2013. The case will then be heard at the Court of Appeal on 16 October 2013, with a date to be decided on 9 November 2013. The Enforcement Authority contacted the applicant to plan the sale of the attached sawmill. In his reply a few days later, the applicant stated that he had removed the sawmill from his property and hidden it. The Authority also handed the applicant a summons for questioning on its premises. On the same day, the District Court assigned a public defender for the applicant. On 27 May 2010, after having held an oral hearing, the D.C. District Court ordered the Enforcement Authority to detain the applicant because he had refused to cooperate and give the required information. The Court ruled in favor of the Authority's request and the applicant was detained. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of Appeal, maintaining its claims. The applicant opposed the appeal, maintaining his claims and adding that he considered that, if he were detained, it would amount to imprisonment to obtain a confession. In reaching its decision, the court found that the measure did not breach the Convention. The court concluded that currently there did not exist such extraordinary reasons to detain the applicant and that detention was proportionate to the aim pursued. It stated that a debtor had to give necessary information about his assets and failure to do so could result in the debtor being detained, if there were extraordinary reasons for detention. It was not necessary to impose a fine initially. Lastly, it noted that it should be informed. The Court of Appeal held an oral hearing on 30 June 2010 and decided to maintain its earlier decision. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the applicant should be kept in detention since he still had not given any information about the location of the sawmill. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court which, on 6 July 2010, refused leave to appeal. On 13 July 2010 the District Court reviewed the applicant’s detention and held a new hearing in the case as required by Chapter 2, section 16, of the Enforcement Code. In its decision, the D.C. District Court noted that the. applicant maintained his refusal to reveal the whereabouts of thesawmill and found, with regard to the proportionality of the. measure, that there were extraordinary reasons for the continued detention. The case was closed on 23 September 2010 when the District Court struck the case out of its list of cases. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of Appeal which, on 13 August 2010, rejected the appeal. On 26 April 2012 the applicant submitted a claim for damages to the Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern), pursuant to the Act on Compensation for Deprivation of Liberty and Other Coercive Measures (Lagen om ersättning vid frihetsberövande och andra tvångsåtgärder, 1998:714), in the amount of SE. The applicant was detained for 42 days and demanded compensation. The Chancellor of Justice rejected the claim. He said the decision to detain the applicant had been taken by a court of law, in accordance with relevant legal provisions. The examination of the case showed no basis for finding that the decision was taken on erroneous grounds and therefore was incorrect, the Chancellor said in a decision made on 15 October 2012. The decision was made by the Chancellor on a case-by-case basis and the applicant was not found to have been detained on false grounds. The claimant was awarded SEK 80,000 for the suffering he had endured during the 42 days he was deprived of his liberty.

name: Anna Białas
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 69129/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Anna Białas, filed an action with the Tarnobrzeg District Court in which she sought a court order against third parties requiring them to remove an electricity cable they had installed on her land. An expert opinion was submitted to the court during that period. The parties were subsequently invited to settle the case, between 15 November 1990 and 6 May 1991 the proceedings were stayed at their request in order to negotiate a settlement. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Jakub Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant repeatedly sought exemption from payment of the expert’s fee. She was ordered to pay the fee, failing which the evidence provided by the expert opinion would be excluded. The applicant failed to comply with the order. On 31 May 2000 the Tarnobrzeg District Court decided to omit the evidence. It examined as evidence the case files of three other sets of related proceedings and on that basis delivered a judgment dismissing the action. The court agreed with the first-instance court that the defendant had the right of co-ownership to the plot on the date on which the proceedings were instituted and that the applicant's claim was accordingly inadmissible.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13024/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. train_texts: Iranian national Mansour Keshmiri (“the applicant’s” case) was born in 1958. He joined the People's Mojahedin Organisation in Iran in 1985. In 1986 he arrived in Iraq. He was then transferred to Muğla prison as charges were brought against him for illegal entry and falsifying identity documents.

name: Sonja Mendel
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The applicant alleged that her right to access to a court had been violated. She requested damages, but did not claim that there had been a breach of her rights under Article 6 of the Convention. This complaint seems still to be pending before the chancellor of Justice.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49913/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights.
