name: Gérard Vacher
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the French Government (“the Government’) on 7 August 1995. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. On 5 September 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1996. The Court heard addresses by Mr Soyer, Mr Ricard and Mr Dobelle, and also their replies to its questions. The applicant was Mr Gérard Vacher, a company director and lives at Neuilly-sur-Seine. The Commission produced the file on the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions, on 7 May 1996. Mr Vacher was sentenced to a fine of 8,000 French francs (FRF), payment of which was suspended, and ordered to alter the wall so it complied with regulations. The case file for the appeal was registered by the Court of Cassation registry on 19 June 1991. On 14 August 1991 the applicant filed a pleading in support of his appeal. On 3 September 1991 the chief registrar of the court sent Mr Vacher the following letter: “Further to your letter, I have to inform you that the Criminal Division of the Court Of Cassation delivered a judgment on 6 August 1991 dismissing your appeal. Consequently, the pleading received from you at the criminal registry on14 August 1991 will be disregarded as being out of time.“ The judgment in question, which was served on the applicant on 30 October 1995, was based on the following ground: ‘No ground of appeal has been filed in support. of the appeal'

name: Grzegorz Jończyk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19789/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been unlawfully detained in a regular detention centre pending his transfer to a psychiatric hospital. The court found it established that the applicant had committed the offences with which he was charged. However, it found he could not have been held criminally responsible as he was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. It further referred to the experts' opinion and ordered the applicant be placed in a psychiatric Hospital. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was detained in the Nowa Sól Detention Centre. On 7 July 2008 the Żary District Court gave a decision and ordered that the applicant be placed in the Lubiąż Psychiatric Hospital. The applicant subsequently appealed against this decision in so far as it related to the choice of hospital and the case file was transferred to the Zielona Góra Regional Court. On 29 August 2008 the Zielona Góra Regional Court upheld the decision of 7 July 2008. On 15 September 2008 the applicant was admitted to the hospital. It appears that he left the hospital on a later unknown date before February 2009.

name: Anne-Marie Paulsen-Medalen
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the applicants, Ms Anne-Marie Paulsen-Medalen and Mr Sven-Erik Svensson, both Swedish nationals. It originated in an application (no. 16817/90) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 November 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Mrs Westerberg and Mr Ehrenkrona. The first applicant is the mother of two children, P. and J.; the second applicant is J’s father. The applicant came into contact with the social authorities in 1984 while expecting her first child P. Following his birth, he and his mother stayed with her parents, then with her second applicant and, as from May 1985, with his father. After the birth of her second son J. in 1986 the first applicant became involved in legal proceedings. The first applicant moved to Högsbohöjd in 1986. Since 1989 she has been living at Västra Frölunda in order to be closer to her parents. The children were placed at the Bö Children’s Home in Gothenburg. The first applicant appealed against the decision to take the children provisionally into care. However, the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) and the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarräotten) upheld the decision and the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. The applicant and her sons were returned to their parents. The first applicant's right to see her children was restricted to a 2½ hours’ visit in the foster homes every second week. The County Administrative Court quashed the decision in a judgment of 20 June 1990. On appeal by the Social Council that judgment was overturned on 6 July 1990. The first applicant appealed against the Administrative Court of Appeal’s judgment to the Supreme Administrative Court which, on 5 November 1990, refused leave to appeal. On 22 January 1991 the first applicant and the children, represented by their mother, applied for leave to Appeal to the United States Supreme Court. The appeal was rejected on 11 January 1991. On 5 February 1991 Mrs Westerberg submitted the following request to the relevant authority on behalf of the second applicant. The second applicant’s access to his son J. was granted on 23 July 1991. On 28 June 1993 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ judgments as regards the restrictions on access. According to the Government, the delay in giving judgment appeared to have been due to the fact that it was awaiting the Strasbourg Court's ruling in the case of Margareta and Roger Andersson v Sweden (judgment of 25 February 1992, Series A no. 226‑A) which raised similar issues in relation to restrictions on telephone communications between mother and child. The second applicant did not pursue the matter but appears to have contacted the social authorities at Frölunda to enquire about his access to J. The authorities replied: “A right of access to a child for a person other than the custody holder does not exist under domestic law. It is however appropriate that a child also meets his or her relatives.” The County Administrative Court has decided that [J’s] access to his mother should be limited to two visits a year, which may be increased to the extent agreed by [J.]. His access to other relatives should be considered in light of this. Admittedly, [J.] has not appeared more than a few times during the last year. Social District Council said grandparents' access to their grandchildren was not regulated in the law. Request could, nevertheless, be examined in the context of the social authorities’ general powers to decide on the personal conditions of the children. Decisions made under these general powers were not subject to any review. The grandparents were advised to contact the social authority responsible for the foster home to discuss the possibilities of access. The access requested did not appear to be consistent with the children’s needs. By letter of 22 November 1992 the grandparents insisted on having a formal decision on the subject. On 4 December 1992 the Social District Council decided that the request did not call for any further action.

name: Wacław Płoski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26761/95) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application alleged that the refusal to allow him to attend the funerals of his parents was in breach of Article 8. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The decision was made under Rule 52 of the Rules of Court. The applicant applied for leave to attend the funeral of his mother. The Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused the permission to grant the applicant leave considering that he “was a habitual offender whose return to the prison cannot be guaranteed” The judge’s decision was worded as follows: “Further to the application of 3.07.1994 for compassionate leave I hereby inform you that, after analysing the case, I have not found grounds for granting such leave because there are no compassionate circumstances as referred to in Art. 59 § 1 of the Code of the Enforcement of Sentences.” Wacław Płoski was convicted of larceny and received a prison term. He applied for leave to attend the funeral of his father but was refused. He was released from prison on 27 February 1996 and later convicted of another crime. He has been in and out of prison since his release. He is currently serving a sentence of 10 years in prison for larcenies. He wrote to the President of the Wrocław Regional Court asking for an explanation of why he had not been allowed to attend his mother and father's funerals. The president refused to provide an explanation and said that the applicant had been a recidivist posing a risk of absconding. The application was rejected.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 December 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was heard by the Chamber of the European Court of Justice in December 2001. The hearing was held at the Court’s Wrocław, Poland, headquarters. The applicant applied for leave to attend the funeral of his mother. The judge rejected his application on 5 July 1994. In August 1994 the applicant’s father died. On 6 August 1994 he made an application for leave. The application was in the following terms: “I kindly ask you to grant me a compassionate leave because my father Wacław Płoski has died. The funeral will take place on 8.08.1994 and I would like to attend it and to pay last respects to him.” The judge said there were no grounds for granting the leave because there were ‘no compassionate circumstances’. The application was accompanied by the statement of a prison officer who confirmed that the applicant’s “behaviour was beyond reproach” and that he “stayed in touch with his wife and children” Wrocław-Śródmieście District Court refused permission to grant the applicant leave. The court gave the following reasons for its decision: “The charges against the accused involve a significant danger to society. The accused Wacław Płoski is a habitual offender within the meaning of Article 60 § 2 of the Criminal Code.” On 26 May 1995 the applicant was convicted of larceny and received a prison term.

name: Edward Skałka
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43425/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Adam Bezucha, a lawyer practising in Kłodzko. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) "Any little cretin, whether he wears a gown or not, should vent his need to intimidate others by making allusions to legal responsibility [for their acts] on his mistress, if he has one, or on his dog, but not on me. I am not going to be afraid of any such clown who wants to intimidate me, but the truth is that my request of 18 August 1994 was addressed to the court, not to some fool," he says. The judge "write rubbish about my alleged request for a pardon, which my request was absolutely not, but he also intimidates me," he adds. "If he is such a brilliant lawyer that he is able to reply to questions that were not asked – and his legal skills can be seen if the content of my letter is compared with his reply" The court found that on 15 November 1994 the applicant had sent a letter to the President of the Regional Court in which he referred to all judges of the Penitentiary Division as “irresponsible clowns” The Sosnowiec District Court convicted the applicant of insulting a State authority and sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment. The court considered that it was beyond any doubt that the applicant who had written the impugned letter. The analysis of its content and form led to the conclusion that he had acted with the firm intention of insulting the Regional. Court as a judicial authority. He had first addressed himself to the judges of that court as a group, and then focused on one unidentified judge. Accordingly, it had to be understood that the applicants had insulted the court as the State authority. Katowice Court of Appeal and Bielsko-Biała Regional Court both upheld the first-instance court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the contested judgment on 2 June 1997. The applicant's lawyer argued that the conviction had been in flagrant breach of Article 237 of the Criminal Code in that the applicant's acts, in the light of his submissions as to his motives, did not amount to a punishable criminal offence. The court referred to the grounds of appeal in which it had been argued that he had intended to insult a specific person, not an institution. The sentence imposed corresponded to the degree of the applicant’s guilt and with the seriousness of the offence. The Supreme Court went on to state that the applicant's abusive letter, referred to and quoted by the Regional Court, had clearly exceeded the limits of acceptable criticism. No new arguments had been submitted to the Supreme Court to show that there had been any procedural shortcomings in the proceedings, the court said. The Supreme Court therefore dismissed the cassation appeal as unfounded. The appeal was dismissed as not being in compliance with the requirements laid down by the applicable procedural provisions. The court emphasised, it was worth noting that the. name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of an exclusion order on him and his expulsion to Bulgaria violated his right to respect for private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. On 22 March 2007 a Chamber of that Section delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 8. The respondent Government should pay the applicant 5,759.96 euros in respect of costs and expenses. The Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene. The applicant was born in October 1984 and currently lives in Bulgaria. He was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment, thirteen of which were suspended on probation. The sentence was accompanied by an order to undergo drug therapy. The applicant was granted an unlimited settlement permit (Niederlassungsbewilligung) on 8 March 1999. In February 2000 the applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between June 1999 and January 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Deuretsbacher and Mr Trauttmansdorff, as well as their answers to questions put by a number of judges. On 25 May 2000 the Vienna Juvenile Court convicted the applicant on eighteen counts of aggravated burglary and attempted aggravated burglary. The court noted the applicant’s confession as a mitigating circumstance, and the number of offences committed and the rapid relapse into crime after the last conviction as aggravating circumstances. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten-year exclusion order on the applicant. The applicant, assisted by counsel, appealed that the exclusion order violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention. He stressed that he had come to Austria at the age of six, his entire family lived in Austria and he had no relatives in Bulgaria. The applicant came to Austria only at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and could not speak Bulgarian. He had no relatives or other social contacts in Bulgaria and stressed the fact that he was still a minor. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the exclusion order was justified under Article 8 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia. According to information given by counsel at the hearing, the applicant did not commit any further offences in Bulgaria. The Government informed the Court that the inclusion order will expire on 3 January 2011.

name: Lars Lillo-Stenberg
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13258/09) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Norwegian nationals, Mr Lars Lillo-Stenberg and Mrs Andrine Sæther (‘the applicants’), alleged that their right under Article 8 had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. On 20 August 2005, the applicants married in a private ceremony which took place outdoors on an islet in the municipality of Tjøme in the Oslo fjord. In the last photograph, the bride was barefoot with her wedding dress raised above her knees to avoid getting the dress wet. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine. The magazine appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett), which by judgment of 2 September 2008 found against the applicants, by three votes to two. The Supreme Court has considered legal questions relating to violation of privacy in the judgments Rt-2007-687 (Big Brother) and Rt/2008-489 (Plata). In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [the applicants], the appeal should be allowed. The provision in section 3-6 refers, at any rate primarily, to violation. of section 390 of the Penal Code and Article 8 of the Convention. The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships within the family are clearly of a personal nature. The question under consideration is whether a violation of privacy took place. There would have been no question of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the basis of an overall evaluation of the article, cf. paragraph 64 of the Big Brother judgment with further references. I would add that I see nothing in the article indicating that the couple had given the magazine permission to report on the wedding in return for payment. The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. Both [applicants] are well-known figures, but neither of them has had a prominent role either in the public administration or in any other public body. The article clearly has a purely entertainment value. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 of the Human rights Convention is the most relevant principle to be weighed. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The case was heard by the Munich Regional Court in 1997 and 1998. The court found that the muscle had not been cut and that no liability of the defendants could be establish. The applicant appealed against the dismissal of his appeal in 2004. On 7 December 2005 the Federal. Constitutional Court refused to accept his constitutional complaint for examination. The appeal was dismissed in 2004 and the case was dismissed again in 2005.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11564/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, a gynaecologist, was born in 1956 and lives in İzmir. He alleges that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. In particular, he complains of having received electric shocks, of having been suffocated, and of being beaten and threatened. He also alleges that during the first three days of his detention, he had been deprived of food and medication and prevented from sleeping. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. The prosecution noted that none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events. None of the medical reports, dated 19 October 1999, 23 October 1999 and 25 October 1999 save for one dated 11 November 1999, i.e. fifteen days after the events, noted any physical findings of ill-treatment.

name: Andrzej Kaźmierczak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4317/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was indicted on several charges of fraud while acting in an organised criminal group. The court attached importance to the serious nature of the offences with which he had been charged and the likelihood of a heavy sentence being imposed. The applicant has been held in detention since July 2003. He has been charged with a string of serious offences. The judge has ruled that his continued detention is necessary in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the gravity of the anticipated sentence. The applicant has made numerous unsuccessful applications for release on bail or under police supervision and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against decisions extending his detention. name: Paweł Kurczewski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18157/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 4 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29§ 3 of the convention, the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was lodged by a Polish national, Mr Paweł Kurczewski (“the applicant”), on 7 May 2004. The applicant was indicted before the Gdańsk District Court. He was charged with robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Hearings scheduled for 9 October and 11 December 2003 were cancelled due to, among other things, the failure to bring the co-accused to trial from prison. On 28 July 2004 the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He appealed on 7 December 2004. His detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. In all those decisions the courts stated that the grounds originally given for the applicant's detention were still valid. They repeated the grounds previously given for his continued detention. All the appeals and applications for release lodged by the applicant were to no avail. Appeal hearings cancelled for various reasons, such as illness or absence of defence lawyers, and the need to obtain evidence. Gdańsk Regional Court quashed the applicant's detention order on 3 February 2006. He was released on the same date. It appears that the first-instance judgment was upheld on 11 July 2007. It is not known whether he has been found guilty of the charges against him or whether the charges have been dropped. He is still being held in a Polish detention centre. The case is still pending in the Polish Supreme Court. The appeal was due to be heard on 13 October 2005, but the hearing was later postponed.

name: Mehmet Pehlivan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4233/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Pehlivan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was charged under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code, and with killing B.C. in 1992. The applicant made statements before the first-instance court, denying the charges against him. On 22 November 1999 the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand. The court subsequently postponed the hearings until 24 December 1998 on account of the failure of the gendarmerie command to submit the relevant information. The judge held that there were strong indications that he had committed the offence defined in Article 125: carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. The applicant was convicted under Article 448 of the Criminal Code of homicide and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 26 March 2002 because the applicant had been unable to examine three witnesses against him during the trial. The case was subsequently remitted to the First Division of the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The court found no convincing evidence that the offence committed by the applicant was linked to terrorist activities and ordered the applicant’s release from prison in view of the length of his detention during judicial proceedings. On 8 April 2004 the Court ofCassation upheld this judgment.

name: Jarosław Kąkol
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3994/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. It decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he was charged and the severity of the anticipated penalty. It also considered that the prolongation of detention was justified by the need to obtain DNA evidence in order to corroborate evidence previously obtained. The trial began on 28 December 2001. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court held three hearings per month. During the hearing held on 30 January 2002 the trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when the prosecutor was reading the bill of indicted. On 11 September 2002 the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw the case against him. The court also ordered the applicant to be held in custody until 30 September 2002. Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant and his 17 co-defendants be kept in custody until 30 June 2003. Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's and eighteen of his co-Defendants' detention until 31 December 2003. On 1 September 2003 a new legal-aid counsel was appointed for the applicant. The previous counsel was discharged by the trial court from his duties at his own request and following a number of court rulings. The trial court had taken various procedural steps in order to accelerate the proceedings. The risk of absconding or tampering with witnesses in the present case did not have to be supported by any concrete facts, but resulted from the above presumption. The applicant and other defendants were free to make use of their procedural rights, the abuse of those rights undoubtedly led to delays in the trial. The Court of Appeal in Gdańsk prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. The reasons for the delays were the obstructiveness of the defendants and the abuse of the rights of the defence. By March 2006 the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. He maintained that the length of his detention was excessive and that the charges against him lacked a basis in law. The court ruled that keeping the applicant in custody was necessary to prevent him from interfering with the trial, given the reasonable risk of such interference. The case is still pending before the first-instance court in Gdańsk, Poland. The trial had to commence de novo due to the serious illness of the judge rapporteur. The applicant was released on 19 October 2005 after appealing against the Court of Appeal's decision to extend his detention until January 2006. The case appears to be still pending at the first court. It is believed that the case has been settled on a. sufficiently strong basis. It appears that the proceedings are still pending in the first Court of First Instance of the Gda Court of Appeal. The application was made in March 2005 and the trial court made a severance order with a view to expediting proceedings.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59526/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government was represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki and Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was charged with large-scale fraud to the detriment of the State Treasury. There were two other defendants in the case. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 9 years' imprisonment and a fine in 1998. He appealed against his conviction, arguing that his detention was excessive. On an appeal lodged by the applicant, the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. The Regional Court held the first retrial hearing on 20 June 2000. The retrial was to begin on 28 March 2000 but was adjourned since one of the defendants had to undergo a psychiatric examination. The hearing scheduled for 9 May 2000 had to be adjourned due to the illness of a lay judge. Subsequent hearings were held on 12, 18 and 19 July, 22 August, 20, 21 and 28 September, 17 and 18 October, 28 and 29 November and 20 December 2000. The applicant appealed, invoking, inter alia, Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. He submitted that his right to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial was not respected. He also maintained that his detention was so excessive that it amounted in reality to serving a prison sentence. The Szczecin Regional Court dismissed an application for release on bail or subject to other guarantees or conditions. On 16 November 1999 the Regional Court extended the applicant's detention until 30 April 2000, repeating the grounds mentioned in the previous decisions. On 11 January 2000 the Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It stressed that both the fact that the applicant had earlier evaded justice and the nature of his, in the court's words, “criminal relations” with certain witnesses involved in the case. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant had misconstrued Article 263 §§ 3 and 4 of the 1997 Code. The court found it necessary to extend his detention until 30 October 2000 because the summer holidays were approaching. The applicant requested that the three sets of criminal proceedings conducted against him before the courts in Szczecin, including the trial of the accused, be halted. The application was denied by the Regional Court of Poland, which said that the charges against the accused were without merit and that he had already been convicted at first instance. The appeal was heard by the Polish Supreme Court, which upheld the decision to extend the detention. On 13 October 2000 his request was refused. On 18 October 2000 the Szczecin Regional Court prolonged the applicant's detention until 30 January 2001. The applicant's appeal, based on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, was rejected by the Court of Appeal on 31 October 2000. name: Gerhard W. Luedicke
train_texts: The case originated in three applications against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission by Mr. Gerhard W. Luedicke, Mr. Mohammed Belkacem and Mr. Arif Koç. The Commission ordered the joinder of these three applications on 4 October 1976. The application was lodged on 1 October 1977, the request on 10 October. Their purpose is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 3 (e) and 14 (art. 6-3-e, art. 14) of the Convention. The Government filed their memorial on 30 January 1978. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on 17 April that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply. On 8 May, he communicated to the Registrar a note containing “the applicants’ observations on the question of the application of Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention“ and Mr. Koç’s observations. The Government undertook, inter alia, responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments or statements (Rule 27 para. 3). The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Stras. Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights on 25 May this year. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government and by Mr. Ermacora, Mr. Trechsel and Mr. Pawlik for the Commission. Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings. They are made up of “the fees (Gebühren) and expenses of the Treasury’. Section 17 para. 2 of the last-mentioned Act provides that “for the purposes of compensation, interpreters shall be treated as experts’ If an accused is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. Some courts read the Act as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to pay costs in the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued. This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Gerhard W. Luedicke is a citizen of the United Kingdom and was a member of the British Forces stationed in the Federal Republic of Germany. In May 1972, the Bielefeld District Court (Amtsgericht) convicted him of a road traffic offence. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. On 30 June 1972, he entered an appeal against this assessment of costs; he maintained that the assessment was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. Following the refusal of the auditor (Bezirksrevisor) to modify the assessment, the matter was referred to the Biellefeld Regional Court. Mohammed Belkacem is an Algerian citizen, born in 1954. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in Algeria, he rejoined his father in the Federal Republic of Germany. He was involved in a dispute in a Berlin night-club during which another client lost his coat. He paid the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs on 4 May 1973, on his return to Algeria. Mr. BelKacem was awarded the damages of around €6,000 by the court of appeal in Berlin. The appeal was dismissed on 31 August 1972 by the D. feld District Court. On 8 February 1973, following an “immediate appeal’ by Mr. Luedicke, the Bielefeld Regional Court confirmed the decision. Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court convicted him of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to four weeks’ imprisonment (Dauerarrest) and to a fine of DM 500. Mr. Belkacem filed an appeal against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. He submitted that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. On 13 June 1974, the Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal. The Regional Court reasoned that since no assessment of costs had yet been made, there had been no decision capable of being challenged on appeal. Arif Koç, a Turkish citizen born in 1940, has been employed in the Federal Republic of Germany in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. On 6 December 1973, the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court (Schwurgericht beim Landgericht at Aachen) convicted Mr. Koç of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a year’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commuted. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), in a fully reasoned decision delivered on 5 June 1975, set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The court ordered the applicant to bear the costs of the proceedings ‘with the exception, however, of the costs occasioned by the assistance of the Turkish-language interpreter, which costs are to be borne by the Treasury’. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. The intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. According to the payment vouchers (Kassenanweisungen), the fees paid to the interpreter amounted to DM 311.50 for the hearing on 4 December 1973, DM 510.50 on 5 December and DM 112.50  on 6 December - making a total of DM 934.50. The applicant was not served with a notice to pay the costs for which he was liable, including the interpretation costs, since it was noted that he had a wife and four children to support, that his income was modest and that there was thus no prospect of recovering the costs. It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. Nor does the consideration that a foreigner should not receive worse treatment in the matter of costs than a national, dictate the conclusion that permanent exemption from costs is necessarily implied. In their applications, lodged respectively on 23 July 1973, 20 December 1974 and 28 July 1975, Mr Luedicke, Mr. Belkacem and Mr. Koç claimed to be victims of a violation of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. In its report of 18 May 1977, the Commission expressed the opinion: ‘The decisions concerning the interpreter’s costs in the applicants’ cases were in breach of Article6 para. 4 (1) (1-3)’ The Government of Germany requested that the Court strike the case out of its list insofar as the applicant Koç was concerned.

In accordance with Rule 21 paras. 3 (b) and 5, Mr Wiarda, the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber and assumed the office of President of the chamber. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 16 March 1989. It originated in an application (no. 9310/81) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 (art. 13) of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir Vincent Evans, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza for the Government, by Mr Busuttil for the Commission and by Ms Hampson for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. The first applicant, Richard John Powell, is a director of a mining concern and lives with his family at Esher, Surrey, in a house which he bought in 1957. Since 1972 it has lain under a flight departure route from Heathrow in operation for about one third of the year, usually during the summer months. Following objections to the level of noise disturbance, the route was divided into two sections in 1975. Michael Anthony Rayner lives in a bungalow in Colnbrook, Berkshire. He farms with other members of his family on land that has been in his family for some generations. It falls within a 60 NNI contour, which is regarded as an area of high noise-annoyance for residents. About 6,500 people around Heathrow Airport experience a noise exposure equal to or greater than that suffered by Mr Rayner and his family. About half a million other people live within this contour area. The average height of arriving aircraft over his property is 450 feet and the averageheight of departing aircraft varies between 1,235 and 2,365 feet according to aircraft type. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours (high noise-annoyance zone). Every increase of 10 in that scale represents approximately a doubling of the loudness. Compensation for the loss of value of houses and land as a result of airport noise is provided for by the Land Compensation Act 1973. However, such compensation is payable only in respect of new or altered public works first brought into use after 16 October 1969. Intensification of an existing use is, for reasons of principle and practice, not compensatable. Mr Powell and Mr Rayner would have no entitlement to compensation under this Act, writes Mr Powell. The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport. In December 1986, after the completion of the fourth terminal (see paragraph 11 above) and privatisation of the Authority, the successor company to the Authority announced a scheme for the purchase of noise-blighted properties close to Heathrow Airport. This scheme provided for purchase by the company of property severely affected by aircraft noise at Heathrow (within the 65 NNI contour) where the owner had acquired the property before 17 October 1969 and wished to sell but could not do so except at a deflated price. Claims had to be made between 1 January 1987 and 31 December 1988. The main forum for international co-operation seeking to make aircraft quieter is the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) The broad thrust of ICAO’s work has been towards the development of a series of standards, leading to the phasing out of aircraft unable to meet them. In the United Kingdom effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. For the exemption to apply there must be compliance with the statutory provisions referred to in section 76(1) of the 1982 Act. In practice this means the Air Navigation Order 1985 as amended, the Air navigation (General) Regulations 1981 as amended and the Rules of the Air and Air Traffic Control Regulations 1985. A 1984 Order gave effect to new ICAO standards and to regulations based upon recommendations of the European Civil Aviation Conference. In the event of an infringement of the noise limit, the Airport informs the airline by letter and sends a copy to the Department of Transport. The effect of recent bans on non-noise-certificated aircraft has been to keep the rate of compliance to around 99% by day and 98% by night. The Secretary of State is empowered by section 78 of the Civil Aviation Act to deny Heathrow’s facilities to operators who fail to comply with noise abatement measures but to date it has not been found necessary to invoke this provision. A helicopter link between Gatwick Airport and Heathrow Airport was introduced in 1978. A scheme for sound insulation of dwellings was introduced for Heathrow in 1980. The application (no. 9310/81) was first lodged with the Commission on 31 December 1980 by the Federation of Heathrow Anti-Noise Groups. On 15 March 1984 the Commission rejected the Federation’s complaint, but the application was continued by Mr Powell and Mr Rayner, together with a third applicant whose claim has since been settled. In common with other persons living within the 60 NNI contour, Mr Rayners qualifies for a full noise-insulation grant. The applicants invoked Articles 6 § 1, 8 and 13 (art. 6-1, art. 8,. art. 13) of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (P1-1) The cases of Mr Powell and Mr Rayner were declared admissible under Article 13 of the convention but inadmissible for the rest. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the dissenting opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government maintained the final conclusions in their memorial, whereby they requested the Court ‘to decide and declare that there has been no violation of Article 13’.

Heathrow is one of the busiest international airports in the world. Over 22% of passengers use the airport as an interchange point. It is currently used by over 70 airlines and serves 200 destinations worldwide. The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport unless it could show that the acquisition of the property was necessary for the proper performance of its function. The Noise Abatement Act 1960 specifically exempts aircraft noise from its protection. Aircraft operators' liability is further limited by section 76(1) of the Civil Aviation Act 1982. An action will lie at common law for nuisance in respect of an activity which unreasonably interferes with the use and enjoyment of land. If liability is established, damages may be awarded or, in certain circumstances, an injunction granted. The 1982 Act does not exclude all liability on the part of aircraft operators for trespass and nuisance caused by aircraft in flight. The exemption applies only in respect of aircraft flying at a reasonable height above the ground. The main forum for international co-operation seeking to make aircraft quieter is the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) The broad thrust of ICAO’s work has been towards the development of a series of standards, leading to the phasing out of aircraft unable to meet them. These standards are not operative within the I CAO member States unless and until they are given effect in national legislation. In the United Kingdom effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. A 1984 Order gave effect to new ICAO standards and to regulations based upon recommendations of the European Civil Aviation Conference. In the event of an infringement of the noise limit, the Airport informs the airline by letter and sends a copy to the Department of Transport. According to the Government, the effect of recent bans on non-noise-certificated aircraft has been to keep the rate of compliance to around 99% by day and 98% by night. The Secretary of State is empowered by section 78 of the Civil Aviation Act to deny Heathrow’s facilities to operators who fail to comply with noise abatement measures, but to date it has not been found necessary to invoke this provision. Since 1972 a system of regularly alternating the landing runway has been implemented at Heathrow during westerly operations. The main objective is to achieve a fair sharing of periods of relative quiet among the communities of West London affected by noise from landing aircraft. Under this scheme, which cost the British Airports Authority approximately £19 million, over 16,000 house owners or occupiers applied for grants. The application (no. 9310/81) was first lodged with the Commission on 31 December 1980 by the Federation of Heathrow Anti-Noise Groups. On 15 March 1984 the Commission rejected the Federation’s complaint, but the application was continued by Mr Powell and Mr Rayner, together with a third applicant whose claim has since been settled. Mr Powell and Mr Rayner invoked Articles 6 § 1, 8 and 13 (art. 6-1, art. 8, and art. 13) of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (P1-1) They argued that they had been the victims of a violation of Articles 6 and 8. with the operation of Heathrow Airport. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a. violation of Article 13 of the convention in relation to Mr. Rayner’s claim. The full text of the Commission's opinion and of the dissenting opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment.

Michael Anthony Rayner lives in a bungalow in Colnbrook, Berkshire. It falls within a 60 NNI contour, which is regarded as an area of high noise-annoyance for residents. The NNI is a long-term average measure of noise exposure which is used in the United Kingdom to assess the disturbance from aircraft noise to communities near airports. Intensification of an existing use is, for reasons of principle and practice, not compensatable. Mr Powell and Mr Rayner would have no entitlement to compensation under this Act. The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport. In December 1986, after the completion of the fourth terminal, the successor company to the Authority announced a scheme for the purchase of noise-blighted properties close to Heathrow Airport. This scheme provided for purchase by the company of property severely affected by aircraft noise at Heathrow (within the 65 NNI contour) where the owner had acquired the property before 17 October 1969 and wished to sell. Claims had to be made between 1 January 1987 and 31 December 1988. By virtue of the contour limitation the applicants’ properties were excluded from the scheme. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention. The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in Regensburg at night. The applicant was accordingly transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital on 15 December 2005. On 25 October 2007 the Regensberg Regional Court prolonged the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital. The execution of his preventive detention was interrupted in order to execute the sentence against the applicant, which had been ordered by two previous courts. The court considered that it was very likely that the applicant, if released, would commit further serious offences resulting in considerable physical or psychological harm to the victims. The court further quashed its decision of 26 October 2005 to execute the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison in accordance with Article 67a § 3 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital to Straubed Prison on 19 June 2008. On 22 July 2008 the Nuremberg Court of Appeal reversed the decision of the Regional Court and returned the case back to the Regensburg Regional Court. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal as ill‑founded. The psychiatric expert report drawn up by expert K. was clear and conclusive and complied with the minimum standards required for such reports. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. It found, accordingly, that the applicant's continued preventive detention was lawful and proportionate. The decision was upheld by the Regional Court in March 2008. The applicant was detained in a separate wing of Straubing Prison for persons in preventive detention from 13 November 1997 to 31 March 2004. The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. From 2002 to 2004 he participated in a discussion group in prison. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. It remitted the case-file to the Nuremberg Court of Appeal in order for it to review whether, applying a stricter standard of proportionality, the applicant's preventive detention was to continue. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. It had not been shown that the applicant, owing to specific circumstances, was highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act (see paragraph 39 below) The applicant was transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital thereupon. The sentencing court orders preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years’ imprisonment. The court may review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied or whether it should be declared terminated. For persons in preventive detention, this time‑limit is two years. The first period of preventive detention may not exceed ten years. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). Article 67d of the Criminal Code was amended by the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act of 26 January 1998, which entered into force on 31 January 1998. The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The court may subsequently transfer a person against whom preventive detention was ordered to a psychiatric hospital or to a detoxification facility if the person’s reintegration into society can be better promoted thereby. The duration of the placement is determined by the provisions which apply to the measure ordered in the judgment. Transfer for enforcement of a different measure of corrections and prevention. The detention of the mentally ill person with diminished criminal responsibility (M. v. Germany) If a person has spent ten years in preventive detention, the court shall declare the measure terminated (only) if there is no danger that he will commit serious offences. A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. The Act on Therapy and Detention of Mentally Disturbed Violent Offenders (Therapy Detention Act – Gesetz zur Therapierung und Unterbringung psychisch gestörter Gewalttäter) entered into force on 1 January 2011. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention were incompatible with the constitutional right to liberty of the persons in preventive detention. It found that those provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot). These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. In its reasoning, the Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. name: Jan Nowiński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25924/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right of access to a court had been violated as a result of the court's refusal to accept his statement of claim. On 17 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant had to move out of the apartment he had previously occupied at Gajowa Street in Wrocław. On 16 May 2005 the District Court ordered that the statement of claim be returned to the applicant. The applicant filed an interlocutory appeal against that decision. The court held that the applicant had failed to indicate his place of residence. Since he had stayed at different addresses he should have indicated a place where he spent most of his time and where his daily activities were located, the court said. The decision was upheld on appeal on 9 December 2005 and the applicant paid the required court fee for lodging his appeal.

name: Fedai Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21773/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in Turkey. He was taken into custody within the context of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the TKP/ML – TIKKO (the Turkish Communist Party-Marxist Leninist - Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army) The case was remitted to the Istanbul Assize Court for re-trial. The applicant appealed the decision. The proceedings are currently pending before the Court of Cassation. The case relates to the activities of the TKP/ML – TIKKO with a view to undermining the constitutional order of the State. The court found the applicant guilty of the alleged offence and sentenced him to life imprisonment, pursuant to Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The judge ruled that the applicant had been involved in armed attacks, the killing of several individuals and robberies. The application has been rejected and a new trial has been scheduled for September 2009.

The applicant was convicted as charged by the Istanbul State Security Court and sentenced to death. The appeal is currently pending.

The court examined only the proceedings before the Regional Court, namely from 17 August 2005 to 12 December 2005, and held that there were no delays for which the Regional court could be held responsible. It noted that the court, when deciding on administrative and procedural matters, acted without delay. It further considered irrelevant the fact that at the material time the trial had not yet commenced. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 27 September 2006. The proceedings are still pending. The case was referred to the Katowice Regional Court for consideration. On 17 May 2006 the court discontinued the proceedings, since the applicant had withdrawn his complaint on 5 May 2006 about the length of the proceedings before the District Court. The application was later dismissed on 20 May 2006. The case was settled out of court in 2007. The applicant was awarded a fine of more than £10,000, plus costs and legal fees. The appeal was dismissed on 22 May 2006, after the applicant withdrew his complaint about the court's length of proceedings, and the case was dismissed. name: Karin Andersson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice on 29 May 2012 and concluded on 2 June 2013. The Court of Appeal rules in favour of the applicants and the Swedish Government. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. The distance from their properties to the “corridor” or the specific stretch of the railway fixed in later proceedings vary; the houses appear to be situated 300 – 2500 metres away. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case – Ms Bring, Mr Bäcklund and Mr Osterman – petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for a judicial review. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. They also asked the Environmental Court in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. The railway plan for the area in question was adopted on 21 June 2005. Twelve applicants appealed to the Government against the railway plan. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected the petition in December 2008. The court considered itself bound by the Government’s decision as to the permissibility of the railway project and thus limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures, as indicated by the decision of the Environmental Court of Appeal. It found that the specific stretch chosen in the railwayPlan was situated within the permitted “corridor” and thus rejected the appeals. The railway plan was in line with the European Convention on Human Rights and the EU Habitats Directive. The court considered that the question of permissibility of a railway project was within the power of the Government. The Government’s decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. The Supreme Administrative Court further stated that, if private interests were affected by the location of a. railway project, judicial review could be obtained by petitioning the court in. proceedings against the Government's decision. A dissenting judge said that a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court. in its earlier decision on the issue of the railway plan. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard at the High Court in London on Tuesday. The hearing was adjourned until February 8, 2015. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 December 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Martinez and Mr Michelson as well as replies to its questions. The applicants owned a property in Gryta, adjacent to land on which a company - Västmanlands Avfallsaktiebolag (VAFAB) - takes delivery of and treats household and industrial waste. VAFAB has been authorised to engage in this activity on the land in question since 1 July 1983. It had been discovered in 1979 that refuse containing cyanide had been left on the dump and analyses of drinking-water emanating from a nearby well had shown excessive levels of cyanide. In 1983 excessive levels of cyanide were found in six wells near the dump. The use of the water from these wells too was prohibited and the landowners concerned, including the applicants, were temporarily provided with municipal drinking-water. VAFAB asked the Licensing Board to renew its permit and to allow it to expand its activities on the dump in July 1986. The applicants appealed to the Government, challenging the conditions set for the permit. The Government, as the final instance of appeal (see paragraph 13 below), upheld these and dismissed the appeal on 17 March 1988. In June 1984 the National Food Agency (livsmedelsverket) recommended that the maximum permitted level of cyanides be raised from 0.01 mg to 0.1 mg per litre. As a result, the municipality stopped supplying the above-mentioned landowners with water.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the court which tried and convicted him. It declared inadmissible the remainder of his complaints. The applicant and his co-accused were charged with distributing illegal leaflets and carrying identification cards and driving licences belonging to third parties. The search of their houses had uncovered the internal regulations of the party whose aim was to establish an independent Kurdish State on the territory of the Turkish State through dissemination of propaganda. The court sentenced the applicant and four of his co.accused to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred them from public service indefinitely. The applicant appealed. On 7 October 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The case was heard at the Ankara State Security Court on 7 November 1996. The judge ruled that the applicant was guilty of an offence under Article 168 and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act.

They were sentenced to a suspended two-year prison sentence, suspended for a year and a half, respectively. The sentence was suspended for two-and-a-half years if it was upheld. name: Elena Riera Blume
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37680/97) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application concerned the detention of the applicants, who are presumed members of a “sect”, for nearly ten days following a preliminary investigation directed by Barcelona investigating judge no. 6. The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5, 8 and 9 of the Convention. The case was examined by the Court of Appeal and declared admissible on 9 March 1999. The Court ruled that the application was not in breach of Article 25 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Riera Blume and Others v Spain (dec.), no. 37680/97, ECHR 1999-II. The applicants, Ms Elena Riera. Blume, Ms. Concepción Riera Blumes, Ms María Luz. Casado Perez, Ms Daría Amelía Casado. Perez,Ms María Teresa Sales Aige and Mr Javier Bruna Reverter, concerning their deprivation of. liberty (Article 5 of the Convention) and the interference with their right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. The Court declared the remainder of their application inadmissible. It decided that if there was not a friendly settlement of the case, a public hearing would be held. Sales Aige, Javier Bruna Reverter, born in 1954, 1952, 1950,. 1950, 1950, 1951 and 1957 respectively and live in Valencia (Spain) The applicants were arrested in 1984 and taken to the seat of the investigating court. A judge decided to release the applicants but gave oral instructions to the police that those detained, including the applicants, should be handed over to their families. The judge in question confirmed his oral instruction in a decision of 26 June 1984. In that decision he also ordered the chief of the Catalan police (mossos d’esquadra) to interview and question all those detained during the searches who had subsequently been released. The applicants were allegedly subjected to a process of ‘deprogramming’ by a psychologist and a psychiatrist at the request of Pro Juventud. On 30 June 1984 the applicants left the hotel. The applicants lodged a criminal complaint alleging false imprisonment, offences against the exercise of personal rights, falsification of documents, usurpation of functions and misappropriation of goods. In a judgment of 7 March 1990 the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial acquitted the accused, holding that the acts complained of had been prompted by a philanthropic, legitimate and well-intentioned motive. The prosecution and the applicants lodged appeals on points of law, which were dismissed by the Supreme Court on 23 March 1993. The applicants lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court. In their appeal they alleged violations of the right to religious freedom (Article 16 of the Constitution) They asked the court to quash the judgments of the Audiencia Provincial and the Supreme Court, to order the officials complained of to pay five million pesetas as compensation for the damage sustained. They also asked for a declaration to the effect that the Generalitat of Catalonia was liable in default. In conclusion, the offence of false imprisonment cannot be said to have been committed since there was no intention on the part of the defendants to deprive anybody of his or her liberty. Mr José Victor Riera Blume was held to have withdrawn on account of failure, through his own fault, to comply with a formal requirement. The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants, seeing that they were limited to declaring that the acts with which the defendants were charged did not amount to the offences for which they were being prosecuted. The Constitutional Court pointed out, firstly, that there was no fundamental right to have a person convicted and, secondly, that it could not protect fundamental rights by quashing final substantive judgments whereby defendants had been acquitted. It also pointed out that, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties.

The case originated in an application (no. 37680/97) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The case was heard by a three-judge panel of the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) and returned to the Commission on 10 March 1999 for further proceedings. The Court sent the parties the text of its decision on the admissibility of the application (Riera Blume and Others v Spain (dec.), no. 37680/97, ECHR 1999-II) and requested them to submit such further evidence and observations as they wished. It also asked the applicants to submit their claims for just satisfaction under Article 41 of the Convention (Rule 60) The Court placed itself at the disposal of the parties with a view to securing a friendly settlement of the matter, but found that there was no basis on which such a settlement could be reached. In accordance with the Chamber’s decision, a hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 1999. Sales Aige, Javier Bruna Reverter, were born in 1954, 1952, 1950,. 1950, 1950, 1951 and 1957 respectively and live in Valencia (Spain). At an unknown date in 1983 the Public Safety Department (“the DGSC”) of the Generalitat (government) of Catalonia received through Pro Juventud, an association formed to fight against sects, a request for help. Several people alleged that members of their families had been ensnared by a group known by the name of CEIS (Centro Esotérico de Investigaciones) According to the families’ complaints, those who ran the CEIS managed to bring about a complete change of personality in their followers. On 21 June 1984, they were taken by members of the Catalan police in official vehicles to a hotel some thirty kilometres from Barcelona. While at the hotel the applicants were allegedly subjected to a process of ‘deprogramming’ by a psychologist and a psychiatrist at the request of Pro Juventud. On 30 June 1984 the applicants left the hotel. As soon as they had regained their freedom, the applicants lodged a criminal complaint alleging false imprisonment, offences against the exercise of personal rights, falsification of documents, usurpation of functions and misappropriation of goods. In a judgment of 7 March 1990 the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial acquitted the accused, holding that the acts complained of had been prompted by a philanthropic, legitimate and well-intentioned motive. The applicants lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court. In their appeal they alleged violations of the right to religious freedom (Article 16 of the Constitution) and the rights of the defence during their detention. The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants. It also pointed out that, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer, as such, a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties. The issue is not whether or not use was made of an effective judicial remedy (section 43(1) of the CCA [Constitutional Court Act]) but whether the remedies afforded by the judicial process chosen have been exhausted.
