name: Zygmunt Mączyński
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings in his case were not concluded within a reasonable time. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. On 1 November 2001 the Court effected a change in the composition of its Sections and the present case was re-allocated to the new Second Section. The case was settled at the Court of Appeal on 25 July 2004 and the decision was published on 4 July 2005. Hearings took place on 28 May, 30 June and 6 August 1997. During the first of these hearings, the plaintiff replied to forty-one questions submitted by the applicant in 1995. On 8 January 1997 the applicant asked the Vice-President of the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) to transfer the case-file to the Pruszków District Court immediately. He pointed out that the Regional Court had decided his procedural request on 25 November 1996 and the casefile had been lying since then in the archives of the regional court. As a result, no judicial activity had taken place during that period. On 6 February 1997 the. applicant filed with the trial court three requests concerning an expert witness and the disputed property. The applicant appealed against a procedural decision taken by the Pruszków District Court. He threatened to commit suicide in the courtroom and set fire to the court building if the proceedings in his case were not concluded speedily. Between 16 July 1998 and 26 May 1999 the District Court held four hearings and issued one decision. During that time, the court received written pleadings on six occasions. The proceedings are apparently still pending. The applicant has not been found guilty of any crime and the case has been adjourned until after the end of the current financial year in September 2013. The case is currently being heard at the Warsaw Regional Court.

name: Adnan Levent Çamlar
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs in 1997. The Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release in 1998. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible on 24 June 2013. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Adnan Levent Çamlar (“the applicant”), on 4 August 2004. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The case was heard at the Court of Appeal. In 1997 the Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand in absentia. The applicant denied his involvement in the trafficking of illegal drugs. He requested to have certain witnesses, including his counsel in the United Kingdom, heard. The court rejected that request, finding that the statements of the witnesses called by the applicant would not contribute to the case. In 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. He was acquitted of all charges on 18 February 2003, mainly on the basis of the investigation conducted in the. United Kingdom and the evidence obtained during another set of proceedings concerning the same offence. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine. He appealed against the conviction on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. On 9 April 2009 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and heard the submissions of the applicant’s lawyer. Finally, the higher court upheld the judgment of the İzmir Assize Court with a minor procedural correction. The higher court indicated that the offence at issue concerned the exportation of illegal drugs and accordingly the case differed from that concluded in the United Kingdom. The high court dismissed the applicant's remaining grounds for appeal without further elaboration.

The applicant was placed in detention on remand in absentia. In March 2003 the applicant submitted his written defence to the court and requested his acquittal. He was acquitted on 18 February 2003. The court deferred the examination of the case to the subsequent hearings, awaiting information as regards certain accused in the United Kingdom. The application was dropped on 23 February 2004 and the applicant was released pending trial. The case was reopened on 7 March 2005 but the application was dismissed again on 11 March 2005. The appeal was dismissed on 17 March 2006. The judge who heard the case has since retired. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twenty four years’ imprisonment and a fine. On 31 March 2003 the applicant appealed against that judgment. He argued that he could not be found guilty on the basis of evidence which according to the British court was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. In June 2005 the applicant requested the reassessment of his case and the application of the more favourable clauses in the new Code. On 3 July 2008 the İzmir Assize Court sentenced the applicant to twenty years and ten months of imprisonment. Finally, the higher court upheld the judgment with a minor procedural correction. The high court dismissed the applicant’s remaining grounds for appeal without further elaboration.

name: Dietrich Rösslhuber
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32869/96) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and requested the parties to submit further observations. Thereupon the applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).I. The circumstances of the case: The applicant is a certified accountant and tax consultant, residing in Salzburg. During the preliminary investigations, which concerned a network of more than 300 firms, about 1,800 bank accounts were examined and about 8,000 volumes of documents were seized and studied. A special computer programme was designed in order to cope with the large volume of data. Most of the time was consumed by the preparation of an expert opinion, whereby the team of accounting experts first had to clear the balance sheets of the companies. On 16 September 1996 the trial started before the Salzburg Regional Court sitting with two professional and two lay judges. A motion brought by the applicant and his co-accused challenging the two professional judges for bias was dismissed, as was their further motion challenging the experts for bias. 46 days were dedicated to hearing the accounting experts. On 19 January 1998 a hearing had to be held in a hospital in Vienna due to the applicant’s illness. The applicant announced that he would file a plea of nullity and an appeal (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde und Berufung) On 16 June 2000 the written version of the judgment, comprising about 1,100 pages, was served on the applicant. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. The case was decided in favor of the French Republic by the Court of Justice. Claude Mazurek was born in 1942 and lives at La Grande-Motte. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. The applicant claimed that Article 760 of the Civil Code, which restricts the inheritance rights of adulterine children, was discriminatory and incompatible with Articles 8 and 14. The Court of Appeal ruled that Article 760 did not discriminate against children born to adulterous parents. The Court ruled that the amount transferred to the not-for-profit company was not intended as a gift to the children. The court ruled that it was not in line with the principle that children should be treated equally in all circumstances. The Appeal found that the provision was not a violation of the Convention, but was in fact designed to protect the rights of the children of the couple who had given the gift of the money to the non-profit corporation. The case was decided by the court of appeal, and the decision was appealed to the Supreme Court. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. Article 760 was a provision necessary for the protection of the rights of others. It was a French legal principle of public policy and not contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant subsequently received one quarter of the amount paid to the notary dealing with the estate.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23279/14) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention breached his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the. Convention and the prohibition on retrospective punishment under Article 7 § 1. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by two of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens and Mrs K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who had been granted legal aid. The applicant stabbed a female cyclist in the back in a life-threatening manner for sexual gratification. He was diagnosed with sexual deviance, a personality disorder and psycho-organic syndrome. As long as the applicant did not drink alcohol, those abnormalities did not affect his criminal responsibility as he was able to control his aggression. But combined with the consumption of alcohol, they led to the applicant's criminal responsibility being diminished. The court endorsed the experts’ finding that the applicant’s personality disorder could no longer be treated because his sexually deviant aggressive behaviour had lasted for decades. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing the applicant in preventive detention. The Lüneburg Regional Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention at regular intervals. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication. The court had consulted the Celle Prison authorities and the prosecution as well as his counsel, who represented him throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts. By 11 June 2011 he had served ten years in preventive detention. It was only following the entry into force of the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act on 31 January 1998 (see paragraph 51 below) that the courts responsible for the execution of sentences could prolong preventive detention without any maximum duration. An external psychiatric expert it had consulted, in his report dated 8 June 2013, confirmed the findings made by a number of previous experts. Expert W. had confirmed that the applicant suffered from sexual sadism, a sexual deviance, and was addicted to alcohol, even though he had not drunk since being detained. The Regional Court found that, as required by section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, there was still a very high risk that, owing to specific circumstances relating to his personality and his conduct, the applicant would if released commit the most serious sexually motivated violent offences, similar to those of which he had been convicted. The court found that that order was necessary to guarantee the applicant sufficient care while in preventive detention. Expert W. had stressed – as he had already done in 2012 – that the prison authorities must at least attempt to treat the applicant, who was willing to undergo treatment with medication. The anti-hormonal therapy to be offered had proved to diminish sadistic fantasies and the libido, and could therefore reduce the applicant’s dangerousness. On 2 September 2013 the Celle Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. Endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, it confirmed that the requirements laid down in section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code had been met. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the decisions of the Lüneburg Regional Court and the Celle Court of Appeal. He claimed that the order for the continuation of his preventive detention violated his constitutional right to liberty, read in conjunction with the right to protection of legitimate expectations guaranteed in a State governed by the rule of law. On 29 October 2013 the Federal. Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file. no. 2 BvR 2182/13). The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 7 November 2013. The decision of the Federal constitutional Court is published in full here. The applicant had been held in preventive detention in a wing of Celle Prison. He had stopped attending a group for addicts and refused to take medication to reduce his libido for fear of side effects. Since 2 June 2013 the applicant has been detained in the new Rosdorf centre for mental health. The conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention prior to the period of detention at issue are outlined below. The applicant is currently being held under the Therapy Detention Act. The application is based on a ruling made by the Celle Court of Appeal on 31 January 2012 that detention under that Act could only be ordered once the preventive detention of the person concerned had been terminated. The conception of preventive detention in the centre was developed in order to comply with the constitutional requirement to differentiate between preventive detention and imprisonment. Detainees are placed in apartment units measuring some 23 square metres containing two furnished rooms and a bathroom. The rooms are equipped with a controlled access to the internet including e-mail, telephone, television, CD and DVD player and radio. There are common rooms for residential groups consisting of some seven detainees, which include a kitchen, a dining room, a television room and rooms for games, handicraft work and exercise. The outdoor premises, measuring some 1,600 square metres, can be used for sports, recreation or gardening. Persons in preventive detention may work, but are not obliged to do so. The applicant stopped attending group sessions aimed at preventing detainees from relapsing into excessive alcohol consumption. He also regularly participated in group sessions at which detainees discussed their experiences during leave from detention. He did not take part in any structured leisure activities and spent most of his day alone watching television. He refused regular and repeated offers to start a treatment with medication to reduce his libido, which had been recommended by expert W. in 2013, for fear of side effects. In December 2014 he showed willing for the first time to take up such treatment. He proved reliable while on leave from the detention centre under escort on a number of occasions.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. It originated in an application (no. 10842/84) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Commission sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13, 17 and 18 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Article 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: Mr H. Corell, Ambassador, Under-Secretary for Legal and Consular Affairs, Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr S. Tell, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Housing and Planning. Mr Gaukur Jörundsson, Delegate; Mr U. Brunfelter, Lawyer, Mr G. Petrén, former Justice of the Supreme Administrative Court. Mr L. Magnusson, Land Surveyor, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government and Mr Gau kur Jocur Jokur for the Commission as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant bought a property of 2,644 m², Salem 23:1, in the centre of Rönninge in the municipality of Salem. The property was covered by a building prohibition and an area plan adopted in 1972. The ban was issued by the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen, “the Board’) of the Stockholm County on 21 September 1965. The last decision was taken on 11 July 1985 and was valid until 11 July 1987. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987 (Plan - och Bygglagen, ‘the 1987 Act’), the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one (see paragraphs 44-45 below). The applicant also complained to the Parliamentary Ombudsman (justitieombudsmannen, JO) who replied in March 1976. The applicant was denied an exemption from the building prohibition. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. The Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. On 6 June 1983 the Board decided to prolong the building ban for the area in question. In April 1983 the Building Committee wanted to revoke the right of the newly created municipality Rönninge to build on its land. On 23 March 1984 the Board rejected this request, citing changes in the objectives of the planning procedure as a result of the changes of municipal organisation which have occurred during the time of prohibition. The applicant’s property is situated in an area which should be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. On 13 February 1984 the Municipal Council (kommunstyrelsen) adopted an area programme according to which the planning procedure should be given priority. On 11 July 1984 the Board decided to issue a further building prohibition for the area in question. In the decision it was noted that the Municipality planned to carry out certain work during 1984 for the purposes of establishing the necessary plans. The applicant appealed to the Government, which rejected the appeal on 8 November 1984, referring to the on-going planning work. On 24 April 1986 the Government quashed the Board's decision, holding that the Committee's opinion was not a binding decision. The application was made on 10 July 1987. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision on the request for a period of two years. The building permit application was granted on 24 July 1987, but only for a preliminary opinion. The application was for a single or multi-family house development. According to the Government, this is the last step of the preparatory work in the making of a town plan. The approval was granted and the application was approved on 26 July 1987 for construction of a house. The applicant's application was rejected on 31 July 1987 and he applied for a new building permit.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. It originated in an application (no. 10842/84) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Commission sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13, 17 and 18. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government and Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and Mr Tullberg, Mr Petrén and Mr Magnusson for the applicant as well as their replies to its questions. At the hearing both the Agent of the government and the representative of the applicant filed a number of documents. The applicant bought a property of 2,644 m², Salem 23:1, in the centre of Rönninge in the municipality of Salem, a suburb about 20 kilometres south west of Stockholm. The property was also covered by an area plan (områdesplan - see paragraph 26 below), adopted in 1972, which described the property as a public area containing green spaces, streets and car parking. The first building prohibition under section 35 of the 1947 Act covering the applicant’s property was issued by the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen, “the Board’) of the Stockholm County on 21 September 1965. The last decision was taken on 11 July 1985 and was valid until 11 July 1987. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one (see paragraphs 44-45 below). The applicant’s property was supposed to be used for building blocks of flats of more than two storeys. The applicant appealed to the Board claiming that the building prohibition was not valid. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. In April 1983 the Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. In March 1984 the Board rejected this request, stating inter alia that the Board finds that a revocation is not justified. The long duration of the [building] prohibition depends to a large extent on changes in the objectives of the planning procedure which have occurred twice during the time of prohibition. The applicant's property is situated in an area to be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. In 1983 the Municipal Council adopted a building programme to the same effect. On 12 June 1984 the Building Committee stated that it would not be prepared to grant any building permit in view of the existing building prohibition. The applicant appealed to the Board, arguing inter alia that the building prohibition covering his property had ceased to be effective on 6 June 1984. The property was covered by an area plan (områdesplan - see paragraph 26 below), adopted in 1972, and by a building prohibition pursuant to the 1947 Building Act. The first building prohibition under section 35 of the 1947 Act covering the applicant’s property was issued on 21 September 1965 and was valid for one year. This prohibition has subsequently been prolonged by the Board for one or two years each time, leaving the property unaffected for only a few brief intermediate periods. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one (see paragraphs 44-45 below). The applicant’s property is situated in an area that should be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. The applicant appealed to the Government which rejected the appeal on 15 December 1983. In the decision it was noted that the Municipality planned to carry out certain work during 1984 for the purposes of establishing the necessary plans. In a decision of 21 August 1984, the Building Committee conceded that a mistake had been made and quashed its decision of 12 June. The building committee decided to defer the decision for two years (see paragraphs 45 and 46 below). name: Marianna Cieślak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32098/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant, Ms Marianna Cieślak, is a Polish national who was born in 1923 and lives in Bobolice, Poland. The case was heard on 27 September 2007 and a decision was made to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The court ruled in favour of the applicant. Two plaintiffs lodged with the Warsaw District Court a claim for repossession of the expropriated land. The case was transmitted to the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) The Polish Allotment Association appealed. The applicant appealed. On 20 December 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. On 15 June 2006 it issued a writ of enforcement. The court held that the 2004 Act had legal effect from its date of entry into force. It found that there had been no breach of the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time in the period after 17 September 2004. The judge also held that there was no inactivity or undue delay.

train_texts: The case originated in applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was dismissed on 31 January 2003 on the grounds that the Turkish Government had not adequately explained its position on the application. The ECHR ruled that the application was not admissible and dismissed it again on 31 March 2004. The case was referred to the 6th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court where the criminal. proceedings against Mr Ketenoghlu are still pending.

name: Robert Głowacki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1608/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Leszek Robert Głowacki (“the applicant’), on 27 December 2007. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 3 of the. Convention on account of the imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime on him. He further complained about the length of criminal proceedings against him. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was arrested on 18 May 2007. He was placed in the Warsaw Białołęka Detention Centre. On 22 September 2009 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted the applicant of armed robbery, burglary and causing serious bodily harm and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. On 10 April 2010, at the applicant’s request, the detention was lifted and he was released from custody. The applicant lodged an appeal against the last of those decisions on 6 March 2010. He is still serving the prison sentence imposed on 2 March 2011. He did not appeal against this decision. The last of the decisions to keep him in custody was made on 26 September and 22 December 2008. The authorities relied on the original grounds given for keeping him in prison. The applicant was convicted of armed robbery and using fake police uniforms. He was sentenced to seven years and six months in prison. His application for release and appeals against refusals to release him were unsuccessful. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw Regional Court had been excessive, and also sought an award of just satisfaction. The court considered that there had been no significant delays in the proceedings, as the applicant had contributed to the Length of the Proceedings. The Court of Appeal gave a decision and dismissed the applicant’s complaint on 15 December 2009. The application was dismissed and the applicant was released from custody. The Warsaw Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission classified the applicant as a ‘dangerous detainee’ The commission considered that it was necessary to place the applicant in solitary confinement as he had been charged with numerous offences, including armed robbery. The applicant appealed to the penitentiary courts against most of those decisions, arguing that he was suffering from various health problems including hemiparesis and discopathy. The courts gave decisions on 26 May, 29 August and 17 October 2008, 15 April and 24 June 2009, and 4 March 2010. In particular they stressed the risk posed by the seriousness of the offences and the use of weapons and fake police uniforms. The applicant argued that the living conditions in the detention centres in which he was detained were inadequate. The Government submitted that after his initial complaint the applicant had, in direct conversation with the prison authorities, agreed to be held in solitary confinement. The applicant failed to lodge a claim for compensation for damage to his health sustained as a result of inadequate conditions of detention. He was granted leave to attend his mother’s funeral on 8 May 2009. On 29 June 2009 and 2 November 2009 his sister and son visited him on average once a month. The majority of these visits lasted one hour. Between 28 October 2008 and 4 June 2009 he was not visited by anyone.

name: Bernd Karl Baumann
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33592/96) against France lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 21 July 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr F. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 14 March 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 14 November 2000. O.H., who had come to take delivery of the stolen vehicle, and S.B, who had handled it, were arrested. The on-the-spot investigation established that other transactions had taken place and that the two arrested men used to meet in a hotel in Brumath (Bas-Rhin) The investigators seized a German passport in the applicant's name, 7,700 German marks (DEM) and 2,150 French francs (FRF) The applicant's lawyer lodged an application under Article 99 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 6 December 1993, requesting the investigating judge to return the money and other seized items, including the passport. In a letter of 29 April 1996 she renewed her request, stating among other things: “my ex-boyfriend has put me in a difficult position which has seriously changed my life ... I have incurred debts because of him ... it is very important for me to recover my money...”

name: Rajko Medenica
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20491/92) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Assize Court of the Canton of Geneva had tried and convicted him in absentia, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. By a decision of 16 December 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. After consulting the parties, the Court decided to dispense with a hearing of the merits of the case. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant was accused of causing Yugoslavia’s welfare institutions to sustain substantial losses with the complicity of an official at the consulate of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva. He was arrested on 27 October 1982 and charged with fraud, intimidation and forging documents. On 1 February 1984 the applicant paid the stipulated sum and was released. He then travelled to the United States of America, where he acquired American nationality and practised as a doctor specialising in the treatment of certain serious forms of cancer. The case might be set down for trial between January and May 1989. At a hearing on 27 September 1988 the President of the Assize Court informed the parties that the trial would commence on 17 April 1989. A Swiss man accused of failing to attend a trial in Switzerland. The Swiss authorities were given 60 days to respond to an American court order. The applicant was ordered to find replacement doctors for his patients. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the United States of America and requiring him to surrender his passport. The trial at the Canton of Geneva Assize Court began on 17 April 1989. The judge refused to adjourn the trial, holding that the applicant had been absent without good cause. After the hearing he returned to the U.S. after the hearing and the case was adjourned. The President noted that the American order had been made largely in reliance on evidence from the applicant’s patients, in other words on information of no scientific weight. The applicant had consistently benefited over a number of years from the support of American figures who were highly influential in South Carolina. The Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. It also made an order excluding him from Swiss territory for ten years. The President observed that the decision appeared very favourable to the applicant, who had not appealed against it. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Court of Cassation in 1991. The Court of Justice had dismissed his application for relief on the grounds that he was 'irresponsible' and that without his care the patients would be certain to die. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun. On 8 March 1990 the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina set aside the order of 28 March 1989 and ordered the return of the applicant’s passport. It held that the argument concerning the refusal to remit the case had been conclusively disposed of. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He alleged a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant’s absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure. The applicant could not avoid his obligation to appear before the Swiss courts by relying on a decision that was ultimately based on equivocal and even knowingly inaccurate statements. The applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States. In the Federal Court’s opinion, it was possible to infer from the foregoing that it was the applicant's own fault that he had been unable to attend his trial. At the hearing one of the lawyers for the defence indicated that he envisaged making ‘an application for an adjournment of the trial’ One of the applicant’s American patients applied to the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, Charleston Division, for orders requiring the applicant to continue to treat him until he could be replaced by another doctor. He maintained that his life would be in danger if there were any interruption in the treatment he was receiving from the applicant. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the U.S. and requiring him to surrender his passport. The Swiss authorities, including the Principal Public Prosecutor of the Canton of Geneva, were given sixty days in which to respond. The applicant confirmed that he would attend the trial. The applicant had known for a long time that he would stand trial. He had been told the approximate date of his trial in June 1988 and the exact date in September 1988 and it had accordingly been his duty as a doctor to ensure that there was a replacement for him if he really wished to appear for trial. The applicant lodged an application with the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina to have the restraining order of 28 March 1989 set aside. In a judgment of 26 May 1989 the Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure. He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his application for an adjournment had been dismissed. name: Nigar Gözüm
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8, taken separately or together with Article 14, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) On 9 November 2010 she applied to the registry office for the registration of her forename as that of the mother of E., relying on the new Regulation. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative change.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55434/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand pending his trial by court martial was in breach of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. By a decision of 25 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court ruled that the application was admissible and that the Government had not breached the Convention. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955’ A short note by the CO (“referred to Higher Authority”) constitutes the sole record before the Court of that hearing. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. The applicant was given a four-page document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him immediately thereafter. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. On 22 February 2000 the CO of the MCTC released the applicant from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. He was initially orally informed that the review would take place on 15 February 2000 but was then informed on 16 February 2000 that thereview had not taken place. On 2 March 2000, the same CO swore an affidavit setting out the reasons for the applicant's release. The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. The judge ruled that the interests of justice could be met by releasing the Applicant into open arrest despite the allegation against him being that he had committed rape and indecent assault. He also ruled that there was evidence that he, with others, concocted a story and interfered with a witness.

The applicant was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment and stripped of all his civil, civic and family rights for ten years. Fabrice Gardel was convicted of sexual abuse of a minor under the age of 15 by a person in authority. Gardel applied to the Créteil Post‑sentencing Court to have his sentence suspended. The application was refused on the grounds that, according to the expert medical reports, ‘the applicant’s survival is not in doubt, nor is his state of health incompatible in the long term with detention’ Gardel also suffered from congenital heart disease which made any physical activity impossible. The court also referred to a psychiatric expert report from November 2004 according to which the applicant's psychological development ‘appears very limited’ I acknowledge having been informed that: I have been finally convicted of an offence carrying a sentence of ten years or more. I am required to provide proof of my address by reporting in person every six months. Failure to comply with these obligations is punishable by a term of two years’ imprisonment and a fine of 30,000 euros. I take note of the fact that if I leave the country my obligation to report in person will be suspended for the duration of my stay abroad but that I must continue to provideProof of my addresses by means of a registered letter with recorded delivery to the authority managing the Sex Offenders Register. I further acknowledge that I have the following rights: (i) under the Data Protection Act and Article 706-53-9, I may obtain a copy of all the information concerning me in the register. “If the decision forming the basis for my placement on the register was issued by a foreign judicial authority, I may apply to the public prosecutor at the Nantes tribunal de grande instance to have the information in the register rectified or deleted,” he said. “I may also have the frequency of reporting reduced to once a year, in accordance with Articles R 53-8-27 et. seq. by applying to thepublic prosecutor in whose district I am resident,’ he added. ‘I can also ask for the information to be rectified, deleted or to be reduced in frequency.’

The first applicant on 27 November 1996 complained about the delays in the processing of his application. On 18 February 2000, NIPo informed the first applicant that, although the application had been received on time, it maintained its decision to shelve the application because he had not met the substantive requirements indicated to him on 9 May 1994. The required tests were therefore superfluous, in his view, according to the applicant. NIPO refused the application on the ground that the applicant had not made it probable that the subject-matter of the application had the alleged technical effect. NIPO informed the first applicant on 30 August 2001 that it had annulled its decision to discontinue the matter and gave him until 28 February 2002 to respond to its letter of 5 May 1999. The Board of Appeals took a different view and indicated a new formulation of the patent claims which might lead to a patent, but only for sea vessels. By a decision of 14 November 2005, the Board of. NIPO asked the Military Supreme Command whether the application should be kept secret on national security grounds, which the latter answered in the negative in March 1993. The first applicant on 27 November 1996 complained about the delays in the processing of his application. On the ground of the first applicant’s. failure to comply with the time-limit of 5 November 1999, NIPo decided to discontinue (henlegge) its examination of his. application under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. Upon reconsideration of the matter, Nipo informed the first. applicant on 18 February 2000 that, although the application had been received on time, it maintained its decision to shelve the application. because he had not met the substantive requirements indicated to him on. The first applicant applied for a patent on 5 May 1999. NIPO refused the application on 2 October 2001. The first applicant appealed to the Board of Appeals (Patentstyrets annen avdeling) on 27 November 2001. By a decision of 14 November 2005, the Board concluded that the invention in application no. 19905214 had a technical effect, but the Board did not consider whether other patent requirements had been fulfilled. Thereafter, mostly both applicants, occasionally only the first applicant, acted as claimants in the relevant proceedings (to simplify “applicants” is used in the following). The applicants had received information about the patentability of their claims. The applicants, represented by Mr. H. Berge, filed a new complaint to the Parliamentary Ombudsman on 13 March 2006 concerning the proceedings before NIPO. On 29 November 2007, they were informed that the Board, after having examined the case, had found it clear that the conditions for granting a patent had not been fulfilled in so far as concerned aircrafts. The application might succeed in respect of a more limited field of sea vessels. In the alternative, the part of the application that related to air transport might be disjoined from that which related to sea transport. The applicants were given until 29 January 2008 to comment and were warned that the case might be determined on the basis of the case-file as it stood as at that date. The applicants had been advised that in order to succeed, the patent requirements would have to be defined so as to exclude aviation but had not been willing to do so. The application as presented did therefore not fulfil the conditions for grant of patent. On 22 September 2008 the Board of Appeals confirmed NIPO’s refusal of the patent requested (see paragraph 25 above), albeit on a different reasoning. Unlike NIPo, the board of Appeals found that the application could have succeeded in a limited area of sea transport. The invention was based on additional features that had made the invention patentable. from no. 19905214. When comparing the EPO patent claims with no.19905214, one would observe that the former had been based on more features that made the Invention patentable in the first place. This was not the case in the case of the second invention, which was not based on any new features. The invention was in fact based on a previous invention that was not patentable at the time of the first patent, but was later deemed patentable by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) in the second patent.

name: Anders Fredin
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 13 April 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) The Government of the Kingdom of Sweden (‘the Government’), within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 September 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Trechsel and Mr Axelsson, as well as replies to a question put by it. Mr Fredin applied for a special extraction permit, so that he could continue to extract gravel from the pit. The revocation of the permit, and the lack of a court remedy against this and a related measure, gave rise to an earlier case before the Court, which held in a judgment of 18 February 1991 (Series A no. 192) that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1. The application was dismissed by the Board on 14 March 1989. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was rejected by the Government on 21 June 1989. The Supreme Administrative Court, sitting with five judges, dismissed the latter request by three votes to two, finding that there were no grounds under section 9 of the Administrative Procedure Act 1971 for holding a hearing. As to the merits, on the basis of written observations submitted by the. applicant and the County Administrative Board, it concluded unanimously that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. The case has been referred to as the 'Swedish pit case' and has been described as 'one of the most significant environmental decisions in the history of Sweden' It was not possible under Swedish law for the applicant to appeal from the Supreme Administrative Court’s decision of 13 December 1990. They noted that certain essential points of MrFredin's case remained unclear, since there was disagreement as to whether the above-mentioned restoration plan required the further extraction of gravel from the pit.

name: Altan Karakullukçu
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr Ç. Hasdemir, a lawyer practising in İstanbul. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 21 October 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the process to the Government. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court on 1 November 2004. It was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant appealed against the decision and requested the suspension of the execution of the judgment. The Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on 16 November 1995. The Istanbul Administrative Court awarded the applicant an amount of compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage with legal interest running from 18 February 1992. On 18 September 2000 the applicant was paid the due amount of compensatory damages. The case-file was sent to an expert. The expert submitted its report to the Court on 29 December 1998. On 30 April 1999 the judgment became final. The applicant was ordered to pay compensation to the Turkish authorities.

It found that even though the car was used by somebody else the applicant, as the registered owner has to check that the car undergoes regular inspections. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court in which he complained, inter alia, that the IAP had convicted him in absentia. The Administrative Court refused to deal with the complaint under section 33a of the Administrative Court Act since the amount of the penalty did not exceed EUR 750 and no important legal issue was at stake. name: Adnan Khurshid Mustafa
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10. The applicants were represented by Mr U. Isaksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm, and by Ms S. Wikström, lawyers of the Stockholm Tenants' Association. The Swedish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C.-H Ehrenkrona, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. Landlord initiated proceedings before the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. Landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. Tenants' Association examined the installation on 26 August 2004. Engineer found that it was very stable but recommended that, for safety reasons, a steel wire be fixed between the dish and the stand. The applicants made the recommended addition. They claimed that they had now complied with the landlord's demand that the earlier satellite installation be dismantled. Landlord's liability for damage to persons and property could not reasonably be incurred unless it were able to prevent the mounting and use of the satellite dish. Landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code, to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. It concluded, contrary to the findings of the Rent Review Board, that its placement breached Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants had been fully aware of the importance that the landlord attached to the issue of the placement of satellite dishes and of the consequences that could follow from a refusal to comply with the landlord's instructions. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord that order and good custom be upheld. The first applicant now had much longer and costlier trips to and from work.

The applicants claimed that, by mounting satellite dishes for the reception of television programmes, some of which were broadcast in their mother tongues, they were exercising their freedom to receive information, as protected by the Swedish Constitution, Article 10 of the Convention and EC law. The new installation was, they claimed, in conformity with the rules of the tenants' tenancy agreement and complied with the landlord's demand that the earlier satellite installation be dismantled. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code, to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended, pursuant to Chapter 12,. section 46, subsection 1(1) of the Rent Review Board's decision on 21 October 2004. The first applicant now had much longer and costlier trips to and from work and the applicants' three children had had to change nursery and school.

name: Wiesław Chodecki
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 10 August 1998. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Sosnowiec. On 12 June 1994 he was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. He was charged with homicide and remanded in custody until 12 August 1994 in connection with the investigation against him. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant was detained on remand from July 1994 until 12 September 1994. The Sosnowiec District Court ordered that two psychiatric reports be obtained in order to establish the applicant’s criminal responsibility. On 28 March 1996 the Katowice Regional Court gave judgment. The court convicted the applicant as charged, and sentenced him to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 30 May 1996 the applicant appealed. The hearing scheduled for 17 February 1998 was adjourned. The case was remitted for re-examination. The applicant was released on 1 June 1998. The trial court held hearings on 10 December 1996, 27 February, 28 February, 26 March, 30 April, 8 May and 28 October 1997, as well as 14 and 22 January 1998. The applicant was convicted of homicide and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. The Katowice Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 29 January 1999 in view of the applicant's conviction and sentence the month before. The applicant challenged that decision before a court which did not have the necessary jurisdiction. On 6 March 2000 the Supreme Court dismissed that appeal. The matter was transferred to the Katowice Court of Appeal, which on 25 February 1999 dismissed both of his appeals. The case was later referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which dismissed the appeal in March 2000. The appeal was subsequently dismissed.

name: Mustafa Tamamboğa
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1636/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr M.A. Altunkalem, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 6 June 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants were sentenced to life imprisonment on 29 July 1997. On 14 July 1997 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment in respect of fourteen of the accused, including the applicants. The applicants failed to attend some of the hearings. At each hearing the court, relying on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence and the content of the case-file, decided to prolong their remand in custody. The judges dealt with procedural matters and adjourned many hearings, since one of the co-accused could not be found and the statements of another one residing in Germany couldn't be taken. The court also considered releasing the applicants pending trial both ex officio as well as upon their own requests. The first applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to 12 years and six months' imprisonment. On 17 March 2003 the Court of Cassation upheld this judgment. By an additional judgment, the first applicant's sentence was reduced to six years and three months's imprisonment on 22 June 2005. The applicant was given time to prepare his observations on the merits. The court, taking into account the amount of time the first. applicant had spent in remand in custody, ordered his release pending trial. The judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge, sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. The first applicant has since been released from prison.

name: Kristina Sheffield
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court as two separate cases (Sheffield v. the United Kingdom and Horsham v the United UK) by the European Commission of Human Rights on 4 March 1997. The object of the requests was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the cases disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). On 19 March 1997 the then President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, decided, under Rule 21 § 7, that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both cases simultaneously. Joint hearing of both cases took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 February 1998. The Court decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, together with the other members and the four substitutes of the original Chamber, the latter being Mr P. van Dijk, Mr V. Butkevych, Mr J. Casadevall and Mr A. Spielmann (Rule 51):. Pantiru. . Pantiru (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 5). The first applicant, Miss Kristina Sheffield, is a British citizen born in 1946 and currently resident in London. At birth the applicant was registered as being of the male sex. Prior to her gender reassignment treatment (see paragraph 13 below) she was married. She has one daughter from that marriage, which is now dissolved. She states that she was required to obtain a divorce as a precondition to surgery being carried out. Following the divorce, the applicant’s former spouse applied to the court to have her contact with her daughter terminated. The applicant states that the judge granted the application on the basis that contact with a transsexual would not be allowed. Her new name has been entered on her passport and driving licence, but her birth certificate and various records including social- security and police records continue to record her original name and gender. She was dismissed by her employers in 1986 as a direct consequence of her gender reassignment and has found it impossible to obtain employment in the respondent State in her chosen profession. She also notes that she is obliged under the Perjury Act 1911 to disclose her former sexual identity in certain contexts under pain of criminal sanction. The applicant maintains that her decision to undergo gender. reassignment surgery has resulted in her being subjected to. discrimination at work or in relation to obtaining work. She is a pilot by profession. The second applicant, Miss Rachel Horsham, is a British citizen born in 1946. She has been living in the Netherlands since 1974 and acquired Netherlands citizenship by naturalisation in September 1993. The second applicant was registered at birth as being of the male sex. She left the United Kingdom in 1971 as she was concerned about the consequences of being identified as a transsexual. Thereafter she led her life abroad as a female. She underwent gender reassignment surgery on 21 May 1992 at the Free University Hospital, Amsterdam. She states that she is forced to live in exile because of the legal situation in the United UK. She plans to marry her male partner but has been informed by the OPCS that as a matter of English law she would be precluded from contracting a valid marriage. Under English law, marriage is defined as the voluntary union between a man and a woman. Under section 11(b) of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 any marriage where the parties are not respectively male and female is void. The sex of the child must be entered on the birth certificate. The criteria for determining the sex of a child at birth are not defined in the Act. The practice of the Registrar is to use exclusively the biological criteria (chromosomal, gonadal and genital) as laid down by Mr Justice Ormrod in the above-mentioned case of Corbett v. Corbett. A birth certificate accordingly constitutes a document revealing not current identity but historical facts. The 1953 Act provides for the correction by the Registrar of clerical errors or factual errors. The official position is that an amendment may only be made if the error occurred when the birth was registered. No error is accepted to exist in the birth entry of a person who undergoes medical and surgical treatment to enable that person to assume the role of the opposite sex. A transsexual continues to be recorded for social security, national insurance and employment purposes as being of the sex recorded at birth. A male-to-female transsexual will accordingly only be entitled to a State pension at the State retirement age of 65 and not the age of 60 which is applicable to women. The ruling of the ECJ was applied by the Employment Appeal Tribunal in a decision handed down on 27 June 1997 (Chessington World of Adventures Ltd v. Reed [1997] 1 Industrial Law Reports) The majority of member States now make provision for such recognition. Out of thirty-seven countries analysed, only four do not permit a change to be made to a person’s birth certificate in one form or another to reflect the re-assigned sex of that person. To tolerate such discrimination would be tantamount, as regards such a person, to a failure to respect the dignity and freedom to which he or she is entitled and which the Court has a duty to safeguard. The full text of the Commission’s opinions in the two cases and of the dissenting opinions contained in the reports is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The applicants in their joint memorial requested the Court to decide and declare that the facts of the case disclose a breach of their rights under Article 8 of the Convention and/or Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8, and to award them just satisfaction under Article 50. The Government requested the court to declare that there had been no breach of the applicants’ rights. The Court declared the facts to be in accordance with those requested by the Government (i. animously).

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 51279/99) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, a violation of their freedom of expression. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The Government, but not the applicants, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application partly admissible on 4 September 2001. The European Commission requested the Observatoire géopolitique des drogues (OGD) to prepare a report on drug production and trafficking in Morocco in 1994. The Commission asked the Observatory for a revised version of the report, with the names of the drug traffickers deleted. The report contained twelve chapters with the following titles. It related how, over a period of ten years, there had been a tenfold increase in the area of land that had historically been used for cannabis production in the region of Er Rif. The current levels of production made “the sharif kingdom a serious contender for the title of the world’s leading exporter of cannabis”. It was published in a book sold by the OGD entitled Etat des drogues, drogue des Etats (“State of drugs, drugs of States”) and containing a chapter on Morocco. Le Monde reported that Morocco had become the world’s leading cannabis exporter. The report casts doubt on the sharif authorities’ determination to put an end to the trafficking, despite the ‘war on drugs’ they declared in a blaze of publicity in the autumn of 1992. Corruption guarantees the drug-trafficking rings the protection of officials ‘ranging from the humblest customs officer to the King's inner circle ...’ The King of Morocco made an official request to the French Minister of Foreign Affairs for criminal proceedings to be instituted against Le Monde. Mr Colombani and Mr Incyan were summoned to appear in the Paris Criminal Court on charges of insulting a foreign head of State. Le Monde found guilty of insulting a foreign head of State and sentenced to fines of 5,000 French francs (FRF) Each. They were ordered to pay King Hassan II, who had successfully applied to be joined as a civil party to the proceedings, FRF 1 in damages and FRF 10,000 pursuant to Article 475-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal also ordered Le Monde to make additional reparation in the form of a report publishing details of the convictions. The applicants appealed on points of law against that judgment. In a judgment of 20 October 1998, the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed their appeal, approving the court of Appeal’s view that “what [made] the article insulting [was] the suspicion with which the King of Morocco's determination to put an end to drug trafficking in Morocco was viewed” Court of Appeal found that the charge of duplicity had been repeated twice and that the insistence on drawing the reader’s attention to the King in person was tainted with malicious intent. The article portrayed Morocco as the world's leading hashish exporter and alleged direct responsibility on the part of the Moroccan government and members of the royal family. The charge that pernicious statements had been made to dramatic effect solely in order to preserve the country's image’ was found to be ‘pernicious’ and ‘unsubstantiated’ by the Court of Appeal. The court found that ‘the charge that [the article] was made to preserve [Moroccan] image was unfounded’.

name: Jadwiga Hulewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35656/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The decision was made by the Court of Justice. The applicant twice requested the Minister of Justice to grant her leave to file an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court. Her first request was rejected on 10 October 1994. Her second request was granted on 31 January 1997. The Supreme Court quashed both judgments given in the applicant’s case and remitted the case to the court of first instance. It held that the lower courts had committed serious errors of fact and law. The Lębork District Court joined the applicant's case with similar proceedings against seven other members of the co‑operative. On 29 December 1998 the Słupsk Regional Court rejected her appeal. On 1 March 2002 the District Court gave judgment. On 8 April 2002 the applicant appealed against this judgment.

name: Fatma Ormancı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43647/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants were represented by Mr Dinçer Söğütlü, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. By a decision of 27 November 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The decision was made by the European Court of Human rights (ECH) in Strasbourg, France, on 8 November 2005. The outcome of the case will be published in a book of the same name, The Case of the Applicants: The Case for Human Rights in Turkey. The case was notified to the defendant on 29 April 1992. The court awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary and pecuniary damage together with interest from the date of the action. The defendant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision of the Gaziantep Administrative Court on 9 December 1996. The case was adjourned until 20 December 1996 when it was decided that the applicants should pay the necessary fee for the communication of the decision to the parties. The applicant's husband A.O. was killed in July 1992. He was found dead in his home in the town of Ormancı, in the province of Elbistan. The applicants' husband was killed by a bullet to the head. The applicants submitted their observations to the Supreme Administrative Court on 13 February 1997. The case was allocated to the 10th Division. of the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The applicants were paid the amount awarded to them on 5 November 1997 and 30 April 1998. The application was rejected on 10 March 1998 by the first-instance court. The appeal was dismissed on 9 March 1998. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org for details. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 27 November 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was transferred to the newly composed Second Section. The case was notified to the defendant on 28 May 1992. The Ankara Administrative Court declared itself incompetent ratione loci and sent the case file to the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The court also appointed an expert to calculate the amount of pecuniary damage the applicants had sustained as a result of the death of A.O. The applicants paid an advance on the court fees. the court awarded the applicants compensation for non-pecuniary and pec uniary damage together with interest from the date of the action. The defendant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision. The decision was made on 27 September 1996. The case was allocated to the 10th Division. of the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The applicants were paid the amount awarded to them on 5 November 1997 and 30 April 1998. The case file was received by the Supreme Administrative Court on 28 March 1997. The court upheld the decision of the first-instance court on 10 March 1998 and the case was dismissed. The appeals were dismissed again on 6 July 1998 and 7 July 1998. An appeal was also heard on 6 August 1998 and 6 September 1998.
