name: Mark William Grayson
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 19955/05 and 15085/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Each applicant alleged that, in confiscation proceedings following his conviction for drugs offences, the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure, in breach of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Court decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1). The judge examined property received by the applicant during the six-year statutory period. He concluded that the applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69. The judge was further satisfied that so large a consignment would not have represented the applicant’s first venture into drug trafficking and that he had financed the purchase with the proceeds of previous drug dealing. The final item of expenditure taken into account by the judge was GBP 70,000 which an associate of the applicant, who claimed to have an income of approximately GBP 40,000 a year, had paid for the applicant's legal fees. Police had found realisable assets of GBP 236,000, including cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest, a car and some business stock. The judge observed: “The fact that the police have traced a certain amount of property is not of itself a reason to find it is the only property available to the [applicant]. Also credibility is a real issue. This Defendant is cunning, devious and intelligent. Giving evidence he sought to mislead at every turn, wary that the truth would reveal assets he didn’t want to and that he had hidden assets prior to conviction. He has lied persistently and blatantly and his credibility is nil’ Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII, and observed that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant. Court added that although the accountancy report raised a suggestion of possible double-counting by the prosecution when it came to an analysis of realisable property, that was “irrelevant, since the judge’s order did not depend upon any calculation of realizable property.” The second applicant (Mr Barnham) was convicted of two conspiracy charges involving plans to import large consignments of cannabis into the UK. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, the judge describing him as the lead organiser in a sophisticated, established and internationally based drug trafficking business. The applicant claimed to have been entirely unsuccessful in his attempts at drug dealing and to have earned a living by singing in bars. Of the total benefit figure, it was submitted that 94.4% was expenditure and the remaining 5.6% received had been dissipated over the years of the applicant’s imprisonment in Spain and Portugal and in the United Kingdom. His car, worth GBP 11,615, had also been confiscated by the Portuguese authorities. Since his conviction his wife was living with their son in England and supporting herself with a cleaning job. Judge finds that the applicant and his wife had lied about their activities and their sources of income. He made a confiscation order equal to the amount which he had assessed as the benefit, namely GBP 1,525,615, with five years, three months’ imprisonment if the applicant had not paid within 18 months. The applicant appealed against the judge’s ruling regarding his realisable assets, asserting that Article 6 of the 1994 Act was ‘inadequate’ and he should not have received the benefit. The judge ruled in favour of Mr Barnham, saying that he had made a ‘clear and cogent’ case for why the benefit was not fully realisable. Court of Appeal rejected argument that there was a difference between cases where the prosecution had proved benefit by evidence and those where the benefit had been calculated through the use of assumptions. At the second stage the burden of proof shifts to a defendant to establish, if he can, his realisable assets to the satisfaction of the court. The Court of Appeal found, however, that the judge had made an error of calculation and reduced the order to GBP 1,460,615. The expression ‘hidden assets’ is indicative of the fact that the prosecution can have no means of knowing how and where a defendant may have dealt with or disposed of his criminal activities. The Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general public importance for appeal to the House of Lords concerning Article 6 of the Convention. The appeal was brought by a member of the European Court of Human Rights. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights for review. The Court of appeal ruled that the case was not of public importance. The European Court of Human Rights found that Article 6 was a matter of "general public importance" and rejected the appeal. The European Court of Human rights found the case to be a matter of public importance and asked the House of Lords to rule.

The judge examined property received by the applicant during the six-year statutory period. He concluded that the applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69. The final item of expenditure taken into account by the judge was GBP 70,000 which an associate of the applicant, who claimed to have an income of approximately GBP 40,000 a year, had paid for the applicant's legal fees. The police had found realisable assets of GBP 236,000, including cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest, a car and some business stock. The judge observed: “The fact that the police have traced a certain amount of property is not of itself a reason to find it is the only property available to the [applicant]. Also credibility is a real issue. This Defendant is cunning, devious and intelligent. Giving evidence he sought to mislead at every turn, wary that the truth would reveal assets he didn’t want to and that he had hidden assets prior to conviction. He has lied persistently and blatantly and his credibility is nil’ The Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII, and observed that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant. The judge followed the scheme of the Act in arriving at his conclusions, and in the context of a man who was caught when engaged in importing heroin which had cost well over £1 million. The level of assets available to a defendant is normally peculiarly a matter within his own knowledge. In those circumstances, this was, we are satisfied, a large confiscation order. It was, however, one which it was plainly proper for the judge to make. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, the judge describing him as the lead organiser in a sophisticated, established and internationally based drug trafficking business. The applicant and his wife gave evidence, to the effect that their only asset was their house in Spain, which they owned jointly. Since his conviction his wife was living with their son in England and supporting herself with a cleaning job. The case was heard at the Court of Justice of the United Kingdom (CJ), which ruled in favor of the appeal. The appeal was heard in the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom (ISC), which found in favour of the appeal and the appeal was dismissed.

The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure, in breach of Article 6 of the convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Chamber decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1) The case was heard by a jury of seven judges, one of whom was the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal. The judge found that the applicant had benefited to the amount of GBP 1,230,748.69. The judge was satisfied that so large a consignment would not have represented the applicant’s first venture into drug trafficking and that he had financed the purchase with the proceeds of previous drug dealing. The largest element emerged from an analysis of 17 bank accounts which the applicant held at one time or another. The banking records demonstrated unexplained credits to the applicant's account in the two trading years ending April 1998 and April 2000 which exceeded the turnover of his business as recorded in the accounts by approximately GBP 153,000. During the intervening year, ending April 1999, the bank statements showed deposits at GBP 83,000 below the business trading turnover. Police had found realisable assets of GBP 236,000, including cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest, a car and some business stock. The judge observed: “The fact that the police have traced a certain amount of property is not of itself a reason to find it is the only property available to the [applicant]. Also credibility is a real issue. This Defendant is cunning, devious and intelligent. Giving evidence he sought to mislead at every turn, wary that the truth would reveal assets he didn’t want to and that he had hidden assets prior to conviction. He has lied persistently and blatantly and his credibility is nil’ The Court of Appeal referred to Phillips v. the United Kingdom, no. 41087/98, ECHR 2001-VII, and observed that the reverse onus of proof in relation to the statutory assumption at the calculation of the benefit stage is fully Convention compliant. The Court added that although the accountancy report raised a suggestion of possible double-counting by the prosecution when it came to an analysis of realisable property, that was “irrelevant, since the judge’s order did not depend upon any calculation of realizable property.” The second applicant (Mr Barnham) was convicted of two conspiracy charges involving plans to import large consignments of cannabis into the UK. The applicant was sentenced to eleven years’ imprisonment, the judge describing him as the lead organiser in a sophisticated, established and internationally based drug trafficking business. The applicant claimed to have been entirely unsuccessful in his attempts at drug dealing and to have earned a living by singing in bars. Since his conviction his wife was living with their son in England and supporting herself with a cleaning job. The defence submitted that there was no evidence capable of supporting a finding of assumed ‘hidden’ assets. The judge found that the applicant and his wife had lied about their activities and their sources of income. The applicant appealed against the judge’s ruling regarding his realisable assets, asserting that Article 6 of the 1994 Act was ‘unconstitutional’. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35141/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 of the. Convention in relation to the contact restrictions following the taking into public. care of her three children. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the contact. restrictions to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant herself contacted the Child and Youth Psychiatric Clinic (Barn- och ungdomspsykiatrin; hereafter “BUP”) In 2005 the applicant contacted BUP in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit (social beredskap) went to the applicant’s home, accompanied by police and a chief physician from the adult psychiatric clinic. The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water. The applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care in accordance with the Act on Compulsory Psychiatric Care (Lagen om psykiatrisk tvångsvård, 1991:1128). The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. Social Council applied to the County Administrative Court for a permanent care order in respect of all three children. The council maintained that the applicant had shown a serious lack of ability to care for her children. S. had nightmares and had been afraid of sudden movements. D. had been late in her speech and motor development. T. had no limits towards adults and wanted to control everything and everyone around her. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall. On 9 January 2006 the Administrative court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in full. The Social Council contested the appeal. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. The applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children were being deprived of contact with her. The Social Council decided to restrict the applicant’s contact rights to all three children. This meant that each parent should meet with the children once every three months in a neutral environment where the family home parents and the social worker responsible for the file should be present. The decision was based on an investigation carried out by the Social Council, in consultation with BUP, into the children’s situation. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited in order to ensure their secure and positive development. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. She could see no reason for such restricted contact and found it to be contrary to the best interests of the children as they would forget their mother. They had lived with her until May 2005 and they had had a close and warm relationship. The Social Council contested the appeal. It submitted that the children were currently in the process of developing and learning things that they had not had the opportunity to learn before. It noted that the last meeting between the applicant and her children, on 23 January 2007, had passed without incident, partly because eight adults had been present to ensure the children’s well-being. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining her claims and adding that she wished to see her children at least once a month in order to ensure that they would not forget her. She felt that the family home parents had a negative attitude towards her and that this influenced the children. Social Council observed that despite the applicant’s visits having been planned and very structured, the children had still had negative reactions before and after each meeting. The court decided to increase the applicant's contact with her children to four times per year, for four hours each time. It noted that the limited contact had been in place for roughly two years and had contributed to the children developing positively during this time. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining that she wanted contact rights with her. children during one weekend per month, without the presence of others, in order to ensure that she and the children would establish a good contact. The applicant voluntarily underwent a neuropsychological examination during two days at Stavanger University Hospital, upon request by the Social Council. The examination concluded that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) that was mainly inattentive in nature. It concluded that it would not be in the best interest of the children to increase the applicant’s contact rights further than decided by the lower court. The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. A week later, she was released from psychiatric care and returned to her home. Social Council applied to the County Administrative Court for a permanent care order in respect of all three children. The council maintained that the applicant had shown a serious lack of ability to care for her children. All three children had worn nappies when they arrived at the temporary family home, although T. only at night, and they had been dirty and had an endless appetite. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall. The Administrative Court upheld the lower court’s judgment in full on 9 January 2006. The Social Council contested the appeal but the decision of the Social Council was upheld. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. name: Alexander Findlay
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 8 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22107/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Alexander Findlay, a British citizen, on 28 May 1993. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Alexander Findlay was a member of the Scots Guards. He had served in the Falklands campaign in 1982 and was injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. He suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. His service was due to terminate in November 1992 when he would have received a resettlement grant and, at the age of sixty, an army pension. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1996. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Mackenzie and Mr Havers. The applicant, a lance-sergeant, was sent with his regiment to Northern Ireland. On 29 July 1990, after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested. On 31 July 1990 an ex-naval psychiatrist, Dr McKinnon, examined Mr Findlay and found that he was responsible for his actions at the time of the incident. However, a combination of stresses (including his back injury and posting to Northern. Ireland) together with his heavy drinking on the day, had led to an “almost inevitable“ event. The court martial consisted of a president and four other members. All of the members of the court martial were subordinate in rank to the convening officer and served in units stationed within London District. None of them had legal training. Mr Findlay was acquitted of all charges against him by the jury. He was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 10 years and a maximum of 15 years. The sentence was suspended for a period of three years and suspended for two years after the conclusion of the trial. The jury returned a verdict of acquittal, with the maximum sentence of life with a maximum term of five years. It was not possible for the jury to reach a verdict before the end of the sentence. The trial was adjourned until January 1991. Mr Findlay appeared before the general court martial, at Regent’s Park Barracks in London, on 11 November 1991. He pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence), two charges of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline (a military offence) and two counts of threatening to kill. The defence put before the court martial the medical reports referred to above (paragraphs 11-13) and called Dr Reid to give evidence. The latter confirmed his view that the applicant suffered from PTSD, that this had been the principal cause of his behaviour, and that he was in need of counselling. Mr Findlay was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, reduction. Alexander Findlay was sentenced to six months in prison and dismissal from the army. He appealed by way of petition to the first of the “reviewing authorities’ (see paragraph 49 below) On 14 December 1992 the Divisional Court refused leave to challenge the validity of the findings of the court martial. He claimed that the sentence imposed was excessive, the proceedings were contrary to the rules of natural justice and that the judge advocate had been hostile to him on two occasions during the hearing. The judge advocate's advice was not disclosed to the applicant, nor was he given reasons for the decisions confirming his sentence and rejecting his petitions. Mr Findlay commenced a civil claim in negligence against the military authorities, claiming damages in respect of his back injury and PTSD. In March 1994 the civil action was settled by the Secretary of State for Defence, who paid the applicant £100,000 and legal costs, without any admission of liability. The settlement did not differentiate between the claims inrespect of PTSD and the back injury. Mr Findlay's case was settled out of court and he was awarded £200,000. The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 8 December 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22107/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 28 May 1993. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. Alexander Findlay is a British citizen born in 1961 in Kilmarnock, Scotland, and now lives in Windsor, England. He joined the British army in 1980 and became a member of the Scots Guards. In 1982 he took part in the Falklands campaign and witnessed the death and mutilation of several of his friends. In 1987 he sustained an injury during training for service in Northern Ireland. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (“PTSD”) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. This disorder was not diagnosed until after the events of 29 July 1990 (see paragraph 10 below) The applicant, who had become a lance-sergeant, was sent with his regiment to Northern Ireland. On 29 July 1990, after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested and charged with a number of offences. The medical evidence shows that he was responsible for his actions at the time of the incident. However, a combination of stresses (including his back injury and posting to. Northern Ireland) together with his heavy drinking on the day, had led to an “almost inevitable“ event. Mr Findlay was remanded for trial on eight charges arising out of the incident of 29 July 1990. He decided that he should be tried by general court martial. The court martial consisted of a president and four other members. All of the members of the court martial were subordinate in rank to the convening officer and served in units stationed within London District. None of them had legal training. The assistant prosecuting and defending officers were both officers from the Second Scots Guards stationed in the London District and the assistant defending officer was from the Postal and Courier Department, Royal Engineers (Women’s Royal Army Corps), which is under the direct command of the Ministry of Defence. Mr Findlay pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence) and two charges of threatening to kill (a military offence) The defence put before the court martial the medical reports referred to above (paragraphs 11-13) and called Dr Reid to give evidence. The latter confirmed his view that the applicant suffered from PTSD, that this had been the principal cause of his behaviour, that he had not been responsible for his actions and that he was in need of counselling. The court martial retired to consider their decision on sentence, accompanied by the judge advocate. On their return they sentenced the applicant to two years’ imprisonment, reduction. Alexander Findlay was sentenced to a reduced term of imprisonment and dismissal from the army. No reasons were given for the sentence (see paragraph 46 below). The decision of the court martial had no effect until it was confirmed by the ‘confirming officer’ Mr Findlay petitioned him for a reduction in sentence. This petition was rejected on 10 March 1992. The applicant applied to the Divisional Court for leave to challenge by judicial review the validity of the findings. He claimed that the sentence imposed was excessive, the proceedings were contrary to the rules of natural justice and that the judge advocate had been hostile to him on two occasions during the hearing. On 14 December 1992 the Court refused leave on the basis that the court Martial had been conducted fully in accordance with the Army Act 1955. Mr Findlay commenced a civil claim in negligence against the military authorities, claiming damages in respect of his back injury and PTSD. In March 1994 the civil action was settled by the Secretary of State for Defence, who paid the applicant £100,000 and legal costs, without any admission of liability. The settlement did not differentiate between the claims inrespect of PTSD and the back injury. Mr Findlay received a payout of more than £200,000. During the battle of Mount Tumbledown he witnessed the death and mutilation of several of his friends and was himself injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (‘PTSD’) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. He was then arrested and charged with a number of offences arising out of the incident on 29 July (see paragraph 14 below). train_texts: The case originated in three applications against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was arrested in the Netherlands on 31 January 1999. He was charged with the attempted importation of 163 kilograms (compressed weight) of cocaine with a potential street value of GBP 11 million. The applicant sought to challenge the admissibility of telephone interception evidence. He ultimately pursued an appeal to the House of Lords, which delivered its judgment against the applicant on 24 March 2000. The trial subsequently commenced in the Crown Court in June 2000. After the jury had already retired to consider their verdict a prejudicial document was discovered within the jury bundle. The fault for this lay with the prosecution, a matter admitted at the time. The 1994 Act provides for the making of a confiscation order in the event of a conviction for drug trafficking offences. On 5 June 2001 the applicant was found guilty of the offences charged. On 6 June 2001 he was sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In 2004 he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. He was released from prison in February 2006 and, on 17 November 2006, he abandoned his appeal (see further paragraph 29 below) The confiscation proceedings took place between June 2001 and December 2001. The applicant was convicted of drug trafficking in June 2001. Defence counsel was unable to address the judge on the point of “exceptional circumstances’ owing to his lack of familiarity with the case. The matter was adjourned to 4 December 2001 to review progress. Defence gave notice that it wished to challenge the validity of the postponement of the confiscation hearing on the basis that the Crown Court had no jurisdiction. The judge set a timetable for the service of skeleton arguments on the jurisdiction point and fixed 14 March 2002 for legal argument on the matter. In early March, as a result of informal discussions between junior counsel for both sides regarding a case pending before the Court of Appeal, the 14 March 2001 date was vacated. In the event, the pending appeal case was subsequently conceded by the prosecution so no oral argument took place. On 22, 23 and 27 May 2002 two defence applications submitted by newly instructed leading counsel were heard. The first was to stay the confiscation proceedings on grounds of abuse of process; the second was for an order declaring that there was no jurisdiction to continue the proceedings. The judge found that the original adjournment was to afford the defence more time, that no defence response had been forthcoming to the prosecution statement and that further delay had been caused by the applicant wishing to instruct new solicitors. He found that there had been a misunderstanding between counsel as to whether any undertaking had been given and that no abuse therefore arose. Following the ruling, the confiscated proceedings were adjourned and fixed for September 2002 to allow the defence to prepare. The judge considered the applicant’s case to be distinguishable on the facts. For unknown reasons, matters proceeded more slowly than the parties had expected and the September confiscation hearing did not go ahead. A further judgment in a similar appeal was handed down by the Court of Appeal on 16 December 2002 (R v Knights (Richard Michael) and others [2002] EWCA Crim 2954). An appeal against that judgment was lodged with the House of Lords. The judge allowed a one-week adjournment to obtain an update from the judicial office of the Lords. He was reminded by the applicant that he would again need to formally postpone the confiscation Hearing. The House of Lords handed down their judgments in two jurisdiction appeals on 21 July 2005. The applicant was released from prison on 1 February 2006, having served half of his sentence. On 17 November 2006, apparently following adverse outcomes on various issues relating to his appeal, the applicant abandoned his appeal against conviction. It is unclear whether a hearing took place in September or whether further adjournments were agreed in light of the applicant’s pending appeal. The matter was listed for a hearing in late January 2007. At the hearing on 25 January 2007 it was agreed to seek suitable dates in April 2007. The prosecution served the amended statement in January 2007 and the applicant was given until the end of May to respond. A procedural hearing was agreed for 6 July 2007. On 1 November 2007 the parties appeared before the judge. The substantive hearing was listed for 20 July 2008, with a time estimate of two weeks. The judge delivered his ruling on the confiscation on 19 December 2008. He identified the total amount of the applicant’s benefit from criminal conduct as GBP 1,840,563. He found the principal realisable asset to be a farm, which was valued at GBP 690,000. A confiscation order was made with a three-year term of imprisonment to be served consecutive to the main sentence in default of payment. Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal itself. Decision upholds the confiscation order and finds no violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Now for the applicant to seek other remedies. C.I.C. of the Court of Appeal. Hearings on the merits of the appeal took place before the full court to decide on 17 March 2010. The judge ruled that the delay in disposal of the proceedings had breached the applicant’s right to a fair trial and to a trial within a reasonable time under Article 6.0. The appeal was dismissed by the court on 28 June 2010, after a hearing in which the judge agreed that the judge had erred in including the current value of the farm. Court of Appeal ruled that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in about the spring or early summer of 2002. The Court of Appeal considered that it was in the applicant’s interests to await the eventual authoritative ruling of the House of Lords. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40694/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged in particular, that the civil proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, Government's Agent. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 28 May 2002 the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The application, but not the Government, filed observations on the merits. The case was heard in the Warsaw Regional Court. The court observed that the applicant had lost the capacity to work and was disabled in the so-called second degree. On 11 April 1990 the applicant was granted the first degree status of disability (serious disability) The monthly supplementary pension was increased to 100 PLN as a result of a settlement between the parties. The case was remitted to the Warsaw District Court, as the latter had become competent following the increase of the applicant's claim. In February 1995 the applicant requested the court not to schedule any hearings in the period from 1 until 18 March 1995. The application was dismissed in May 1995. The case was heard in the Warsaw Regional Court. The parties asked for an adjournment in order to reach an out-of-court settlement. On 19 April 1995 the applicant increased the claim. On 14 November 1995 the court requested the applicant's former employer to submit certain documents. The documents were submitted on 21 November 1995. On 1 December 1995 the hearing was adjourned to give the applicant two weeks to submit his comments on the documents received by the court. The court refused and closed the hearings in the case. On 16 January 1998 the court re-opened the proceedings. The applicant requested the court to appoint a new expert. He once more challenged the expert opinion. The applicant filed an appeal against the decision of 29 December 1998. The Warsaw Court of Appeal remitted the case to the Warsaw Regional Court. The applicant requested the court to appoint a lawyer under the legal aid scheme with a view to lodging a cassation appeal. He lodged also a “personal” cassation. to be taken. The court rejected his appeal on the merits of the case for failure to comply with the procedural requirements. The judge ruled that the applicant could lodge a request to reinstate the time-limit for submitting the documents requested by the court. The appeal was dismissed on 29 April 1999 and the applicant appealed again on 30 April 1999. The applicant's appeal against the decision of 29 December 1998 was rejected on 5 August 1999. On 20 August 1999 the applicant's lawyer lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court in order to reinstate the time-limit for lodging the cassation appeal. The Supreme Court quashed the decision on 7 December 1999 for having been reached without due consideration to the applicant’s pending legal aid application. The applicant increased his claim on 12 January 2001. The judgment was served on the applicant on 8 June 2001. on 20 December 2001 the court rejected the appeal, considering that it had not been shown that arguable grounds existed which would justify the examination of the appeal.

The Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The applicant received child benefit in the sum of GBP 150.20 per month. His wife died on 6 May 1997 leaving four children, the last born in 1987. He applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. He was informed on 29 June 2000 that the Benefits Agency was unable to accept his application as a valid claim because there was at that time no legislation providing an equivalent of the widows’ benefits concerned to widowers. On 1 October 2000 the applicant made a claim for Widow’s Bereavement Tax Allowance to the Inland Revenue for the years 1997‑1999.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53911/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants run a fishing farm in Schalchen since 1976. They allege that the regulation works on a small river in the vicinity of the applicants' estate without permission under the Water Act (Wasserrechtsgesetz 1959) constituted an interference with their water-rights. On 20 June 2002 the First Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) on 13 January 1971. On 11 February 1971 the Regional Governor dismissed this request. On 3 June 1975 the District Authority held a hearing and ordered the Municipalities to take specific steps to ensure the water supply of the fishing farm before 31 December 1976. On 2 December 1975 the. Regional Governor found that their water rights were not violated by the granted permission. On 27 January 1976 the Federal Minister rejected the applicants'. predecessors' appeal as belated. Subsequently, they lodged a. request for leave to appeal out of time (Wiedereinsetzung in den vorigen Stand) on 2 April 1976. The Federal Minister granted this request and, consequently, had to take a decision on the merits on the appeal. The applicants filed an appeal against the decision to grant ex post permission for the regulation works. Several technical experts were appointed in order to establish whether the regulation. works had damaged the well. The applicants lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court as well as with the Administrative Court. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the Federal Minister on 14 October 1996. The Federal Minister had to take a decision on the merits. whether the applicants' water rights had been prejudiced by the regulationWorks. The Administrative Court quashed this decision on 6 August 1998 on the ground that the Minister had failed to take into account the expert reports submitted by the applicants. On 27 April 2000 the applicants challenged the experts appointed by the Minister for bias. The proceedings are still pending. The applicants agreed with the Federal Minister on the further conduct of the proceedings. The Federal Minister would furnish a questionnaire to the expert in order that he supplemented his report. Thereafter the applicants would be given the opportunity to comment on the revised report and another hearing would be held. The hearing is set to take place on November 17 and 18 this year. name: Peter Maxwell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 3 August 1993 by. the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision. as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach. by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c) Peter Maxwell was found guilty of assault by a Scottish jury in 1990. He was sentenced to five years in prison. Mr Maxwell was given legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. There appeared before the Court: Mr I. Christie, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord Rodger of Earlsferry, QC, Lord Advocate, Mr R. Reed, Counsel, Mr I I. Jamieson, Mr A. Dickson, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Mr Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The applicant lodged a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows. The applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him. To do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction. There had been insufficient evidence to establish that the assault had resulted in the victim’s permanent disfigurement. The appeal was adjourned until after a further adjournment of the hearing of his appeal. His legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. Mr Maxwell was granted legal aid to pay for representation at the hearing. The Board informed Mr Maxwell that his application had been refused as the Board was not satisfied, as it was required to be under the relevant legislation. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. On 21 March 1991, the applicant addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal.

The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 18949/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 March 1991. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). The applicant indicated in a letter postmarked 22 July 1993 that he did not wish to take part in the proceedings. On 17 November 1993 he submitted a claim for just satisfaction. Legal aid had been made available to the applicant for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Lord Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The applicant, Mr Peter Maxwell, is a British citizen born in 1944. He lives in Perth, Scotland. Two masked men broke into a private house, situated in Stevenston, Scotland, on 14 or 15 February 1990. They assaulted the occupant causing him severe injury and permanent disfigurement. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction. (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence; (e) his legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally and addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal on 21 March 1991. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. The Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal.

name: Krzysztof Paszkowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42643/98) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that that his pre-trial detention had been inordinately lengthy. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 8 January 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg, France. The decision is expected to be delivered by the end of this month or beginning of next month. The judge is Mr. J. Wojewódzki (“the applicant’s lawyer”). The applicant was indicted together with eleven other persons on charges of robbery and extortion. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 106 witnesses. On 26 July 1995 the applicant lodged an application for release. He submitted that his wife had been placed in a mental hospital and that their daughter had been left without care. On 18 August 1995 the Gdańsk Regional Court upheld the detention order. The court held that keeping the applicant in custody had been necessary to ensure the proper conduct of the proceedings. The Supreme Court granted the application and prolonged his and eight other co-accused’ detention until 30 June 1997. On 13 August 1997 the Supreme Court extended the applicant’s detention until 1 December 1997. The trial court still had to hear evidence from 50 witnesses. The court stressed that the case was particularly complex as it concerned several co-accused. The composition of the trial court had to be changed due to the presiding judge’s illness. On 22 October 2002 the Regional Court gave judgment. It sentenced the applicant to four years’ imprisonment. The trial court listed 31 hearings, of which 17 were cancelled or adjourned. The judge held that the detention had already been prolonged three times by the Supreme Court but to no avail, as the proceedings had still not been terminated. In his opinion, any prolongation of his further detention on remand would be tantamount to serving a prison sentence.

name: Christopher Ian Scott
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 September 1995. It originated in an application (no. 21335/93) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British national, Mr Christopher Ian Scott, on 2 September 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 paras. 1 and 3 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30) The applicant is a British citizen born in 1958. He is currently detained in Her Majesty’s Prison, Leicester. A Finnish national, Ms T., made a statement to the police in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife, Canary Islands, in which she alleged that the applicant had raped her the night before. Ms T. underwent a medical examination and on 9 March 1990 flew back to Finland. The applicant had escaped from Sudbury Prison, West Midlands, on 22 December 1989. An international warrant for his arrest for the murder of his father had been issued against him on 31 January 1990 by a judge at Birmingham Crown Court. He had a false passport and was suffering from serious alcoholic intoxication requiring medical attention. Mr Scott was arrested in Puerto de la Cruz in March 1990. A formal request for extradition was filed on 27 April 1990. The applicant denied the murder allegations and resisted extradition. The British Embassy in Madrid wrote to the Audiencia Nacional that in the applicant’s case the sentence actually served upon conviction for murder was not likely to be more than ten years. In a decision (auto) of 22 February 1991 a section of the Criminal Division of the Audiancia Nacion ordered Mr Scott to be detained pending trial. Mr Scott was sentenced to 30 years in prison in March 1991. He was released on bail. The applicant was arrested on 23 March 1990 for the murder of his father. On 7 March 1991 the investigating judge in Puerto de la Cruz extended the applicant’s detention pending trial in the rape case. On 24 June 1991 the public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be kept in detention pending his trial for rape unless he could be temporarily handed over to the United Kingdom authorities. On 6 March 1992 the British Embassy in Madrid wrote to the Audiencia Nacional indicating that his re-extradition to Spain could not be guaranteed. On 17 March 1992, taking 23 March 1992 as the date of the beginning of the applicant's detention for the rape offence, the judge ordered his provisional release (libertad provisional) He was, however, keep in detention under orders made in the extradition proceedings. The Audiencia Nacional decided to extend his detention under Article 504 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 10 (3) of the Extradition Act for a period not exceeding two years, that is until 23 March 1994. The applicant lodged an appeal (recurso de súplica) against this decision but on 18 June 1992 a full court of the Criminal Division dismissed the appeal on the ground that he had been detained in the extradition case on 23 March 1990, independently of his earlier detention for a different matter, and that the risk of his absconding was considerable. In his submissions the public prosecutor had again referred to the case pending in Puerto de la Cruz. Another application for release by the applicant on 7 September 1992 was rejected. The applicant was charged with, inter alia, rape and forgery of documents. The prosecutor sought a prison sentence of sixteen years in respect of the rape offence and a further prison sentence. In a judgment of 21 March 1994 the Audiencia Provincial of Santa Cruz de Tenerife acquitted the applicant on the rape charge on the ground that the only evidence incriminating him was Ms T’s statements, which contained many inconsistencies. With respect to the forgery offence the applicant was convicted and sentenced as charged. The applicant was handed over to the United Kingdom authorities, pursuant to the international arrest warrant and theAudiencia Nacional's decision of 22 February 1991 allowing extradition. On 9 November 1995, following a trial at Birmingham Crown Court, Mr Scott was convicted of the murder of his father. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Hard. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65507/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Glynn, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. By a partial decision of 10 September 2002 the Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. It also decided to join the application to other applications. The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Yeovil. His wife died on 17 December 1996, leaving one child born in 1991. The applicant applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. The Benefits Agency refused his claim for WMA. The appeal was then sent to the Social Security Appeals Service. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was upheld and the applicant receives child benefit in the sum of GBP 70.20 per week. However, no social security benefits were payable to widowers under the domestic law.

name: Mustafa Yalgın
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 of Protocol no. 11). The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 of the Rules of Court). The Court declared the complaints inadmissible on 11 January 2000. In 1981 the applicant was questioned by the police officers at the Ankara Security Directorate. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court, composed of two civilian judges, two military judges and an army officer, convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the killing of B.B., bomb attacks, acting as an armed look-out for several crimes and opening fire on a grocery shop. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, permanently debarred from employment in public service and placed under judicial guardianship.

name: Eie Enhorn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court decided that the application was admissible and that the Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. The decision was published in November 2004. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1987 Act. He is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for the fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. The applicant explained that before 1994 he had had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. His partners were partly old acquaintances, partly new ones, whom he met in parks and so on. The boy, who was 15 years old when they met, took the initiative both emotionally and sexually. Today [the applicant] realises that he infected the boy. While on the run, the applicant had had no sexual relations. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer.’ The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant has a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the. applicant returned to Stockholm and went to Norrköping on a few occasions in order to deal with money matters. The applicant had lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations’ A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The applicant suffers from a paranoid personality disorder and from alcohol abuse. The German Federal Bar Association (Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer) was granted leave by the Vice‑President to intervene as third party in the case. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The case was heard by the Federal Court of Justice and the German Government were represented by their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens and Mrs K. Behr. The public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He asked the bank not to reveal the request to the applicant. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. The information received was analysed by the police and the public prosecutor. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. Therefore, everyone who had access to the case file, such as the lawyers of the co‑accused, also had access. to the applicants’ banking information, including the names of his clients who had transferred. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. On 24 April 2012 the applicant asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to hand over to him all data received from the bank and destroy all related data at the public prosecution office. In his request the applicant emphasised his role as a criminal defence lawyer, which was known to the acting public prosecutor, and the consequences for his clients, whose names were accessible through the banking information. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily and that the documents could therefore only be returned to the bank. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint. It found that the decision was proportionate and that the safeguards were not applicable. The bank could not be considered a person assisting the applicant or a person involved in the professional activities of the applicant under Article 53a of the CCP (see paragraph 27 below) The judge ruled that the bank had acted voluntarily and that there had been sufficient suspicion for such an extensive analysis of his banking transactions. The judge also found that there were several safeguards in place concerning the seizure of documents (see paragraphs 26-29 below)

The German Federal Bar Association (Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer) was granted leave by the Vice‑President to intervene as third party in the case. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Germany and the jury was instructed to rule in favour of the applicant. The outcome of the case is to be decided by the Court of Appeal. Public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He based his request for information on Articles 161a, 51 and 70 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. The information received was analysed by the police and the public prosecutor. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. Therefore, everyone who had access to the case file, such as the lawyers of the co‑accused, also had access, including the names of his clients who had transferred. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily, and that the documents could therefore only be returned to the bank and not to the applicant. Nonetheless, in order to safeguard the client‑lawyer privilege, it also decided to separate the documents in question from the general court file and only grant access to them if reasons proving sufficient interest were provided. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court. It found that the decision was proportionate and that the safeguards were not applicable. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, without providing reasons (case no. 2 BvR 2268/12) On 19 September 2013 the applicant's constitutional complaint was refused to be admitted by the Federal Court of Justice. The case was heard by the Court of Appeals in Hamm on 13 September 2012. The applicant's case was decided on 15 September 2012 by the Hamm court of Appeal. The appeal was heard again on 17 September 2012 and the case was settled on 15 October 2012.

name: Ryszard Jakubczyk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17354/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) had been violated, as he had had no opportunity to examine the main witnesses in the criminal proceedings against him. On 24 April 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The case was heard on 15 January 2002. Kielce. ce Regional Court held a hearing at which the prosecutor sought to read out statements made by a certain W.P. as well as by J.K., B.S., and G.C. The applicant’s lawyer objected to this, submitting that the statements in question had been made before the Austrian courts in another set of criminal proceedings in which those individuals had been the accused. He also submitted that the Polish authorities had made no attempt to hear those individuals in Poland at the preparatory stage of the proceedings. The court based its decision on Article 587 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and others, which allowed statements by both witnesses and accused to be read out. The court found that the applicant had acted together with three accomplices. The court sentenced the applicant to nine years’ imprisonment and a fine. Some of the evidence referred to above had been collected in another set of criminal proceedings against the applicant (regarding charges severed in 2001, see paragraph 10 above) The court examined at length the results of the searches of the laboratory, which had been conducted by several experts, who had collected about 100 samples of chemical substances as well as video and photographic evidence. The written reasons of the judgment in this respect are detailed and extensive. As regards the applicant, the trial court referred to comparisons made by Polish and German experts ofchemical substances found in the laboratory to ecstasy pills. The trial court assessed the credibility of statements obtained from W.P. and others by the Austrian courts and investigating authorities. The court considered this evidence to corroborate what had been established by experts, namely that the drugs found abroad had in fact been produced in the laboratory in B. The appeal challenged the trial court’s finding that the applicant had been producing drugs up to 15 December 2000. On 8 April 2004 the Krakow Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) held a hearing and upheld the impugned judgment. The applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment, alleging that it had been sufficiently proved that he had acted as a leader of an organised criminal gang. Appeal court dismissed the arguments that the applicant had not been producing any illegal substances immediately before and after 12 December 2000. The court considered that the police had secured in his laboratory large quantities of substances for the production of narcotics. On 15 July 2004 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) The Supreme Court decided not to hear the cassated appeal and refused to prepare written reasons for its decision. The Court of Appeal analysed at length the statements made by W.P. and other witnesses heard in Austria and assessed their usefulness and veracity. It underlined that the. applicant had never contested that he knew W. P. and had met him on several occasions.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Ryszard Jakubczyk (‘the applicant’), on 22 April 2004. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the convention had been violated, as he had had no opportunity to examine the main witnesses in the criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Kielce. ce Regional Court held a hearing at which the prosecutor sought to read out statements made by a certain W.P. as well as by J.K., B.S., and G.C. The applicant’s lawyer objected to this, submitting that the statements in question had been made before the Austrian courts in another set of criminal proceedings in which those individuals had been the accused. The court based its decision on Article 587 of. the Code of Criminal Procedure and others, which allowed statements. made by both witnesses and accused in another. set of proceedings to be read out. It agreed that it had not been obvious whether this provision could be applicable to a. situation where the actions of foreign authorities had not. been taken at the request of the Polish authorities. The applicant was convicted of the following offences, committed on an unspecified date between 1997 and 15 December 2000: storing and possessing large quantities of psychotropic substances, particularly amphetamines. The court found that the applicant had acted together with three accomplices; however it acquitted him of the charge of leading an organised criminal gang. The trial court sentenced the applicant to nine years’ imprisonment and a fine. Some of the evidence referred to above had been collected in another set of criminal proceedings against the applicant (regarding charges severed in 2001, see paragraph 10 above) The court examined at length the results of the searches of the laboratory, which had been conducted by several experts, who had collected about 100 samples of chemical substances. The trial court assessed the credibility of statements obtained from W.P. and others by the Austrian courts and investigating authorities, and determined that they were worthy evidence (pełnowartościowy materiał dowodowy) The court considered this evidence to corroborate what had been established by experts, namely that the drugs found abroad had in fact been produced in the laboratory in B.C. The appeal challenged the trial court’s finding that the applicant had been producing drugs up to 15 December 2000. The Krakow Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) held a hearing and upheld the impugned judgment. Appeals court considered that the police had secured in his laboratory large quantities of substances for the production of narcotics. Court noted that the applicant had never contested that he knew W.P. and had met him on several occasions, allegedly in the capacity of an expert consultant in chemistry. Supreme Court decided not to hear the cassation appeal and refused to prepare written reasons for its decision. In addition to the above-mentioned circumstantial evidence, the Court of Appeal analysed at length the statements made by W. P. and other witnesses heard in Austria and assessed their usefulness and veracity. The court noted that W. p. had disclosed many elements of his dealings, which only in part concerned the applicant, without attempting to minimise his own role.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the convention had been violated, as he had had no opportunity to examine the main witnesses in the criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was made on 22 April 2004 by Mr Ryszard Jakubczyk (“the applicant’s” case) The case was heard by the President of the Fourth Section on 24 April 2008. The judge ruled on admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Kielce Regional Court refused the applicant’s request for W.P. and B.S. to be heard in person without specifying the reasons for the refusal. The court based its decision on Article 587 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and others, which allowed statements made by both witnesses and accused in another set of proceedings to be read out. It agreed that it had not been obvious whether this provision could be applicable to a situation where the actions of foreign authorities had not be taken at the request of the Polish authorities. However this doubt had been dismissed by the Supreme Court in its decision of 28 March 2002. The applicant was convicted of the following offences, committed on an unspecified date between 1997 and 15 December 2000. The court found that the applicant had acted together with three accomplices. However it acquitted him of the charge of leading an organised criminal gang. He was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment and a fine. The trial court examined at length the results of the searches of the laboratory, which had been conducted by several experts. Some of the evidence referred to above had been collected in another set of criminal proceedings against the applicant (regarding charges severed in 2001, see paragraph 10 above) The court further examined the involvement of each of the co‑accused in the activities with which they had been charged. Experts considered that it was most probable that the drugs found abroad had been produced in the laboratory in B.C. The link between the applicant, the other co‑accused, and the activity of the laboratory was established on the basis of various pieces of evidence examined at length by the trial court as well as circumstantial evidence. The trial court considered that W.P. in his statements had been incriminating himself to a far greater extent than the applicant. The Krakow Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) held a hearing and upheld the impugned judgment on 8 April 2004. Appeal court dismissed the arguments that the applicant had not been producing any illegal substances immediately before and after 12 December 2000. The court considered that the police had secured in his laboratory large quantities of substances for the production of narcotics. The Court of Appeal analysed at length the statements made by W.P. and other witnesses heard in Austria and assessed their usefulness and veracity. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) on 15 July 2004. The Supreme Court decided not to hear the cassated appeal and refused to prepare written reasons for its decision on 19 October 2004.
