name: Maciej Ziembiński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. In issue no. 33 of 18 August 2004 the applicant published an article entitled “Elegantly wrapped dung” (“Łajno – elegancko opakowane”). It read, in so far as relevant: “A poser is someone who does everything to produce external effects by his conduct, speech and, in particular, with the populism he preaches” The Radomsko District mayor was accused of defamation in 2005. He wrote that quail breeding would not solve the unemployment problem in the region. The mayor and his spokesman accused him of using words such as ‘numbskull’, ‘dull boss’ and ‘dim-witted official’ The judge ruled in favour of the district mayor, and the case is now being heard in the court of appeals in the city of Poznań. The case is expected to be heard in March or April next year, and will be heard by the Supreme Court of Poland in April or May. The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case. Private prosecutors sought an order requiring the applicant to publish an apology in the weekly newspaper. They also sought reimbursement of their legal costs and payment by the applicant of 5,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) to a charity. On 8 February 2006 the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court gave its judgment. It held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” in respect of K.H. had defamed them as local government officials. Journalist had written about the quail farming initiative. He referred to the author of the initiative as a ‘poser’, ‘numbskull’ and ‘dim-witted official’ The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. They had not been mentioned by name, but they had been easily identifiable on account of the publicity generated by the project. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. Maciej Ziembiński intended to derive satisfaction from doing them moral harm. The court found that the acts had constituted a blatant abuse of freedom of speech and professional ethics. It imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt.“Dull” means not sharp, unintelligent, intellectually retarded. “Dung” has a cruder equivalent, and undoubtedly that equivalent was meant to describe K.H.’'s contribution to the development of local entrepreneurship. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity. The judge ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006.

The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 March 2010. The judge ruled in favour of the Polish Government. The Radomsko District's mayor and two other officials accused him of defamation. They said he used the word 'numbskull' and 'dull boss' in an article about a local economic development programme. He said that neither quail breeding, nor mushroom growing, nor Eternit will solve the unemployment problem in the villages of our region. But no numbskull will convince me that I am wrong, he says. The time is approaching when pilgrimages of men from all over Poland, and maybe even the European Union, will come to Radoms Ko to taste quail eggs and later begin procreating, he writes. The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case. Private prosecutors sought an order requiring the applicant to publish an apology in the weekly newspaper. They further sought reimbursement of their legal costs and payment by the applicant of 5,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) to a charity. On 8 February 2006 the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court gave its judgment. It held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” in respect of K.H. had defamed them as local government officials. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. They had not been mentioned by name, but they had been easily identifiable on account of the publicity generated by the quail farming project and the earlier articles published by the applicant's newspaper. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media to serve the State and society. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. The trial court noted that the present case involved a conflict between constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and the right of each citizen to have his reputation protected. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt, also culpably. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The applicant appealed. The Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment.

The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. In issue no. 33 of 18 August 2004 the applicant published an article entitled “Elegantly wrapped dung” (“Łajno – elegancko opakowane”). It read, in so far as relevant: “A poser is someone who does everything to produce external effects by his conduct, speech and, in particular, with the populism he preaches” In 2005 M.D., the mayor of the Radomsko District (starosta), G. D., the head and spokesperson of the district’s marketing department, lodged a private bill of indictment against the applicant. They accused him of defamation committed through the mass media under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code. In particular, they alleged that the copious use of words such as “numbskull”, “dull boss” and “dim-witted official” was defamation. “This is not a venture of the quail variety by some smart poser or populist who is able to sell his dull bosses dung nicely wrapped in words. And he actually sells it. ...” The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case, and transmitted the private bill of indictment to the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court. The trial court held two hearings. The court found that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” had amounted to insult (zniewaga) committed through the mass media, within the meaning of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The judge convicted the applicant under that provision and ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 10,000 (approximately 2,630 euros (EUR) The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context is legally irrelevant. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. The trial court noted that the present case involved a conflict between constitutionally guaranteed freedom of speech and the right of each citizen to have his reputation protected. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt, also culpably. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The judgment was served on the applicant on 29 May 2006. The Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment and ordered the application to pay the costs. The judge ruled that fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted. But it did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity.

The court convicted the applicant under that provision and ordered him to pay a fine of PLN 10,000 (approximately 2,630 euros (EUR) The court observed that, since March 2004, the applicant’s newspaper had been publishing articles which were critical of M.D., the mayor of the Radomsko District, and his officials. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The trial court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. The fair criticism and objective coverage, free from personal emotions, which is desired in journalism, gave way to the private interest of the defendant, pursued through expressions which remain offensive and disrespectful. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. By using insulting words in respect of the district officials, Maciej Ziembiński intended to derive satisfaction from doing them moral harm. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt. Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court (‘the Regional Court’) upheld the first-instance judgment. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21413/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled in favour of the applicant, who is now living in Oldham, Greater Manchester. A building society advanced 150,000 pounds sterling (GBP) and GBP 116,250 respectively to the applicant. On 23 March 1988, the applicant's wife collected part of the advance, GBP 104,000, and took it to India in a bin liner. The applicant was subsequently charged with two offences of obtaining property by deception contrary to section 15(1) of the Theft Act 1968. He was also charged with removing property required to be delivered to the official receiver and failing to account for the loss of property while bankrupt. On 18 February 1992, he was convicted of the four offences charged and was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment. In 1995, the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain decided to remove his licence to practise as a pharmacist. Court of Appeal ruled that the answers given to the official receiver were in breach of Article 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. The House of Lords ruled in favour of the applicant on 29 November 2001. The decision was upheld in a further appeal by the Court of Appeal on 9 March 2006. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of England and Wales on 11 March 2007. The court of appeals ruled that it was the duty of the court of appeal to uphold the conviction. The judge said the original conviction was unsafe because it was based on answers given under compulsion during the bankruptcy examination. The case was dismissed on 13 March 2008. The Appeal Court returned the case to the original Court of Appeals on 14 March 2009.

name: Johann Widmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42032/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of the administrative proceedings exceeded the reasonable time requirement under Article 6 of the Convention. On 20 March 2001 the Court communicated the above complaint to the Government and declared the remaining complaints inadmissible. By a decision of 6 June 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicant appealed to the Agricultural Authority of first instance (Landesregierung als Agrarbehörde erster Instanz - “the Agricultural Authority”) to grant him the necessary quantity of timber for the maintenance of existing and the edification of new alpine cabins. The Agricultural Authority held a hearing and on 20 June 1989 a forestry expert delivered his opinion. On 4 September 1989 the Agricultural. Authority gave its decision, ordering the Federal Forestry Administration to provide the applicant with a certain quantity of. timber within four weeks. On 27 June 1990 the applicant filed a complaint against this decision with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of sufficient prospects of success and remitted the case to the Administrative Court. The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 28 January 1998. It confirmed that the applicant was entitled to obtain a variable quantity of timber dependent on the need to maintain his alp's cabins, but not a fixed annual quantity. The applicant's further appeal was dismissed on 11 December 1997. It found that the legal instrument of 1868 only conferred a right to obtain timber for the maintenance of cabins.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 60177/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were employed by the Culture and Education Department of the Sincan District Council in Ankara and were involved in the organisation of public activities and events during religious and national days. On 27 April 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants were taken into police custody on 5 February 1997 and the first applicant on 6 February 1997. They were accused of disseminating propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation, namely the Hezbollah. During their police interrogations, the applicants denied the charges against them. On 15 October 1997 the Ankara State Security Court found that the applicants had aided and abetted a terrorist organisation. It found the applicants guilty as charged, sentenced them to three years and nine months’ imprisonment and debarred them from public service for three years. On 21 September 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the Ankara City Security Court.

He was placed in Ümraniye Prison. In December 2000 the applicant was sent to Kandıra F-type Prison. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant and 398 others were accused of starting a riot in the prison and of damage to public property. The Istanbul State Security Court ordered the applicant's release pending trial on 9 February 2001 but he was not released as his detention on remand had been ordered on 25 December 2000 in connection with the incidents in the Ümraniye Prison. On 7 July 2001 at around 8.30 p.m. the applicant was released from prison. In 2004 the State Security Courts were abolished following a constitutional amendment and the case before the Istanbul Assize Court was transferred to the Istanbul Juvenile Court. The case was accordingly remitted before the Court of Cassation to determine which court had jurisdiction to examine the case.

name: Guy Ankerl
train_texts: Case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (“the Government”) on 10 July and 28 August 1995 respectively. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3(d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L. Wildhaber, the elected judge of Swiss nationality. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 May 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr P. Boillat, Head of the European Law and International Affairs Section, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr A.D. Schmidt, former judge in the Canton of Geneva, Counsel. For the Commission Mr F. Martínez, Delegate; (c) the applicant. On 24 September 1996 the Court removed the documents in question from the file (Rule 37 para. 1) The Court heard addresses by the applicant himself, Mr Schürmann and Mr Boilat. Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva in 1978. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA. The company was itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA (“Chrysanthemums“), the owner of the building. In a letter of 8 May 1987 Naef gave the company notice to quit the flat with effect from 29 February 1988. The applicant then applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement. He maintains that he did so. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance, alleging that the applicant was occupying the premises unlawfully. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court thus had to determine whether the conduct of the protagonists amounted to an agreement to enter into a lease after the termination of the subtenancy. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. The transcript of the testimony reads as follows: “...Mr Jean-Gabriel Linder ... When I resumed [the management of the building in March 1988], Mr Ankersl was occupying premises but he had no written or oral lease or even a tacit one.” Mr Dominique Veuillet: We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises. In 1986 or 1987 he came to see me and told me that his position vis-à-vis Régie Immobilière was a rather special one. The defendant asked that we should draw up a lease in his name. At the same time he had asked us to collect the rent direct from him. He told me he did not wish to proceed in the matter and he didn't give me the reasons. I myself handed the file over to another property-management company on 31 December 1987, and at that time, as far as we were concerned, his position remained as we had described in our letter. Mr Ruffieux and Mr Ankerl were forced out of their flat in 1989. The court ruled that there was no lease agreement between the parties. The tenant was ordered to move all property and persons from the flat and restore it to the plaintiffs in good condition. The lawsuit was settled out of court in 1994. The plaintiffs are still living in the flat, but have moved into a new flat. They are waiting for their case to be heard in court again in June. The case is expected to last until the end of the year. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. Mr Ruffieux, the director and shareholder of the plaintiffs, told the Court that he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. Mr Ankerl had been supplied personally with GPR Degenève’s account number and wrote to that company on 29 February 1988 to inform them that in future he would pay the rent into their account. The Court reaches the conclusion that, in the circumstances of this case, no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. In the instant case no lease has been signed since the termination of the sublease. Guy Ankerl was denied a lease by the landlord, Chrysanthemum SA, for flat at no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, second floor. He appealed to the Canton of Geneva Court of Justice, which dismissed the appeal on the grounds that there was no relationship between the parties. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal in the Federal Court of France, which was also dismissed on the same grounds. In the end, it was decided that the landlord was entitled to raise his ownership against the subtenant, and that the defendant was on the premises unlawfully. The landlord is entitled to rely on Article 641 para. 2 [of the Civil Code] applies in this case. The case was brought by a man whose wife had to take an oath to testify against him. The man claimed that the cantonal courts had violated Article 6 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Federal Court said that the appeal did not comply with the requirement that reasons must be given for a breach of the law. The First Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and14 of the Convention (art. 6, art. 14) of which the appellant makes a bald assertion without providing any explanation. The appellant’s wife was heard only for information purposes and without taking the oath. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. ... The present appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible.““Mr and Mrs Ankerl left the flat in issue on 16 October 1991. ’s statement into consideration.”‘The appellant did not show in what way the cantonal appellate court had unsustainably interpreted the statements made by the sworn witness Jean-Gabriel Linder.’

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L. Wildhaber, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Art 43) and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 May 1996. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr P. Boillat, Head of the European Law and International Affairs Section, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr A.D. Schmidt, former judge in the Canton of Geneva, Counsel. For the Commission Mr F. Martínez, Delegate; (c) the applicant. The Court heard addresses by the applicant himself, Mr Schürmann and Mr Boilat. On 24 September 1996 the Court removed the documents in question from the file (Rule 37 para. 1) Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva, in 1978. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA (“Régie Immobeille SA’), itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA. On 14 November 1986 Régie Naef SA informed the applicant that renovation and building work was going to be carried out on the block. The applicant then applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement. No settlement had been reached. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance, alleging that the applicant was occupying the premises unlawfully since his subtenancy agreement had been terminated. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court held a hearing on 19 May 1989. It heard Mr Linder (GPR Degenève), Mr Veuillet (Naef) and Mrs Ankerls; Mr Ruffieux (Chrysantshemum) and the applicant also gave evidence. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. Mr Dominique Veuillet: We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises. In 1986 or 1987 he told me that his position vis-à-vis Régie Immobilière was a rather special one. The defendant asked that we should draw up a lease in his name. He did not give me the reasons. I did not myself communicate the shareholder’s position to Mr AnKERl but, on the other hand, I did send the file to our lawyer. ... I myself handed the file over to another property-management company on 31 December 1987, and at that time, as far as we had described in our letter of 14 July 1987. Mr Ruffieux: Mr Linder never asked us to look for a flat elsewhere. Mr Ankerl: When I concluded the lease with Régie Immobilière, I did not realise that it was a subtenancy. “On 12 October 1989 the court held that there was no lease agreement between the parties. The court ordered Mr AnKERl to move all property and persons from the flat and restore it to the plaintiffs in good condition.” The judgment reads as follows: “... Mr Veuillet, an employee of [Naef], told the Court that the tenant, Régie immigration SA, had asked Naef to collect the rent direct from Mr AnKerl. This arrangement was accepted, the payments being received as an indemnity for unlawful occupation’ Mr Ruffieux, the director and shareholder of the plaintiffs, told the Court that he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. Mr Ankerl had been supplied personally with GPR Degenève’s account number and wrote to that company on 29 February 1988 to inform them that in future he would pay the rent into their account. The Court reaches the conclusion that, in the circumstances of this case, no lease was entered into orally (the existence of an oral agreement has not been proved) or even implied by the clear conduct of the parties. ... In law the only issue which it is necessary to resolve is whether the defendant, since his sublease was terminated, has been given a lease by the landlord. Guy Ankerl had a sub-leased apartment in Geneva, Switzerland. He was refused a lease by the landlord, Chrysanthemum SA. He appealed the decision, but the appeal was dismissed by the Canton of Geneva Court of Justice. The judge said that there was no legal relationship between the parties and that the landlord was entitled to raise his ownership against the subtenant. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal. The case was heard by the Federal Court of Appeal, and the judge ruled in favour of the landlord. The landlord was found to have violated the terms of the sub-leasing contract by refusing to grant an extension of the lease. “... the fact that [the cantonal courts] allowed the representative of a party to be heard as a witness on oath created a flagrant inequality vis-à-vis the other party, who by the force of circumstance was not able to call witnesses to whom the oath could be administered. The equality of arms guaranteed both in the Federal Constitution and in the European Convention on Human Rights was not ensured.“The First Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention (art. 6, art. 14) The appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible. The applicant’s wife was heard only for information purposes and without taking the oath. The appellant did not, moreover, show in what way the cantonal appellate court had unsustainably interpreted the statements made by the sworn witness Jean-Gabriel Linder. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. It merely found that Mr Linder would pass on to the landlord Guy Ankerl’ s wish to enter into a new lease’.

name: Dimiter Pobornikoff
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It originated in an application (no. 28501/95) against the Republic of Austria. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c). The Government’s application referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Austria had recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46) The Court decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant was found guilty of the murder of his wife and sentenced to life in prison. He then filed a plea of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) and an appeal (Berufung) The Supreme Court set the hearing date for the applicant's plea ofnullity and his appeal for 27 January 1994. The applicant did not request to attend the hearing of the hearing before the Supreme Court. The application was dismissed and the appeal was rejected. The appeal was dismissed on 25 January 1994 and the case was dismissed. The decision was upheld by the Appeals Court on 2 February 1994 and he was sentenced to death by lethal injection. The Supreme Court found that the applicant had rightly claimed as a mitigating circumstance that he had no prior convictions. The sentence of life imprisonment was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The applicant was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 25 years in prison. The judge ruled that the sentence was not too harsh because the applicant acted for base motives. The court also found that cruelty had not been factually established as an aggravating circumstance. The conviction was upheld on appeal and the jury was unable to reach a verdict on the appeal because of the lack of evidence. The jury also found the conviction not to be too harsh on the basis that the defendant had acted for particularly base motives and had acted in self-defence.

The case was referred to the Court by the Austrian Government on 5 July 1999. It originated in an application (no. 28501/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) The Government’s application referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Austria had recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). After consulting the Agent of the Government and the applicant, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant was found guilty of the murder of his wife and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed the sentence and filed a plea of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) and an appeal (Berufung) The Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) fixed the hearing date for the applicant's plea ofnullity and his appeal for 27 January 1994. The applicant received a notification, which stated that his counsel would be summoned to the hearing. He did not request to attend the hearing before the Supreme Court. The application was dismissed and he was released on bail. The case was decided by a jury at the Feldkirch Regional Court. The Supreme Court found that the applicant had rightly claimed as a mitigating circumstance that he had no prior convictions. The sentence of life imprisonment was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The Court also found that cruelty had not been factually established as an aggravating circumstance. However, there was evidential support for the conclusion that the. applicant had acted for particularly base motives. On 27 January 1994 the Supreme Court, after having held a hearing in the absence of the applicant but in the presence of his new official defence counsel, Mr. K., rejected his plea of nullity as well as his appeal. The case was dismissed.

The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. It originated in an application (no. 28501/95) against the Republic of Austria. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany indicated that they did not intend to intervene in the case. After consulting the Agent of the Government and the applicant, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing. The applicant was found guilty of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed the verdict and the Supreme Court heard his plea of nullity and appeal in 1994. The applicant was represented by official counsel, Mr. A. He was detained during the hearing of the plea of Nullity and the appeal was adjourned to January 1994. He did not request to attend the hearing before the Supreme court. The appeal was heard on 27 January 1994, and the applicant was released on bail until the appeal hearing was held on 15 June 1994, when he was allowed to return to Germany. The application was heard by a jury at the Feldkirch Regional Court (Landesgericht) The jury decided that there were no mitigating circumstances. The applicant could not be brought to the court to hear his appeal. A new official defence counsel was appointed as Mr A. would be unable to attend. The Supreme Court found that the sentence of life imprisonment was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The court rejected his plea of nullity and his appeal as well as his appeal for the sentence. The applicant was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 30 years. The sentence was suspended for 20 years on the grounds of good behaviour. The judge ruled that cruelty had not been factually established as an aggravating circumstance, but that the applicant had acted for particularly base motives.

name: Türkan Yavuz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67137/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Türkan Yavuz (‘the applicant’) was taken into custody on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation, namely the TKP/ML0. According to the search protocol drafted on the same day by the police officers and signed by the applicant, the police found a number of documents, guns, ammunition and dynamite. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the İstanbul State Security Court. She acknowledged the contents of her police deposition. She stated that during her custody, four or five police officers had sexually harassed her by touching her breasts and buttocks. She claimed that she was also punched. On the same day, the applicant was released and no criminal proceedings were brought against her. The applicant signed her deposition. He denied having given any “information about the investigation proceedings“ and relied on Articles 6 and 10 (art. 6, art. 10) of the Convention. The proceedings in the Criminal Cassation Division of the Vaud Cantonal Court were dismissed on the grounds that the disclosure of criminal complaints had been lodged was not information about an investigation. The actus reus of the offence punishable under Article 185 CC is therefore made out. Mr Weber himself admits that the breach of the confidentiality of the investigation was intentional. His submission based on a kind of necessity is devoid of merit since it was open to him to appeal to the Indictment Division against the orders for the sequestration of the Franz Weber Foundation’s and the Helvetia Nostra association’’ accounts, as he did two days later. The decision is therefore well-founded on that point. The disclosure of the challenge is not information about an investigation. The appellant was therefore rightly convicted. ...“ Finally, the Criminal Cassation Division set aside of its own motion the entry of the fine in the cantonal register.”. Mr Weber lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He relied on Articles 10 and 6 (art. 10, art. 6) of the Convention. In his view, Article 6 applied because of the criminal nature of the fines. On this point cantonal law differed from federal law. It noted that under Vaud law and notwithstanding that they were convertible into days of imprisonment (arrêts), the fines for “procedural offences’ were disciplinary in nature. The applicant argued that Article 185 of the Vaud Code of Criminal Procedure (Vaud CCP) violates freedom of expression. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 November 1983. The ECHR provides expressly that such restrictions are permissible where they are necessary in a democratic society, in particular for maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The rule enacted in Article 185 Vaud CCP clearly conforms to these principles. A weighing of the competing interests at stake leads to the same conclusions. While it may indeed be readily appreciated that the applicant had grounds for rebelling against the sometimes unorthodox course taken by the proceedings against him, it must not be forgotten that the usual remedies were open to him. The prohibition against communicating information about an investigation until its completion and the penalties attaching to the offence are undoubtedly consistent with the proportionality principle. The fine was convertible into ten days’ imprisonment under Article 12 of the Vaud Order on the recovery of fines and their conversion into imprisonment. The possibility of conversion into a custodial sentence makes no difference, since conversion is possible only in the event of the appellant’s refusing to pay the fine out of sheer unwillingness. The safeguards provided for in Article 6 § 1 (art. 6-1) ECHR were therefore not applicable in the instant case.“ The applicant paid the fine in January 1985.‘The fine imposed in the. instant case was not a negligible one, but it nonetheless came into the category of penalties. which by their nature, duration or manner of execution are deemed not to be appreciably detrimental.

name: Nigel Eastaway
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74976/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The parties replied to the Court in writing. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. At the conclusion of the criminal trial, the applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The case was adjourned until after the defendants had served their evidence. The case was to be decided on the basis of undisputed facts. The defendants were allowed to serve their evidence in reply on 10 July 1997. The hearing was continued until 9 February 1998 when the case was settled. The judge ruled that the case should be settled on the grounds that the facts were undisputed and that the defendants did not have the right to delay the case. The trial was finally settled on 9 March 1998, and the defendants were ordered to serve the rest of their evidence by 1 April 1998. The decision was overturned on 11 April 1998 and the case went back to court again. The applicant met the Secretary of State on 5 March 1998. to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement. At a directions hearing on 23 March 1998, the time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. On 4 October 1998 the applicant broke off the settlement negotiations. On 29 July 1999 there was a pre-trial review in the disqualification proceedings, at which the court gave detailed trial directions. The trial was set down to begin on 4 October 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant renewed his judicial review application before the Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing the application on 15 February 2001. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal in April 2001 and the decision was returned to Mr Eastaway. The appeal was dismissed on 8 March 2001, the decision by the Supreme Court in June 2002 was upheld, and the application was dismissed again on 9 March 2001. A large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of MrEastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.’” “Mr Eastaway does not now suggest that the delay has been such that a fair trial is impossible.”‘“The applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of four and a half years, commencing on 25 June 2001.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The Secretary of State’s evidence was not complete at the time he commenced proceedings, and he applied for an extension of time for the serving of evidence. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), and the parties replied in writing to each other’S observations. Criminal charges had been brought against the applicant and three other defendants in the Blackspur proceedings on 1 July 1992. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The defendants were ordered to provide evidence by 17 January 1997. They failed to do so and the case was adjourned until 8 February 1998. The judge ruled that the case should continue and ordered the defendants to provide further evidence. The case was settled out of court in July 1998 and the defendants were cleared of any wrongdoing. The trial continues in the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom at a later date, and the jury has been unable to reach a verdict. The jury's verdict is still pending. The defendants are appealing the decision to dismiss the case against them on the grounds that they did not meet the terms of their bail. They are also appealing to the Court of Appeal for reconsideration. The court of appeals has yet to make a decision. The applicant attempted to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement with the Secretary of State. On 30 June 1999 the applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the secretary of state’s decision not to discontinue the proceedings on grounds of delay. The application was refused by the Court of Appeal on 15 March 2000, following an oral hearing. On 2 February 2000 the applicant renewed his judicial review application. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999, and the trial began on 8 December 1998. The disqualification proceedings were adjourned on 29 July 1999 after a pre-trial review. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissed it on 15 February 2001. The Court of Appeal refused leave to apply for judicial review. In the judgments of the Court of appeal given in November 1997, Mr Eastaway was granted leave to appeal against the decision of the Secretary of State to continue the proceedings. A large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of Mr. Eastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the. Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.” The application was dismissed by the Vice-Chancellor and the Court of Appeal on 13 September 2001. The applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of four and a half years, commencing on 25 June 2001.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required, the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. At the conclusion of the criminal trial, the applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The case was adjourned for more than a year. It was eventually settled on the basis that the defendants had not served their evidence in time. The case was heard again in April 1998, and the judge ordered the defendants to serve their evidence. The defendants did not comply and the case was re-opened on 9 February 1998. The judge ruled that the case should be adjourned until the next hearing on 6 June 1998. This was the first time the case had been adjourned since it began in 1994. The court then adjourned the case for a further three months and the defendants were ordered to serve the evidence. They did not do so and the hearing was called again on 10 July 1997. The applicant tried to negotiate a 'Carecraft' settlement with the Secretary of State. On 5 March 1998 the applicant was told that he would accept a settlement based on a disqualification period of five years. On 23 March 2000 Buxton LJ refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In the course of a considered judgment, Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’, because the arguments on delay could, and should, have been made during the disqualification proceedings. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. Mr Eastaway found a violation of Article 6 of the Human Rights Act, but the decision was dismissed on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal refusing leave to apply for judicial review. A large proportion of the undoubtedly long time which has elapsed since these proceedings were commenced is due to the various actions taken by Mr Eastaway. Those actions were taken not to obtain but to avoid a fair and public hearing by an independent or impartial tribunal either within a reasonable time or at all. In my view there has been no breach of Mr. Eastaway’s Convention rights under Article 6 and for the. Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them.” ‘Mr Eastaway does not now suggest that the delay has been such that a fair trial is impossible.’

name: Artur Lewandowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29437/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of his pre‑trial detention had been unreasonable. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided on 17 March 2005 and the judgment was published on 21 March 2006. The decision was made to admit the application. The applicant was convicted of having committed armed robbery in January 1999 and was sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed but on 31 August 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It appears that the proceedings ended on an unspecified later date. The appeal court quashed the remainder of the impugned judgment in so far as it concerned the applicant's conviction for armed robbery. in January and February 1999. The court remitted this part of the case and the proceedings are pending before the Supreme Court. The application for release is still pending. The arguments for and against the appeal can be found in the case at: http://www.wrocław.org.uk/cases/appeal/conviction-of-armed-robbery.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26461/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the bankruptcy proceedings against him were not terminated within a reasonable time. By a decision of 22 January 2008, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court also heard that the applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1) The applicant was a partner in a commercial partnership, a banking and stockbroking firm called Vekselerfirmaet Hugo Petersen I/S (hereafter “the Partnership”).  bankruptcy proceedings commenced against the Partnership in 1988. The Partnership estate was closed on 5 December 1995 with distribution of dividends. Court sessions were held on 6 November, 6 and 21 December 1995, 14 February and 17 April 1996. The accounts of the applicant’s bankruptcy estate could not be prepared, however, until formal accounts were available in the estates of the co-partners Hugo Petersen’S Børsmæglerselskab A/S, CHN and FVM. The Bankruptcy Court adjourned the proceedings pending the preparation of accounts. The latter proceedings were finalised in 1999. On 4 April 1997, the trustee informed the Bank bankruptcy Court that the draft accounts for the Partnership had been prepared. By 1997 the bankruptcy proceedings against the other partners of the Partnership were terminated. On 26 March 1998, the Bankruptcy Court declared that the estate would be closed. In accordance with the draft distribution accounts, preferential claims would be fully covered. An amount of approximately DKK 5.4 million remained for distribution to so-called section 98 claims. During the period between November 1998 and October 1999 an amount of DKK 750,000 was made available to the applicant. Before the final deadline for notifying claims in the estate, which the applicant missed, a distribution on account was made in respect of the ordinary claims. The amount of the distribution was made on account for the period November 1998 to October 1999. Thirty-two Partnership creditors lodged claims for interest in the estate. Eight creditors then issued a writ against the bankruptcy estate, and the applicant intervened as a third party. The creditors declared that they did not wish to appeal against the judgments unless the applicant did so. The applicant subsequently appealed against the. judgments to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), hereafter the. High Court. On 26 June 2001, the. Bankruptcy Court invited the applicant and the creditors to consider whether the estate could be closed under. section 144 of the Bankruptcies Act by setting aside funds to cover the contested claims pursuant to section 149. According to the former provision, the estate can be finalised and the surplus assets handed over to the debtor if the creditors had. obtained full payment. The applicant objected to the Bankruptcy Court closing the estate. The High Court found against him on 22 March 2002. The Supreme Court passed judgment finding against the applicant on 19 September 2005. The applicant failed to request leave to appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) The Ministry of Justice (Justits Justice) disputed the Government's assertion that the application had been dismissed in vain. The case was settled by the High Court in February 2003 and the appeal proceedings were concluded on 24 January 2003. The appeal proceedings concerning the disputed deferred claims for interest were adjourned until October 2003, when the applicant was granted leave to appealing against the judgment. The applicant raised his complaints about the length of the bankruptcy proceedings before the court, where the case was pending. ministeriet) invited the applicant to raise his complaints. The applicant was not able to do so due to the nature of the case and the court's adjournment. The case is still pending in the court and is expected to be heard by the end of the year. The application will be heard in court on November 20, the ministeriet said. The case originated in an application (no. 26461/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the bankruptcy proceedings against him were not terminated within a reasonable time. By a decision of 22 January 2008, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The case is now being heard by the European Court of Justice. The application was brought by a Danish national, Mr James Valentin (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2006. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen. The Partnership’s assets, including the individual partners’ assets, were estimated at about 8 million Danish kroner (DKK) The Partnership estate was closed on 5 December 1995 with distribution of dividends. Court sessions were held on 6 November, 6 and 21 December 1995, 14 February and 17 April 1996. The Bankruptcy Court adjourned the proceedings pending the preparation of accounts. The accounts were being prepared, but could not be completed until, inter alia, the outcome of proceedings initiated by the Ministry of Taxation against Hugo Petersen's Børsmæglerselskab A/S was known. The latter proceedings were finalised in 1999. By 1997 the bankruptcy proceedings against the other partners of the Partnership were terminated. On 26 March 1998, the Bankruptcy Court declared that the estate would be closed. During the period between November 1998 and October 1999, an amount of DKK 750,000 was made available to the applicant. An amount of approximately DKK 5.4 million remained for distribution to so-called section 98 claims (section 98 of the Bank bankruptcy Act, which included deferred claims for interest). The bankruptcy proceedings were adjourned on 25 August 1998, a distribution on account was made in respect of the ordinary claims. The accounts and report had been prepared and sent to theApplicant for his comments. Thirty-two Partnership creditors lodged claims for interest in the estate. Eight creditors then issued a writ against the bankruptcy estate, and the applicant intervened as a third party. The creditors declared that they did not wish to appeal against the judgments unless the applicant did so. The applicant subsequently appealed against the verdicts to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), hereafter the High court. The hearing was adjourned pending the outcome of the lead cases. On 20 November 2001, at a hearing at the Bankruptcy Court, the trustee recommended that final distribution accounts be prepared in respect of the deferred claims, which were not the subject of the pending appeal proceedings. The applicant appealed against the finalisation of the estate in accordance with section 149 of the Bankruptcy Act. The High Court found against him on 22 March 2002. The applicant failed to request leave to appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) In October 2006 the Ministry of Justice (Justits Justice) disputed the Government's decision to hand over the remaining assets of the Estate to the applicant. The Court decided to approve the accounts and to make contributions in respect of the claims, which were not the subject of the pending appeal proceedings. Finally, the estate was finalised by setting aside the remaining funds to cover the disputed claims. The application was made while the bankruptcy proceedings were still pending. The judge invited the applicant to raise his complaints about the length of the proceedings. The application was dismissed without further action, the judge said. The case is still pending at the bankruptcy court in Bucharest, Bucharest and elsewhere in the world. name: Roy H.W. Johnston
train_texts: The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 21 May 1985. The case originated in an application (no. 9697/82) against Ireland lodged with the Commission in 1982 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Roy H.W. Johnston, an Irish citizen, Janice Williams-Johnston, a British citizen, and their daughter Nessa. The request sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Articles 8, 9, 12 and 13. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 23 and 24 June 1986. Immediately before they opened, the Court had held a preparatory meeting. There appeared before the Court: Mrs. Liddy, Deputy Legal Adviser, Department of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. D. Gleeson, Senior Counsel, and Mr. J. O’Reilly, Counsel, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Senator M. Robinson and Dr. Duncan for the applicants, as well as replies to questions put to them by the judges. Roy H.W. Johnston married a Miss M in 1952 in a Church of Ireland ceremony. Three children were born of this marriage, in 1956, 1959 and 1965. In 1978, the second applicant, with whom Roy Johnston had been living since 1971, gave birth to Nessa. He consented to his name being included in the Register of Births as the father (see paragraph 26 below) Under the Constitution of Ireland, the first applicant is unable to obtain, in Ireland, a dissolution of his marriage. He has taken the following steps to regularise his relationship with her and with his wife and to make proper provision for his dependents. The third applicant has, under Irish law, the legal situation of an illegitimate child. Her parents are concerned at the lack of any means by which she can, even with their consent, be recognised as their child. They are also concerned about the possibility of a stigma attaching to her by virtue of her legal situation, especially when she is attending school. She has adopted the first applicant’s surname, which she uses amongst friends and neighbours, but for business purposes continues to use the name Williams. According to her, she has felt inhibited about telling employers of her domestic circumstances. She would like to become an Irish citizen by naturalisation, but has been reluctant to make an application, not wishing to put those circumstances in issue.

In 1978, the second applicant, with whom Roy Johnston had been living since 1971, gave birth to Nessa. He consented to his name being included in the Register of Births as the father. The first and second applicants state that although they have not practised any formal religion for some time, they have recently joined the Religious Society of Friends (the Quakers) in Dublin. This decision was influenced in part by their concern that the third applicant receives a Christian upbringing.

name: Fahriye Çetinkaya
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicants’ alleged ill-treatment in police custody. The applicants were born in 1978 and 1980 respectively and live in Istanbul. They were arrested on suspicion of having participated in an illegal demonstration which took place in Ümraniye on 29 July 2001. The first applicant, who was identified by the police as one of the protesters, was arrested on the spot. The second applicant was arrested following a chase. The police prevented him from being lynched. The applicants were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examinations both in the evening of 3 August 2001 and in the morning of 4 August 2001. The medical reports drafted on these dates concluded that there were no signs of blows on the applicants’ bodies. On 7 August 2001 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicants with aiding and abetting the PKK under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The applicants denied all the allegations made against them. They contended that they had been forced to sign police statements without reading their contents. The court ordered their detention on remand. The first applicant contended that, although there was no marks on her body, she had been tortured in police custody. The applicants’ lawyer filed two separate petitions with the Fatih public prosecutor, complaining about the applicants' ill-treatment during their arrest and detention in police custody. November 2001 the first hearing was held before the Istanbul State Security Court. The court gave a decision of non-jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Ümraniye Criminal Court of First Instance. The applicants were acquitted on account of lack of evidence on 16 February 2004. The investigation against the police officers against the applicants was dropped on 9 August 2002. The case against the four police officers who were allegedly responsible for the ill- treatment of the applicants is ongoing.

name: Serdar Güler
train_texts: The case was brought by two Turkish nationals under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants were represented by Mrs Y. Yeşilyurt, a lawyer practising in İstanbul, and the Government was represented by their Agent. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29) The applications were lodged in 2005 and the decision was made in 2009. The applicants claim that they were denied access to the court because they had not filed the applications in time. They also claim that the application was denied on the grounds of a lack of evidence. The court ruled that the applicants were entitled to a hearing. According to the applicants, they were beaten and insulted during and after their arrest. The same day they were taken to the Bayrampaşa Health Clinic for a medical examination. The doctor who examined the applicants concluded that both of them were unfit to work for seven days. On 2 November 2004 the Beyoğlu public prosecutor issued a decision of non-prosecution in respect of the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. In his decision, the public prosecutor considered that the force used by the security forces had been in line with Article 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police. The Beyoğlu Criminal Court acquitted the applicants of the charges against them in March 2006. The court found it established that the applicants were not amongst the demonstrators who had been carrying ‘Halkevleri’ flags and had attacked the police officers. The police had therefore been proportionate, the court said. The case was heard in front of a panel of judges from the Istanbul Assize Court. Five police officers, who were wounded during the incident, joined the proceedings as intervening parties. They were acquitted on 7 March 2006 after the court heard a video recording of the incident and witness statements. The applicants were acquitted of all charges. The prosecution had accused them of taking part in an illegal demonstration without prior authorisation.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5786/08) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Swedish State had failed to comply with its obligation under Article 8. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 21 June 2012 a Chamber composed of Dean Spielmann, President, Elisabet Fura, Karel Jungwiert, Mark Villiger, Ann Power-Forde, Ganna Yudkivska, André Potocki, delivered its judgment. It unanimously declared it admissible, holding, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of that provision. The applicant was born in 1987 and lives in Ludvika. In September 2002, when she was 14 years old, she discovered that her stepfather had hidden a video-camera in the laundry basket in the bathroom, which was in recording mode. Immediately after the incident, the film was burned without anyone seeing it. On 21 October 2005 the public prosecutor indicted the applicant’s stepfather for sexual molestation (sexuell) The applicant was granted anonymity on 12 March 2013. On 22 March 2013, the President of the Grand Chamber acceded to her request to lift the anonymity granted to her. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 3 April 2013 (Rule 59 § 3) Stepfather was charged with sexual molestation for allegedly looking through the window of the applicant’s room when she was undressing in the late summer of 2003. The applicant, represented by counsel, submitted a claim for damages of 25,000 Swedish kronor (SEK): SEK 15,000 in compensation for violation of her personal integrity and SEK 10,000 for pain and suffering, to be joined to the criminal proceedings. She based her private claim on “the criminal act for which her stepfather was being prosecuted”, without invoking any specific sections of the Tort Liability Act. He was not sure whether the camera had been in recording mode or whether a film had been recorded, but it had been an impulsive act. The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was also ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. The court found it established that he had had a sexual intention in hiding the camera in the laundry basket and directing it at the part of the bathroom where it was usual to undress. The buzzing sound from the camera heard by the applicant strongly suggested that the camera was switched on and was actually recording. Whether a recording had actually been made, however, was unclear. The man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. The Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and the applicant's claim for damages was dismissed.

The Court heard addresses by Mr Crafoord, Mr Lewis, Mr Södergren and Mr Rönquist, as well as their replies to questions put by Judges Ziemele, Sicilianos, Pinto de Albuquerque and Zupančič. The applicant, her stepfather, her mother and her cousin gave evidence before the District Court of Falun (Falu Tingsrätt) The applicant’s stepfather explained that he had lived with her mother from 1997 until the autumn of 2003. They had separated on account of the incident in question, among other things. He had wanted to try to film with a hidden camera, but it had been an impulsive act. He was not sure whether the camera had been in recording mode or whether a film had been recorded. The applicant had not reported the incident to the police until 2004, when she had heard that the applicant's cousin had also experienced incidents with the accused. The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was also ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. In assessing whether the act legally constituted sexual molesting within the meaning of Chapter 6, Article 7 § 3, of the Penal Code, the Court of appeal referred to a previous case in which the stepfather had been found guilty of sexually molesting his cousin. The court concluded that it could under the circumstances be considered established that the applicant's stepfather actually filmed her while she was naked. The man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. However, since no charge of that kind had been brought against the applicant's stepfather, the court could not examine whether he could be held responsible for such a crime.
