In conclusion, despite finding his behaviour extremely reprehensible, he was acquitted and the applicant's claim for damages dismissed.

name: Tommaso Cuscani
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32771/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he did not receive a fair trial on account of the absence of interpretation at his hearing on sentencing. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 26 June 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant, but not the Government, filed observations on the merit of the case, which were dismissed. The applicant was declared bankrupt in September 1994 as a result of civil proceedings brought by the Inland Revenue to recover unpaid tax. The various companies were all registered for Value Added Tax (VAT) purposes but failed to make any VAT payments or returns to the Customs and Excise authorities. The resulting loss of VAT was assessed at approximately 460,000 pounds sterling (“GBP”) and the accumulated losses in respect of Income Tax and National Insurance contributions were assessed at GBP 360,000. The applicant was represented throughout the proceedings by a Queen's Counsel, who was also a Recorder, a very experienced junior counsel and two different firms of solicitors. The applicant was convicted of fraud and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. The court asked the applicant's counsel for an interpreter at the subsequent hearing. The applicant's brother was present and the court agreed to make use of him, if need be. In May 1996 the applicant applied to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division seeking leave to appeal against sentence. In his application, the applicant was represented by the same legal team that had defended him at trial. He did not maintain in his application that he had been unable to understand the proceedings at the trial or to communicate effectively in court; nor did he allege that he should have been provided with the services of an interpreter. Leave to appeal was refused by the Single Judge on 3 May 1996 and by the full Court of Appeal on 15 July 1996. The applicant wrote to the Home Secretary, admitting that he had not declared GBP 2,000 per week for staff wages due to the recession, and claiming that the real amount of the fraud was GBP 140,000 and not GBP 800,000. He further complained that his counsel had failed to secure him the services of an interpreter at the trial on 26 January 1996 and that this was of “paramount importance” for the purposes of the plea in mitigation. He also complained about his counsel, who, he claimed, did not understand Italian but nevertheless did not insist on an interpreter. The Commission accepted that the applicant would have been able to understand the generality of the prosecution case. The Commission found that too little time had been spent by the applicant's lawyers explaining the case to him. However, the Commission noted that the Court of Appeal no longer had the power to allow an appeal against conviction if it did not think the conviction was unsafe but was dissatisfied in some way with the trial process. The applicant was released from prison on licence on 25 November 1996. In the view of the Commission, whilst the. applicant's conviction was arguably unsatisfactory, it could not be said to be unsafe. Since the Commission did not consider that there was a real possibility that, if referred to the Court. of Appeal, the conviction and sentence would not be upheld, it decided not to make such reference.

name: Sahro Osman
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8. The application was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen, from Ministry of Justice. The applicant's father returned to Denmark in November 2003 and was summoned for an interview with the Immigration Service. He was informed that he, who had been recognised as a refugee, had visited his country of origin. On 9 August 2005, three months before the applicant turned eighteen years old, she contacted the Danish Embassy in Nairobi with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in Denmark. The Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Alien Act. The applicant appealed against the decision to revoke her residence permit in April 2007. She claimed that it had not been her decision to leave the country. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. It stated among other things: “... The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed...”. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated in Esbjerg, Denmark. The case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant, and said that it was preferable for foreign minors to arrive as early as possible. The High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org. In the U.S. call the National Suicide Prevention Line on 1-800-273-8255.

name: Anthony Boner
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 3 August 1993 by. the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government’), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). Anthony Boner is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Between 29 March and 10 April 1990 he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. During the trial a prosecution witness, Mrs G., entered the courtroom prior to giving evidence. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Lord Rodger and Ms Rae as well as replies to its questions. Mr Boner instructed new solicitors, who asked a different counsel to advise on the prospects of an appeal and to draft a note of appeal. In his opinion dated 10 June 1990 counsel stated his view that the only possible ground of appeal related to the ‘admissibility of the evidence of Mrs G.’ and to the question ‘that the trial judge erred in exercising discretion in allowing her to be present’. The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. Mr Boner lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction. The application to extend legal aid to the appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. Despite the advice of his solicitors and counsel, Mr Boner decided to proceed with the appeal. The applicant, who had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions, presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in Edinburgh and acting as an appellate court. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The appeal court considered the appeal court's decision to admit Mrs G.’s evidence as admissible. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The court found the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. As the applicant did not address the court on the remaining grounds of Appeal, these were not considered by the court. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. The appeal was dismissed on all grounds except for those raised by Mrs G, who was found not guilty of any offence. She was found guilty of a single count of misconduct in public office and sentenced to two years in prison.

The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 18711/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 4 April 1991 by a British citizen. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) ( art. 6-3-c). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Maxwell v the UK should be heard by the same Chamber. The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Between 29 March and 10 April 1990 he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. During the trial a prosecution witness, Mrs G., entered the courtroom prior to giving evidence. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Lord Rodger and Ms Rae. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter. He found that the relevant legal conditions were satisfied and permitted Mrs G to give her evidence. In her evidence, Mrs G stated that the applicant had been at her home the evening before the robbery and had spoken of robbing the post office. The following morning he had left the house and returned later with a bag, in a state of nervousness. The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. Mr Boner's application for legal aid to extend appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. Legal Aid Board asked the applicant to provide an opinion from counsel on the prospects of success. In this latter opinion counsel reiterated the view that the appeal rested on the question whether Mrs G.’s evidence was admissible. But he again stated that he had not been provided with sufficient material on which to assess the merits of the appeal. Mr Boner decided to proceed with the appeal and presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary, sitting in Edinburgh and acting as an appellate court. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The court held that the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. As the applicant did not address the court on the remaining grounds of Appeal, these were not considered by the court. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. The appeal was dismissed on all other grounds, as well as the grounds raised by Mrs G., and the case was adjourned until a later date.

name: Guy Laumont
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. On 27 October 2000 the Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 31 August 2000. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the French Government. The appeal was rejected on 2 December 2000 and the case was dismissed on 6 December 2000. A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. An employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing. The judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit) and made a partial discharge order. The Indictment Division of the Versailles Court of Appeal ordered further investigations to be made and appointed for that purpose the investigating judge at theVersailles tribunal de grande instance. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Créteil public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention but had received no reply. The applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily. In a judgment of 19 August 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on 19 January 1995 a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of [the applicant], who was under investigation for offences including armed robbery.” The application was refused in the judgment now appealed against on the grounds that the investigating court did not lay itself open to the objections raised. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. He was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment at the Versailles Assize Court. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 18 December 1997. In a judgment delivered on the same day on the civil claims the applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages. The initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken.

name: Thomas John Crompton
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. He was made redundant from the Territorial Army in 1994. He later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical store-man post remained vacant. He also applied for a number of other clerical posts within the Army but was refused for them. In 1994 the applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal. His claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board of the Defence Council. The Army Board found in the applicant's favour as regards his argument that he ought to have been, but was not, given priority before five selection boards. It ordered that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. In November 2001 a further offer of settlement was made to the applicant, which he rejected. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary, a redundancy payment estimated on the basis of the applicant’s actual earnings during the relevant period, and a compensation payment. The High Court ordered the Court of Appeal to make an order to pay the damages. The appeal was denied on the grounds that the amount was too low. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which rejected the appeal. The court then ordered the payment of the full amount of the damages to be made in full. The payment was made in July 2004, but was delayed by a year and a half. The award was finally made in May 2006. The damages were paid in full after a further two years, but the appeal was rejected again in March 2007. The High Court ruled that the award was not excessive and that it should be reduced to £50,000. The Army Board awarded the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47 on 24 May 2005. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. No further action was taken against the applicant. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal for the Courts of Justice of the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled in favour of the applicant on the grounds that the award of 24 May2005 had been incorrectly reached.

The case originated in an application (no. 42509/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The application was brought by a British national, Mr Thomas John Crompton (‘the applicant’), on 20 November 2005. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ms H. Moynihan, Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was heard by the Fourth Section of the Court of Appeal on 13 May 2008. The applications were heard by a panel of three judges. The applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal, but his claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board met to reach a determination on 11 April 2001. It issued its decision on 16 July 2001, ordering that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary ( minus the applicant's actual earnings during the relevant period); a redundancy payment estimated on the basis of the Army Act 1955; and a further offer of settlement. The applicant disputed the calculation of the compensation. The High Court rejected the offer on the basis that it did not include any compensation for the loss of time. A further offer of GBP 153,000 was made in 2004, but was also rejected. The case was adjourned until 2007, when the court ruled in favour of the original offer. The court also ordered the claimant to pay back the full amount he was owed. The award was later reduced to GBP 150,000. The judge ruled that the amount was too low because the compensation was not paid within the required time period. The appeal was finally settled in 2007 when the judge ruled in favor of the initial offer. The Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47 on 24 May 2005. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. In addition to the compensation, the applicant was awarded an interest-free loan of £100,000. The settlement was agreed between the two parties in January 2006. The terms of the settlement were finalised in March 2007.

name: Lorraine Dickson

Whether the child might expect to be without a father or mother for an important part of its childhood years. Auld LJ relied in principle on the judgment of the Court of Appeal in R (Mellor) v Secretary of State for the Home Department ([2001] 3 WLR 533). He pointed to the similarity of the arguments put by the applicants in the present case and in the Mellor case. He then noted that on occasions the Secretary of. State had “dis-applied the policy” when the circumstances had merited it. “To the extent that [the applicants have] suggested that he Secretary. of State has irrationally misapplied his own policy to the circumstances, or has otherwise acted disproportionately in applying it, I would. I would say it is not open to them to seek to re-open the validity of the policy which this court has held in Mellor is rational’ Mance LJ: “There is no basis for saying that the Secretary of State’s approach can be equated, as [the applicants] suggested, with the extinction of a fundamental right. reject the suggestion.” The other judges also relied on the judgment in Mellor, Mance said. “The case of Mellor is also clear authority that considerations and potential consequences of public interest over and above a narrow view of the requirements of good order and security in prison can play a role in a decision whether or not to permit such artificial insemination,” he said. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15737/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 10 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice on 6 November 2009. The decision was made by the majority of three judges. The Izmir State Security Court held its first hearing on 11 May 1999. The judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time. The applicant retracted his earlier submissions, claiming that he had made them under duress. He further contested the verbatim records of the reconstruction of events and other evidence which incriminated him. On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges sitting on the bench of the State Security Courts were replaced by civilian judges. The next hearing was held on 7 October 1999 where the court heard evidence from one complainant, Mr R.G., who had not witnessed the incidents. The Court of Cassation quashed the conviction as regards his conviction under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 13 June 2001 the applicant appealed. In his petition, he submitted that, apart from evidence obtained under duress at the pre-trial stage, there was no evidence to demonstrate that he had taken part in these acts. He further complained that there was nothing to indicate that he was part of an illegal organisation and that therefore Article 168 should not have been applied to him. By letter dated 16 June 2008 the applicant’s representative informed the Court that the applicant was no longer in prison. The appeal was dismissed and he was released from prison.

The case originated in an application (no. 15737/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant admitted, inter alia, to taking part in three separate acts of arson together with Mr M.K. and Mr F.D. in order to protest against the arrest of Abdullah Öcalan. The applicant and his lawyer were accused of setting fire to a car on 19 February 1999 and settingFire to two buildings on 13 and 14 March 1999. The applicant retracted his earlier submissions, claiming that he had made them under duress. He further contested the verbatim records of the reconstruction of events and other evidence which incriminated him. The court did not respond to the applicant's lawyer’s request to make additional defence submissions under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The next hearing was held on 7 October 1999 where the court heard evidence from one complainant, Mr R.G., who had not witnessed the incidents. Ms F.K., the sister of one of the accused, maintained that she and her brother had been subjected to torture in custody. The applicant was convicted of arson under Article 168 of the Criminal Code. He appealed the conviction, claiming that there was no evidence that he had taken part in arson. The Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court's decision. The applicant was sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison. He has since been released from prison after a three-year appeal process. The application was rejected on the grounds that Article 168 should not have been applied to the applicant. The case was referred to the High Court of Justice for further proceedings. It is not known whether the applicant is still in prison or has been released. The appeal was dismissed on the basis of a lack of evidence that the applicant was part of an illegal organisation.

Soldiers O, P, Q and R were instructed to position themselves in a wooded area to the south of the Loughgall Road, near what is known as Ballygasey Cottage (Position 4) Soldiers S, T and U were positioned in a woods to the rear of St Luke’s Church and to the east of the R UC station (Position 5) Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. One of the sons was brought outside to fill it with diesel. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house and placed in the bucket of the digger. The soldiers reported a number of sightings of the blue Hiace van passing in front of the RUC station in both directions. Reports that the van had been hijacked, and that a digger was acting suspiciously in the area. The soldiers were on full alert when, between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m., the blue van came from the Loughgall direction and parked outside the station on the far side of the road facing Armagh. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van and began to shoot at the R UC station. Soldiers A to E, who had positioned themselves at windows on the first floor of the station began to return fire without warning. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Soldier V fired at a man in a blue boiler suit crossing the road in a crouched manner. Soldier K saw a man whom he apprehended, tied his hands and feet and handed him over to the R UC who arrested him. This man was a Mr Tennyson who was not involved in the attack. He happened on the shooting, and had left his car to seek cover. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. Soldier X checking the body found that the man was holding a cigarette lighter. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van (with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork) and a white Citroen car (with about 34 bullet holes) The vehicles were directed to positions of safety by soldiers as soon as the opportunity arose. When the shooting ceased the soldiers and members of the RUC were airlifted back to their barracks. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. Debris on the rifle suggests that this person was lying on the ground before the explosion. The pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was lying in a lane-way opposite the premises of the Loughgall Football Club. This body was not wearing a boiler suit and there was a cigarette lighter close to the right hand. Post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel) Spent cartridge cases were recovered from all over the crime scene. name: Timothy Walker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37212/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the obligation imposed on him as a man in employment over age 60 to pay national insurance contributions, which did not apply to a woman in work of over that age, was in violation of Article 14 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a decision of 16 March 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant paid 10% of his earnings (between the primary threshold of GBP 385 and the upper earnings limit of 2,535) in NICs (Class 1), amounting to GBP 215 per month and GBP 2,580 per annum. A woman of 60 years or more who continued to work would not be required to pay any NICs on her earnings. The applicant wrote to his Member of Parliament and the Paymaster General complaining about the difference in treatment for men and women. Both replied stating that since liability to pay national insurance contributions is linked to the state pension age, the treatment of men and woman would equalise in 2020.

name: Krzysztof Ruminski
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Krzysztof Ruminski alleged that his physical problems had been caused by his former employment as a driver. The Social Insurance Office (Försäkringskassan) appointed an in-house specialist in orthopaedic surgery who concluded that there was not a high degree of probability (hög grad av sannolikhet) that any harmful element in the applicant’s former employment had caused his problems. The circumstances of the case are described below. The applicant’s back problems had appeared after barely two years in the industry and he suffered from degenerative changes to his back. The Social Insurance Office questioned the conclusions in the medical statement as they were based on information about exposure which was to a high degree uncertain. In a judgment of 27 October 2008, the Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the lower court‘s judgment in full. The court found that, although it was scientifically known that employees in the food industry had a statistically high risk of injury, the circumstances in the applicant's case had to be taken into account. The judge said that the medical and other evidence in the case does not demonstrate that the applicant has been exposed to any such harmful influences. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Högsta förvaltningsdomstolen) in 2009. He complained of the lack of reasoning in the Administrative Court of Appeal’s judgment. He argued that that court's refusal to hold an oral hearing had infringed his right to a fair trial within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was declared inadmissible by the Court on 21 May 2013 for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. On 30 December 2013, the applicant lodged a claim for compensation for the alleged breaches of the convention. He requested 50,000 Swedish kronor (SEK) fornon-pecuniary damage. On 15 January 2015 the Chancellor of Justice rejected the applicant's claim. In accordance with the Court’s case-law, a less strict standard applied to the requirement to hold a hearing before the appellate court. The Administrative Court of Appeal had taken a stance on the central and decisive question in the case, that is, whether the applicant had been exposed to harmful influences in his work. While the Chancellor noted that it would have been preferable, for pedagogical reasons, for the court to have given clearer grounds for why the applicant’'s evidence had not been sufficient, she concluded that the reasoning was not so deficient that the applicant's right to a fair trial had been infringed under Article 6 of the Convention. The standard of proof was somewhat mitigated on 1 July 2002, but that amendment did not apply to the applicant’s case. name: Fazlı Kaya
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24820/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 18 January 2011 the application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance during the applicant’s police custody and his inability to question some of the witnesses were communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant is currently serving a prison sentence in Edirne, Turkey. The application was filed by Mr Fazlı Kaya (“the applicant”), on 13 June 2005. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal organisation. He was found guilty and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. In December 2004 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal. This decision was deposited with the registry of the first instance court on 5 January 2005. The applicant was sentenced to 12 years and 6 months’ imprisonment under Article 168 of the former Criminal Code. In delivering its decision, amongst other items of evidence, the trial court relied on the statements of the co-accused, and also took into consideration the. statements of İ.H., E.G. and A.S.

name: Tony Michael Chalkley
train_texts: The case stems from an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained about the use of a surveillance device in his home. The Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on just satisfactions. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and his partner, Mr Tony Michael Chalkley. WDC Fletcher briefed three officers about purported grounds for arresting the applicant and his partner for credit card fraud, without informing them of the intended installation of the device. Officers from the Regional Crime Squad then used the house key to enter the applicant’s home and install the listening device. The trial was at Peterborough Crown Court in October 1996. An application was made, in a voir dire procedure, on behalf of the defendants for the tape recorded evidence to be excluded under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 on the basis that it had been obtained unlawfully and in breach of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The tape-recordings amounted to confessions of serious crimes involving the possible use of firearms. The judge ruled the evidence admissible. The applicant and his co-defendant changed their pleas to guilty. They were each sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment. On 18 December 1997, after being granted leave to appeal, the applicant’s appeal against conviction was dismissed by the Court of Appeal (R. v. Chalkley and Jeffries [1998] 2 All ER 155). On 15 June 1998 the House of Lords refused the applicant's petition for leave to Appeal. In early 2001, the application was released on licence.

name: Naim Aktar
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3738/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant bought seven plots of land in the Bozcaada region of Çanakkale from a private person by way of a bill of sale in 1977. On an unspecified date, a land registry survey was carried out in the region, as a result of which the plots in question were registered in the name of the Treasury. The court held that there was no record of ownership in the land register in respect of these three plots and the applicant had therefore acquired title to them. Bozcaada Cadastral Court relied on a number of sources, including on‑site inspection reports, statements from witnesses and local experts, title deeds, tax records, bills of sale, sketch plans and agricultural and technical expert reports. On 18 June 2003 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's rectification request. This decision was served on the applicant on 11 July 2003. The conditions for adverse possession of unregistered land had not been fulfilled by the applicant in the instant case. The applicant, therefore, could not claim title to the plots in question. The Bozcaada cadastral court upheld the judgment on 4 February 2003.

name: Arnaldo Otegi Mondragon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2034/07) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. In view of the information available to it, the Court decided that no hearing was necessary. The case was heard by the Third Section of the Court, which decided that it was not necessary to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Basque Country High Court of Justice has jurisdiction to try the applicant because of his status as a member of parliament. The public prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for ‘serious insult against the King’ on account of his remarks made on 26 February 2003. The applicant argued that his remarks had constituted political criticism directed against the Head of the government of the Basques Country. He added that to say that the King of Spain was the Supreme Head. of the Civil Guard did not imply any intention to undermine dignity or honour; it was merely. merely merely political criticism. The criminal proceedings in the Basque. Country High court of Justice began on 7 April 2003. The High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. The court found that his remarks had been “clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality’ The Constitution does not guarantee the right to freedom of expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct, the court found. “... This is not an issue concerning the private life of the Head of State but one of rejection of the ties of political power deriving from the hereditary nature of the institution which he personally symbolises” The court also found that criticism of a constitutional institution is not excluded from the scope of the right of expression. The public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. In the view of the public prosecutor, it was clear that the King had been performing official duties and that he was a figure in the public eye; however, that did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court's case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year’s imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to pay a fine. Supreme Court considered the impugned remarks to have been value judgments rather than statements of fact. Judge P.A.I. issued a dissenting opinion in which he argued that the comments complained of had been of a political nature. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour but had been directed solely at his institutional role as Commander-in-Chief of the Spanish armed forces. The applicant had not claimed that the King was responsible for actual acts of torture, only that he was strictly liable as Head of the State apparatus. In a decision (auto) of 3 July 2006, served on 11 July 2006,. the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s amparo appeal inadmissible. as manifestly devoid of constitutional content. The Constitutional Court noted at the outset that the right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered, namely the warm welcome extended to the King of Spain by the government of the Basque Country in the wake of the closure of the daily newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria. The court said there was no denying the ignominious, vexatious and derogatory nature of the impugned remarks, even when directed against a public figure. The King occupied a neutral position in political debate. This implied that he was owed institutional respect of a kind that was ‘substantively’ different from that due to other State institutions. The Constitutional Court held that the applicant’s remarks, on account of their obviously derogatory nature, had clearly gone beyond what could be considered legitimate. The applicant was imprisoned on 8 June 2007 after the Supreme Court upheld a judgment of the Audiencia Nacional of 27 April 2006 sentencing him to fifteen months’ imprisonment for publicly defending terrorism. According to the Government, his sentence was remitted on 16 July 2009. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 27644/95) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by twelve Swiss nationals. The applicants complained that they had not had access to a “tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6.0. The Commission declared the application admissible on 7 April 1997. On 14 January 1999 a panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber. The applicants live in the villages of Villigen, Würenlingen, Böttstein and Kleindöttingen. The Beznau II nuclear power plant consists of a dual-loop pressurised water reactor. The site is situated five kilometres from the German border. The application for an operating licence for the plant was made on 18 December 1991. The Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial and replied to the questions of the Court. The Court decided that it was not necessary to hold a hearing. Complainants requested the Federal Council to refuse an extension of the operating licence and to order the immediate and permanent closure of the nuclear power plant. The Federal Council dismissed all the objections as being unfounded and granted NOK a limited operating licence expiring on 31 December 2004. The licence was subject to compliance with various specific conditions concerning, for instance, threshold levels for radioactive substances, tests of the safeguard system, improvements of the feedwater system, for ageing surveillance and various other continuous technical improvements. NOK was also requested to submit periodically updated safety reports. The decision relied on a safety evaluation report established by the Swiss Nuclear Safety Inspectorate. The Federal Council relied on an opinion of the Nuclear Technology and Safety Section of the Federal Energy Office. The report gave the results from the point of view of nuclear safety and radiation protection, including conclusions and proposals for licence conditions to be formulated in the licensing decision. The Federal Council observed that although power stations built twenty years earlier certainly no longer met current technical standards, they could nonetheless be maintained and modernised so that they could continue to operate quite safely. It referred to the emergency standby system and improved power supply system (NANO), put into operation in 1992, and the filtered containment venting system. Furthermore the results of the probabilistic safety analysis carried out at the Beznau II nuclear power plant showed that a nuclear accident was unlikely. The Federal Council observed that by voting against the popular initiative of 23 September 1990 (see paragraphs 20-21 below) “For the Progressive Abandonment of Nuclear Energy” the Swiss people and the majority of the cantons had expressed the wish to continue using nuclear energy. With regard to the reactor accident at Chernobyl, the Federal Council stated that the reactor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant was technically not comparable to a light-water reactor like that of the Beznau II power plant. Council also pointed out that, in accordance with the Agreement of 10 August 1982 between the government of the Swiss Confederation and the Federal Republic of Germany, the German authorities had been provided with the relevant documents. The condition of the power plant with regard to nuclear safety and radiation protection and also to its operation had been rated as good. The relevant documentation examined by the HSK had not revealed any safety-relevant gaps in the maintenance programmes. All the safety systems installed at the Beznau II nuclear power plant for the purpose of preventing nuclear accidents were very seriously flawed compared with more modern pressurised water reactors in central Europe. The safety systems for their failure to ensure that the back-up components were physically separate and protected from fire. The standard of the emergency cooling system and residual heat removal compared to modern light water pressure reactors in Central Europe. From 30 November to 11 December 1998 a team of eleven experts of the International Regulatory Review Team (IRRT) reviewed the working methods of the HSK. During the mission six members of the team also visited the Beznau II nuclear power plant. In their report of January 1999 the reviewers identified “a number of good practices which had been recorded for the benefit of other nuclear regulatory bodies” The report compared the attitude adopted in the last few years to older, Westinghouse-type, first-generation pressurised water reactors by the supervisory authorities in various countries of Europe, the USA and Japan and reached the conclusion that the standards applied in the licensing procedure were far below those applying in other central European countries.

Council further observed that by voting against the popular initiative of 23 September 1990 (see paragraphs 20-21 below) “For the Progressive Abandonment of Nuclear Energy’ The German-Swiss Commission on the Safety of Nuclear Installations (Deutsch-Schweizerische Kommission für die Sicherheit kerntechnischer Einrichtungen – “DSK”) presented annual reports giving a concise evaluation of the conditions. The licence at issue continued to tolerate the serious safety deficiencies which had already been mentioned in previous expert reports of 1992 and 1994. The lack of protection against outside influences rendered the plant much more vulnerable to a plane crash or to action by third parties. The standards applied in the licensing procedure at issue were far below those applying in other central European countries – i.e. risks were accepted that would no longer be tolerated in other countries. The report further referred to the OSART mission which was conducted in 1995 and the criticism expressed by the experts with regard to the organisational structures and management at the Beznau II power plant. In their report of January 1999 the reviewers identified “a number of good practices which had been recorded for the benefit of other nuclear regulatory bodies”

The Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case. Complainants requested the Federal Council to refuse an extension of the operating licence and to order the immediate and permanent closure of the nuclear power plant. The Federal Council dismissed all the objections as being unfounded and granted NOK a limited operating licence expiring on 31 December 2004. The licence was subject to compliance with various specific conditions concerning, for instance, threshold levels for radioactive substances, tests of the safeguard system, improvements of the feedwater system, for ageing surveillance and various other continuous technical improvements. NOK was also requested to submit periodically updated safety reports. More than 99% of the objections were photocopies. The complaint was filed by the Federal Energy Office, a large part of which came from Germany and Austria. The Federal Council was satisfied that certain complainants lived in zone 1 around the nuclear power plant and were therefore entitled to take part in the proceedings. The Federal Council observed that although power stations built twenty years earlier certainly no longer met current technical standards, they could nonetheless be maintained and modernised so that they could continue to operate quite safely. It referred to the emergency standby system and improved power supply system (NANO), put into operation in 1992, and the filtered containment venting system. Furthermore the results of the probabilistic safety analysis carried out at the Beznau IInuclear power plant showed that a nuclear accident was unlikely. The Federal Council said that the reactor of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant was technically not comparable to a light-water reactor like that of the Beznau II power plant. Council further observed that by voting against the popular initiative of 23 September 1990 (see paragraphs 20-21 below) “For the Progressive Abandonment of Nuclear Energy” the Swiss people and the majority of the cantons had expressed the wish to continue using nuclear energy. The Federal Council also pointed out that, in accordance with the Agreement of 10 August 1982, the German authorities had been provided with the relevant documents relating to the requested operating licence. There would be no risk for the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. The condition of the power plant with regard to nuclear safety and radiation protection and also to its operation had been rated as good. The relevant documentation examined by the HSK had not revealed any safety-relevant gaps in the maintenance programmes. All the safety systems installed at the Beznau II nuclear power plant for the purpose of preventing nuclear accidents were very seriously flawed compared with more modern pressurised water reactors in central Europe. The safety systems for their failure to ensure that the back-up components were physically separate and protected from fire. The standard of the emergency cooling system and residual heat removal compared to modern light water pressure reactors in Central Europe. Lack of protection against outside influences rendered the plant much more vulnerable to a plane crash or to action by third parties. No demand had been made for an actual emergency system, such as was required for the more recent western European pressurised water reactors. The standards applied in the licensing procedure at issue were far below those applying in other central European countries – i.e. risks were accepted that would no longer be tolerated in other countries. The report further referred to the OSART mission which was conducted in 1995 and the criticism expressed by the experts with regard to the organisational structures and management at the Beznau II power plant.

name: Wiesław Pióro
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8362/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants’ father’s land “Terebella” was expropriated for the purpose of an agrarian reform programme in 1944. On 29 January 1949 the Minister of Agriculture quashed this decision. On 20 May 1994 the applicants filed a motion for annulment of the 1949 decision. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected their appeal on the ground that they had failed to exhaust the available remedies i.e. they had not filed a request with the Minister for reconsider. The applicants applied to the Minister of Agriculture for leave to file out of time a motion for reconsideration (wniosek o ponowne rozpatrzenie sprawy) of the decision of 5 September 1996. The applicants lodged an appeal against that decision with the Supreme Administrative Court. On 3 November 2000 the court quashed the Minister’s decision of 12 May 2000 and remitted the case. On 11 February 2004 the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court gave judgment quashing the challenged decision of the Minister. The Minister upheld his decision on 18 November 2004. Upon an appeal by the second applicant, on 24 May 2005 the Warsaw regional Administrative Court quashed both decisions. The 1949 decision was issued in breach of the procedural law but refused to declare it null and void on the ground that it had produced irreversible effects. The authorities instructed the applicants to proceed with a claim for compensation for the unlawfully expropriated land under Article 160 of the Code of Administrative Procedure. The applicants were further instructed that, in the event they were not satisfied with the outcome of the administrative proceedings for compensation, they were free to file with a civil court an action for tort under Article 417 of the Civil Code. In January 2008 the applicants filed with the Minister of Agriculture a claims for compensation. The proceedings are currently pending. The applications for compensation are under appeal.

name: Yasser Chraidi
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Yasser Chraidi, was born in 1959 in Lebanon. At the time of lodging his application, he was detained in Berlin. He is currently living in Lebanon and was arrested by the police in Lebanon in 1992. He was acquitted of E.’s murder but convicted of forgery and sentenced to one year and six months’ imprisonment in 1994. On 24 May 1996 the applicant was extradited to Germany and subsequently held in detention on remand on account of the arrest warrant issued in 1990. On 21 November 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application. Berlin Regional Court rejected a request by the applicant for release in 2000. Appeal ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand. The danger of his absconding still persisted because the applicant had been extradited to Germany only in May 1996 and had neither a fixed dwelling nor social ties in Germany which would prevent him from abscond if released. The court moreover referred to the lifelong prison sentence the applicant faced and underlined that more lenient preventive measures would not be suitable. Lastly, there had been no breach of the obligation to proceed speedily (Beschleunigungsgebot) (German law) The Berlin Regional Court convicted the applicant on three counts of aiding and abetting murder. The court alluded to the tensions between the United States and Libya which had arisen following terrorist attacks in 1985. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed appeals on points of law by the applicant and the public prosecutor. On 28 April 2005 the applicant was released from prison. He was sentenced to 14 years’ imprisonment, but was released in April 2005 after serving just eight months of his 14-year sentence. The applicant was initially detained in Lebanon with a view to extradition in connection with the present case. This period of detention was to be deducted from his prison sentence at a ratio of 1:3 until 30 April 1994 and from 1 May 1994.

name: Morten Sørensen
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber constituted within the First section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected. Third-party comments were received from the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions (Landsorganisationen – LO) A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. In the spring of 1996 he did his national service. On 10 May 1996 he applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (“FDB”). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. The applicant informed his employer and the shop steward that he did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership of SID. On 24 June 1996, the applicant was dismissed for not satisfying the requirements for obtaining the job as he was not a member of a trade union affiliated to LO. The applicant, represented by Denmark's Free Trade Union, instituted proceedings before the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) against FDB, requesting that FDB be ordered to acknowledge that his dismissal was unlawful and to pay him compensation. The High Court ruled that the domestic courts should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He was offered a job at a nursery on condition that he became a member of SID. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He was a member in the mid-1980s, but resigned his membership after a few years as he felt unable to support its political affiliations. He is a former member of the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening I/S) and a former president of the Norwegian Labour Party (NLM). He has been married to the former NLM president, Jens Bremen, since 1998.

He then rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He was offered a job at a nursery on condition that he became a member. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined the union. He died on 4 June 2007, at the age of 74. He is survived by his wife, three children and a step-granddaughter. He has also written books about SID and the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening).
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By decisions of 20 March 2003, the applications were declared partly admissible. In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber constituted within the First section relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. Third-party comments were received from the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions (Landsorganisationen – LO) A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 2005. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. In the spring of 1996 he did his national service. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (‘FDB’). In a letter of 20 May 1996, the applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. The applicant was dismissed for not satisfying the requirements for obtaining the job as he was not a member of a trade union affiliated to LO. He alleged that section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act of 9 June 1982 violated Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant said he did not want to pay the subscription to SID because he had been told that, as a holiday relief employee, he would not be given full membership of SID. The High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant did not comply with this requirement.” The High Court ruled that the domestic courts should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. On appeal, the Supreme Court (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The second applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Haderslev, Denmark. He is a gardener by profession. He became a judge in 1999. A former member of SID became a member of the Christian Trade Union (Kristelig Fagforening I/S) The applicant was offered a job at a nursery on condition that he was a SID member as the employer had entered into a closed-shop agreement with that trade union. The applicant commenced the job on 17 May 1999 and rejoined SID, although he still did not agree with its political views. He died in August 2006, at the age of 69. He was buried in a cemetery near his home in Kristelig, Norway, near the village of Kvitkov, where he used to live.

name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1638/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the residence prohibition against him violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 2 June 2005. The Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene (Article 36) in the case. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was convicted of 18 counts of partially completed and partially attempted aggravated burglary. He was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment, 13 of which were suspended on probation. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten years’ residence prohibition on the applicant. He appealed against the prohibition, but the decision was upheld by the Vienna Juvenile Court on 19 July 2002. The applicant served his prison term until 24 May 2002. He did not benefit from early release from his prison sentence. The court found that the public interest in the prevention of disorder and crime outweighed the applicant's interest in staying in Austria. The applicant came to Austria at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and was not able to speak Bulgarian. He drew attention to the fact that he was still a minor and had no relatives and other social contacts in Bulgaria. He was arrested on 27 November 2003 and deported to Sofia on 22 December 2003. The application was rejected by the Constitutional Court for lack of prospects of success and he was deported to Bulgaria in December 2003 after being detained for a year. The case was upheld by the Vienna Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektion) on 18 August 2003 and the applicant was deported on 22 November 2003.

The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant alleged, in particular, that the residence prohibition against him violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. By a decision of 2 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant was born in 1984 and currently lives in Bulgaria. He was convicted in 1999 of 22 counts of aggravated gang burglary and extortion. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant in 2005. The applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between June 1999 and January 2000. On 11 February 2000 the Vienna Juvenile Court remanded him in custody. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten years’ residence prohibition on the applicant. The applicant appealed, but the court ruled that further stay in Austria was contrary to the public interest. He was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment, 13 of which were suspended on probation. The court noted the applicant’s confession as a mitigating circumstance, the number of offences committed as well as the rapid relapse into crime. The applicant filed complaints both with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) and the Constitutional Court. He stressed that he had come to Austria at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and was not able to speak Bulgarian. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the residence prohibition was justified under Article 8 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. The Vienna Federal Police Authority requested the applicant to leave Austria. The applicant was arrested on 27 November 2003 and deported to Sofia on 22 December 2003. He was still a minor when he was deported.

name: Frans Vermeulen
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Kingdom of Belgium. It originated in an application (no. 19075/91) against Belgium lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 6 November 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). Professor J. Van Compernolle was appointed to sit as ad hoc judge. On 24 May 1995 the Chamber relinquished jurisdiction in favour of a Grand Chamber. On 8 June 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the additional judges. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 30 August 1995. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Debrulle, Head of Department, Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr L. Simont, avocat, Mr E. Jakhian, counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr Danelius, Mr De Boel, Mr Traest, MrJakhian and Mr Simont, and also their replies to a question put by one of its members. It had heard the opinion of the deputy procureur du Roi but had not heard the applicant himself, who was in custody in Ghent prison on account of criminal proceedings against him for forgery, uttering, fraud and misappropriation. The applicant applied to the court to set aside that judgment and rehear the case. The court declared the application admissible, ordered that the proceedings should be reopened and put the case on the special list pending the outcome of the criminal investigation. Antwerp Court of Appeal acquitted the applicant of all the criminal offences with which he had been charged. The judge rapporteur, Mr Vermeulen’s lawyer and Mr du Jardin, the avocat général, made oral submissions and subsequently took part in the court’’ deliberations. The applicant was acquitted on 17 March 1995 of all charges against him. The trial was held in the courtroom of the procureur genéral in Antwerp, Belgium. The hearing was held between 13 and 16 March 1995, in front of a jury of eight. The jury found the applicant not guilty on all charges and acquitted him.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68694/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr T. Fırat, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was filed by twelve Turkish nationals, who were detained in the Buca prison, in İzmir, at the time of the present application. Preliminary investigation was instigated by the İzmir public prosecutor's office into the allegations of the applicants. The applicants reiterated that they were beaten by the gendarmes and the prison wardens. A forensic expert examined Ahmet Güven, Kadri Sönmez, Metin Göktepe, Neslihan Gök tepe, İzzettin Koç, Kadir Issı, Mehmet Kışanak, Rıdvan Karatay, Ali Kemal Yıldız and Ms Emsihan Karaty in prison. The investigation concerning the incident in Buca prison is still ongoing. The doctor observed swellings and erythemas on the upper part of the back, underneath the chin and around the nose and mouth as a result of blows. He concluded that the injuries rendered Mehmet Kışanak unfit for work for ten days and that he would recover within twenty days following a medical treatment. The doctor decided that Rıdvan Karatay should be referred to the ophthalmologist at the Izmir State Hospital. The medical report referred to pain in the head, wounds on the right eye orbit, swellings in the right arm and to ecchymosis behind the ear. The injuries rendered Ahmet Güven unfit for five days. Yaşar Avcı was hospitalised on 20 July 1995 with the diagnosis of ‘general body trauma’ He was discharged from the hospital on 28 July 1995 and was re‑examined on 9 October 1995. The expert concluded that the injuries had not been life threatening but had rendered him unfit for work for ten days and that he would recover. The prosecutor decided not to prosecute the Director of Buca Prison and his staff for alleged ill-treatment of the applicants. The applicants objected to this decision. On 25 June 1996 the Karşıyaka Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection. On 11 April 1996 the prosecutor transferred the investigation file concerning the gendarmes to the İzmir Administrative Council. Ahmet Güven was convicted of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of a part of the national territory under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. He was sentenced to death on 2 December 1998 and had his sentence commuted to life imprisonment on 6 September 2002. The Government decided not to bring proceedings against the gendarmes responsible for the transfer of the applicants to court on 20 July 1995. The applicants claimed they were never informed of the outcome of the proceedings and that they learned of the decision of the İzmir Administrative Council when the Court delivered its judgment in the case of Satık and Others (no. 31866/96, 10 October 2000) The applicant was diagnosed in 2003 as suffering from hypertension and amnesia. The Government submitted a number of documents as regards the applicant's transfer to various medical centres for check-up and the results of his analyses. They noted that he was receiving drug treatment and that he could physically continue to take care of himself within a prison facility. The applicant was released from prison on 1 November 2005, on 1 Nov 2005, the applicant was sentenced to five years in prison. As regards Rıdvan Karatay, the medical report referred to an ery thema and a swelling on the right eye orbit,  and to an ecchymosis behind his ear. The medical report also referred to pain in Ahmet Güven's head, wounds in his right arm and around his eyebrows. Yaşar Avcı, who was hospitalised on 20 July 1995 with the diagnosis of ‘general body trauma’, had sustained the following injuries at the time of the hospitalisation: ecchymoses on the back and on both shoulders, a graze of 2 x 2 cm on the right zygoma, erythemas in the forehead, sensitivity on the left tibia. The prosecutor decided not to prosecute the Director of Buca Prison and his staff for alleged ill-treatment of the applicants. The applicants objected to this decision. Ahmet Güven was convicted of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of a part of the national territory under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. His health deteriorated and he was prescribed medication as well as a special diet. He took part in hunger strikes on various occasions and that as a result his health deteriorated.
