name: Davood Amrollahi
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56811/00) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Iranian national, Davood Amrollahi. The Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2, in fine). The Government filed additional observations concerning exhaustion of national remedies. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by Mr Jørgen Lange, a lawyer practising in Copenhagen. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Hans Klingenberg. In 1992 he was granted a residence and work permit by the Danish government. In 1998 he was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to three years in prison. In 2008 he was released on bail. He has three children, one of whom was a daughter from a previous relationship. He also has a son and a daughter who were born in the 1990s. He is still living in Denmark and works as a carer in a retirement home for the elderly. He was granted permission to return to Iran in 1998 but returned to Denmark in 1998. In 2009 he was charged with drug trafficking for allegedly trafficking in heroine and was jailed for three years. The applicant had served two-thirds of his sentence and was due to be released on parole. He did not consent to the deportation and refused to leave the country voluntarily. He was detained as from that date in accordance with the Aliens Act with a view to being repatriated. The immigration authorities found, on 13 January 1999, that the applicant would not risk persecution in Iran of a kind which could constitute a basis for his remaining in Denmark. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Refugee Board (Flygtningenævnet), which on 16 April 1999 requested the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to provide more information on the situation in Iran. By judgment of 14 February 2000 the City Court revoked the decision to expel the applicant. The applicant was released from his detention on 11 May 2000. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision of 3 March 2000 as it agreed that a request for a review of an expulsion order pursuant to section 50 of the Aliens Act could only be examined once by the courts. On 7 September 2000 the Supreme Court agreed that the case could not be re-examined. The application was rejected and the applicant returned to the UK. The case was heard by the British Supreme Court in September 2000. It was the first time the court had heard the case since the case began in March 1999. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant, and the case was dismissed.

The immigration authorities found, on 13 January 1999, that the applicant would not risk persecution in Iran of a kind which could constitute a basis for his remaining in Denmark. The applicant was released from his detention on 11 May 2000. On 7 September 2000 the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision of 3 March 2000. The Supreme Court agreed that a request for a review of an expulsion order pursuant to section 50 of the Aliens Act could only be examined once by the courts. The High Court ruled that the application could not be made again before it was heard on 7 September. The applicant is a Swedish citizen resident in Stockholm. Since 1973 he has spent a total of eight years in prison for the commission of serious economic offences. The applicant claims that on two occasions, in April-June and June‑July 1991, he was the victim of kidnapping and extortion perpetrated by three persons. The applicant applied for compensation to the Criminal Damage Compensation Board (Brottsskadenämnden - hereinafter “the Board’) under the Criminal damage Act 1978. He said he had sought compensation for personal injury in the amount of SEK 160,000 in the proceedings against L. and that he had reserved his right to make any further claims with regard to future damage. The Stockholm District Court convicted L., sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay SEK 144,350 in damages to the applicant. The Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) reversed the District Court’s decision on the ground that the charges against L had not been proven. Nor is there any other reason for changing the decision.”“He had more or less repeated the same evidence he gave to the District Court.’’ “He was not able to make any further submissions.‘‘He was unable to make further submissions’. ‘“The Board did not consider that he had made any other submissions. “‘There was no reason for us to change our previous decision’

name: Mehmet Ümit Erdem
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42234/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant claimed that he was in the crowd that day when police officers from the Rapid Response Force used excessive force on them. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The events of 14 October 2001 were cited as the reason for the application. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) was represented by their Agent. The application was dismissed. The applicant was kicked and beaten up with truncheons. He felt pain in his arms, legs, chest and ribs. The applicant had a closed fracture on the right eleventh costal cartilage. The criminal investigation of the applicant’s complaint of ill‑treatment will be held in October 2011. The application has been dismissed with no further action to be taken against the police officers involved in the incident. The case will be heard in court in October next year. The complaint has been rejected by the court and is no longer a case of ill-treatment, but rather of a miscarriage of justice. The court will now decide how to proceed with the case. In November 2001, the Kadıköy public prosecutor requested authorisation from the Istanbul governor to prosecute the police officers allegedly responsible for the applicant’s ill-treatment. An Istanbul deputy police chief was appointed to carry out a preliminary investigation on behalf of the governor. The report recommended that authorisation for prosecution should be declined. The applicant lodged an objection to the governor's decision with the Regional Administrative Court. On 8 January 2002, the prosecutor decided not to bring any criminal proceedings against the security forces at the Rapid Force Department of the Istanbul Security Headquarters. An objection by the applicant to the prosecutor's decision was rejected on 18 January 2002. Istanbul Regional Administrative Court upheld the Istanbul Governor’s decision. applicant to this decision was dismissed by the Üsküdar Assize Court on 15 March 2002. On 2 May 2002 the Istanbul Regional administrative court upheld the governor's decision. The case was heard in the Istanbul High Court of Justice, which heard the case in November 2000. name: Liban Mohamud Ahmed
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59727/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Somali national Mr Liban Mohamud Ahmed. The applicant provided the immigration authorities with a false name and a false immigration history in order to avoid being sent back to the Netherlands. Although the asylum application was unsuccessful the applicant was granted exceptional leave to remain until 2004. In December 2007 he was convicted of a public order offence and of failing to surrender. He was sentenced to four and a half months’ imprisonment. Deportation order signed on 29 October 2008 and he was thereafter detained under paragraph 2(2) of Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971 pending his removal from the United Kingdom. On 2 June 2009 removal directions were set for 17 June 2009. They were cancelled on 16 June 2009 when the applicant made an application to this Court (application no. 26023/09), which granted an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. The form from July 2009 includes the following statement in reference to the Rule 39 measure: “Whilst this means that enforced removal is not possible, [the applicant] could reduce the length of time he spends in detention by withdrawing voluntarily” A similar point features in some, if not all, of the later forms. The applicant filed a claim for judicial review, contending that his ongoing detention was unlawful. Pursuant to the principles set down by the High Court in R. v. Durham Prison Governor ex parte Hardial Singh [1984] 1 WLR 704, the Secretary of State cannot lawfully detain a person pending removal for longer than a reasonable period. In a judgment dated 14 November 2011 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim. It noted that in deciding whether or not there was a realistic prospect that deportation would take place within a reasonable time, the risk of absconding or re-offending were ‘of paramount importance’ The Administrative Court considered whether alternatives to detention could be used such as electronic tagging, monitoring by telephone and regular reporting. Given the applicant’s history of absconding, it concluded that the alternatives would not have been sufficient and there was an absence of adequate assurances from the applicant. The court did not accept that there was not, at the time the interim measure was indicated, a realistic prospect of removing the applicant within a reasonable time. It therefore did not consider his continued detention up to 13 July 2011 to be unlawful. The applicant was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. He restated his arguments concerning the Hardial Singh principles which had been advanced in the court below. The Court of Appeal conducted an extensive review of the circumstances of the case. It accepted that at the time of receipt of the Rule 39 measure in the applicant’s case, there was nonetheless a reasonable prospect of their being concluded and of removal being effected within a reasonable time. Lord Justice Elias dissented on one point only: acknowledging that “there is no one right answer to the question what is a reasonable period”, he believed that the period of two weeks which elapsed following the judgment in Sufi and Elmi was too long for the applicant to be detained. The applicant argued that his detention was in breach of Article 5 of the Convention. It took into consideration the fact that the rule 39 measure applied in his case did not involve any specific assessment of risk towards him. Court accepted that if the applicant were able to show that the decisions to maintain his detention were vitiated by public law he would succeed in establishing that the detention was unlawful and would have a claim of false imprisonment. Court of Appeal found that although some of the passages in the review forms were not very happily expressed, they did not involve any legal error. Supreme Court refused the applicant leave to appeal on 26 March 2013. The court found that Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention added nothing of substance in the present case. In reaching this conclusion, it rejected the applicant’s assertion that Mikolenko v. Estonia, no. 10664/05, 8 October 2009 was authority for the proposition that the lack of a realistic prospect of deportation within a defined period rendered detention unlawful.

name: Gerard Magee
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged he was ill-treated while in detention and that he was denied a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. On 17 December 1988, the applicant complained to the same doctor he had seen the day before of ill-treatment during the second and third interviews on the previous day. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. At 1 p.m. the applicant was allowed to consult with his solicitor, who made notes on the applicant's allegations. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. The applicant was then interviewed for the last time about an unrelated matter. He was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.M. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions. The applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. On 3 March 1989 the applicant made an official written statement to the Complaints and Discipline Branch of the Royal Ulster Constabulary complaining about his ill-treatment by one team of two detectives while at Castlereagh police station. On 17 September 1990 the trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant did not subsequently give evidence at the trial. On 21 December 1990 the trial judge gave judgment. He noted that the only evidence against the applicant was the admissions and statement made while in custody at Castlereagh police station. The trial judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials. As to the ESDA evidence, the judge said it was impossible to accept that ill- treatment could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. The appeal was rejected on 16 June 1993. On 17 December 1993 the applicant’s appeal against his sentence was rejected. The case was settled by the Supreme Court of Ireland, which ruled that the trial judge had had the great advantage of seeing the applicant give evidence and that both an accused and police officers involved can equally have an incentive to lie.

On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. On 8 February 1993 the applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. That court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. Accordingly, on 16 June 1993 the applicants appeal against his sentence was rejected. On 17 December 1993, the applicant appealed against his prison sentence. The appeal was rejected on 17 June 1993, and the applicant returned to prison. The applicant was released from prison on 12 July 1994. The case was settled at Belfast Crown Court in March 1995.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. On the same day the applicant was interviewed five times by two teams of two detectives. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.m. on 17 December 1988. On 18 December 1988, the applicant. was visited by the same doctor who asked the applicant if he had any further allegations of ill-treatment. and the applicant replied that he had not. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. On 19 December 1988 the applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. On 3 March 1989 the applicant made an official written statement to the Complaints and Discipline Branch of the Royal Ulster Constabulary complaining about his ill-treatment by one team of two detectives while at Castlereagh police station. On 17 September 1990 the trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The trial judge rejected the application, admitted the applicant's admissions and statement into evidence and adjourned his detailed judgment. The applicant was found not guilty of ill-treatment by the court on 21 December 1990. The trial judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials of the allegations made by the applicant. The judge also found that not one single objective sign of the ill- treatment which the applicant alleged was found by any of the doctors who examined the applicant; and that on the morning of 18 December 1990, the applicant did not make any complaint about ill-treated despite the fact that he claimed he had suffered the worst treatment of all during the previous day. The applicant was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment in 1991. His appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland in 1993. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. On 17 December 1993 the applicant's appeal against his sentence was rejected. The application was dismissed on 13 March 1994. The appeal was dismissed again on 16 June 1995. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against him and was released on bail. The case was settled at Belfast Crown Court in September 1998. The trial judge found that it did not substantiate the applicant’s submission as to the lack of authenticity of the interview notes. The judge ruled that he was fully entitled to convict the applicant.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19165/08) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that his trial was unfair because of the non-disclosure of the sources of the evidence of a Chief Superintendent without adequate counterbalancing measures. The application was communicated to the Government on 4 January 2012. Written submissions were received from the Irish Human Rights Commission, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party. The Irish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr P. White, of the Department of Foreign Affairs. Five men who remained in the estate were arrested and charged with being members of an illegal organisation. Two of the men in the back of the van were dressed in clothing that gave the appearance of, and made them look like members of An Garda Síochána. When the Nissan Almera was later examined by the police they found it contained false registration plates which corresponded to its tax and insurance discs, these, in fact, being those of an identical car that had previously been stolen. The owner of the car was later identified as being MB. During police investigations, the Nissan Micra car which had left Corke Abbey after dropping off a man named O’Snodaigh was also found. Papers found which contained the phone number of the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) and the man in the driver’s seat of the Transit van (PB) The trial court later found that, at the very least, the applicant was acquainted with one of the men arrested on 10 October 2002 and with the owners of the car (see paragraph 22 below). On 18 November 2004 the SCC delivered its judgment convicting the applicant and his co-accused (NB) of the charges. The trial lasted 8 days. 54 prosecution witnesses were heard. The accused did not give any evidence at trial nor was any other evidence tendered on his behalf. The SCC considered four strands of evidence tendered by the prosecution. Chief Superintendent PK testified that he believed that, on 10 October 2002, the applicant was a member of the IRA. When asked to identify his sources, he claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK’s sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him (Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000-II) The SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK's evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial. The accused, it held, was entitled to some enquiry into the basis of PK. Chief Superintendent produced files which told him the accused were members of the IRA. The SCC found that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. The court rejected a suggestion put to the Chief Superintendent PK, in cross-examination that his evidence was a fiction. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The trial court held that the demands of justice required that it should not convict solely on the basis of PK’s evidence so the SCC went on to examine whether there was evidence which supported and corroborated the belief of PK. It found that PK had formed that belief ever before the ‘Corke Abbey’ events of 10 October 2002. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The SCC was satisfied beyond any doubt that this packaging and receipt matched the torch found in the Transit van. It was further satisfied that the dark green Nissan Micra observed by the police at Corke. Abbey was the property of Ms K, the partner of the applicant and that he, the applicant, had had control of the. motor vehicle on the evening in question. The trial court accepted that the documentation established that the applicant was, at the very least, acquainted with the driver of the Transit van (PB) and the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) The court was satisfied that not only were the relevant statutory provisions invoked and adequately explained to each accused but each was given an opportunity to protest in the event that he had not understood that explanation, an opportunity which was ignored. The video-recordings of the interviews were shown to the trial court. It noted that, not only did each remain totally silent during the course of interview, but each appeared to take no ostensible interest whatsoever in what was going on. They sat bolt upright showing remarkable self-control throughout. The court had ‘no doubt’ that, as provided for by section 2 of the 1998 Act, it was entitled to and did, in fact, draw the inference from the failure of each accused to answer those questions. The court was satisfied that their silence amounted to corroboration of the belief evidence given by Chief Superintendent PK. As the court did not doubt the evidence of PK that he believed each was a member of the IRA, the court was persuaded beyond all reasonable doubt that each of the accused was guilty of charged. The trial court added that it was not convinced that, standing alone, either the activities at Corke Abbey or the documentation found upon a search of their homes necessarily indicated activities or membership of an unlawful organisation.  applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (‘CCA’) was refused on 28 November 2006. The applicant sought leave to appeal against his conviction to the CCA claiming that the trial court had erred in law. He objected to any review by the trial judges, as adjudicators of guilt or innocence, of material underlying the belief of Chief Superintendent PK on the grounds that to do so was unlawful and contrary to the case-law of this Court. The Supreme Court in DPP v. Kelly ([2006] IESC 20) had found this limitation necessary and properly counterbalanced. The CCA held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. A statement to the contrary was explicitly made in the judgment itself. The CCA also considered that the events at Corke Abbey and an association with those events, the vehicles and the contents of the vehicles, the materials found during searches as well as the meetings between both accused at the time when the applicant’s house was being searched, were all matters which came within the ambit of ‘movements, actions, activities, or associations on the part of an accused person’ The CCA confirmed the association with events at Corke Abbey could not be considered in isolation. The court also found that the evidence was enough to support the conclusion that the men were members of the IRA. The case was referred to the Supreme Court, which said the right to silence was not an absolute right and must be balanced against the need to protect witnesses. The Supreme Court ruled in favour of the prosecution, and the case was heard again in November 2013. The trial was adjourned until January 2014, when it would be heard again on the merits of the case. The decision to uphold the conviction was returned to the Court of Appeal on January 24, 2014. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court. The CCA rejected the submission that the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence and it was clear from the SCC's review that there were no such documents. Moreover, the undisclosed documents were demonstrably not determinative as the applicant had suggested. The trial court had explicitly stated this to be so in its judgment. The applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the trial Judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents. The case originated in an application (no. 19165/08) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by an Irish national, Mr Kenneth Donohoe (“the applicant”), on 8 April 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms C. Almond, a lawyer practising in Dublin. The Irish Government (”the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr P. White, of the Department of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 4 January 2012. Written submissions were received from the Irish Human Rights Commission which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party. The Nissan Almera remained on the estate parked near the Transit van. One of the men walked away from the group while four of them got into the back of the van and one into the driver’s seat. A lump/sledge hammer; two pickaxe handles; a torch; eight plastic bags of cable ties; black balaclavas with single or double openings; woollen gloves; rolls of masking tape; a sky blue shirt marked ‘security’; a yellow fluorescent jacket with the word “GARDA” labelled on it. Five men of the original eight who remained in the estate, and who were in the Ford Transit van, were arrested and charged with being members of an illegal organisation. On 24 October 2002 the applicant was arrested under section 30 of the Offences against the State Act 1939, as amended (“the 1939 Act’). He was brought to the police station where he was questioned about membership, contrary to section 21 of the 1939 Act, of an unlawful organisation. The applicant did not make a statement and was released from custody. On 30 October 2002 he was arrested on suspicion that, on 10 October 2002, he was a member of the IRA. He and a co-accused (NB) were interviewed at length by police officers. Numerous questions were put to them concerning the events in Corke Abbey and the evidence gathered by the police. Trial court considered four strands of evidence tendered by the prosecution. Chief Superintendent testified that he believed applicant was a member of the IRA. When asked to identify his sources, PK claimed privilege stating that disclosure would endanger lives and State security. SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK’s evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial. The accused, it held, was entitled to some enquiry into the basis of PK's evidence. The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK's sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him. The Chief Superintendent claimed that the accused were members of the IRA. The SCC ruled that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. As the head of the Special Detective Unit, PK was the person best placed to learn of the activities of the accused. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The trial court held that the demands of justice required that it should not convict solely on the basis of PK’s evidence so the SCC went on to examine whether there was evidence which supported and corroborated the belief of PK. The court rejected a suggestion put to the Chief Superintendent PK, in cross-examination that his evidence was a fiction. Packaging from a Rayovac torch and a receipt dated 10 October 2002 were later found in the Nissan Micra when it was searched. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The court accepted a piece of paper containing the drawing of a key and a telephone number which the court accepted was that of MB, the owner of the Nissan Almera with the false number plates. It was also satisfied, having heard abundant evidence which included sightings of the applicant and his co-accused together, that they were ‘well known’ to each other. The court accepted that the documentation established that the applicant was, at the very least, acquainted with the driver of the Transit van (PB) and the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) The video-recordings of the interviews were shown to the trial court. It noted that, not only did each remain totally silent during the course of interview, but each appeared to take no ostensible interest whatsoever in what was going on. They sat bolt upright showing remarkable self-control throughout, in that their only movement was an occasional blink of the eyes but they made no effort to engage with the interviewers. It was clear to the court that each was deliberately and offensively ignoring all that was being asked of them. Each accused was asked to affirm or deny that he was a member of the IRA. Each was asked whether he knew the men arrested at Corke Abbey on the night of 10 October 2002, it being clear that each knew one or more of them. The trial court had no doubt as to the materiality of a vast number of the questions put to each accused. The court was satisfied that their silence amounted to corroboration of the belief evidence given by Chief Superintendent PK. It was persuaded beyond all reasonable doubt that each of the accused was guilty of charged. The judge did not believe that either activity or documentation indicated activities or membership of an unlawful organisation.  applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (‘CCA’) was refused. CCA rejected the submission that the SCC, which decided on guilt or innocence, should not have carried out this review having regard to this Court’s case-law. It found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the belief of the Chief Superintendent. The belief of Chief Superintendent PK was simply admitted as being evidence, no more and no less, and this was already well established in the prior jurisprudence. Such a witness could be cross-examined but he was entitled to claim privilege in respect of underlying facts or sources. The applicant’s case held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. The CCA also considered that the events at Corke Abbey and an association with those events, the vehicles and the contents of the vehicles, were all matters which came within the ambit of the phrase ‘movements, actions, activities, or associations on the part of an accused person’ found in section 3(1)(b)(i) of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act, 1972, as amended (“the 1972 Act”). The trial court was entitled to look at the established facts, when taken in conjunction with the inferences which it had properly drawn to see whether these supported or corroborated the belief evidence of the Chief of Staff. The court found that all the matters taken together were sufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the two men were members of the IRA. The Court of Appeal then refused to grant the application under section 29 of the 1924 Act. The Supreme Court ruled that the application was not of ‘exceptional public importance’ and that the right to silence did not apply to the case. The case was decided on the basis that the fact that the evidence was ‘proved’ was not enough to support the claim that the men were involved in an IRA plot. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence and it was clear that there were no such documents. The CCA noted that the applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the trial judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents or the documents. Moreover, the undisclosed documents were demonstrably not determinative as the applicant has suggested and the trialCourt had explicitly stated this to be so in its judgment. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19165/08) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that his trial was unfair because of the non-disclosure of the sources of the evidence of a Chief Superintendent without adequate counterbalancing measures. The application was communicated to the Government on 4 January 2012. The Irish Human Rights Commission had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party (Article 36 § 2 of. the Convention and Rule 44§ 2 of the Rules of Court, as in force at the material time) Five men arrested on suspicion of being members of an illegal organisation. Nissan Almera found to contain a lump/sledge hammer; two pickaxe handles; a torch; eight plastic bags of cable ties; black balaclavas with single or double openings; two identical navy ties resembling those worn by members of An Garda Síochána; woollen gloves; rolls of masking tape; a sky blue shirt marked ‘security’; a yellow fluorescent jacket with the word “GARDA” labelled on it. A number of remote controlled radios and election posters in respect of a man named O’Snodaigh. The applicant was arrested under section 30 of the Offences against the State Act 1939, as amended (“the 1939 Act’). He was brought to the police station where he was questioned about membership, contrary to section 21 of the 1939 Act, of an unlawful organisation (the Irish Republican Army, “IRA”). The applicant did not make a statement and was released from custody. On 24 October 2002 a lawful search of the applicant’s home took place. Papers were found which contained the phone number of the owner of the Nissan Almera (MB) and the man in the driver's seat of the Transit van (PB) The trial court later found established that, at the very least, the applicant was acquainted with one of the men arrested on 10 October 2002. The trial court considered the evidence of a Chief Superintendent who testified that he believed that, on 10 October 2002, the applicant was a member of the IRA. The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK’s sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him (Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000-II). The prosecution, which had no access to the confidential source material, opposed the applicant's request on the principle of informer privilege. The SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK's evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial in favour of the prosecution. Chief Superintendent PK had 25 years’ service as a police officer most of which was devoted to combating subversion. As the head of the Special Detective Unit, PK was the person best placed to learn of the activities of the accused. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The SCC was persuaded beyond any doubt by the belief evidence of PK that the accused were members of the IRA as charged. Moreover, the trial court was satisfied that PK had formed that belief ever before the ‘Corke Abbey’ events of 10 October 2002 or any matters discovered following the arrest of five persons on that occasion. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The court accepted a piece of paper containing the drawing of a key and a telephone number which the court accepted was that of MB, the owner of the Nissan Almera with the false number plates. The SCC was satisfied beyond any doubt that this packaging and receipt matched the torch found in the Transit van. It was further satisfied that the dark green Nissan Micra was the property of Ms K, the partner of the applicant, and that he had had control of the motor vehicle on the evening in question. The trial court accepted that the documentation established that the applicant was, at the very least, acquainted with the driver of the Transit van. A thumb print on black tape found in the Almera was accepted as being that of the co-accused. The court was satisfied that not only were the relevant statutory provisions invoked and adequately explained to each accused but each was given an opportunity to protest in the event that he had not understood that explanation, an opportunity which was ignored. Each availed of the opportunity to consult a solicitor before and in the course of several police interviews. It was clear to the court that each was deliberately and offensively ignoring all that was being asked of them. The trial court had no doubt as to the materiality of a vast number of the questions put to each accused and it was clear that each had made no effort whatsoever to answer them. For example, each accused was asked to affirm or deny that he was a member of the IRA. Each was asked whether he knew the men arrested at Corke Abbey on the night of 10 October 2002. The court was satisfied that their silence amounted to corroboration of the belief evidence given by Chief Superintendent PK. The trial court was persuaded beyond all reasonable doubt that each of the accused was guilty of charged. The applicant, in particular, was specifically asked about his use of his partner’s car.  applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (“CCA”) was refused. He objected to any review by the trial judges, as adjudicators of guilt or innocence, of material underlying the belief of Chief Superintendent PK on the grounds that to do so was unlawful and contrary to the case-law of this Court. The Supreme Court in DPP v Kelly ([2006] IESC 20) had found this limitation necessary and properly counterbalanced by matters not dissimilar to those arising in the present case. The exercise of the trial court’s discretion to review the files furnished by the Chief Superintendent did not infringe the right to a fair trial. The CCA held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment. The CCA also considered that the events at Corke Abbey and an association with those events, the vehicles and the contents of the vehicles, the materials found during searches as well as the meetings between both accused at the time when the applicant’s house was being searched, were all matters which came within the ambit of the phrase ‘movements, actions, activities, or associations on the part of an accused person’ found in section 3(1)(b)(i) of the Offences Against the State Act, 1972. The Court of Appeal ruled that the evidence pointed to the existence of a criminal organisation. The court ruled that this evidence was sufficient to establish that the men were members of the IRA. The Court of appeal then took the case to the Supreme Court for review. The Supreme Court found that the right to silence did not apply to the evidence presented in this case. The case was then referred to the High Court for further scrutiny. The High Court returned a verdict that the case could not be dismissed as a case of mistaken identity because the evidence was consistent with the public interest. The appeal was then remanded and the case was re-opened for further examination. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court which required that the withholding of any such documentation had to remain at all times in the supervisory control of judges themselves. The CCA rejected the submission that the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence. The applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents or the documents. name: Antun Petrovic
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 5 December 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20458/92) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Antun Petrovic, on 3 August 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31) Antun Petrovic claimed a parental leave allowance (Karenzurlaubsgeld) in 1989. His claim was turned down by the local employment office (Arbeitsamt) on the ground that only mothers could claim such an allowance when a child was born. He appealed against that decision to the Vienna Regional Employment Office. He again argued that section 26(1) of the Unemployment Benefit Act 1977 (see paragraph 14 below) was discriminatory and, therefore, unconstitutional. On 19 September 1997 the Commission produced various documents from the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 October 1997. The Constitutional Court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. It added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments (section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below) The applicant's complaint was unfounded, seeing that the legislature had a certain amount of time in which to adapt new rules to changes in society (Anpassung gesetzlicher Vorschriften an geänderte Verhältnisse).

The case originated in an application (no. 63879/00) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. In a decision of 29 November 2005 the Chamber declared the application admissible. Neither the Government nor the applicant filed further written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who is currently detained in Muret Prison. The Principal Public Prosecutor – the only appellant – submitted that the applicant should be sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment and permanently excluded from French territory. The applicant appealed on points of law and filed additional submissions in which he reiterated his argument that Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not comply with the principle of equality of arms enshrined in Article 6 of the Convention. On 1 July 1999 the Lyons Court of Appeal upheld the judgment as to the issue of guilt and the permanent exclusion from French Territory. In so holding, and in so far as Article 505 does not deprive the applicant of his right to appeal, the appeal by the Principal Public prosecutor must be declared admissible. “The judges applied the law correctly ...” says the judge. The judge says the prosecution had a right to use a different remedy to that used by the Principal Public Prosecutor. The prosecution used a remedy that could have been used by that prosecutor, the judge adds. The prosecutor was given different conditions and time-limits from those applicable to the Principal public prosecutor, he says. The court said the judge's decision was correct and that the judge had a duty to give the defendant the remedy he was entitled to use, not to use it as a substitute for the Prosecutor’s remedy. The judges said that the defendant was given a remedy he could use, but was not given the right to do so as a result of the law.

name: Mehmet Tanay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18753/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. On 20 November 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Mehmet Tanay (“the applicant”), in February 2004. The Court of Cassation held that the case had been time-barred on 17 September 2000. The Directorate appealed the decision and the case was dismissed in July 2003. In November 2003 the Court ofCassation upheld the final ruling. The case was re-opened in December 2003. The application for rectification by the Directorate was dismissed by the Court in March 2003 after the applicant argued that it was she who had been ill, not her client. The Court ruled that rectification would not affect the outcome of the case and dismissed the rectification request. The appeal was dismissed again on 13 November 2003 and the appeal was dropped.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 20 November 2007. It also decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the treaty) The applicant was represented by Mrs Fatma Kalsen Demirdaş, a lawyer practising in Tunceli. The Turkish Government were represented by their Agent. The Tunceli Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision, quoting the applicant’s name, instead of that of his representative, as the person who had been ill. In an application for rectification Mrs Demirdaş argued that it was she who was ill, not her client, and that the Court had made a factual error which should be rectified. On 12 May 2003, the Court of. Cassation held that “amending the factual error would not affect the outcome’, and dismissed the rectification request. The Directorate appealed. On 13 November 2003 the Court  upheld the final ruling.

name: Collette Hemsworth
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58559/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants mainly complained under Article 2 that there had been an unlawful use of lethal force against the deceased, Mr John Hemsworth, and that the State had not fulfilled its procedural investigative obligations in that respect. The application was communicated to the Government on 18 October 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 11 January 2012 the Irish Government declined to exercise their right to intervene. John Hemsworth died from a cerebral infarction on 1 January 1998. The RUC began an investigation supervised by the Independent Commission for Police Complaints. An expert in forensic medicine instructed by the first applicant found that it was “highly likely” that the assault was the sole underlying cause of death. The applicants claimed that the original pathologist later expressed his agreement with these later two expert opinions. The Coroner opened a pre-inquest hearing, in 16 cases including into John Hemsworth’s death, to hear submissions on the implications of the judgments of this Court of 4 May 2001 in certain cases concerning deaths in Northern Ireland. First applicant applied for legal aid for the inquest under the Lord Chancellor’s Extra-Statutory Scheme (established in July 2000) On 5 June 2001 she began a judicial review action. The action continued in order to challenge that limitation on funding. On 7 January 2003 the High Court found against her as did the Court of Appeal (9 March 2005) In February 2002 limited legal aid was proposed but in a manner she considered inconsistent with the State's approach. The first applicant again issued judicial review proceedings. On 26 April 2004 the High court found in her favour. The applicants claimed that, during that hearing, the Coroner advised that there was no evidence that the deceased had been struck by RUC officers. The first applicant applied to the Coroner to recuse himself. The Coroner refused but indicated that he would receive further representations as to why RUC witnesses were required. The first applicant began a judicial review action. On 9 March 2009 the High Court found in her favour. The inquest began on 21 September 2009. It did not sit each day and certain witnesses were unavailable through ill-health. On 8 October 2009 the jury discharged the jury due to evidence which had emerged. It emerged that Officer M had been a member of the RUC at the time of the alleged assault. He was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and, in addition, he was due to be called as a witness. Private G had seen an officer in the RUC Blues OSU assaulting a civilian with a baton in an area close to the location of Mr Hemsworth’s alleged assault. Given the time it would take to recall witnesses and to call Private G, the Coroner considered it preferable to discharge the jury and conduct the inquest afresh. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them in relation to the death of John Hemsworth. Officers unconnected with the original investigation should conduct this disclosure exercise. The inquest was scheduled to begin on 21 January 2010. On 22 April 2010 the first applicant obtained an expert medical report which found that marks on the deceased's face and back were consistent with allegations of assault by police baton. John Hemsworth died on 7 July 1997. The inquest jury accepted that his injuries included fractures to both the right and left hand sides of his jaw bone, tramline bruising to the left jaw, neck and lower left side of his back. Since the RUC Blues OSU were the only police on therelevant street on the relevant night, it was “highly probable” that one or more of those officers was responsible for the injuries to Mr Hemsworth. The Coroner announced that he would refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (“DPP”) and ensured the production, from public funds, of a transcript of the inquest proceedings. The applicant initiated civil proceedings against the PSNI on 5 September 2001. On 10 August 2011 a Notice of Intention to Proceed was served. In July 2012 the Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file. In his report of 1 May 2007 he considered that the medical experts did not agree on the extension of a causal link between the July 1997 injuries and the subsequent death. There was no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death and he could identify nothing further that he could do to take the matter forward.

The inhabitants of the applicant’s village were suspected of ‘aiding and abetting terrorists’ The applicant filed a petition complaining about the burning down and forced evacuation of his village by gendarmes. The applicant alleged that a delay in releasing him from prison had given rise to a violation of Article 5 of the convention. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. No further appeal lay against the decision. The applicant was released from prison on 14 April 2000 and served with a copy of the Court's decision by the governor of the Tarnów Mościce Prison. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61444/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a “reasonable time”, as required under Article 6 § 1 of the convention. He also alleged a breach of Article 13 of the treaty. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant's wife, Mrs Józefa Krasuska, informed the Court’s Registry that the applicant had died on 30 December 2004. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late husband's stead. The case was brought in the Zielona Góra Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) in Poland. The applicant and his wife had concluded a contract with E.W. and W.W., the owners of a company that was to carry out building work on the applicant’s house. On 24 November 1994 the applicant, considering that the company was in breach of the contract, withdrew from it. The judge gave judgment and dismissed the claim. The plaintiffs appealed. In 2000 the judge decided to obtain a fresh expert report. The Government maintained that in the course of the hearing the plaintiffs had modified their claim. On 12 October 2000 the court refused the plaintiffs' application for an exemption from payment of the court fee for the increased claim. The Government maintained that at the hearing on 8 May 2001 the plaintiffs had increased their claim and had stated that they would not seek an exemption. The applicant denied that they had altered their claim. He maintained that, in a pleading of 11 May 2001, he had indeed extended the amount of the damages sought to 300,000 Polish zlotys (PLN), mostly because he had been forced to do so by the court. A hearing scheduled for 12 July 2001 was adjourned at the plaintiffs’ request. A subsequent hearing was held on 6 September 2001.

name: Arnaud Bédat
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 1 July 2014 a Chamber of that Section delivered its judgment (see A.B. v. Switzerland, no.56925-08, 1 July2014), in which it declared the application admissible and held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 10. The applicant is a journalist by profession. On 15 October 2003 he published an article in the weekly magazine L’Illustré entitled ‘Drame du Grand-Pont à Lausanne – la version du chauffard – l’interrogatoire du conducteur fou’ (“Tragedy on theLausanne Bridge – the reckless driver’s version – Questioning of the mad driver”). The article in question concerned a set of criminal proceedings against M.B., a motorist who had been remanded in custody after an incident on 8 July 2003 in which he had rammed his car into pedestrians. The incident, in which three people had died and eight had been injured, had caused much emotion and controversy in Switzerland. M.B. had been ‘charged with premeditated murder [assassinat] and, in the alternative, with murder [meurtre], grievous bodily harm, endangering life and serious traffic offences’ and that he “appear[ed] to show no remorse”. The article also included a brief summary entitled ‘He lost his marbles...’ (“Il a perdu la boule...”), and statements from M.B’s wife and from his doctor. ‘I would like to phone my big brother in Algeria’, he subsequently begged. He finally announced on 11 August that he had come to a ‘final decision’: he dismissed his lawyer on grounds of ‘lack of trust’ M.B. was sentenced to one month’s imprisonment, suspended for one year. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. His appeal was dismissed on 30 January 2006 by the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Vaud. The Federal Court dismissed the appeals on 29 April 2008. Its decision was served on the applicant on 9 May 2008. In accordance with Article 293 of the Criminal Code, he had the duty as a professional journalist, under Article 32, to publish it owing to what he sees as the obvious interest of the so-called ‘Lausanne Bridge’ case to the general public in French-speaking Switzerland. Anyone who makes public all or part of documents, investigations or deliberations of an authority which are secret by law or by virtue of a decision taken by that authority, acting within its powers, will be punished by a fine. The court may decide not to impose any penalties if the secret thus made public is of minor importance (see paragraph 3). According to case-law, this provision proceeds from a formal conception of secrecy. In its Stoll v. Switzerland judgment of 10 December 2007, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that this formal conception was not contrary to Article 10 ECHR inasmuch as it did not prevent publication. All investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The present case concerns secrecy imposed by the law rather than by an official decision. The appellant is charged with the publication of records of interviews and correspondence contained in the case file of a live criminal investigation. The Federal Court is prevented from determining whether the interference in issue was compatible with Article 10 ECHR, by assessing, in the context of its examination of Article 293, paragraph 3, of the Criminal Code, the justification for classifying a given piece of information as secret, and weighing up the interests at stake, on the other. The aim is to maintain the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights has already had occasion to deem such a purpose legitimate in itself. This is the inescapable conclusion as regards the records of interviews of the accused. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation and before the trial. We might point out here that it appears from the impugned publication that it is also the only possible conclusion as. regards the letters sent by the accused to the investigating judge, which focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer. The content of the correspondence between the detainee and the investigating judge is not disputed. The appellant submits that he had the professional duty (under former Article 32 of the Criminal Code) as a journalist to publish the information in question because of what he describes as the obvious interest in the ‘Lausanne Bridge’ case. He considers that in the light of European case-law, the basic assumption should be that publication is justified in principle unless there is a pressing social need to maintain secrecy. In the instant case the information published by the appellant, in so far as it concerned the content of his interviews and his correspondence with the investigatingJudge, cannot be described as a secret of minor importance. The accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion. It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage. However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest. The public interest is manifestly lacking as regards the letters that were published. This type of information provides no relevant insights into the accident or the circumstances surrounding it. It relates to the private life, or indeed intimate sphere, of the person in custody. The cantonal court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not, as he claims, to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’, ‘the reckless driver's version’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a mad driver. The European Court of Human Rights reiterates that neither it, nor the domestic courts for that matter, should substitute their own views for those of the press. Journalist asked whether the driver was in fact doing his best to ‘make himself impossible to defend’. The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case, without the least respect for the principle of presumption of innocence (see judgment appealed against). The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged, how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship. The decision appealed against does not violate federal law as interpreted in the light of the Convention provisions relied upon by the appellant.”

The European Court of Human Rights has already had occasion to deem such a purpose legitimate in itself. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation and before the trial. It is also the only possible conclusion as regards the letters sent by the accused to the investigating judge, which focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 7). We might point out here that it appears from the impugned publication that it is possible that the accused may have tried to influence the decisions taken by the investigatingJudge and the trial court. In the instant case the information published by the appellant, in so far as it concerned the content of the records of his interviews and his correspondence with the investigating judge, cannot be described as a secret of minor importance for the purposes of Article 293, paragraph 3, of the Criminal Code. The information was only accessible to a restricted number of persons (the investigating judge and the parties to the proceedings) Furthermore, the investigating authority was desirous to keep them secret, with not only a legitimate interest in doing so but an obligation under the Cantonal Code of Criminal Procedure, the justification for which was mentioned above. The only remaining point at issue is the existence of justification. The court finds that while the accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion, it had nevertheless, in legal terms, been simply a road accident with fatal consequences. It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 8, to which the cantonal judgment refers) However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute a public interest. Nor is it clear, as regards the records of his interviews, what political question or matter of public interest would have arisen or been worth debating. The cantonal court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a mad driver. The European Court of Human Rights reiterates that neither it, nor the domestic courts for that matter, should substitute their own views for those of the press as to what technique of reporting should be adopted by journalists. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case. The appellant did not explicitly criticise the amount of the fine imposed on him. Nor did he challenge the refusal to grant him a probationary period after which the fine would be struck out (former Article 49, point 4) under Swiss law. The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged, how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship. The decision appealed against does not violate federal law as interpreted in the light of the Convention provisions relied upon.

name: Mustafa Erçıkdı
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52782/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were the Nazilli district directors of the Labour Party (Emeğin Partisi) at the time of the events. On 31 March 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The pair were sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment and to a fine of TRL 1,433,333. The sentences of Ms Çamoğlu and Mr Kazan were suspended as they did not have a criminal record. On 6 April 1999 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court and sentenced them to a year and a half’s imprisonment. The sentence was suspended until the end of the second term of the Turkish parliament in May 1999. This was the first time in Turkish history that two members of the same family had been sentenced to such a long term sentence.

name: Rıdvan Saruhan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5298/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) In 1974, a third person named B.A. inherited a plot of land from her mother, a Syrian national. She did not have the land registered in her name at the time. The applicants claimed that she had failed to transfer the ownership of the land to them, although they had paid the purchase price. On 30 December 2003 the court dismissed the action. As the land had been owned by the State since 1966, the court concluded that the sale agreement was void. The Court of Cassation dismissed the plea of unconstitutionality and upheld the first instance court’s decision. This decision was not served on the applicants and they learned about the outcome of the proceedings by tracking their application through the court's web site. On 7 July 2005 the Court ofCassation rejected the applicants’ request for rectification. The court ruled that the decree of 1966 was valid and that the applicants' appeal should be accepted. The appeal was rejected on July 7, 2005, and the appeal was denied on July 10, 2005. The case was decided on July 13, 2006. The decision was upheld on July 17, 2006, and was delivered on July 21, 2006 at 9.30am local time.
