train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention about his trial by court-martial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The parties each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits of the complaints. The case was adjourned pending the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Grieves v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 57067/00, ECHR 2003‑XII. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. They are: The applicant was born in 1976 and, at the time of the application, was still a minor. The applicant was living with his family in Germany, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in the Support Unit of the Rhine Garrison. On 8 February 1994 the applicant was charged with the murder of a young civilian woman. The German authorities waived jurisdiction pursuant to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement 1951 (see paragraph 21 below). The applicant was returned to Germany in time for his court-martial which commenced on 21 April 1995. The applicant returned to England in April 1994 where he was detained. Despite his father’s return, the applicant remained subject to military law as the proceedings had already commenced (see paragraphs 25 and 26 below) The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, gave judgment on 30 July 1996, dismissing the appeal. The appeal court certified a question of law for law for the applicant to be tried in Germany. He had all the safeguards which a defendant in any court-martial is entitled to enjoy. Had the appellant been held in Germany to await trial, as he could have been, his claim to trial in England would have appeared weaker. The greater availability of such witnesses as a trial in Germany was a legitimate reason for favouring trial there. We are satisfied that these proceedings were not an abuse of process. The House of Lords granted leave to appeal on 9 July 1997. The appeal was dismissed on 16 December 1997. Lords Slynn of Hadley and Hope of Craighead expressed the view that at first sight the decision to prosecute the applicant by court-martial had been inappropriate. The Court of Appeal ruled that the 1955 Army Act had been used to bring the applicant to trial in the local civil courts and that the proceedings were not an abuse of process. The case was settled at the High Court on 8 June 1998. The Appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeals on December 16, 1997, after the applicant’s appeal was heard by the Lords. Many of the witnesses were German and that they could not be forced to attend a trial in England. The defence had not yet indicated what evidence would be agreed. The Director thought that, while some of their evidence might be agreed, it was unlikely that this would include the police and forensic experts. He added that one of the forensic scientists who was responsible for examining secretions and bloodstains was being difficult to deal with. Lord Bingham of Cornhill CJ said in his judgment that it was clear, with the benefit of hindsight, that the trial could have been conducted in England without due difficulty. But the Director of Public Prosecutions would have had to have taken his decision well before the trial. The proceedings were conducted within the rules laid down by Parliament. There is no sound basis for thinking that, at the time when a decision about this would have had to have been taken, a prosecution in the English courts within a reasonable time would have been seen to be practicable. The alternatives lay between taking proceedings by way of court-martial in Germany, leaving the matter in the hands of the German public prosecutor or taking no proceedings at all. The Army Act 1955 provides: “(1) Any person subject to military law who commits a civil offence, whether in the United Kingdom or elsewhere, shall be guilty of an offence against this section” The Act identifies in its Fifth Schedule the civilians outside the United Kingdom who are subject to Part II of the Act when not on active service. They include, at paragraph 5: “Persons forming part of the family of members of any of Her Majesty’s Naval, Military, or Air Forces and residing with them or about to reside.” The trial of those who have ceased to be subject to military law is expressly provided for by section 131. Since the Armed Forces Act 1976, where a civilian defendant is to be tried, civilian Crown servants can be detailed as members of the court-martial. Most criminal offences allegedly committed by a civilian dependent would be tried by a Standing Civilian Court (similar to a Magistrates’ Court) The basic rule of the common law is that the jurisdiction of the criminal courts in the United Kingdom is confined to crimes committed within the territory of each court. An exception is provided by section 9 of the 1861 Act, which gives jurisdiction to British courts in respect of alleged murders and manslaughters committed by British citizens anywhere in the world. The Offences against the Person Act 1861 is cited as the basis for the ruling by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in the case of the murder of a British woman in Switzerland in 2009. The case was referred to the ECHR by the Court of Criminal Appeal, which decided in favour of the prosecution of the woman.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28648/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the convention on the ground of his religion. Members of recognised religious societies holding religious functions comparable to the applicant’s functions were exempted from military service. The application was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicant was represented by Mr R. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 3 April 2003. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. It concluded that the applicant had not convincingly shown that no fault lay with him within the meaning of section 29 of the convention. On the same day he lodged a further complaint against another penal order of the IAP concerning also illegal employment of foreigners. The Constitutional Court joined these proceedings and, on 24 September 1996, granted the applicant's requests for suspensive effect. On 17 May 1999 the Administrative Court obtained the Iap's submissions. On 3 September 2002 it dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The applicant's conviction concerning illegal employment. of three other Polish nationals was also confirmed on 3 October 2002. These decisions were served on the applicant and his counsel on 3 July 2002. The Administrative Court instituted preliminary proceedings on 6 April 1999.

name: Carl G. Holm
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 11 December 1992 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 15 February 1993 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. It originated in an application (no. 14191/88) against Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Carl G. Holm, on 24 January 1987. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. In 1974 the applicant formed together with others a foundation named Contra. According to him its aim was to scrutinise governments of communist regimes in Eastern Europe and the Swedish Social Democratic Workers Party. In 1985 a publishing house published a book entitled “Till höger om neutraliteten’ (To the right of neutrality) which contained a survey of right-wing organisations and individuals. The author of the book, Mr Sven Ove Hansson, was then employed by the publisher and had previously served as an ideological adviser to the SAP. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson, Mr Malmlöf and the applicant himself. In 1986 a Swedish man sued the author and the publisher of a book for aggravated libel. He claimed that the book contained allegations implying that he belonged to certain nazi and fascist groups. In view of the wide distribution of the book and the applicant’s central position in the Swedish Federation of Industries, the libel was aggravated. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and awarded him 200,000 Swedish kronor in damages. The book was published by Tidens förlag AB, owned by a company owned by the Swedish Petroleum Company (SAP) The SAP was responsible for the majority of the shares in the company, which was controlled by the SAP directly. The defendants, but not the applicant, asked for the case to be considered with a jury. The question whether a criminal offence had been committed was to be examined by a jury, composed on the basis of a list of two groups of names. The list, which had been published by the Stockholm County Council (Stockholms läns landsting), indicated the jurors’ political affiliations. The first group comprised sixteen persons, seven of whom were members of the SAP, five of the Conservative Party, two of the Liberal Party and one of the Communist Party. The second group included eight names, of whom four were members to the SAP. A jury of nine members was constituted. Of these, five were members of the SAP - one of them was subsequently replaced by another SAP member -, two of the Conservative Party, one of the Liberal Party and one. of the Communist Party. The jury replied in the negative to the questions put to it concerning the alleged unlawfulness of the impugned passages of the book. The District Court dismissed the charges made by the applicant and his claims for damages. In view of the conclusions reached on the merits, it ordered him to pay 67,860 Swedish kronor in costs. It was not possible under Swedish law for the applicant to appeal against the jury’s verdict (see paragraph 16 below)

The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson, Mr Malmlöf and the applicant himself. The applicant formed together with others a foundation named Contra. According to him its aim was to scrutinise governments of communist regimes in Eastern Europe and the Swedish Social Democratic Workers Party (Sveriges socialdemokratiska arbetareparti - the “SAP’) The author of the book, Mr Sven Ove Hansson, was then employed by the publisher and had previously served as ideological adviser to the SAP. On 15 April 1986 the applicant brought a private prosecution for aggravated libel (grovt förtal) against Mr Hansson in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Stockholm. In the same proceedings he sued both the author and the publisher for damages, claiming 200,000 Swedish kronor. He contended that the book contained allegations implying that he belonged to certain nazi and fascist groups, calculated to cast doubt on his honour and to expose him to contempt. In view of the wide distribution of the book and the applicant’s central position in the Swedish Federation of Industries, the libel was aggravated. The impugned passages included allegations which can be summarised as follows: (a) in 1973 the applicant had chaired the youth section of the World Anti-Communist League's Conference in London, an organisation whose membership was said to consist largely of neo-nazis. The trial of the Swedish National Union in Lund and Malmö was to be heard by a jury. The jury was made up of members of the SAP and the Conservative Party. The defendants, but not the applicant, asked for the case to be considered by the jury. In support of his request, the applicant argued that Tidens förlag AB was the “mouthpiece’ of the social democratic movement. The District Court rejected his request on 10 November 1986, finding that, regardless of whether the publisher could be seen as a ‘mouthpiece' as described, the reasons invoked by the applicant were valid. In an appeal against this decision to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea Hovrätt), the applicant submitted, in addition to the above arguments, that the contents of the book were of a political nature and that the case had political undertones. In view of the conclusions reached on the merits, it ordered him to pay 67,860 Swedish kronor in costs. It was not possible under Swedish law for the applicant to appeal against the jury’s verdict (see paragraph 16 below).

name: Torsten Leander
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 12 December 1985, he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the De delegate would present his observations at the hearing. On 28 April, the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. Torsten Leander worked as a temporary replacement in a post at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. The museum is adjacent to the Karlskrena Naval Base which is a restricted military security zone. The applicant maintained before the Court that the intention was that he should work for ten months in this post, while its ordinary holder was on leave. He alleged that on 3 September he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control which had to be carried out on him in accordance with the Personnel Control Ordinance 1969 (personal-kontrollkungörelsen 1969:446 - see paragraphs 18-34 below) The applicant complained to the Government and requested that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. He pointed out in particular that he had left a permanent position in Dalarna, in the North of Sweden, on being told that he was accepted for employment at the Naval Museum. The Government requested the opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces (överbefälhavaren), who in turn consulted the Commander in Chief of the Naval Navy. In his original complaint, and also in a letter of 4 December 1979, Mr. Leander further requested that he be given information about the reasons for his not being accepted. The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces considers that Mr. Leander may properly be employed by the Naval Museum provided that the holder of the appointment does not require access to the Naval Base. The applicant requested that the Government should, before taking a decision on his request of 22 October 1979, give him the right to be apprised of and to comment upon the information thus released. On this matter, the Government sought the opinion of the Board. In its reply of 22 February 1980, the Board proposed that the applicant’s complaints be dismissed. It added: “The entering of information in the register of the Security Department is based mainly on a 1973 Royal Decree which is secret’ The Government rejected the whole of the applicant’s complaint. Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. At the relevant time, he had not belonged to any political party since 1976. Earlier he had been a member of the Swedish Communist Party. He had also been a. member of an association publishing a radical. publication. after decision by the National Police Board in plenary meeting. At least three of the six members of the Board who are appointed amongst parliamentarians should be present when decisions are taken in matters of personnel control. In the case of the Applicant, all six members were present. During his military service, in 1971-72, he had been active in the soldiers’ union and a representative at a conference in 1972. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that, according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He had also been active. in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association and he had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe. He was sentenced to three years in prison.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5138/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was taken into custody during a military operation carried out by the Turkish armed forces on suspicion of being a member of an illegal armed organisation. On 4 January 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody to the Government. The trial of the applicant and his seven co-defendants began on 20 August 1998 before the Diyarbakır State Security Court. The applicant joined the PKK in 1995 and had received military training. The applicant also stated, during the hearings, that he had been forced to put his thumbprint on the statement taken from him at the gendarme station. The Diyarbakır State Security Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to death. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. On 16 September 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The court found it established, on the basis of, inter alia, the statements taken from the applicant after his arrest and the testimony given by him during the trial, that. he had carried out a number of illegal activities.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged in particular that the quashing of their convictions by the Independent Administrative Panel upon an official complaint by the relevant Federal Minister violated Article 6 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. They also complained under Articles 6 and 13 about the length of the proceedings and lack of an effective remedy in that respect. On 18 June 2007 and 28 August 2008 respectively, the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the cases at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant was found guilty of the offence of drunk driving under sections 5(1) and 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act. He was sentenced to a fine of EUR 1,162 with seventeen days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The applicant appealed, repeating his argument as regards the alleged imprecision of the breathalyser test. After holding a hearing, the Upper Austria Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat) allowed the applicant’s appeal in part. In its decision of 17 June 2002 it found that an alcohol level of 0.59 mg/l could be considered to have been confirmed, since allowance had to be made for a possible inaccuracy. The Independent Administrative Panel’s decision of 17 June 2002 was served on the Federal Minister for Traffic, Innovation and Technology. On 18 February 2005 the Administrative Court quashed the decision and referred the case back to it. It found that the decision had applied the law incorrectly, since there was no ground to make allowance for inaccuracy in the breathalyser test. Consequently, his conviction under section 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act was upheld. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, claiming several violations of Article 6 of the Convention. He submitted that the proceedings had been unreasonably lengthy and that he had no remedy in this respect. The applicant alleged that the proceedings were unfair, and violated the ne bis in idem principle. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint as being unfounded. The judge ruled that the breathalyser used had been correctly calibrated and that the result of the test could not be deemed to be completely accurate. The applicant was found guilty of drunk driving under sections 5(1) and 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act. He was sentenced to a fine of EUR 872.07 with 13 days’ imprisonment in the event of default. The case is currently being heard by the European Court of Human Rights. On 12 March 2002 the Upper Austria Independent Administrative Panel held a hearing. It questioned the applicant and an expert on weights and measurements. Even making allowance for possible inaccuracy a breath alcohol level of 0.57 mg/l could be established beyond all doubt. The offence therefore fell under section 99(1)(b) of the Road Traffic Act and the fine was to be reduced to EUR 700, with nine days’ imprisonment in the event of default. On 25 January 2005 the Administrative Court, following the official complaint, quashed the decision of 19 March 2002 and referred the case back to it. It observed that a driver who was required to undergo a breathalyser test had the right to request that a blood sample be taken. The applicant was convicted under section 99(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act. The Independent Administrative Panel dismissed an appeal by the applicant against the penal order of 17 January 2002. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 14 July 2006 the Administrative Court, referring to its previous decision, dismissed the applicant's complaint as unfounded. The judgment was served on the applicant and his counsel on 14 August 2006. The applicant was fined EUR 872 for the offence at issue and sentenced to ten days in prison. The hearing was adjourned until 2 November 2007. The Administrative Court has dismissed the complaint.

name: Burghard Theodor Mooren
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11364/03) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr D. Hagmann, a lawyer practising in Mönchengladbach. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case continues. The applicant was suspected of having evaded turnover taxes of 57,374 euros (EUR) and income taxes of EUR 133,279. He had to be placed in pre-trial detention because of a danger of collusion (Verdunkelungsgefahr) The documents seized were incomplete. There was therefore a risk that the applicant, if released, might destroy the missing documents or conceal further business transactions and accounts. The applicant argued that there was no risk of collusion or of his absconding. The Mönchengladbach District Court heard representations from the applicant and his defence counsel. The District Court’s review of the detention order took place on 16 August 2002. The Mönchengladbach Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the District Court's decision dated 16 August 2002. It found that there was a strong suspicion that the applicant had evaded income, turnover and trade taxes. There was a danger of his absconding within the meaning of section 112 § 2 no. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 41 below) The applicant had connections in foreign countries and faced a heavy sentence. The Regional Court found that it was impossible to assess whether the information given in this manner would be sufficient. The Court of Appeal's review of the detention order was upheld on 16 September 2002. On 17 September 2002 the Mönchengladbach Regional Court decided, without giving further reasons, not to amend its decision of 9 September 2002. The applicant claimed that he had a constitutional right to be given access to the facts and evidence on which the detention order was based. The Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, in its submissions to the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal, stated that it was not prepared to give the applicant access to case files. Pursuant to section 114 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below), the facts leading to a strong suspicion that the accused had committed a particular offence and the reasons for detention had to be revealed. Court of Appeal: The facts and evidence on which the suspicion and the reasons for the defendant’s detention on remand were based had to be described in sufficient detail to enable the accused to comment on them. be set out in the detention order. The Court of Appeal noted that, in its decisions on the applicant's detention, the District Court had, however, merely stated that the applicant was strongly suspected of tax evasion ‘on the basis of the business records seized when his home was searched’ This defect had not been remedied in the course of the subsequent decisions. As counsel for the defence had also been refused access to the case files under section 147 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, these defects amounted to a denial of the right to be heard. The applicant’s counsel was given copies of four pages of the voluminous case files containing an overview by the Düsseldorf Tax Fraud Office of the amounts of income and taxes evaded. The Mönchengladbach District Court then issued a fresh detention order against the applicant. It stated that there was a strong suspicion that the applicant had evaded taxes on some twenty occasions between 1991 and June 2002. He faced a lengthy prison sentence which could no longer be suspended on probation, had not notified the authorities of his place of residence for several years and had claimed that he was living in the Netherlands. Mönchengladbach Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the detention order on 7 November 2002. The applicant lodged a further appeal on 8 November 2002, complaining that his counsel had still not been granted access to the case files. On 18 November 2002 the Public Prosecutor's Office granted the applicant's counsel access to files. The files had been at the Regional Court and had only recently been returned to the public prosecutor. The request for access was granted on 20 November 2002 and the applicant withdrew his further appeal in December 2002. In his submission, the applicant argued that his right to liberty had been breached by his illegal detention on the basis of a void detention order. The applicant argued that the Court of Appeal’s refusal to quash the detention order and to take a decision itself had also breached his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The Federal Constitutional Court, without giving further reasons, declined to consider his constitutional complaint. On 9 March 2005 the Mönchengladbach District Court convicted the applicant on eight counts of tax evasion and sentenced him to a total of one year and eight months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. The court found that the applicant, who had confessed to the offences, had evaded turnover taxes of DEM 129,795, income taxes of Dem 344,802 and trade taxes ofDem 55,165.
